Al-Haqq begins Surat al-Nisa' with His saying:

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from one soul and created from it its mate and dispersed from both of them many men and women. And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs. Indeed Allah is ever, over you, an Observer.﴾ (1)

When Allah, glorified is He, calls mankind to His taqwa, He says: "O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from one soul." The meaning of "fear your Lord" is: make between yourselves and Him a protection (wiqaya). And what should I do to fear our Lord?

The first taqwa is that you believe in Him as God (ilah), and that you believe with your intellect that He is God. He, glorified is He, presents to you the rational case for people, saying: "O mankind, fear your Lord." He did not say "fear Allah," because Allah, in its concept, means worship. The ilah is one who is worshipped, who has commands and prohibitions. The truth has not yet reached people to this point; they are still at the level of rububiyya (lordship). The Rabb (Lord) is the one who takes charge of the upbringing of a thing: creating it from nothing, and sustaining it from nothing. But is it not the right of the one who creates a thing and raises it that he should set for it a law of maintenance?

It is his right and responsibility to set for the creature a law of maintenance. We see now that every inventor or maker sets for his invention, or for the thing he made, a law of maintenance. By Allah, would He, glorified is He, create human beings from nothing and then leave them to act as they wish? Or would He say to them: do this and such, and do not do that and such, so that you may fulfil your mission in life? He has set the constitution of the call to faith, so He said: "O mankind, fear your Lord who created you." So what is required of them is that they fear (taqwa), and to fear means to set up a protection for themselves by carrying out the commands of this Lord, the God who created them. And by Allah, would He make their creation a cause unless it was witnessed to be His? He, glorified is He, says: "Fear your Lord who created you." Our Lord's creation of us is witnessed; otherwise, if it were doubted, we would say to Him: "You did not create us," and to Allah belongs the highest likeness.

You hear someone say to you: "Be good to so-and-so, who did such and such for you." Do you acknowledge that he made it or not? If you acknowledge that he made what he made, then you respond to whoever says such words to you. So the saying of Allah: "O mankind, fear your Lord who created you" implies that Allah's creation of people is not a matter of dispute or doubt by anyone. He, glorified is He, wanted to draw us to Himself and bring us to His presence through something we all believe in, which is that He, glorified is He, created us for what He wants, which is that we receive from Allah what protects us from the attributes of His majesty. He, glorified is He, used the word "Rabb" and did not say "fear Allah," because the concept of Rabb is the one who creates from nothing and sustains from nothing, and cares for, and is the Nurturer, and brings the human being to the level of perfection that is intended for him. He is the One who created the whole universe and perfected its creation and making. For this reason the Truth says:

﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon?" they would surely say, "Allah." So how are they deluded?﴾ (Al-Ankabut 61)

So the matter of creation is an established matter. And since it is an established matter, its meaning is: since you have believed that I am your Creator, then I have power; this is one. And I am your Nurturer, so I have wisdom. A God who has power and has wisdom: either we fear His power and so dread Him, or we thank His wisdom and so acknowledge Him. "O mankind, fear your Lord who created you from one soul." If the Truth had not said "and created from it its mate," it would not be complete. Why? Because He will say in other verses about creation:

﴿And of everything We created pairs, that you may remember.﴾ (Al-Dhariyat 49)

So His creating you from one soul and creating from it its mate here, and people want to enter a maze. Does "created from it" mean the creation of Eve from Adam's rib, that is, from Adam's own soul? Some people said so, and some people said: no, "from it" means from its kind (jins). They argued for this by saying: when Allah says:

﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ (from verse 128, al-Tawba)

Did Allah take Muhammad (ﷺ) from our souls and our being? No. Rather, he is a messenger from our human kind. It is as if He, glorified is He, pointed to an evidence; because the creation of Eve has had its features obliterated from us, and because He gave us the explanation of the creation of Adam, his shaping from clay, and the stages of his creation until he became a human being. Therefore it is permissible that He made the creation of Adam the pattern for the creation of the first kind, and after that Eve is like him. So His saying, glorified is He, "created from it" means from its kind: He created her from clay, then shaped her, etc. But the experience with Eve has not been reported to us as it was with Adam. Or the intended meaning of His saying "from it" is from the rib, and this is something we did not witness from its beginning. And what a person did not witness, the proof concerning it comes from one who witnessed it. And He, glorified is He, wanted to spare us from the labyrinths of speculation on this matter: how He created us, and how we came.

The manner of your creation is no concern of yours. The One who created you is the One who tells you, so listen to His word, because this is a matter that does not relate to experimental science. For this reason, when Darwin came and wanted to be arrogant and speak, the modern theory came to demolish his words. The modern theory said to Darwin: the factors that affected the first ape to become a human, why did they not affect the rest of the apes so that they too would become humans, and the kind of apes would vanish? This is a question Darwin does not answer. So we say: this is a matter we did not witness, so we must listen to the One who did it. And the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves, and I would not have taken the misleaders as helpers.﴾ (Al-Kahf 51)

Since He did not make them witness it, can any of them bring knowledge about it? No one brings knowledge about it. Then He responds to whoever comes with a claim of knowledge, saying: "and I would not have taken the misleaders as helpers." The meaning of "misleaders" is that they will mislead you about creation. It is as if Allah has given us immunity against the false sayings that might arise from this, when He said: "and I would not have taken the misleaders as helpers." He has made clear to us the nature of those who mislead concerning the origin of creation and the manner of creation. They were not with Allah to help Him at the time of creation, so that they could inform mankind of how creation happened. So if you want to know, know that it is He, glorified is He, who tells how you were created and in what form you were. But whoever says such-and-such, they are the misleaders. And "the misleaders" are those who turn you away from the truth towards falsehood.

"O mankind, fear your Lord who created you from one soul." Why did He not say "created you from two" and stop there? Because when a thing is traced back to two, one of the two may have a desire; but this has been traced back to one only. So there should not be conflicting desires among you, because you are traced back to one soul. As for the theory of Darwin and what he said, Allah has provided for the cause of religion, and especially the cause of Islam, scholars from among non-Muslims who were guided to evidence that agrees with the Qur'an. The French scientist Monnier stood up, when he wanted to respond to the myths they tell about the origin of man, and said: I am amazed at those who think in this way. Does chance produce what we call a "male," then chance produces a person we call a "female," who is of the same kind but differs from him in type, such that when the two meet they produce a male like the first or a female like the second?

How does chance perform this process?

Let us grant that chance created Adam. Did chance also create for him one of his own kind? But she differs from him in type, such that when they meet a strong emotional current arises between them, which is the most intense of instincts, and then from them there arises a fertilization that produces a male like the first or a female like the second. What kind of chance is this? This chance is wise and purposeful. Call it chance, and we call it Allah.

Monnier, may Allah guide him to Islam and forgive him, thought that he had brought the proof with which he refutes Darwin. We say to him: the Qur'an has touched on this matter when it said: "fear your Lord who created you from one soul and created from it its mate." This is the greatness of it: He created the man and created the woman, who is of his kind, but differs from him in type, such that when they meet, Allah produces from them men and women. So it is a purposeful process, with care, purpose and wisdom. Thus the saying of Allah, glorified and exalted is He: "who created you from one soul and created from it its mate." This is what the French scientist Monnier was finally guided to.

"And He dispersed from both of them many men and women." Look at the greatness of the expression in His saying "and dispersed" (wa bath), which means "spread out" (nashr). We will pause at the word "spread out," because mankind must spread across the earth, so that they all may take of Allah's bounties throughout the earth.

"Nashr" means scattering what is folded in a space. There is something folded, and there is something else spread out. In the folded thing there is gathering, and in the spread thing there is dispersal and distribution. So the space of a gathered thing is narrow, and the space of a dispersed thing is wide. This means that when Allah, glorified and exalted is He, says "and dispersed from both of them," that is from Adam and Eve, "many men and women," and He was content to say "women" and did not say "many women," why? Because it is expected that in every male kind the number should be fewer than the female. If you look, for example, at a field with palm trees, how many male palms and how many female palms do you find? You will find one or two males.

So the scarcity of males is intended, because the male is fertilizing, and a male can fertilize thousands. So when Allah says "and dispersed from both of them many men," the male is the element that is supposed to be much fewer, so what about the second element, femaleness? It must be more. The Qur'an comes to alert you to the indications in the wording, because the speaker is Allah. But if you look at His saying "and dispersed from both of them," that is from Adam and Eve, and they are two, "many men and women," it is plural, to show you that what multiplies begins with a few and then ends with abundance.

We want to understand this so that we may take from it the statistical evidence for the existence of the Creator. He "dispersed from both of them many men and women," and the human multitude that appeared from the two will disperse more from it. Then from the second dispersed group a third dispersed group will come. The further we extend in dispersal, abundance arises. When you look at any country, you find its population a century ago far less than its population now. For example, the population of Egypt a century ago did not exceed five million, and two centuries ago it was fewer, and ten centuries ago it was fewer, and twenty centuries ago it was fewer. So the further the future extends for you, the population grows, because He, glorified is He, disperses from the maleness and the femaleness many men and women, and He will disperse from them an even greater number.

So whenever time advances, population increases. We see this in a single family: a single family is usually made up of a father and a mother, and then from them children may come, and grandchildren, and when Allah prolongs the life of one of the parents, he sees the grandchildren, and perhaps sees the grandchildren's grandchildren. So whenever time advances for the multiplying from two, it increases, and whenever you go back into the past, it decreases. Those who were a million a century ago were half a million two centuries ago, and so on until they are only ten, and the ten were four, and the four were two, and the two are Adam and Eve.

So when the Truth says that He created Adam and Eve, and you try to trace the whole world back, you will trace it back to them. And since multiplication arises from the two, from where did they come? The Truth, glorified is He, clarifies this for us in His saying: "Indeed We created you from male and female," and with that He relieves us of the science of statistics. It was necessary for this verse to come in order to solve for us the riddle of statistics. Whenever the future time comes, the world grows, and whenever we go back into the past, the count decreases until it becomes and ends at two. Beware of saying "one," because from one there is no multiplication; multiplication comes from two. And from where did the two come? Someone must have created them, and He is able to do this. Allah teaches us this when He says: "He created you from one soul and created from it its mate and dispersed from both of them many men and women." We take from "dispersed" the meaning of "spreading out." And if Allah had not said this, modern minds would have become lost and fallen into

And Allah, glorified and exalted, has addressed the orphan, who is the very embodiment of weakness among humankind, and He wished to lay down a law for him, so He said: ﴿And give the orphans their property, and do not substitute the bad [property] for the good, and do not consume their property along with your own property. Indeed, that is a great sin.﴾

And how can we give the orphan his property when he has not yet reached the stage of men, and we fear that if we give him the money he will squander it?

Consider the precision of the expression in His saying, after that: ﴿And test the orphans until, when they reach marriageable age, if you perceive in them sound judgment, then release to them their property﴾ (part of verse 6, Surat al-Nisa').

And before that, what do we do? Do we hand them the money? Allah makes clear that when you are guardian (wali) over an orphan's property, you must be very careful to give this orphan his property in full only after he has fully matured. You are a guardian (hafiz) over this property, so beware of mixing your wealth with his or of substituting from it, that is, taking the fine and valuable from his and giving him from your own what is less fine or less beneficial.

So His saying "And give the orphans their property" means that Allah made the property belong to the orphan, and did not grant the one in charge of him any right to dispose of this property except in a manner of preservation. Also, there is another point, explained to us by "And test the orphans." There are people who want to prolong the period of guardianship over the orphan so that one of them may benefit from this property. Allah, glorified is He, therefore makes clear: do not wait until he reaches maturity and then say, "We will keep him waiting." No. You train him through experience in some dealings and observe whether he manages well or not.

The saying of the Truth, "And test the orphans," means: examine them, can they take care of their own affairs alone? If they can, then be assured that when they reach the age of discernment they will manage well; give them their property after the test, because the orphan lives in a deficiency of age (qusur 'umri), whereas Allah distinguishes between the orphan and the safih (the one lacking sound judgment). The safih does not suffer from a deficiency of age but from a deficiency of reason. When Allah spoke about this matter He said: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾ (part of verse 5, Surat al-Nisa').

Is it your property? No. When a person is a safih, know that he has no management over his own possessions, and the management of ownership passes to whoever disposes of the property wisely. So be careful to manage the property of the safih as if you were its owner, because he has no ability to dispose of it well. But when the orphan reaches the stage of ba'ah (readiness for marriage), marriage and maturity, the Truth says: ﴿then release to them their property﴾ (part of verse 6, Surat al-Nisa').

He, glorified is He, says once in the context of guardianship, "your property," and in the giving, He says "their property." So He wants you not to squander the wealth. Then He clarifies: be careful with the wealth of the orphan or the safih as if it were your own, because as long as he is a safih, the responsibility of guardianship is required of you, and the property is not yours. Take from it what corresponds to the management of the property during the time of foolishness or orphanhood. After that, the Truth, glorified and exalted, comes to inform those in charge of the affairs of orphans or of the foolish who do not manage their property well, and says: ﴿and provide for them from it﴾ (part of verse 5, Surat al-Nisa').

Make the provision come from what it yields, and beware of keeping it in your possession; otherwise, what is the value of your guardianship, your trusteeship, and your charge over the affairs of the safih or the orphan? You must make the property fruitful for him, not consume it or mismanage it so that it diminishes each day. No. "And provide for them from it": the "min" here is causal, meaning provide for them by means of it, provide for them with a provision that comes out of it.

"And give the orphans their property and do not substitute the bad for the good." The bad (khabith) is the unlawful (haram) and the good (tayyib) is the lawful (halal). "Do not substitute the bad for the good": it may be that within the orphan's property there is something fine, and the guardian takes it for himself and replaces it with something of similar but ugly quality. For example, if among the orphan's property there is a fine horse, while the guardian has an ugly horse, he takes the fine one and says, "A horse for a horse"; or a buffalo in place of a buffalo; or a good palm tree in exchange for a palm tree that does not bear fruit. Here the Truth says: ﴿do not substitute the bad for the good﴾.

And His saying, glorified and exalted: ﴿do not consume their property along with your property﴾ means: beware of not making a distinction between their property and your property, so that you consume this together with that. Rather, distinguish between consuming your own property and preserving theirs. Why? The answer comes: ﴿Indeed, that is a great sin (hawban kabiran)﴾, that is, a grievous transgression.

Then the Truth moves on to another matter, in which the weakness of orphanhood and the weakness of gender come together. The weakness of orphanhood applies whether the orphan is male or female, but if she is female the trial is greater, for she is burdened by both weaknesses at once. Naturally, when an orphan girl is under the guardianship of her guardian (wali), he may say to himself: "She owns property, so why not marry her so that I may take the wealth?" This happens often.

For this reason the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And if you fear that you will not deal justly with the orphan girls, then marry those women who please you, two, three, or four. But if you fear that you will not be just, then [marry only] one, or what your right hands possess. That is more suitable, that you may not incline toward injustice.﴾

Here the Truth emphasizes the command to keep away from orphans, for the orphan is liable to be wronged because of his weakness, especially if the orphan is a girl. Wronging anyone is forbidden in general, other than orphans, but wronging a weak woman is a greater offense, for she cannot defend herself, whereas a mature woman of sound judgment may be able to defend herself against injustice. As for His saying, "And if you fear that you will not deal justly," it comes from "aqsata", meaning he acted justly. The root qist is among the words whose meanings get confused in the mind. "Qist" is sometimes used to mean "justice" when the qaf is kasra (qist with a kasra), as the Truth says:

﴿Allah testifies that there is no deity except Him, and the angels and those of knowledge [also testify], [that He is] maintaining justice (qā'iman bil-qist). There is no deity except Him, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran)

Thus we know that the word "qist" comes sometimes to mean justice and sometimes to mean injustice.

"Qasta", "yaqsitu", "qasatan" and "qusutan" mean he acted unjustly, with a fatha on the qaf in "qasata" and a damma in "qusut".

Qist with a kasra on the qaf is justice; qast with a fatha on the qaf, as we have said, is injustice. There is a second verbal noun, "qusut", but the verb is one. When the Truth says, "And if you fear that you will not deal justly (tuqsitu)," from "aqsata", it means: if you fear failing to be just, that is, injustice. In the language there is what we call the hamzat al-izala (the hamza of removal), a hamza that enters a verb and removes its meaning. An example: "fulan 'ataba 'ala fulan", meaning he rebuked him for some conduct. Whoever receives the rebuke, when he responds to the one who rebuked him, is said to "a'tabahu", meaning he reassured his heart and removed the cause of the rebuke.

It is said: Muhammad rebuked ('atiba) 'Ali. So what was 'Ali's response? It is said: he "a'taba Muhammadan", meaning he pleased him and removed the rebuke. It is also said "a'jama al-kitab", and you should not understand from this that he made the book foreign (mu'jam); rather, he removed its ambiguity and obscurity. Likewise "aqsata" means he removed injustice and wrong. Qist therefore means justice from the outset, but "aqsata, iqsatan" signifies that there had been oppression or injustice which was then lifted. The matter ultimately returns to justice. So justice that comes from the outset is qist with a kasra; if it comes after an injustice that has been removed, it is iqsat. Thus when one says "aqsata" and "tuqsitu" with a damma, the meaning is that there had been injustice and oppression which was lifted. Therefore when we read the Qur'an, we find it says:

﴿As for the unjust (al-qasitun), they will be fuel for Hell.﴾ (Surah al-Jinn)

Here "al-qasitun" derives from "qast" with a fatha and from "qusut" with a damma, meaning from injustice and oppression. The Noble Qur'an also says:

﴿And if you judge, judge between them with justice. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly (al-muqsitin).﴾ (part of verse 42, Surah al-Ma'idah)

That is, Allah loves those who, when they see injustice, remove it and put justice in its place.

Here in Surah an-Nisa' the Truth says: "And if you fear that you will not deal justly with the orphans," meaning: if you fear that you will not lift injustice from the orphans. To fear failing to be just is because you are righteous and know how to save yourself from the places of slipping. That is: if you, O believers, fear that you will not lift injustice from the orphans, then keep away from them, and let every believer block this avenue against himself, so that his soul does not prompt him to wrong an orphan girl and oppress her. If a man wishes to marry, there are many women outside the orphans before him.

Since women are many, plural marriage becomes permissible. He did not say: leave one and take one; rather He clarified: leave the orphan girl, for there are many women before you. So it suited the situation that the matter of plural marriage should come here, because He, glory be to Him and exalted, wants to turn the guardian away from marrying orphan girls, lest he wrong them, so He commanded him to leave marriage to the weak orphan, since there are many other women. "And if you fear that you will not deal justly with the orphans, then marry those women who please you, two, three, or four."

His saying, "those women who please you" means other than the forbidden women mentioned in His saying:

﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already occurred. Indeed, it was an immorality and hateful and an evil way.﴾ (Surah an-Nisa', 22)

And in His saying:

﴿Prohibited to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brother's daughters, your sister's daughters, your mothers who nursed you, your sisters through nursing, your wives' mothers, and your stepdaughters under your guardianship who are from your wives with whom you have consummated marriage—but if you have not consummated the marriage with them, there is no blame upon you—and the wives of your sons who are from your loins, and that you take two sisters in marriage simultaneously, except what has already occurred. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful. And [prohibited are] married women, except those your right hands possess—the decree of Allah upon you.﴾ (Surah an-Nisa')

So "what pleases you of women" other than the forbidden ones are those who are lawful for the man: "So marry those women who please you, two, three, or four. And if you fear that you will not be just, then [marry only] one, or what your right hands possess. That is more suitable, that you may not incline toward injustice." Here we must understand why this text came, and why it mentions two, three and four here.

He, glory be to Him, wants to make people averse to marrying orphan girls, lest a man, in a moment of weakness, marry an orphan girl and wrong her. So He made clear: leave the orphan girl, for there are many other women; before you are two, three and four. Stay away from the orphan girl, lest you be desirous of her wealth, or look upon her weakness, or because she no longer has any guardian to care for her apart from you.

We want to pause here before His saying, "Then marry those women who please you, two, three, or four." What is the meaning of "mathna"? It is said "mathna", meaning two by two, repeated, as one might say: "The people came mathna," meaning they walked in a file formed of two and two. This indicates a unity that is coming.

It is said: "The people came thulath", meaning they walked in a file of three; and it is said: "The people cameruba'", meaning the people came in a file in which every four walk behind four others.

If someone says: the intended meaning of mathna, thulath and ruba' is that what is permitted is nine women, we say to him: if we calculated as you calculate, the matter would include what Allah did not intend, for mathna means four, thulath means six, and ruba' means eight, and thus the total would be eighteen. But you did not understand, because Allah does not address one person; rather Allah addresses a group, saying: "And if you fear that you will not deal justly with the orphans, then marry those women who please you, two, three, or four."

If a teacher says to his students: "Open your books," does this command mean that one student should open all the books? No; it is a command to each student to open his own book. For this reason, the correspondence of plural with plural requires distribution among individuals.

When the teacher says: "Take out your pens," it means each student must take out his pen. When it is said: "Board your cars," it means each person should board his own car. So the correspondence of plural with plural requires distribution individually. The Truth's saying, "then marry those women who please you, two, three, or four; and if you fear that you will not be just, then [marry only] one, or what your right hands possess; that is more suitable, that you may not incline toward injustice," is a address to a group: one marries two, another marries three, and a third marries four.

The Truth, glory be to Him, when He legislates a ruling, legislates it sometimes as an obligation and sometimes as a permission. He did not make that obligatory upon the man, but He permitted it to him, and there is a clear difference between obligation and permission. Marriage itself, even to one woman, is permitted. So there is a difference between Allah obliging you to do something and Allah permitting you to do it. When Allah permits you to do something, what tips the balance in your action? It is merely your desire.

But when you take a ruling, take it in all its aspects. Do not take the ruling on permitting plurality and then cease to uphold the ruling on justice, for otherwise corruption will arise on earth, and the first of this corruption is that people will doubt the judgment of Allah. Why? Because if you take plurality and refrain from justice, you have taken one half of the ruling and not the other half, which is justice. People then incline away from plurality and turn from it, why? Because people have suffered greatly from plurality, taking Allah's ruling on plurality while abandoning Allah's ruling on justice.

The divine method must be taken whole. Why does a wife dislike plurality? Because she finds that when a husband marries a second wife over her, he turns his entire self, his goodness, his smile and his tenderness, toward the new wife. Therefore it is necessary that a woman dislikes her husband marrying another woman over her.

Those who take Allah's ruling on the permissibility of plurality must also bind themselves to Allah's ruling on justice. If they do not, they spread rebellion against Allah's ruling, and people will find justifications for this rebellion, and it will be said: "Look, so-and-so married another and neglected the first, or left his children without care and turned to the new wife."

How can you take Allah's permission in one matter and not take His obligation in another? One who does so casts doubt upon Allah's ruling among people, and makes people rebel against Allah's ruling. Superficial thinkers say: "They are excused." This reasoning is untenable.

The bane of rulings is that a partial ruling is taken without regard to all the circumstances, and whoever takes a ruling from Allah must take the whole method of Allah.

Bring me a man who is just in companionship, in maintenance, in spending the night, in lodging and in time, and who does not favor one over another. The first wife, if she does something, will find no justification before people; but when the matter is otherwise, she will find a justification for objecting. The clamour we hear these days arises from the fact that some have taken Allah's ruling on the permissibility of plurality without taking Allah's ruling on justice among those with plural wives. Justice applies to matters in which the man has a choice; as for matters in which the man has no choice, Allah has not required them of him.

Some superficial people say: "Allah said: be just, then He ruled that we cannot be just." We say to them: By Allah, is this legislation? Does Allah give with the right hand and take back with the left? Did not the Truth legislate on inability, saying:

﴿And you will never be able to be equitable between wives, even if you should strive to do so. So do not incline completely [toward one] and leave her as if suspended. And if you amend and fear Allah, then indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (Surah an-Nisa', 129)

Since He legislated on the inability to achieve absolute justice, He has kept the ruling and not annulled it. The believer must not make Allah's method in the movement of his life into "parts" (`idin), meaning that he takes a ruling that suits him and leaves a ruling that is against him. The method from Allah is taken as one whole from all people, because any deviation in an individual of the Islamic community harms the whole. Every right you have is a duty for someone else, so if you wish to take your right, then fulfil your duty. Those who take Allah's ruling on the permissibility of plurality must also take Allah's ruling on justice, otherwise they give the enemies of Allah's religion strong arguments for nullifying what Allah has legislated, and for changing what Allah has legislated under the pretext of what they see as the effects of taking one ruling and neglecting another.

The justice required in plurality is equal distribution in lodging, meaning that each of the wives has a dwelling equal to that of the others; in time; in the furnishings of the dwelling; and in what concerns the man's own belongings. He may not make something valuable for one wife and something worthless for another. For example, he may not bring a woollen nightgown (manama) and place it with one wife, and bring another made of cheaper cloth and place it with another. No. Equality is required, not only in her goods, but in your own belongings that you use with her, to the extent that some of the early Muslims would equalise between them even in the sandals worn in the house, so that...

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 4:

After that, the Truth (al-Haqq) says: ﴿And give the women their dowries (ṣadaqāt) as a free gift (niḥlah). But if they willingly remit to you any part of it, then consume it with enjoyment and pleasure.﴾

What is meant by "ṣadaqātihinna" (their dowries) is the mahr (bridal gift), and "niḥlah" is a gift (ʿaṭiyyah). Is the ṣadaq a gift? No. It is a right (ḥaqq) and a wage for the use of the body (ajr buḍʿ). But God wants to make clear to us: let the giving of the mahr to the women be a niḥlah, meaning a restraint of conscience (wāziʿ dīn), not a judicial ruling (ḥukm qaḍāʾ). Niḥlah means a gift.

Look at the divine subtleties and the divine manner of expressing the meanings, for if you look at the reality you will find the following:

A man marries a woman. The man has enjoyment in the woman, and the woman also has enjoyment; that is, each of them has enjoyment and partnership in this, and in the desire for offspring. It would have been expected that she should take nothing, since she will be the one who enjoys, and she may also bear a child for herself, and she will work in the home while the man toils outside the house. But this is a gift God has decreed as an honour to women: "And give the women their dowries as a free gift." As for the command in "give" (ātū), to whom is it addressed? Either it is addressed to the husband, so that His saying "give the women their dowries" indicates that the woman has become the man's wife and the man has become obliged to pay the dowry, and it may be a debt if he married her with a mahr owed in his responsibility, which he pays to her when he is well-off. Or the command is addressed to her guardian (walī amrihā), such as one who would marry off his sister, taking the mahr for himself and leaving her without giving her dowry. The command in this verse is therefore either addressed to the husbands or to the guardians. When the Truth legislates to protect rights, it opens the door to the generosity of virtue (arīḥiyyāt al-faḍl).

Therefore He says: "But if they willingly remit to you any part of it, then consume it with enjoyment and pleasure."

The Truth has first made rights known by addressing the husband or the guardian that the wife's mahr belongs to her, since it is the wage for the use of the body. But He, glory be to Him, has opened the door of the generosity of virtue: if the wife remits, that is another matter, and this is more likely to establish the marital bond and to bring about harmony (yu'addima) between them. What is meant here is the good pleasure of the soul (ṭayyib al-nafs). Beware of taking anything from the mahr of a wife under your guardianship out of shame; what matters is that the matter be by good pleasure of the soul. "But if they willingly remit to you any part of it, then consume it with enjoyment and pleasure." Hanīʾ is the food that is consumed and that you relish as it enters your mouth. But you may eat something pleasant in taste, in chewing and in eating, yet it brings a harmful bodily consequence. It is hanīʾ, but not marīʾ. What is meant is that it should be pleasant in taste and have no bad health consequences. It differs from the pleasant but not wholesome food which a person eats and then seeks treatment afterwards.

So every meal that is hanīʾ is not necessarily marīʾ, and in eating we must take care that it be hanīʾ marīʾ.

The Imam ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him and honour his face, was approached by a man complaining of an ache. The Imam ʿAlī, as we know, is the city of knowledge and of legal opinion (madīnat al-ʿilm wa al-fatyā), and God had granted him the capacity to give opinion and legal ruling.

The Imam ʿAlī was not a physician, but the man was seeking a remedy from the understanding and illumination of Imam ʿAlī.

Imam ʿAlī said to the man: "Take two dirhams from your wife's dowry, buy with them honey, dissolve the honey in rainwater that has just fallen, that is, recently come from God, and drink it. For I heard God say about water that descends from the sky:

﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water﴾ (part of verse 9, Surah Qaf).

And I heard Him, glory be to Him and exalted, say about honey:

﴿In it is healing for mankind﴾ (part of verse 69, Surah al-Naḥl).

And I heard Him say about the wife's mahr:

﴿So consume it with enjoyment and pleasure﴾ (part of verse 4, Surah al-Nisāʾ).

So if blessing, healing, the pleasant and the wholesome are combined in the medicine, may God grant you wellbeing, God willing. Imam ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him and honour his face, took four elements in order to blend them and make from them an effective medicine, as a physician prepares a treatment from various ingredients; and Imam ʿAlī made a remedy from the verses of the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 5:

After this, the Truth moves on to the matters of orphans, the foolish (al-sufaha'), wealth, guardianship and maintenance, and so He, glorified is He, says:

﴿And do not give the foolish your property, which Allah has made a means of support for you, but provide for them from it and clothe them and speak to them words of kindness.﴾

And who is the safih (foolish person)? He is the one who has no soundness in his reason and cannot spend his wealth wisely. And who gives his wealth to a fool? The Truth says this to teach us how to manage wealth. As an example, the Truth says:

﴿And do not defame one another﴾ (part of verse 11, Surat al-Hujurat).

Does any of us defame himself? No, but a person defames his opponent, and defaming the opponent leads to defaming oneself, because his opponent will defame and disparage him, or because you are equal. So the words of the Truth, "And do not give the foolish your property," mean that Allah wants to say: the foolish person does own the wealth, but his foolishness prevents him from managing it well. Failure to manage wealth wisely takes it away and corrupts it, and when a person is foolish, the wealth is not under his management and disposal, but belongs to whoever will put it right through guardianship (qiwamah).

Or, the Truth, glorified is He, addresses an issue that existed in society: when a man has children and they grow up a little, he wants to escape the movement of life and hand over to them the right to dispose of the wealth. If their disposal does not accord with wisdom, it is as if He, glorified is He, said: "No! Beware of giving your wealth to the foolish on the pretext that they are your children. And beware of giving your children what Allah has bestowed on you of your provision, for Allah has made your wealth a means of support for you, and beware of placing your own support in the hand of another."

"And do not give the foolish your property, which Allah has made a means of support for you, but provide for them from it." Does the foolish person not live? Does the foolish person eat less than the wise person eats? Does the foolish person wear less than the wise person wears? Does the foolish person live in a lesser dwelling than the wise person? Does a person smile at the wise but not at the foolish? No; therefore the Truth commands and says: "but provide for them from it and clothe them and speak to them words of kindness." This is a command to treat the foolish person well, and beware of reproaching them for their foolishness, for what they suffer from in their foolishness is sufficient.

Then the Truth turns back to the orphans: ﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age; then if you perceive in them sound judgment, release their property to them, and do not consume it extravagantly and hastily before they grow up. Whoever is wealthy should abstain, and whoever is poor may eat according to what is reasonable. Then when you release their property to them, have witnesses over them; and sufficient is Allah as Reckoner.﴾

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 6:

Almighty Allah commands, in dealing with orphans, that the guardian (wali) begin testing the orphan and training him to manage his wealth before reaching maturity (rushd). That is, do not wait until the orphan reaches the age of puberty and only then test him. Rather, before he attains maturity, you must try him in partial matters. If it becomes clear and evident to you that he is guided and acts well with his property, then at that moment you will find the ruling ready, and you will not be compelled to delay handing over the wealth until you test him in his maturity. Rather, you must test him, train him, and examine him while he is under your guardianship, until the time of attaining maturity arrives, when he can take his property from you and manage it himself. And so that not a moment passes over the property from its owner's maturity while it is still with you.

So He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age. Then if you perceive in them sound judgment, hand over to them their property, and do not consume it extravagantly.﴾

So when the orphan reaches maturity, and he has been trained in good management of wealth, and the guardian (wasi) knows that the orphan has become able to manage his property, then immediately upon reaching maturity the guardian must hand over his property to him, and it is not permissible for the guardian to consume the orphan's property extravagantly. Extravagance (israf) is exceeding the limit, because it is not his property; it is the orphan's property. When it was said to a greedy man: "What do you want, O greedy one?" the greedy man said: "I want a bowl of thareed, into which I strike with my hand, just as the wicked guardian strikes into the orphan's property." May Allah save us and you from this situation. And we find the Truth saying: ﴿And do not consume them extravagantly and hastily, fearing that they will grow up.﴾

Almighty Allah warns us against extravagance with the orphan's property during the period before maturity, out of fear that the orphan would grow up while he still has some property with the guardian; that is, that the guardian would be extravagant and spend all of the orphan's property before the orphan grows up and reaches maturity. Almighty Allah, when He legislates, legislates with His perfect majesty, a legislation that does not prevent the guardianship of the poor, just, non-wealthy person. Allah could have said: "Do not give guardianship except to a person who has wealth, because he is independent of the orphan's property."

But the Truth does not prevent the upright poor person who has experience and faith from guardianship.

Therefore, Almighty Allah says concerning the guardian: ﴿And whoever is wealthy, let him abstain, and whoever is poor, let him eat according to what is reasonable.﴾ So let no one say about another: "He is poor," and if we place his hand on the orphan's property, he will consume it. No, this is a statement by human measures. It is not permissible for anyone to prevent a poor believer from being a guardian of an orphan, because we want one who possesses a faithful reserve that raises him above greed for wealth. Therefore the Truth says concerning the guardian of the orphan's property: he bears clear responsibility.

So if he is wealthy, let him abstain, and if he is poor, let him eat according to what is reasonable. They defined "reasonable" as taking the equivalent wage (ajr mithlihi) for the work he performs.

The word ma'ruf means what is customary among people, or that he takes according to his need. And the Truth says: ﴿And when you hand over to them their property, have witnesses over them, and sufficient is Allah as Reckoner.﴾ And observe the protection: He, glorified is He, creates protection for the guardian or the executor, for the Truth knows His creation, and His creation is subject to change, and the guardian over the orphan must exercise guardianship with wisdom and care, so that the orphan does not come to hate him. Perhaps he would indulge him in everything. We say to him: No, give him in moderation, so that you do not corrupt him. If the guardian gives the orphan in moderation, the orphan may come to hate him, because the orphan may desire luxuries that are not suitable for him and do not match his means, and when the orphan reaches the age of maturity, his hatred may focus against the executor, and he says to him: "You consumed my property." Therefore the Truth makes clear to the guardian or executor: just as I protected the orphan through your good guardianship, I protect you from the orphan's maturity.

Therefore, O guardian, when you hand over the property to him, you must have witnesses to it, because you do not control people's psychological changes. Perhaps he will resent you and hate you, because you were strict with him regarding his property, and you used to restrain his hand when he deviated. And if he hates you, he may seek some opportunity and act against you and accuse you of what is not in you. Therefore it is necessary for you to bring reliable (adl) witnesses at the moment you hand over the property. This testimony is only to clear yourself regarding the property; as for clearing yourself regarding religion, that is left to Allah: ﴿and sufficient is Allah as Reckoner.﴾

Furthermore, Surat al-Nisa' addresses the weakness of women and the weakness of the orphan, because the situation in the society in which Islam came was that they did not give inheritance to women or to the young children who had not yet grown strong, and the strange rule among them was: whoever does not thrust a spear, nor defend a harem or property, nor witness battles, does not take from the inheritance. This was the height of the strong oppressing the weak. Islam came to annul this rule. Rather, it imposed and made obligatory that women take their rights, and likewise children, and for this reason Almighty Allah says: ﴿For men is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, and for women is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, whether it is little or much - an obligatory share.﴾

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 7:

﴿For men there is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, and for women there is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, whether it is little or much — an obligatory share.﴾

And who imposes this share? It is Allah, the One who owns, and it is He who has made it obligatory.

Here we notice that the late martyr, the author of "Fi Zilal al-Qur'an" (In the Shade of the Qur'an), Shaykh Sayyid Qutb, observed a fine point: how can the deceased have children or women who are dependent on him and yet not receive anything? Surely the young ones were more deserving of taking, because the older ones have grown strong in body and limb, so the young are more deserving of care. Also, if the laws of "Mendel" (Mendelian inheritance) in heredity show that children inherit from their mothers, fathers and grandparents good or bad qualities, or illness or chastity or physical form, then why do you not also bequeath to them in wealth?

When we hear the Truth's words, "an obligatory share," there must be one who imposes it and one upon whom it is imposed. The imposer here is Allah, the One who owns. There is a subtle difference between "faraḍa" (to impose as a binding due) and "awjaba" (to make obligatory): "faraḍa" implies something coming from above, whereas "wājib" may come from the person himself, since a person may make something obligatory upon himself.

When the Truth speaks of an obligatory share, He has shown that it has a known measure. Since the share has a known measure, its details must be clarified. The Truth did not clarify this except after introducing people who may not be heirs to the deceased, those who are around the dead person but are not among the inheritors.

Al-Sha'rawi explains the call to give to those who have no share (in the inheritance): "Beware lest this prescribed share distract you from those who have no share in the estate."

Therefore the Exalted says: ﴿And when the division is attended by the relatives and the orphans and the needy, provide for them from it and speak to them a kind word.﴾ (4:8)

When the relatives, the orphans and the needy attend the scene of the distribution of the wealth, and each of the heirs among whom the deceased's property is being distributed has had his affairs settled, these non-heirs may say: the heirs are taking a cool windfall that has descended upon them. Such a situation leaves something in the souls of the relatives, the orphans and the needy.

It is true that the relatives, the orphans and the needy are not heirs, and they will not take anything from the estate as a fixed share for them. But they attended the division, and therefore the true command comes: "Provide for them from it and speak to them a kind word." Had they not attended the division, the situation would have been different. The Exalted commands that we provide for the orphans, the relatives and the needy so that we may draw out from them resentment or envy toward the heir, or rancour toward the deceased. In this way a measure of harmony, affection and love of good spreads among people, because they have obtained some good along with these others, and so they do not become resentful toward the heirs or toward the deceased.

The Truth does not limit itself to commanding the provision of these relatives, orphans and needy, but commands that we speak to them a kind word, such as that we pray to God that He increase their provision, that they have wealth, that they leave children and pass on an inheritance to them. And who must carry out such a deed? They are the heirs, if they have reached maturity. But what is the position if the heir is an orphan? Then those present are the ones who say to the relatives, the orphans and the needy: this is an orphan's wealth, and we have no guardianship over it; had we guardianship, we would have given you more. Such speech brings comfort to the heart.

"And when the division is attended by the relatives and the orphans and the needy, provide for them from it and speak to them a kind word": you must, in that situation, bear in mind that if you were the weak, the orphans and the non-heirs, joy would certainly have entered your hearts had we legislated for you a share of the inheritance. So let each of you remember that when God makes a demand of him, you may one day be in the position of one for whom God makes a demand regarding yourself and your children. Thus the legislative ruling is not taken from one side only: it obliges the believer to certain things, but let us also take into account that it obliges other believers toward the believer in certain things.

The legislative ruling gives you, and therefore it takes from you. This is why we said regarding zakat: beware, O you who pay zakat, lest you think that we are taking from you unjustly the fruit of your toil and sweat in order to give it to people. We take from you while you are able, so that we may insure you should you become incapable, and we will take for you from the capable. It is a wise divine insurance.

And then the Truth (al-Haqq) says: ﴿And let those fear [Allah] who, were they to leave behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them. So let them keep their duty to Allah and speak words of appropriate justice.﴾ (9)

A person who leaves behind weak offspring leaves them while fearful that time will ruin them.

If you, O believer, have weak offspring and you fear for them, then whenever you see weak offspring left by someone else, show them kindness, so that others will show kindness to your weak offspring if you leave them behind. Know that our Lord is Watchful (Raqib) and Sustainer (Qayyum), and He does not leave unrewarded the good you have done, but returns it to your offspring. We have mentioned once that Mu'awiyah and 'Amr ibn al-'As met near the end of their lives. 'Amr ibn al-'As said to Mu'awiyah: "O Commander of the Faithful, what share of worldly pleasure remains for you?" Mu'awiyah had become Commander of the Faithful and head of a strong, wealthy state. He said: "As for food, I have grown tired of its finest; as for clothing, I have grown weary of its softest; my share now is a cup of cold water in the shade of a tree on a summer day."

Mu'awiyah fell silent for a while, then asked 'Amr: "And you, O 'Amr, what pleasures of the world remain for you?"

Our master 'Amr ibn al-'As had a commercial genius, and he said: "My share is a gushing spring in a fertile land, which yields a livelihood for my life and for my son after my death."

He is seeking a continuously flowing spring of water in a land where there are livestock and crops that give forth good.

There was a servant serving them, bringing them drinks. Mu'awiyah looked at the servant and wished to joke with him so as to include him in the conversation.

He said to the servant: "And you, O Wardan, what remains for you of the enjoyments of the world?" The servant replied: "What remains for me of the world's pleasures, O Commander of the Faithful, is a favour of kindness that I place upon the necks of noble people, who will not repay it for the duration of my life, so that it will be a legacy for my descendants among theirs." The servant had understood from Allah His saying:

﴿And let those fear [Allah] who, were they to leave behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them. So let them keep their duty to Allah and speak words of appropriate justice.﴾ (Surah al-Nisa' 9)

Those who keep their duty to Allah regarding weak offspring are assured that Allah will provide them with someone who keeps their duty to Allah regarding their weak offspring.

We have also spoken once about the righteous servant to whom Musa (peace be upon him) went: ﴿Musa said to him: "May I follow you, on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, [as] guidance?" He said: "You will not be able to have patience with me. And how can you have patience about that which you do not encompass in knowledge?" He said: "You will find me, if Allah wills, patient, and I will not disobey you in any matter." He said: "If you follow me, then do not ask me about anything until I mention it to you." So they set out until, when they boarded the ship, he tore it open. [Musa] said: "Have you torn it open to drown its people? You have certainly done a grave thing."﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 66–71)

The righteous servant tested Musa regarding the tearing of the ship, as the verses make clear. The righteous servant said: ﴿Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾ ﴿[Musa] said: "Do not blame me for what I forgot, and do not impose upon me hardship in my affair."﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 72–73)

Then came the matter of the boy whom the righteous servant killed, and Musa's words to him: "You have certainly done an objectionable thing."

Then they came to the people of a town and asked them for food. When a wayfarer asks you for food, know that it is pressing need, for if he asked you for money you might think he was hoarding wealth, but if he asks for a morsel to eat, then this is an obligation upon you.

What did the people of the town do when the righteous servant and Musa asked them for food? The Truth says:

﴿So they set out until, when they came to the people of a town and asked its people for food, they refused to host them. Then they found within it a wall about to collapse, so he set it up straight. [Musa] said: "If you had wished, you could have taken a payment for it."﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 77)

This is a miserly town. The righteous servant found in the town a wall that was about to fall and collapse, so he set it upright, and Musa objected, because he had resentment toward the people of the town: they had asked them for food and they had not fed them. Our master Musa said: "If you had wished, you could have taken a payment for it, since these people are base, and it would not have been right for you to set up the wall for them unless you took a payment from them."

Musa failed to grasp what Allah, glory be to Him, did not hide from the righteous servant. By Allah, if the wall had fallen while they were base people who would not feed those who asked them, and then they had seen the treasure left for the orphaned and needy, they would certainly have seized the treasure. Therefore, when I saw the wall about to fall, I set it up, so that I might conceal the treasure from these base people. The Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them, and their father had been righteous. So your Lord intended that they should reach their maturity and extract their treasure as a mercy from your Lord. And I did not do it of my own accord. That is the interpretation of that about which you could not have patience.﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 82)

So the reason behind this action is the protection of the two orphans. Let us pay attention and heed the details of the text: the righteous servant must have set up the wall in a manner that renewed its assumed lifespan, such that when the two orphans reached maturity, the wall would fall before them so that both could see the treasure. The wall was built on the model of a timed bomb, so that when they reached maturity, the wall would collapse and they would take the treasure. It was a divine timing that Allah willed, because the father of the two orphans had been righteous, had kept his duty to Allah regarding what was under his hand, so Allah sent to him soldiers whom He did not let be known and did not arrange, to guard the treasure for his two orphan sons. Therefore, let us understand well how we deal with others. The word of the Truth:

﴿And let those fear [Allah] who, were they to leave behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them. So let them keep their duty to Allah and speak words of appropriate justice.﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 9)

Why? Because when a person is young, his own selfhood is what is present. But as a person advances in years, the selfhood of his children advances in his heart, and he deprives himself to give to his children. When he sees that his dependants are still weak, and the precursors of death have come to him, he grieves at parting from these weak ones. So the Truth shows every servant the path to security: while you are alive you can give strength to the weak, a strength drawn from attachment to the method of Allah, and especially from caring for the orphans who are under your hand. In this way you secure the lives of your children after you, and you die at peace about them.

The words of appropriate justice from guardians are: not to harm the orphans, to speak to them as one speaks to one's own children, with good manners and warmth, and to address them by saying "my son" and "my boy."

And when the believer keeps his duty to Allah regarding what is in his hands, Allah provides him with someone who keeps his duty to Allah regarding his children.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 10:

The Truth (al-Haqq) continues to establish the method (al-manhaj) regarding the matter of orphans: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly are only consuming fire into their bellies, and they will [soon] enter a blaze.﴾ (4:10)

Why does the Qur'an focus on this particular aspect? Because God wants His creation to receive God's decree concerning those they love and those they need with contentment. If a child is small and sees his father striving for his affairs and providing him with every good thing in life, and then the father dies, and the child has seen that one (his father) died, and he is taken in by the community of faith (al-mujtama' al-imani) that lives in guardianship, it compensates him for one father with many faithful fathers. So when this child's father dies, he receives God's decree and His trials without panic. What makes people receive calamities with fear, anxiety and dread is that they see that when a child's father dies and he becomes an orphan, he will be lost, and the child says to himself: "When my father dies, I will become one who is wasted." But if society protected the rights of the orphan, and every believer became a father to the orphan and every believing woman a mother to the orphan, the matter would be different. When God's decree descends upon his father, he receives the decree with contentment and submission.

﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly are only consuming fire into their bellies, and they will [soon] enter a blaze.﴾ (Surat an-Nisa', 4:10).

The most significant aspect of the whole negative and plundering process is eating (al-akl), because eating is what recurs among people, and it differs from clothing: for every season a person needs clothes suited to it, but eating is a daily process; therefore any plundering is for the sake of food. That is why we say in our colloquial proverbs about the plunderer: "So-and-so has a wide belly" – it is a matter of eating.

The Truth has clarified this matter regarding consuming the property of an orphan: you are stuffing fire into your belly. This means that he eats into his belly what leads to the Fire in the Hereafter. This may also happen as punishment in this world, so that the one who consumes an orphan's property suffers in his belly from diseases that burn his insides. On the Day of Resurrection the believers will see these people who consumed the orphan's property, and upon them will be the marks of consuming the orphan's property: smoke will come out of their mouths. Beware of understanding that only the bellies will be filled with fire, and that there will be no fire before the eyes. Rather, there will be fire in the bellies, and they will enter a blaze.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 4, verse 11:

The Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, what is equal to the share of two females. And if there are only daughters, two or more, for them is two-thirds of what the deceased left; and if there is only one, for her is half. And for his parents, to each one of them is a sixth of what he left, if he had children. But if he had no children and the parents inherit from him, then for his mother is a third. And if he has siblings, then for his mother is a sixth, after any bequest he has made or debt. Your fathers and your sons—you do not know which of them are nearer to you in benefit. An obligation from Allah. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ 11

How excellent is the Lord, our Creator! He instructs us concerning our children. Glory be to Him, Lord of the Mighty Throne. It is as if we are dearer to our Lord than we are to our fathers. His noble words, "Allah instructs you concerning your children," show that He is merciful to us and loves us. When we survey the root *wasiyya* (bequest, instruction) in the Qur'an, we find by induction that it is accompanied by the particle *bi* (ب), which denotes attachment. He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿That is what He has enjoined upon you, that you may become righteous.﴾ (Qur'an 6:153)

And He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿He has prescribed for you of religion what He enjoined upon Noah.﴾ (Qur'an 42:13)

And the Truth also says:

﴿And We have enjoined upon man (regarding) his parents: his mother carried him, in weakness upon weakness.﴾ (Qur'an 31:14)

In all these verses, the *wasiyya* is accompanied by the *bi* that comes for attachment.

But when the Qur'an enjoins the parents concerning the children, it says: "Allah instructs you concerning your children." It is as if the bequest is planted and fixed within the children. Whenever you see the container, which is the child, you remember the bequest, and what is the bequest? It is "for the male, what is equal to the share of two females." We have said before that the Truth said: ﴿For men is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, and for women is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave﴾ (Qur'an 4:7).

The share was not specified directly after this verse, but only after it had brought the account of the orphans and warned people against consuming the property of orphans. Why? Because that stirs in the soul a longing for the ruling, and when the soul looks forward to the detailed ruling, and the ruling comes after the soul has sought it, it takes firm hold of it. Something that the soul seeks is prepared to receive it; but when a matter is presented without being sought, the soul accepts it at one time and turns away from it at another. We observe this in the occasion of specifying the shares of inheritance.

For the Truth, glory be to Him, first said:

﴿For men is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, and for women is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave﴾ (Qur'an 4:7).

Then the matter of division was presented, along with the care of orphans, the needy, and the near of kin. Then came the command and ruling regarding the protection of an orphan's property and the warning against plundering it. After that He says: "Allah instructs you concerning your children," and the first item of the bequest comes: "for the male, what is equal to the share of two females." Why did He not say, "for the females, what is equal to the share of the male," or "for the female, half the share of the male"? These meanings could express what is required.

Allah willed that the measure, or the standard, should be the share of the female, and that the share of the male here be related to the female. For had He said, "for the female, half the share of the male," the measure would have been the male. But He, glory be to Him, made the measure the female, saying: "for the male, what is equal to the share of two females."

As for those who say, "This is the first injustice that befalls women; we want equality," we say to them: look at the justice here. The male is required to have a wife whom he supports, and the female is required to have a male who supports her. Thus half the share of the male suffices her if she lives without marriage, and if she marries, the half that is hers will remain hers, and she will have a husband to provide for her.

So which of them is more favoured in the division? It is the female. That is why Allah made her the base and the measure when He said: "for the male, what is equal to the share of two females." So is there injustice in this saying, or favouritism toward women? In this saying there is favouritism toward women; for first He made her share the standard to which the matter is returned, because the man is required to spend on the female, and the female is required to have a husband who spends on her. So what she takes of half the male's share is wholly hers. You should have said: why did Allah favour women? Allah favoured women because she is a "honour" (ʿarḍ), so He protected her: if she does not marry, she finds what to spend; and if she marries, this is a bounty from Allah. Then the Truth says: "And if there are only daughters, two or more, for them is two-thirds of what he left."

I want you to gather your minds well here, so that you may fully recognise the intent of the Truth and the methods of the Qur'an in alerting minds to receive the speech of Allah. Allah honoured man with reason, and reason must be trained. Training means practice in solving problems; when difficulties arise, it prepares itself to resolve them, and possesses the ability to deduce and evaluate. All these are tasks of reason. So the Truth comes to the most important thing concerning man, which is religion, and the guide to religion and the keeper of its method is the Qur'an, and so it gives reason a creative task.

He, glory be to Him, does not present the texts like the articles of law on felonies or misdemeanours; rather, He gives in one place a part of the ruling and leaves the rest of the law to become clear in another place of the Qur'an through another detail, because He wants to show us that the divine method is a single, integrated method, and that it unfolds from one thing to another, completing a ruling across more than one place in the Qur'an. This is so that you may recognise the method as a whole. And if you are engaged with something, do not think that this thing alone is the method; rather, there are matters that come by digression and intertwine with the thing whose divine ruling you seek. An example of this is the matter of the orphan, which intertwines with the rulings of inheritance. This verse gives us such a matter. Why? Because Allah wants you, O possessor of reason, to exercise yourself within the framework that encompasses all of life. What concerns you first is your religion, so exercise your reason in it; when you exercise your reason in religion, you give your reason energy to work in the other domain.

But if your mind drowns in any particular matter, this may lead you away from the general framework, so that you become occupied with details and distracted from the general aim.

Our children can teach us from their games. A child plays with his peers "hide-and-seek," each companion hides in a place, and the child searches for his companions.

We also play with our children: we hide something in a hand, close our hands, and let the son guess by intuition in which hand the thing is. It is a training of the mind in deduction. If the boy is quick-witted, strong in observation, and full of intelligence, he watches his father's hands to compare which hand trembles slightly, or which hand is not natural in the way the father closes it, and he chooses it, and the boy's intelligence prevails. This is a process of training the child in deduction and understanding, and by this the child learns not to take matters as fixed without thought or practice.

The Truth, glory be to Him, wanted His rulings to be distributed across different places. Let us consider His words: "Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, what is equal to the share of two females; and if there are only daughters, two or more, for them is two-thirds of what he left." That is, if the deceased has not begotten a male and has more than two daughters, then for them is two-thirds of what he left.

But if there is a male with them, then each female will take half the share of the male. And if the sole heir is one daughter, the verse gives her half the inheritance: "and if there is only one, for her is half." There remained something for which Allah gave no ruling, namely that the deceased left two daughters. Here we find that the Truth has guaranteed to the two, in the case of three or more daughters, the taking of two-thirds of the estate; so the scholars have said. Why did He not state this clearly? He left this task to reason: a daughter, when she inherits with a male, takes a third of the estate, and when she is with another daughter without a male, she takes a third.

So if she is with a male, who is the one bearing the responsibility of striving, she takes a third; therefore it is logical that each female takes a third if the deceased has left two daughters. And there is another thing, so that you know that the Qur'an comes entirely as a coherent method: there is another verse in Surat an-Nisa' that discusses a part of this matter, leaving reason room to work and to search. He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning the kalāla. If a man dies leaving no child and has a sister, for her is half of what he left, and he inherits from her if she has no child. If there are two sisters, for them is two-thirds of what he left. And if there are siblings, men and women, for the male is the equal of the share of two females. Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray, and Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ (Qur'an 4:176)

Here the Truth brought up two sisters of the deceased and made clear that for them is two-thirds of the estate. Which of them is closer to the deceased, the two daughters or the two sisters? The two daughters of the deceased are closer to him than his two sisters; therefore for the two daughters is two-thirds. A daughter, if she is with her brother, takes a third, and if she has inherited alone, she takes a half. If the female heirs are more than two daughters, they take two-thirds; and if they are two, each takes a third. Why? Because Allah gave the two sisters two-thirds of what the deceased left if he had no children.

And it is remarkable that He used the plural in the first verse, concerning the inheritance of daughters, and used the dual in the verse that gives inheritance to sisters, so that we take the dual there in the verse about the inheritance of sisters to apply to the plural here, and take the plural here in the verse about the inheritance of daughters to apply to the dual there.

The Truth wanted to give reason the task of searching, investigation and deduction, so that rulings are taken with devotion and good understanding. When He, glory be to Him, says: "They ask you," the meaning of "they ask you" is that they ask you for a ruling, and this is evidence that the believer who asked and sought a ruling has come to love the obligation; he wishes to know the ruling of Allah even in matters on which Allah did not begin with a ruling. The early believers asked and sought rulings out of love for the obligation: "They ask you. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning the kalāla." The word kalāla is derived from *iklīl* (a crown), which is what surrounds the head; the kalāla is the kinship that surrounds a person and is neither of his origin nor of his offspring.

﴿If a man dies leaving no child and has a sister, for her is half of what he left, and he inherits from her if she has no child. If there are two sisters, for them is two-thirds of what he left. And if there are siblings, men and women, for the male is the equal of the share of two females. Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray, and Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ (Qur'an 4:176)

This verse completes the first verse. Let us return to the detailing of the first verse concerning which we are sharing our faith-inspired reflections: "And for his parents, to each one of them is a sixth of what he left, if he had children. But if he had no children and the parents inherit from him, then for his mother is a third."

This means that if the deceased had no children, then the mother has a third and the father has two-thirds. If the deceased had full or consanguine siblings, then the mother has a sixth, according to the Qur'anic text: "But if he has siblings, then for his mother is a sixth," after the bequest he made has been carried out and the debt he owed has been paid. The bequest is placed here before the debt, because the debt has claimants: the creditor can demand his debt, whereas the bequest has no claimant. The Truth placed it first to give it care, lest we neglect it. The Truth concludes this verse:

﴿Your fathers and your sons—you do not know which of them are nearer to you in benefit. An obligation from Allah. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ (Qur'an 4:11)

Beware of setting the shares according to what you suppose about the benefit from fathers or the benefit from sons. The benefit from fathers becomes clear when a person says: "My father raised me and created for me the opportunities of the future." The benefit from sons becomes clear when a person says: "My father is departing, and my sons are those who will carry my memory and my name, and life lies ahead of them." The Truth clarifies: beware of judging by such a judgement; you have no say in this matter: "you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit."

As long as you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit, then adhere to the ruling of Allah, who knows the interest and its direction in the shares as they ought to be.

When we hear: "Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise," or hear: "Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful," we hear it within the frame that Allah does not change, and since He was from eternity Knowing, Wise, Forgiving and Merciful—

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 12:

And the Truth says, after that:

﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave, if they have no child. But if they have a child, for you is one-fourth of what they leave, after any bequest they make or debt. And for the wives is one-fourth of what you leave, if you have no child. But if you have a child, for them is one-eighth of what you leave, after any bequest you make or debt. And if a man or woman leaves neither ascendants nor descendants (kalala), and he has a brother or a sister, then for each one of them is a sixth. But if they are more than that, they share in a third, after any bequest that is made or debt, without causing harm. This is a commandment from Allah, and Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing.﴾ (12)

The verses proceed to clarify that the male's share is like the share of two females. This is justice, because when a man's wife dies, he may remarry and rebuild his life, whereas when a woman's husband dies, she takes her inheritance from him while being exposed to the possibility of marrying again, and she will be answerable to a new husband.

The matter, as Allah intends it, achieves complete justice. And kalala, as we said, means that the deceased has neither a parent nor a child, that is, he has no root (asl) and no branch (far') descending from him.

So if a man leaves kalala, with a brother or a sister, then each of them receives a sixth; if they are more than that, they share in a third, and that too is after any bequest that is made or debt. Why is this ruling established? Let us return once more to the verse of kalala that came at the end of Surat al-Nisa'.

The Truth says in it:
