Some who do not know the actual goals of Freemasonry may join them to participate in the apparent good work. We say to each of these: "Look at your religion; you will find it urges you to do such good. Why do you attribute it to Freemasonry and not do it as an Islamic matter? Why do you not attribute this good to Islam and attribute it to other than Islam?"

In this era there is what is called the "Rotary" clubs, and a person takes on the vanity of pride in belonging to those clubs, and says: "I am a member of Rotary." When you ask him: "Why?" he answers: "They are clubs that urge cooperation, communication, affection and mercy." We say to him: "Has Islam forbidden that? Why do you do such good and attribute it to 'Rotary,' and do not do good and attribute it to your religion, Islam? Therefore this is hostility toward the method."

We find those who have strayed from the method are like the man to whom they said: "What does your soul desire now?" The man wanted to oppose Allah, so he said: "My soul wants me to break the fast on a day of Ramadan, with a cup of wine, and I buy this cup of wine with the price of a stolen pig."

He wants to break the fast of Ramadan while it is forbidden, to break it on wine which is forbidden, and with the price of a pig, and the pig is forbidden to the Muslim, and the pig is also stolen. They asked him: "Why all this complication?" He said: "So that this act may be forbidden four times."

Therefore this is harm done to Allah, and this is a man who has strayed from the method. Will Allah accept his repentance? No. "And repentance is not for those who commit evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, 'Indeed, I have repented now.'" At the moment of death, cowardice begins and the traits of rabbits appear. Why did he not persist in his position until the end? Because he came to the moment in which a person cannot lie to himself: "until, when death approaches one of them, he says, 'Indeed, I have repented now.'" But repentance is not accepted, and society will not benefit from it, and the evil of such a person has ended, and his repentance comes when he is no longer able to do any deed. Thus he mocks Allah, and repentance does not benefit him.

But look at the mercy of Allah and His respect for the testimony of faith, in which the believer affirms: "There is no deity but Allah, and Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah."

Allah placed this believer in opposition to the disbeliever, so he receives punishment in proportion to the sins he committed. The Truth's respect for the faith of the summit (īmān al-qimma) appears in His saying: "I bear witness that there is no deity but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." So Allah clarifies: "We will not make you like the disbeliever," as evidenced by the fact that He conjoined to it "nor those who die while they are disbelievers." Rather, the sinful believer is assigned punishment in proportion to the sins he committed, and the Truth honors the faith of the summit, so they enter Paradise; therefore the Truth did not say they are abiding in the Fire. Rather He said: "Those – We have prepared for them a painful punishment," and "those" refers to both categories, the believer and the disbeliever, so the punishment is for each according to his sin.

The Lord says after that:

﴿O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion. And do not make difficulties for them in order to take back part of what you have given them, unless they commit a clear immorality. And live with them in kindness. For if you dislike them - perhaps you dislike a thing and Allah makes therein much good.﴾ [4:19]

We have said: when the Truth calls His servants who have believed in Him, He, glorified is He, says: "O you who have believed," meaning: O you who have believed in Me by your own free choice, and have believed in Me as a God who possesses all the attributes of knowledge, power, wisdom and self-subsistence. As long as you have believed in this God, listen from the God to the rulings which He requires of you. Thus He addresses none but a believer; He addresses one who believed by his own choice and by the preference of his intellect. The Truth says:

﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾ (part of 2:256).

The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, wishes to address an issue related to women and their weakness. Islam came when women in the Jahiliyyah were in deprivation, oppression and injustice. He, glorified is He, said: "O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion." The word "inherit" (waratha) indicates that someone has died and has an heir, and there is something the deceased has left which may be inherited by no one after him; because when He says, "it is not lawful for you to inherit," a testator has died and He is addressing an heir. So the discussion concerns the inherited property, but the inherited property is sometimes lawful, and for this reason God legislated its distribution, which we have discussed before; but the discussion here concerns something left behind which may not be inherited. What is it?

He said: "it is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion." Does this mean that an heir may not inherit from his deceased relative the female slaves he left behind? No. The heir does inherit from his deceased relative the slave-women he left; but when the word "women" is used, it refers to its most honourable application, that is, free women, because the others are regarded, each one of them, as property of the right hand. "It is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion." Is there inheritance of women by consent? And how is a woman inherited?

Let us note here His words, "by compulsion." In the Jahiliyyah the reality was that when a man died leaving a wife, his heir would come and throw his garment over the wife, and she would become his possession; and if she did not accept, he would inherit her by compulsion; or if he had no desire for her, he would detain her with him until she died and he inherited her; or someone would come and marry her to him and take her dowry for himself, as if he were disposing of her as an owner. Therefore the decisive statement came:

"It is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion, nor to make difficulties for them," and "making difficulties" (al-adl) originally means preventing; it is said, "the woman was obstructed with her child" (a-dalat al-mar'ah bi-waladiha). That is the exact root of the derivation. When a woman gives birth, it is among the bounties of God upon her that she has muscles which contract and relax; they relax so that the place of the child's exit widens, and a woman may be obstructed during delivery, so that instead of the muscles relaxing to let the child come out, they contract; and so procedures are then carried out such as the Caesarean section.

Thus the meaning of "adl" is derived from "the woman was obstructed with her child," that is, her muscles contracted and did not relax so that the infant could not come out; and "the hen was obstructed with her egg," that is, when the egg is on its way down the muscle contracts and the egg does not descend, because a functional disturbance has occurred as a result of incomplete movement. And why does the movement come incomplete instead of relaxing? Because the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, did not will to make the causes in the universe operate automatically and mechanically, so that whenever the causes exist the effect exists. No. Above the causes is a Causer; if He wills, He says to the causes, "Stop," and they stop.

Thus all the deviations we see occur contrary to what the causes would produce, and they are indeed evidence of the absoluteness of power. If things proceeded in that way mechanically, people would say: the mechanism is precise and does not fail. But the Truth draws our attention to the fact that He exercises His authority over His dominion; He has not exercised authority once, then created the mechanism and the causes in the universe and left them to act. No: He makes clear to us: I am the Self-Subsisting, who is not seized by drowsiness or sleep; I say to the causes, "Act" or "do not act." Thus we turn our attention to Him as the one who controls.

You find these deviations as exceptions in the universe, so that the monotony of causes does not beguile us, and so that we remember God continually, and a person remains mindful of the Giver of causes and their Creator, so that dullness does not arise in us from the fact that causes are constant. The Truth draws us to His existence, so causes vary to draw your attention to the fact that they are not acting by their own essence, but act because God created them and left them to act; and if He willed, He would nullify them.

We have said this regarding the miracle of Abraham, peace be upon him, when his people threw him into the fire and it did not burn him. God could have saved Abraham by any other means; but is the matter the rescue of Abraham? If that were the matter, they would not have been able to overpower him; but He empowered them over him, and they seized him and he did not escape from them. It was possible for Him to command the sky to rain when they threw him into the fire, and the rain would have sufficed to extinguish the fire; yet the sky did not rain, but rather the fire blazed. After that the Truth says to it:

﴿We said: O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham﴾ (21:69).

By God, is this a vexation to them or not? It is a vexation to them: you had power over him, you threw him into the fire, and afterwards no rain descended to extinguish the fire; the fire was present and Abraham was in the fire, yet the fire did not burn him. This is the greatness of power.

So what is the meaning of "make difficulties for them" (ta'dulu-hunna)? From "adl" we take the word "prevention": a woman was obstructed, that is, her muscles were contracted so the child did not come out; and you would be obstructing her — how? By preventing her from her natural right when her husband dies; and that after completing the waiting period she has the right to marry whomever she wishes or whoever proposes to her. The Truth forbids: "and do not make difficulties for them," that is, do not detain them with you and prevent them; why would you do that? "in order to take back part of what you have given them." This was a separate ruling: "do not inherit women by compulsion" is one ruling, and "nor make difficulties for them" is a second ruling.

An example: when a man dislikes his wife, he says to her, "By God, I will not divorce you; I will leave you suspended and hanging, I will not be a husband to you, nor will I allow you to marry." This is so that she ransoms herself, thereby releasing the man from maintenance and deferred dower; thus Islam protects the woman and forbids such acts.

But when are you permitted to obstruct them? Here the Truth says: "unless they commit a clear immorality," because they would be detaining them; and this was before the legislation of the prescribed punishments. Some jurists said: the husband may take from his wife what she ransoms herself with, whether money or otherwise, if she commits immorality such as adultery or bad conduct; and this is what is called khul', which is divorce in exchange for a consideration sought by the husband.

The Truth continues: "and live with them in kindness." The word "kindness" (al-ma'ruf) has a wider scope than the word "affection" (al-mawaddah). Affection is that you do good to the one who is with you out of love for him, your soul is at ease in its affection for him, you are happy with him and with his presence; but kindness you may extend even if you do not love. This resolves many difficulties: when the orientalists wished to search the Qur'an to find something by which they could claim there is contradiction in it, they say: your Qur'an says:

﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers or their sons or their brothers or their kinsmen. Those - He has decreed within their hearts faith and supported them with spirit from Him. And He will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein; Allah is pleased with them, and they with Him. Those are the party of Allah; unquestionably, the party of Allah are the successful﴾ (58:22).

How could a believer not love his son or his father or anyone of his kin merely for their disbelief? And the Qur'an in another place says:

﴿And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them; but accompany them in this world with kindness﴾ (31:15).

We say: these people did not understand the difference between affection and kindness. "Affection" (wadd) is one thing and "kindness" (ma'ruf) is another. Affection arises from love; but kindness is not necessarily from love: when someone is hungry I will give him food to eat and satisfy his material needs. That is kindness; affection is that I act to satisfy myself. When a believing man shows compassion to his disbelieving father, he does not show it as a result of affection, but as a result of kindness, because even if he were a disbeliever he would still give him kindness.

Did the Truth, glorified is He, not rebuke Abraham regarding a guest who came to him, whom he did not honour because he asked him and learned that he was not a believer, so he did not host him? Our Lord said to him: "Because of one night in which you host him, do you want to change his religion, while I provide for him for forty years though he is a disbeliever?" What did our master Abraham do? He went and caught up with the man, and called out to him. The man said to him: what made it change so suddenly? Abraham said to him: "By God, my Lord rebuked me for what I did with you." The man said: "Your Lord rebuked you though you are His messenger, and I am a disbeliever in Him? What a fine Lord, a Lord who rebukes His beloved regarding His enemies," and he became a Muslim.

This is kindness. The Truth commands us that we must pay attention to these matters during married life, and this is an issue that all Muslims must heed so that they do not ruin homes. They want to build homes on affection and love; but if there is no affection and love in the home, the home is ruined. We say to them: no. Rather, "live with them in kindness" even if you do not love them; and perhaps the only reason is that you dislike the woman because her appearance does not stir your instincts. O you, you have not understood from God: it is not required of a woman that she stir your instinct; rather it is required of a woman that she be an outlet. If your instinct is chemically stirred by its nature, you find an outlet for it. You do not need a woman to entice you so that instinct is moved in you; and therefore the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "If one of you sees a woman and she pleases him, let him go to his wife, for with her is the like of what is with that one" (1).

That is, a piece of flesh is one; if your instinct is stirred by its nature, then any outlet suffices for you. That is why, when a man came to Caliph Umar, may God be pleased with him, and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I dislike my wife and want to divorce her," he said to him: "Were homes not built except on love, then where is consideration?"

The man had thought his wife would remain forever captivating his heart, so that he would enter each day to kiss her; but Umar drew his attention to the fact that this is a matter which first existed, and afterwards in the household there arise things that bind the man to the woman and the woman to the man.

Therefore the Truth says: "And live with them in kindness; then if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike a thing and Allah makes therein much good." You dislike her in one respect, and perhaps the very respect in which you dislike her is the one that will make her excel in several respects, so that by her goodness in the other respects she compensates for this deficient respect. So do not build the matter on your wanting a fashion model to arouse your instincts when you are idle. No. The woman is a natural outlet: if your instincts are stirred by their nature you find an outlet for them. But if you see in the woman only something that inflames instincts, that means you want the woman to be only a courtesan, living with you only for sexual relations. There are many other matters, so do not take from a woman one aspect only, the aspect of sexual excitement; take many aspects.

Know that God has distributed the causes of His bounty among His creatures: this one He gave beauty, that one He gave intellect, another He gave wisdom, another trustworthiness, another faithfulness, another success; there are very many causes. If you wish to be just and wise, take all the aspects; but if you look at the woman from one aspect only, the aspect of stirring instinct, we say to you: this is not the only aspect suitable for assessing a woman. "Perhaps you dislike a thing and Allah makes therein much good."

Look at the precision in the phrase "perhaps you dislike": you dislike, and you may be right in disliking or not. But if you dislike something of which God says, "and Allah makes therein much good," be assured that if you dislike in a woman something not related to her religion, know that if you bear patience with it, God will place in the remaining aspects for you

1 Narrated by al-Khatib from Umar.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 4, verse 20

Then the Truth says, after that:

﴿And if you desire to exchange one wife for another, and you have given one of them a heap of gold, do not take back anything from it. Would you take it by slander and manifest sin?﴾

When matters become straitened for you, after you have lived with her in kindness and it is no longer possible for the marital life to continue within a framework that pleases Allah, and you fear that you may slip from yourself into what Allah has forbidden, what do you do? He, glory be to Him, says: "And if you desire to exchange one wife for another." That is, you have the right to exchange, since the matter will reach the wounding of Allah's method. In this exchange you must observe the faith-based method, just as Sayyidina al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, indicated to a man who was consulting him about one who had come to propose to his daughter. Sayyidina al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "If the righteous man comes to you, marry her to him; for if he loves your daughter, he will honour her, and if he dislikes her, he will not wrong her."

And the Truth says: "And if you desire to exchange one wife for another." This means that the desire has turned away from the first completely, and it cannot be overcome except by deviating from the method. It may happen that a man is distressed with his wife while he does not suffer any urgent pressure in the sexual sphere, so he divorces her and does not remarry; so what are the conditions of the method in this matter?

The Truth says: "And you have given one of them a heap of gold, do not take back anything from it." The word "qintar" (a great measure of wealth) and the word "qantara" (bridge/arch) derive from the sense of something great. Qintar means "wealth." The ancients estimated it as the amount that fills the hide of a cow, and "miskh" is the hide; when the cow is flayed, its hide becomes like a waterskin, and the amount that fills its hide is called a qintar. The qintar known to us today has a weight measure. When the Truth magnifies the dower to a qintar, He says: "And you have given one of them a heap of gold," so He brings us a great example, and He forbids us by saying: "do not take back anything from it." Why? Because you must understand that the dower you pay is not spread out over the time of your relationship with the woman until your lives end; rather, the dower is made as the price of the intimacy that Allah has permitted you, even for a single moment. So do not reckon it by the measure of how long she stayed with you; no, it is the price of intimacy, for she has uncovered herself to you and you have come into her, even once.

So this qintar's life ends at the first moment, the moment of your having her. "And you have given one of them a heap of gold." This is the matter about which Sayyidina Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Umar erred and a woman was right," for he was speaking about the high cost of dowers. A woman said to him: "How can you say that when Allah says: 'And you have given one of them a heap of gold'?" He said: "A woman was right and Umar erred."

From Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that while on the pulpit he forbade increasing a woman's dower beyond four hundred dirhams, then he came down, and a woman of Quraysh confronted him and said: "Have you not heard Allah say: ﴿And you have given one of them a heap of gold﴾?" He said: "O Allah, forgive me; every person is more knowledgeable than Umar." Then he returned, mounted the pulpit, and said: "I had forbidden you to increase the dowers of women beyond four hundred dirhams; whoever wishes to give from his wealth what he likes, let him do so." (1)

And from Abdullah ibn Mus'ab that Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Do not increase women's dowers beyond forty ounces of silver; whoever exceeds one ounce, the excess will be placed in the public treasury." A woman said: "That is not for you." He said: "Why?" She said: "Because Allah, exalted is He, says: 'And you have given one of them a heap of gold.'" Umar said: "A woman was right and a man erred."

Then the Qur'an denies the very idea of taking back, saying: "Would you take it by slander and manifest sin?" Why? Because it is not the price of your enjoying her for a long time, but the price of your having her, and this occurs as soon as you enter upon her. If you take back any part of the dower from her after that, you are sinful, unless she consents to it; and "manifest sin" is the all-encompassing sin.

(1) Narrated by Sa'id ibn Mansur and Abu Ya'la.

Then the Truth (God) proceeds, with greater rebuke, saying: "And how could you take it?" It is a rebuke of the act of taking back some of the dowry, given the ruling (of the matter). He says:

﴿And how could you take it, when you have gone in unto one another, and they have taken from you a solemn covenant?﴾

Even if you were to consider every manner (of taking), you would not find any manner that makes the taking appear permissible. Why? Because the Truth said: "And how could you take it?" And look at the reason (He gives): "when you have gone in unto one another." So the price of intimacy (bud') is the ifdā' (going in unto one another), and the phrase "afḍā ba'ḍukum ilā ba'ḍ" is a phrase of its own kind; it therefore encompasses all the meanings that exist between a man and a woman. "Ifdā'" is derived from "faḍā'" (wide open space), and "afḍā ba'ḍukum" means you entered into one another in an unrestricted entry.

So ifdā' means: you have entered into one another in the widest possible intermingling. And it is enough, as the peak of intermingling, that her nakedness, which she conceals from her father, her brother, and even her mother and her sister, is revealed to you. There is no ifdā' greater than this. You have entered into her in the broadest contact: your breath, your touch, your intimacy, your companionship, your entering, your exiting, in her bath, in the kitchen, in everything, ifdā's have occurred. And since you have gone in unto her and she has gone in unto you, as the Truth also said regarding comprehensive intermingling:

﴿They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them﴾ (part of verse 187, Surat al-Baqarah).

What more could you want! That is why, when a woman is harsh with her husband and he becomes angry, we say to him: it is enough for you that God has made lawful to you from her what He has forbidden to others, and she has given you her honour; so when she is harsh with you, do not become angry, and remember the Hadith of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "The best of you is the best to his family, and I am the best of you to my family" (1).

"And how could you take it, when you have gone in unto one another, and they have taken from you a solemn covenant." The mithaq is a covenant made between two parties. When you asked her guardian, "Marry her to me," and he said to you, "I have married her to you," it is understood that this word of marriage will produce a new family. Every covenant between creatures other than over a woman's honour is an ordinary covenant; but the covenant between a man and the woman he marries is the solemn covenant, that is, not lenient. God did not describe any covenant with this description except the covenant of the prophets, describing it as ghalīẓ (solemn) (2), and He described this covenant as ghalīẓ. In this verse, "afḍā ba'ḍukum ilā ba'ḍ" is the ifḍā', and in another verse each spouse is a garment and a covering for the other: "They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them." For this reason the covenant is solemn. This solemn covenant obliges you, if companionship falters, to bear with it and treat her with kindness; and if it becomes impossible, and there is no benefit in continuing it, then it is permissible to replace her. But if you have given her a qintār, beware of taking anything from it, why? Because that is the price of ifḍā'; and since this qintār is the price of ifḍā' and it has been consummated, do not take anything from it. Ifḍā' is not something spread out over time so that you may distribute it, no.

And the Truth says: "And how could you take it, when you have gone in unto one another, and they have taken from you a solemn covenant." Here we must understand that the Truth, when it legislates rights, does not forbid graciousness (faḍl). The proof is that He said:

﴿But if they give you graciously of it, of their own accord, then eat it with wholesome enjoyment﴾ (part of verse 4, Surat al-Nisa').

So there is a difference between what is due as right (ḥaqq) and what is pleasing to you (ṭāba lakum). It is related of a judge who said to his people: "You have chosen me to judge the dispute between you; what do you want from me? Shall I judge by justice or by what is better than justice?" They said: "Is there anything better than justice?" He said: "Yes, graciousness (faḍl)." Justice is that each takes his right, and graciousness is that you relinquish your right and he relinquishes his right, and the matter ends. Thus graciousness is better than justice. When the Truth, glory be to Him, legislates rights, He sets guarantees, but He does not forbid graciousness among people:

He, may His majesty be exalted, says:

﴿And do not forget graciousness among yourselves﴾ (part of verse 237, Surat al-Baqarah).

And the Truth says in the verse of debt:

﴿And do not be weary of writing it down, whether it is small or large, to its term. That is more just in the sight of God, more upright for testimony, and nearer to avoiding doubt﴾ (part of verse 282, Surat al-Baqarah).

The Truth commands you to document debt, because you protect not only the creditor's wealth but also protect the debtor himself, for when he knows the debt is documented and written against him, he will not deny it; but if it were not written, he might be tempted to deny it. Thus the Truth protects both the creditor and the debtor from himself. He said: "And do not be weary of writing it," and after it He said:

﴿But if one of you trusts another, let the one who is trusted fulfil his trust﴾ (part of verse 283, Surat al-Baqarah).

You may say to one who borrows from you: there is no need to write a receipt or a deed between me and you. This is a generosity that God does not forbid; since one of you trusts another, let each of you be shy (of betraying), let the one who is trusted fulfil his trust, and let him fear God, his Lord.

And since He has allowed room for graciousness alongside the recording of rights, do not forget that. How much more, then, the solemn covenant between man and woman. The solemnity of a covenant is achieved only by what the covenant requires, and there is no covenant more solemn than what God took from the prophets and what is between man and woman, because it touches on a matter not permitted for a wife to any other than her husband, nor for a husband to any other than his wife. The man must give the woman her right and must not diminish anything of it unless she herself relinquishes it. For the Truth has already said:

﴿But if they give you graciously of it, of their own accord, then eat it with wholesome enjoyment﴾ (part of verse 4, Surat al-Nisa').

Since the soul has been pleased, then mutual consent exists between the two parties, and that is a gentle intimacy between man and woman. The mahr is her right, but it need not be paid in fact; it remains a debt upon the husband: if he wishes he may give it all, or defer it all, or give part and defer part. But when the wife separates after consummation, she has full right to her mahr: if he has deferred all of it, then it is obligatory that she take it, or she takes the remainder if he has paid part of it as an advance payment of the dowry.

However, when ownership of the mahr passes to the wife, God opens the door of consent and mutual agreement between man and woman, as He said: "But if they give you graciously of it, of their own accord, then eat it with wholesome enjoyment," for it is a gift that comes out of mutual consent. This confirms the continuance of companionship, affection, love and mercy between the spouses. After that there remains another ruling: suppose the dispute has flared between man and woman.

A situation in which she hates it and wishes to get out of it: there is no blame if she ransoms herself from him with some wealth, because she is averse; and as long as she is averse, he will be compelled to marry a new wife. So there is no objection to a woman seeking khul' from him by giving something to the husband:

﴿But if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of God, then there is no blame on either of them for what she ransoms herself with﴾ (part of verse 229, Surat al-Baqarah).

The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, wished to give us the proof that the woman's right must be preserved for her; therefore He came with a style that treats the husband's taking part of the wife's mahr in a style of wonder:

﴿And how could you take it, when you have gone in unto one another, and they have taken from you a solemn covenant?﴾ (part of verse 21, Surat al-Nisa').

So "And how could you take it" is evidence that there is no aspect of the Truth that permits you to take her mahr. When he asks, "How?", this is an expression of wonder that such a thing should occur. We have said that every covenant between two parties does not grant rights over honour, but the marriage covenant grants rights over honour, and hence the solemnity of the covenant. Every covenant and pact between two parties may concern wealth, may concern service, may concern paying blood-money on his behalf, may concern giving him aid; these are kinds of covenants, except the matter of honour. The matter of honour is a special covenant between the spouses, and hence the solemn covenant.

1. Related by al-Tirmidhi from ʿĀʾisha; related by Ibn Mājah from Ibn ʿAbbās; related by al-Ṭabarānī in al-Kabīr from Muʿāwiya.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 4, verse 22:

After this, the Almighty addresses a matter by which the family's purity, chastity, dignity and honour are preserved, and by which love and affection remain among the members of the family, so that nothing enters that would bring an end to this love and affection and allow the whispering of Satan to enter between them. The Almighty says:

﴿And do not marry those women whom your fathers married, except what has already occurred. Indeed, it was an abomination and hateful and an evil way.﴾ [4:22]

So this was an existing matter: a son would marry the wife of his father who was not his mother. Safwan ibn Umayya, one of the chiefs of Quraysh, succeeded his father Umayya ibn Khalaf in marrying Fakhta bint al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, who had been under his father; when his father died, he married her himself. The Almighty wishes to remove this matter from the sphere of the family. Why? Because between father and son there are relations of love, mercy, tenderness and compassion from the father, and righteousness, good manners, humility and lowering of the wing of humility from the son. When a man marries a woman and has a son, that is evidence that the father had been married to his mother before her, and it is as if the new marriage has intruded upon the family.

The Almighty also wishes that the eye of the son should not look toward the woman who is under his father, and who might please him and attract him. If she pleases and attracts him, then the least of his thoughts is that he says to himself: "After my father dies, I will marry her." When the hope arises in him that after his father's death he may marry her, he may rejoice at his father's death, and this is if he does not strive to rid himself of his father. And you know the frenzy of the instincts when they come, so the Almighty wishes to cut off from the son the hope of union, even by expectation and wishing, and that he must look upon the slave-girl or wife who is under his father with the same gaze he would give to his mother. When he looks at her with this gaze, the impulses of Satan are restrained.

So He says: "And do not marry those whom your fathers married." Here "nikah" (marriage, literally "union") is used, and it may refer to intercourse and consummation, or it may refer to the contract. However, its use for intercourse and consummation, that is the sexual act, is the more common and the preferable, because when God says: "The fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress" (24:3), the meaning is that he has intercourse without a contract and that the sexual act takes place without marriage.

Here the Almighty says: "And do not marry those women whom your fathers married, except what has already occurred." So what is this "already occurred"? What has passed was existing, that is, Islam came and found this practice followed, and Islam came with the prohibition of such a matter. Thus the new time after Islam does not permit such a thing to happen, even if the marriage contract had taken place before Islam. For this reason He said: "except what has already occurred," so He used "mā" (what), which refers to time. It is as if the new time does not contain this.

Suppose a man married his father's wife and then the ruling came. Would one say "what has passed" applies, because you married her before the ruling? We say: No, the time has ended. So His saying "what has already occurred" refers to time, and since the time has ended, the new time contains nothing of such matters. Therefore "mā" was used; had "man" (who) been used instead of "mā," the ruling would have been that whoever married before Islam would remain with her. But He said "except what has already occurred," so it is not valid in the future that anything of this should exist at all, and separation must be enforced between the spouses in respect of that marriage which was in existence.

The Almighty wishes to make clear to us that when He legislates, He legislates what sound human nature requires. He did not say: "If you do that, it will be an abomination," but rather that even though it existed from of old, it was an abomination and a foul act: "Indeed, it was an abomination and hateful and an evil way." It would not have been consistent with human nature for this matter to be in that form, but when people's nature became corrupt, they resorted to a man marrying his father's wife. Therefore, if you examine ancient history, you will find that every man who married his father's wife was called among them a "nikah al-maqt" (marriage of hatred), and the child born from it they called "al-maqtā," that is, the detested one.

So His saying "Indeed, it was" means: before I, Myself, issued this ruling, "it was an abomination and hateful and an evil way." God clarifies: I legislate for you what human nature requires. Human nature may be obscured in some matters, and may not be obscured in others, because some matters are glaring and evident, and their prohibition is established by human nature.

An example of that: a man who married his mother, or his daughter, or his sister. Thus there are things which, even in the Jahiliyya, no one dared to commit. So He brought a ruling that prohibits what the Jahiliyya had dared and transgressed, and in which human nature had been overstepped. So He said: "And do not marry those women whom your fathers married, except what has already occurred," that is, what has passed.

The Almighty described the marrying of sons to their fathers' wives as "was an abomination," that is, ugliness; and "hateful," that is, detestable; and "an evil way," that is, in the building of the family.

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, began to explain to us the forbidden (relations), even though the Jahiliyyah (Pre-Islamic period of ignorance) had agreed upon them. However, when Allah legislates a ruling that the Jahiliyyah was following, He does not legislate it because the Jahiliyyah did it. No, He legislates it because the natural disposition (fitrah) requires it. The fact that the Jahiliyyah did not do it is proof that it is a fitrah which the Jahiliyyah could not change. So the Truth, glory be to Him, said:

﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brothers' daughters, your sisters' daughters, your mothers who have nursed you, your milk-sisters, your wives' mothers, your stepdaughters under your guardianship, born of your wives with whom you have consummated marriage—but if you have not consummated marriage with them, there is no blame upon you—and the wives of your sons who are from your loins, and that you join two sisters in marriage, except what has already occurred. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [4:23].

Who makes lawful and unlawful? It is Allah. Despite their jahiliyyah and their heedlessness of religion, they forbade marriage with close relatives (mahārim). Even one who has not adopted the religion of Islam has prohibitions that he does not approach. That is, they forbade the mother, the daughter, the sister, and so on. From where did these come to them? The Truth clarifies:

﴿And there was no nation but that a warner had passed among them﴾ [35:24].

The method of the heavens was sent down by Allah from ancient times, as evidenced by His saying:

﴿He said, "Go down from it, all of you, as enemies to one another. But when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor be distressed"﴾ [20:123].

So as soon as Allah created Adam and created his wife, and sent down the method for them, this method was complete in its pillars. Therefore, the persistence of the things which Islam came and found in the ruling that Islam wants arose from the residues of earlier religions, even though they took the place of custom and the place of fitrah. That is, people had become accustomed to them and were naturally disposed to them, and it did not occur to them that Allah had legislated them in earlier religions.

Modern sciences have helped us in understanding many of Allah's rulings, because they found that every reproduction, whether in plants, animals, or humans as well, when the two sexes (male and female) are distant from each other, the offspring comes out strong in its characteristics. But if the husband and wife, or the male and female, of any kind—in plants, in animals, in humans—are close relatives in blood and sexual connection, the offspring arises weak. That is why they say in agriculture and animal breeding: "nuhajjin" (crossbreeding), meaning we bring the female a male from far away. And the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, says to us:

("Marry outside your kin and do not become weak.") And he said: "Do not marry close relatives, for the child will be born weak" (1).

So the Messenger commands us, when we want to marry, not to take relatives, but to keep away, because if we take relatives, the offspring will come out feeble. Through observation it was found that families which made it their custom in life to marry only from among themselves, after a period, develop mental weakness, or sexual weakness, or immune weakness. So the saying of the Messenger of Allah: "Marry outside, do not become weak," means: if you want to marry, do not take from relatives, because if you take from relatives you will become emaciated. "Dawa" means "to become emaciated," so if you wish not to become weak, that is, not to become emaciated, then keep away. Before the Prophet said this statement, this had been found through observation in the Jahiliyyah environment. That is why the Jahiliyyah poet says:

I advise whoever is far in concern
Against marrying the sons of paternal uncles' daughters.
For whoever is weakened by illness and affliction does not escape,
For the offspring of close relatives may become weak.

In our popular neighborhoods, when they praise someone they say: "fatwah," meaning a youth not born of a close paternal cousin. In plants they say: if you plant maize in the Gharbiyya governorate, you must bring the seeds from the Sharqiyya governorate, for example, and likewise with the Chilean watermelon. They bring its seeds from America, and they plant them, and the watermelon comes out beautiful and delicious. Some people may refuse to buy such seeds because of their high price, so they take from the seeds of what they planted and make it into seed stock, and the yield comes out weak. But if he keeps bringing it from outside, even if the price of the kilo reaches a large sum, he obtains a good crop.

Likewise in animals, and likewise in us. That is why the Arab used to say: "Ma dakka ru'ūs al-abṭāl ka-ibn al-a'jamiyyah" (Nothing has battered the heads of heroes like the son of a non-Arab woman), because he came from another stock. That is, this heroic man took the complete characteristics from another stock. So the crossing of complete characteristics with complete characteristics gives more complete characteristics. Therefore, the Truth's prohibition, glory be to Him, of marrying one's mother, sister, and all mahārim, although it is a moral matter, is also an organic matter. "Forbidden to you are your mothers and your daughters"—why? Because this relation is a relation of origin, and the other relation is a relation of branch: mothers are the relation of origin, and daughters are the relation of branch. "And your sisters," which is the relation of a brother to his sister, that is, a sonship from one father. "And your paternal aunts, and your maternal aunts, and your brothers' daughters, and your sisters' daughters, and your mothers who have nursed you, and your milk-sisters."

Thus the matter is interwoven in close kinship. Allah desires strength of offspring and strength of procreation, and He desires another matter: that the marital relationship is always exposed to psychological changes. A man marries a woman, and afterward psychological changes come and disagreement arises between them, as we have said regarding His saying, "And if you desire to replace one wife with another" [4:20]; and he dislikes such-and-such from her. So how would the relationship be between a mother and her son if something of this kind happened? It is supposed that she has a bond that obliges him to remain faithful to her, and likewise regarding a daughter, a sister, a paternal aunt, or a maternal aunt. So the Truth commands the man: keep this matter far from the realm of discord.

And it is from good sense and far-sightedness that we do not enter exchange marriages (muqābalāt) in marriage, or what is called "badal marriage," where two men exchange marriages, each marrying the other's sister, for example. If a dispute occurs in one of them, it necessarily occurs in its counterpart, even if harmony prevails. The good discernment tells you: beware of marrying your sister to a man because you will take his sister, for a wife may agree with her husband, but his sister may not be compatible with her husband who is the brother of the other. Imagine what a mother's feeling would be when she sees the stranger comfortable with her son while her daughter suffers and does not find comfort in her husband's house. What would the situation be? We would have widened the circle of discord and hypocrisy among those in whom there should be no discord or hypocrisy.

The divine wisdom is not in one matter only; rather, divine wisdom is comprehensive, encompassing all these matters. "Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, and your sisters"—the forbidden ones here are, by necessity, the mothers, however high they go; the prohibition includes the grandmother, whether a grandmother from the father's side or from the mother's side, and whatever arises from them. And every woman who is a man's wife, her mother is forbidden to him. "And your daughters" includes the daughters of the son and all that arises from them, and likewise the daughters of the daughter. "And your sisters, and your paternal aunts, and your maternal aunts, and your brothers' daughters, and your sisters' daughters, and your mothers who have nursed you."

Why does the Truth forbid "your mothers who have nursed you"? Because through nursing she contributed to forming cells in the one who was nursed. So there is a part of her in him, and this part has the sanctity of motherhood. That is why the scholars said: it is forbidden for a man to marry a woman with whom he shares a milk-relation in which it is probable that cells are formed. Some permitted marriage with a woman from whom a man suckled one or two sips, for example. But Abu Hanifa held the prohibition of any woman from whom a man suckled. The verifying scholars gave the fatwa and said: a woman is not forbidden unless she has nursed the man, or the man has nursed with her five full feedings, or he nurses from the woman for a day and a night and is satisfied with it, and that this occurs within the period of nursing. And that period, by the text of the Qur'an, is two years: "And mothers nurse their children for two complete years" [2:233].

This matter was discussed between our master Imam Ali, may Allah be pleased with him and ennoble his face, and our master Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, when they brought a woman who had given birth after six months, whereas the common pregnancy lasts nine months, and sometimes, rarely, a child is born after seven months; but for a woman to give birth after six months is an unexpected matter. Therefore Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, wanted to enforce the punishment upon her, because since she gave birth after six months she must be guilty. But our master Ali, may Allah be pleased with him and ennoble his face, grasped the matter.

He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, why do you enforce the punishment upon her?" Uthman ibn Affan said: "Because she gave birth after six months, and this does not happen." Allah opened His bounties upon our master Ali and caused the texts to flow over his imagination at the moment of the fatwa, and this is the opening (fath): the text may exist in the Qur'an, but the soul does not notice it, and the matter may not come from a single text but from the combination of two or more texts. Who comes to mind at the moment of the fatwa, sweeping through the Book of Allah and bringing the text that helps and assists him in the fatwa? It is Imam Ali. He said to our master Uthman: "Allah says otherwise." He said: "And what did Allah say about this?" He said:

﴿And mothers nurse their children two complete years, for whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾ [2:233].

So the completion of nursing is in two complete years, that is, in twenty-four months, and dates are reckoned by the Arabic calendar. And the Truth, glory be to Him, also said:

﴿And his gestation and weaning are thirty months﴾ [46:15].

So if the total of the months of pregnancy and nursing is thirty months, and complete nursing is twenty-four months, then the duration of pregnancy equals six months.

Thus did our master Imam Ali, may Allah be pleased with him and ennoble his face, derive the ruling. A person may know one verse while other verses escape him, and Allah has not restricted the goodness of fatwa to a specific time to the exclusion of other times; rather, the bounties of Allah are for all times. One may say: there is no one among the Muslims who reaches by his deeds the rank of the Companions. Whoever says that forgets what the Truth said in Surat al-Waqi'ah:

﴿And the forerunners, the forerunners—those are the near ones, in the Gardens of Pleasure: a multitude of the former peoples and a few of the later peoples﴾ [56:10–14].

That is, the later generations too will not be deprived of having among them those who are near and able to comprehend the texts to derive rulings. So regarding nursing: one or two sips—this is one opinion; ten feedings—another opinion; five full feedings—a third opinion. The majority of jurists adopted the middle position, which is five full feedings making marriage forbidden, but on condition that it be within the nursing period. So if he nursed outside the nursing period, we say: he has become independent of it by eating, and food has become what gives him the strengthening of his constitution.

Thus the matter of nursing is multi-branched, because the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "What is forbidden by blood is forbidden by nursing" (2).

And what is forbidden by nursing is: the mother by nursing, the daughter by nursing, the sister by nursing, the paternal aunt by nursing, the maternal aunt by nursing, and so on. Thus we see that it is a multi-branched process requiring every family to be vigilant, because when we see that the blessing of Allah does not hover over many homes, we must recognize its causes, the causes of distance from receiving Allah's blessing. The divine transmission is continuous, and we want sensitive receiving devices that receive well. If the receiving devices are broken and the transmission is continuous, no one will benefit from the transmission. Suppose the broadcasting station is broadcasting, but the radio is broken: how would the transmission reach people?

Thus the bounties of Allah and His descending blessings are always present. But there are people who do not take these blessings because their receiving devices are not sound. The first device for receiving blessing is that the home is built on lawfulness in everything. That is, the meeting of husband and wife is on lawful grounds, and many people enter into prohibition even without intending it, and this arises from frivolity, mixing, and disorder in the matter of nursing. People nurse their children in this way without restraint, and the ruling is not in their minds. Afterward we say to them: O people, you have taken precautions for your children in what leads to the soundness of their bodies, so that each child has a file containing: the birth certificate, and the appointed time for receiving vaccinations against diphtheria, polio, and other things.

So why, O family of Islam...

And the Truth (exalted is He) says after that: "And [forbidden to you are] all married women, except those whom your right hands possess. [This is] the decree of Allah upon you. And lawful for you is what is beyond that, provided you seek [them] with your wealth, desiring chastity, not unlawful intercourse. So for whatever you enjoy of them, give them their due compensation as an obligation. And there is no blame upon you for what you mutually agree to beyond the obligation. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise." [4:24]

The saying of the Truth: "And all married women" is a statement conjoined to what came in the previous verse regarding the forbidden women; that is, to the previously mentioned forbidden women will be added "the married women among the women." And who are "the married women among the women"? The原 root principle of derivation is that there is usually a common meaning. So this word is derived from "al-hisn" (fortress), which is a place where a people fortify themselves against their enemy; when they are fortified in it, they are protected from their enemy. But if they are not fortified, they are exposed to their enemy raiding them and seizing them. This is the origin of "hisn." And the derivations taken from it are many. Among them is what the Exalted says:

"And Mary, daughter of 'Imran, who guarded her chastity" (part of verse 12, Surat al-Tahrim).

"Ahsanat farjaha" means that she preserved herself and prevented anyone from approaching her. Here, the saying "al-muhsanat" in the verse we are contemplating refers to married women. For as long as a woman is married, her private part is occupied with another, so no one may take it, and she refrains from any new intrusion upon her contract with her husband. This is the meaning of "al-muhsanat min al-nisa'," so "al-muhsanat" here are the chaste ones through marriage. The Truth says:

"And when they are married, if they commit immorality, upon them is half the punishment for free [married] women" (part of verse 25, Surat al-Nisa').

Since slave women are also made chaste by marriage, are they among the "muhsanat" like the free women? No, these are other than those; they are not included among the free "muhsanat," for if they were included among the "muhsanat," the ruling would be one. He, glorified is He, says: "And when they are married, if they commit immorality, upon them is half the punishment for free women," and the origin of "ihsan," which is chastity, is ascribed to the free woman, because a free woman is usually not approached by anyone. This is the wife of Abu Sufyan at the pledge of allegiance of the women; she said: "Does a free woman commit zina?" Zina was specific to slave women, because they are the degraded ones; they have no father, mother, or honor, so any person may dare against them, and they have no strength or family. Therefore their punishment came as half the punishment of the free woman, because around a slave woman there are people who may be tempted to commit immorality.

So "ihsan" is used to mean chastity, and "ihsan" is used to mean being free, and "ihsan" is used to mean being married, and "muhsanat" is applied to free women. The general state of the free woman is what gives her a family, and no one dares against her. But suppose a married woman, then a dispute or war occurred between her people and the believers, and she became a captive of the Muslims, though she was married according to their custom in her land. By captivity she has passed out of that marriage and has come into the Islamic environment and become a slave. Her enslavement and captivity removed her ihsan, so He said: "except those whom your right hands possess." Thus by ownership of the right hand her ihsan is removed, and it is permissible for the Muslim to marry her or enjoy her if she enters his ownership, even if she was married, because there is a difference of the two abodes: she is in the abode of Islam, having come out of the abode of war, and so she has become a possession of the right hand. This is not done except after her istibra' (waiting period to ensure her womb is free of a child she may have brought from her people), in accordance with the Prophet's saying (ﷺ) concerning the captives of Awtas: "A pregnant woman is not to be had until she gives birth, nor a non-pregnant one until she menstruates." This is an honoring of her, because when she was separated from her husband and became a slave by ownership of the right hand, the Truth did not wish to deprive her, but made her enjoy her master and live under his protection, so that she would not be deprived of emotional and physical companionship, rather than her master wallowing in people's honor.

"And all married women, except those whom your right hands possess, the decree of Allah upon you." "Kitab Allah" means: Allah decreed that as a decree upon you, a registered and documented matter; and just as it is a decree upon you, it is also for you. The Truth says: "And lawful for you is what is beyond that." So the forbidden ones are: those forbidden by lineage, those forbidden by nursing, and those forbidden by marital chastity.

"And lawful for you is what is beyond that" means: it is lawful for you to marry them. Therefore He said: "And lawful for you is what is beyond that, that you seek" meaning you seek "with your wealth, desiring chastity." And we know wealth is the fruit of effort. Effort requires exertion and hardship, and every person loves the fruit of his labor, and may defend it even to death for his wealth, because wealth only comes as the fruit of diligence. Even if wealth comes by inheritance, the one who bequeathed it to you only left it to you as the result of toil and labor. We know that one who labors for a period equal to ten years may be given by God what suffices him to live comfortably afterward; one who labors twenty years may be given what suffices for his child to live comfortably; one who labors thirty years, his grandchild lives comfortably.

So all the inherited wealth you see was the result of diligence, struggle, and hardship by the fathers. When the Truth says "that you seek with your wealth," it shows that the consideration for the womb comes from the man. "And that you seek with your wealth," about which our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), said: "O young men, whoever among you is able to marry, let him marry, for it lowers the gaze and guards the private part; and whoever is not able, let him fast, for it is a shield for him."(1)

And since wealth is precious to a person, and it is taken through movement, through diligence, and through sweat, it must benefit him only in what returns to him with immediate good, without forgetting the deferred good. If he achieves an immediate good with it but then becomes heedless of a deferred evil, he has not placed his wealth in its proper place. "That you seek with your wealth, desiring chastity": "muhsinin" has, as we have known, several meanings. "Muhsinin" means abstaining from committing wrongs and falling into people's honor. "With your wealth": that is, place your wealth, which you earned with toil, in what returns to you with immediate and deferred good, and do not waste it on people's honor. For it is possible for a person to seek the company of a woman with his wealth while not being chaste, and we say to him: you achieved a pleasure and immediate benefit, but you were distracted from a deferred evil. Our Lord says of it: "desiring chastity, not unlawful intercourse," and from this the word "sifah" (fornication) is taken.

So beware of paying your wealth in order to take a woman to satisfy a want. The word "muhsinin" means committing to chastity, and the Truth explained "muhsinin" by its counterpart: "musafihin," from "safh," which is pouring; pouring is a heavy falling and descent of water. Water may descend drop by drop, but "safh" is pouring. That is why the slope of a mountain is named "safh," because water descends from the whole mountain poured out.

Here it is noted that when the Truth speaks of men He says "muhsinin" with a kasra on the ṣād, and when He speaks of women He says "muhsanat" with a fatha. He did not say "muhsinat" with a kasra, because the custom is that the masculine is always the seeker of the feminine, and the feminine is always sought.

"Not unlawful intercourse. So for whatever you enjoy of them, give them their due compensation." "Istimta'" is the attainment of enjoyment for the soul, and enjoyment exists first in the betrothal: when a man proposes to a woman, this is enjoyment; then when he contracts marriage to her, and when she is brought to him in procession, all these are long preliminaries to enjoyment. But enjoyment is not the only aim. It tells you: if you enjoy them, you must give them their dowers. Therefore, if a man marries a woman and then divorces her before consummation, we tell him: pay half the dowry, because you took half the enjoyment. If enjoyment were only the sexual act, he would have taken nothing and thus owes nothing of the dowry. But we say that enjoyment consists in his approaching the daughter of so-and-so, proposing, and contracting; all these are enjoyments, and when these occur he has enjoyed to some extent.

The Truth, glorified and exalted, wants us to build family life on purity and on security of the soul. You find that a man, when he is among his family, feels no discomfort in closing the door on her; but imagine his presence with a woman without marriage: the psychic faculties struggle within him, he lies in wait, and we can observe his trembling at any sound, because his faculties are not harmonious; he will satisfy only one faculty. The remaining psychic faculties are terrified, which shows that what he does is not natural, and since it is not natural, the psychic faculties oppose it. The Truth wants the family built on purity and security, and this psychological security gives every faculty of the soul enjoyment.

We said earlier that if a person has a daughter and sees a young man passing often by the girl and looking often at the balcony, and then the father's gaze falls upon him, what is his reaction? All his limbs are agitated. But when the young man or his father comes, knocks on the door, and says: "O so-and-so, I want to propose to your daughter for myself," or "I want your daughter for my son," what is the reaction of the girl's father? Joy and relief, the faculties become content and the soul is at peace, and an announcement of happiness is made, and he calls people and holds a celebration; for the One who created the spouses, male and female, when He legislated their union, placed in the human soul and its particles contentment with this ruling of union.

Therefore it is narrated: "The lawful cut off the nose of jealousy."

That is, the one who is jealous over his daughter is the one who issues invitations for her marriage; as if jealousy has a zeal in it. If a proposal of honor comes from other than the way of the Creator of honors, the soul is necessarily agitated; if it comes in accordance with what the Creator of honors legislated, the soul is at rest. This is a process that may be difficult to imagine: what causes contentment, and who places zeal, anger, and fury in the heart? It is He, glorified is He, who does that.

A human must consider that each of us is composed of multiple faculties. The marriage contract, the words "marry me" and "I have married you," and the presence of witnesses — what does it do in the particles of the soul's composition so that it is delighted? It is the will of the Truth. This is a known matter: when you have a person you know only, and the flowing affection between you and him is still at its beginning, it suffices when you meet him to exchange greetings and the matter ends; but there is another person for whom the friendly flow between you is not enough, rather you must shake his hand, because there is attraction and affection, and each of them has an influence.

So the process of affection and loyalty is something that produces a chemical change in the soul, and repulsion arises if the meeting comes by way of what God forbade, while what comes by way of what God legislated produces attraction. When the poet addressed the one he loved, he said:

"My father, the one I loved, we parted,
and then God decreed our reunion.
I wished him, and when we met,
his greeting was [like] a farewell."

It is as if the poet wants to prolong the duration of the greeting and the distance, so as to nourish the affection he has, and as if he wants to say: I met with the one I love, and he vanished into what I vanished into; and this arises from the blending.

So the emotional formation or flowing affection is created by God as a flow of meeting. This applies when it is in accordance with God's law; in the other case it is a flow of hatred. What causes that? It is a gift from God, who is the creator of man and the creator of woman. When the meeting comes in accordance with what God legislated, do not rule out that the Creator adjusts the particles; when blending happens, fidelity necessarily comes as a natural result, and likewise loyalty, and this harmony is achieved — that is affirmation; but if the meeting is by other than God's way, there is no harmony in it, and that is negation.

So the Truth, glorified and exalted, builds the family on this meaning. And you know that meetings that occur outside God's way occur in secret and their fruit is denied; if an offspring and a child result from them, the infant will be thrown in the street as a foundling, and they may kill him; but the fruit that comes by lawful means, everyone rejoices in it.

So the Truth, glorified and exalted, says: "And lawful for you is what is beyond that, that you seek with your wealth, desiring chastity, not unlawful intercourse. So for whatever you enjoy of them, give them their due compensation." Enjoyment has many aspects, and the Shi'ah came with His saying: "So for whatever you enjoy of them, give them their due compensation," and they said: this is temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'ah), on the evidence that
