The Istita'ah (capacity) means that a thing comes under my control, so that it does not disobey me or refuse me. Suppose I grip a piece of iron and bend it: the piece of iron has then come under my control. An example is the two sons of Adam, when each of them offered a sacrifice to God, and it was accepted from one of them but not from the other. The one whose sacrifice was not accepted said:

﴿Surely I will kill you﴾ (Surah al-Ma'idah, 5:27).

What was the response of the one who received the threat? He said:

﴿If you stretch your hand toward me to kill me, I shall not stretch my hand toward you to kill you. Indeed, I fear God, the Lord of the worlds. Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin, and so be among the companions of the Fire. That is the recompense of the wrongdoers.﴾ Then ﴿his soul made the killing of his brother seem easy to him, so he killed him, and became among the losers﴾ (Surah al-Ma'idah, 5:28–30).

What is the meaning of "tawwa'at lahu" (made easy for him)? Ta'wi'a means: made it within his capacity. When we consider "fa-tawwa'at lahu nafsuhu" (his soul made it easy for him), we find that the "hu" (him) refers to him, and this shows that a human being has several faculties: a faculty that says, "Kill him," and another faculty that says to him, "Do not kill him." His conscience says to him, "Do not do it," while the soul that commands evil says, "Kill," and he is left hesitating between the two.

God's saying, ﴿fa-tawwa'at lahu﴾ (so it made it easy for him), is evidence that his soul was resistant to him. But the soul that commands evil kept pressing him relentlessly, until his acting soul made the killing of his brother seem easy to him. Although his soul had made the killing of his brother easy for him, he afterwards became one of the regretful. After he had satisfied his desire by killing, he felt remorse, and this remorse comes on his tongue:

﴿O woe is me! Am I unable to be like this raven, and conceal my brother's corpse? Then I would be among the regretful﴾ (Surah al-Ma'idah, 5:31).

You are the one who killed him, yet you became among the regretful. Why? Because the faculties of goodness always lift up good deeds and nullify evil deeds. A human being may begin as evil, even if his faculties are predominantly good; he then descends from that high evil and lessens it. But if the faculties of evil are predominant, he begins with a little evil and then raises it up. He says to himself: "So-and-so did such-and-such to me, and I want to slap him," and afterwards he may raise his evil further and say: "Or I will strike him a blow." But when a person is good, he says: "So-and-so plotted against me. I want to shoot him, or hit him twice, or rebuke him." He descends from evil and ascends from good. As in the story of our master Joseph and his brothers, when they said:

﴿When they said, "Joseph and his brother are dearer to our father than we are, though we are a strong group. Indeed, our father is in clear error." "Kill Joseph or cast him out to some land, so that your father's face will be turned toward you, and after that you will be a righteous people." A speaker among them said, "Do not kill Joseph, but throw him into the depths of the well, and some of the travellers will pick him up, if you are going to act."﴾ (Surah Yusuf, 12:8–10).

They were the tribes, the sons of the Prophet Ya'qub (Jacob). They diminished the evil and immediately lessened it, saying ﴿or cast him out to some land﴾, meaning, throw him into a distant land. So in one step they lessened the killing. How did this transition from killing to "cast him out to some land" take place? Then they lessened the matter a second time, so that no beast would devour him or he would not get lost, and they said: ﴿and throw him into the depths of the well, and some of the travellers will pick him up﴾.

So His saying ﴿whoever among you is not able﴾ means whoever is not able to bring a thing under his control, or to reach it with his hands. This is what is meant by "tawl" (means, ability). "Fulan tawwalat yadahu" (his hand reached it) means he became able to do it. "Fulan tatawwal 'alayya" means so-and-so showed me favour with something. "Fulan tatawwal 'alayya" also means so-and-so presumed to act against me without right. All of these come from "tawl." And "tawlan" means a capacity by which you can marry the one you love. That is, you do not possess wealth and you are not able to afford the bridal gift. Then there is another stage: do not take a free woman, because her dowry is usually high. Instead, take from the captive slave-girls, because their maintenance and expenses are light, and they have no clan or family to dispute with you over the dowry. So He said:

﴿Whoever among you is not able to afford to marry free believing women, then let him marry from those whom your right hands possess of your believing young women.﴾

What we perceive in the verse is that marrying those whom the right hand possesses is for someone other than their owner, because their owner has no need of that; he enjoys them and has intercourse with them, because they are the possession of his right hand, and not owned by another.

So God has permitted the Muslim to marry from among those whom another's right hand possesses, on the condition that this be with the permission of her master, because by marriage she takes a portion of her time and service away from the one who owns her. So he must seek permission, so that the matter of her being devoted to her husband, in some of his services, is known to her guardians. And He also commanded us not to belittle them because they are owned and humiliated, so that we do not withhold their dowry. Rather, it is obligatory to give these women their dowries in a fitting manner, that is, according to what is customary, because that is the compensation for intimacy. If God has commanded us to seek the permission of their masters and commanded us to give them their wages, here there is some difficulty, because the slave-woman does not own anything, since the slave and whatever his hands possess belong to his master.

We say to him: Yes, but if you say, "the slave and whatever his hands possess belong to his master," then you must first establish ownership for her, and then what she owns will belong to her master. If you overstep this and give the money to her master, then in this case no dowry has been established for her. So your saying "the slave and whatever his hands possess" means: give her a period and an opportunity to become an owner, by giving her the wage, as an honour to her. As for her property belonging to her master, that is a different matter. After that, you may go and marry her, and that is permissible. So do we understand from this that if you are able to afford it, you may not marry slave-girls? No. Does this diminish the status of slave-girls? No. Why? Consider the lofty wisdoms that none but the Lord would state.

God wants to clear away the matter of slavery. When someone comes and marries a slave-woman owned by another, her children follow her in servitude. Children in religion follow the better of the two parents, but in freedom and servitude children follow the mother. So if a man marries a slave-woman owned by someone else, the children who will come from her will be slaves. And when he leaves her to her master and marries another from among free women, the child he has from her master's household will be free. So He wants to clear away slavery. This is one point. The other point is that marriage is the coming together of a male and a female to become the nucleus of a family. If the husband and wife are equals, the husband does not find in himself any arrogance toward the wife, and the wife does not find in herself any arrogance toward the husband, because each of them is a match for the other. This guarantees the balance of life and the balance of dealing. But when a man marries a slave-woman who has no family, he may consider her weak and may look down on her; he may humiliate her, and taunt her. And when she has children, he may say to them: "You have no maternal uncle," for example. The Lawgiver wants to build a balanced family life, and for this reason He required compatibility, and said:

﴿Wicked women are for wicked men, and wicked men are for wicked women; and good women are for good men, and good men are for good women﴾ (Surah al-Nur, 24:26).

Some people understand, when they see a good woman, that a good man must marry her. We say to them: This is a legislation, and legislation is a responsibility, subject to being obeyed or disobeyed. So when He legislates that good women are for good men and wicked women for wicked men, if you apply the legislation, then matters will be upright. This answers those who say: since our Lord says "Good women are for good men," how can so-and-so marry such-and-such when one of them is good and the other wicked? We say: This ruling is not about a cosmic event that has occurred; rather, it is a legislative matter that requires us to follow it, and to make good men for good women and wicked men for wicked women, so that balance may be achieved. If a wicked man says to her, "You are such-and-such," she should say to him, "You are such-and-such," so that she does not say to him what he has said about her. As for the good man, he softens his side once, and she, being good, softens her side at another time.

﴿Whoever among you is not able to afford to marry free believing women﴾. The word "muhsanat" (chaste, free women) here means free women, because if she were married she would not be a candidate for another's marriage. ﴿then let him marry from those whom your right hands possess of your believing young women﴾. The word "fata" (young man) we use of a free man who has youth and vigour, and we use the word "fatah" (young woman) of any slave-woman even if she is old. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) taught us not to say, "This is my slave, and this is my slave-woman," but rather to say, "My young man" and "My young woman."

﴿from those whom your right hands possess﴾. Some people ask: Does a man marry someone whom he owns? We say to him: No. She is lawful to him, she is his possession by right of ownership, and he can have a child by her. So it means "from those whom the right hands of others possess," because God addresses the believers as one structure. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The believer to the believer is like a building, each part strengthening the others." (1)

And the Truth says:

﴿Do not defame one another﴾ (Surah al-Hujurat, 49:11).

And He says in another place:

﴿When you enter houses, greet one another, a greeting from God﴾ (Surah al-Nur, 24:61).

Does a believer greet himself, or greet those who have entered upon them?

God wants, through legislation, to make the believers like one body. So He also said:

﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ (Surah al-Nisa', 4:29).

That is, do not kill one another. The meaning is that the bond of faith must make us united in one solid unity.

﴿from those whom your right hands possess of your believing young women, and God knows best your faith﴾. You might say that the faith of those owned by right hand is weak, and make it a reason. The Truth says to you: No. ﴿God knows best your faith﴾. Perhaps a slave-woman may be better in faith than you, because this is a matter of the inner depths of hearts, and it is enough for you to know the outward.

God, glorified and exalted be He, when He treats a matter, treats it as a Lord treats it. He knows the reality of what He created and gives every creature what it requires. First He made clear: if you are not able, for lack of means, to marry free women, then marry slave-girls. This is for the sake of further clearing away slavery.

After that He says: ﴿God knows best your faith, one from another﴾. So if you are going to marry, you must keep before your eyes this matter: that ﴿you are one from another﴾, that is, you are all from Adam. And since you have believed, faith has made you equal, so when you go to marry you must place this before your eyes. He, glorified be He, treats a reality.

And He says after that: ﴿So marry them with the permission of their people﴾. This indicates that whoever has a girl under his hand by right of ownership must treat her as a family member, to compensate her for what she has lost among her people there, so that she feels she is under the protection of Islam, just as she was under the protection of her family and fathers, or even more.

So the one who owns must make himself one of the family. In this way, the Truth, glorified and exalted be He, increases the doors to clearing away slavery. And He made clear: if none of you brings the one he owns into these purifying channels, then he will keep her in bondage. Therefore he must feed her from what he eats, clothe her from what he wears, and not burden her with what she cannot bear. If he burdens her with what she cannot bear, he must help her with his own hand. When there is someone with you whom you clothe from your clothing and feed from your food, and when she does a task that is hard for her, you help her; what kind of treatment is this? It is the treatment of family.

See how many matters the Truth treats: He treats the one seeking marriage, He treats the slave-woman, and He treats the masters. It is the legislation of the Lord of all. He does not legislate for one at the expense of another. And since she is owned by the right hand and has a master, this master has interests, and you must seek his permission, for he may not be able to do without her, since she serves him. So He said: ﴿with the permission of their people﴾. But regarding dowries He said: ﴿So marry them with the permission of their people and give them their wages in a fitting manner﴾. So the slave-woman is married with the permission of the one who owns her, so that he knows that someone has entered as a partner in the transaction and takes the intimacy, namely the husband. When the master gives permission and arranges her marriage, he knows that she no longer belongs to him, and thus no one will take her from behind his back. By seeking permission and arranging the marriage, he prepares himself for the fact that intimacy has been closed off to him, and he retains ownership of her person. As for ownership of the intimacy, it belongs to the husband.

﴿And give them their wages in a fitting manner﴾. So beware of saying...

(1) Reported by al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i from Abu Musa.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 26:

﴿Allah desires to make clear to you, and to guide you to the ways of those before you, and to turn to you in forgiveness. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

What does He make clear to us? He, glorified is He, makes clear the laws that govern the ordering of life. We have said that there can be no criminalization except by a text, and there is no punishment except after criminalization. So before He punishes you for a matter, He tells you: this is a crime, and He states it explicitly. He does not come to you saying: you did such-and-such a thing and this is its punishment, because you might say to Him: I did this act before and I did not know it was a crime carrying a punishment. Therefore one cannot be punished unless he has committed a crime, and one cannot be made to be a crime except by a text. So Allah desires to give you insight, through clarification, into what sets the movement of your life right, and Allah is more trustworthy for you than your own selves, because He is the One who created, and He knows whom He created.

He alone legislates what is suitable for His creation. As for you creating and you legislating, that is transgression; for He, glorified is He, legislates for what He knows, and to Allah belongs the highest likeness. We have said before: the engineer who manufactures the television is the one who sets for it the maintenance regulation, because he is the one who designed the machine, and he is the most worthy of laying down its maintenance rules, so he informs us: this key is for such-and-such, this one is for the picture, and this one is for the sound.

The One who created the human being is the One who sets the regulation of his upkeep, embodied in "do" and "do not." He, glorified is He, has left matters on which no "do" or "do not" was revealed; these are left under permissibility (ibahah), so you may do them or not do them. He, glorified is He, says: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you and to guide you to the ways of those before you﴾. The sunnah (the way or established practice) is the governing law of the movement of life. And the Truth says:

﴿The way of Allah concerning those who passed away before, and you will never find any change in the way of Allah.﴾ (Surat al-Ahzab: 62)

The Messengers preceded the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). We know what happened to those who obeyed their messengers, and what happened to those who denied their messengers. The Truth has said concerning them:

﴿So each We seized for his sin: among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of stones, and among them were those seized by the Cry, and among them were those whom We caused the earth to swallow, and among them were those whom We drowned. And Allah was not one to wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ (Surat al-Ankabut: 40)

So Allah desires to make clear to us the sunan of those before us, that is, the methods by which they were governed, and what happened to the people of truth and what happened to the people of falsehood. Thus it is not a deaf legislation, but a legislation preceded by events that confirm and document it. ﴿And guide you to the ways of those before you and turn to you in forgiveness﴾, and He, glorified is He, makes clear, explains, and turns in forgiveness. ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾, because He is the Creator; ﴿All-Wise﴾, who places the command in its place and the prohibition in its place. Wisdom is: placing a thing in its proper place, and He places it with knowledge; knowledge requires the breadth of what is known, and wisdom is placing each known thing in its right position.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 27:

Then He, glorified is He, says:

﴿And Allah desires to accept your repentance, but those who follow their desires desire that you deviate into a great deviation.﴾

He, glorified is He, said in the preceding verse: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾, and then He says: ﴿and guide you﴾, and then: ﴿and accept your repentance﴾. In the verse we are now reflecting upon: ﴿And Allah desires to accept your repentance﴾. So why did He come first with ﴿and accept your repentance﴾, and here, secondly, with ﴿And Allah desires to accept your repentance﴾?

We say: repentance must first be legislated by Allah, for otherwise, could you repent to Allah from a sin if Allah had not legislated repentance for you? Would this repentance be valid? Thus He, glorified is He, first legislates repentance, and after that you repent in the light of what He has legislated, and He accepts the repentance. In this way we have three stages: first, the legislation of repentance by Allah, out of mercy toward us; then the servant's repentance; and after that Allah's acceptance of the repentance of whoever repents, out of His mercy, glorified is He. So the servant's repentance lies between two repentances from the Lord: a repentance of legislation and a repentance of acceptance.

﴿And Allah desires to accept your repentance﴾. Since He, glorified is He, has legislated repentance, would He legislate it and not accept it? No. Since He has legislated it and taught me to repent, this means He has opened for me the door of repentance, and the opening of the door of repentance is from the mercy of the All-Knowing, the All-Wise toward His creation. For when the Truth created man, He endowed him, unlike the rest of the creatures, with a capacity for active choices; that is, man is able to do this or to do that, and He made his faculties suitable for command and prohibition. The eye is fit to see a sign in Allah's creation and take a lesson from it, and the eye is also fit to stretch toward what is forbidden. The tongue is fit for slandering with it, and fit for mentioning Allah with it, saying: "There is no god but Allah", and all other kinds of remembrance. The hand's muscles are fit for raising it and striking with it, and fit for lifting up with it a stumbling person who has fallen on the road.

This is the meaning of choice in speech, in action and in the limbs. Choice is an absolute capacity which the will of the chooser directs. If you look at the hand, you will find that when you want to raise it, you know nothing of the muscles you use in order to raise the hand. What is it that raises the hand, and which muscles serve this raising? You see this, for example, in the mechanical man, or you see it in the crane that lifts heavy things. Look how many operations are needed to do that! You know nothing of this matter within yourself, yet as soon as you want to move your hand, you move it and it obeys you. When an engineer wants to move a robot, he directs it with specific calculations so that it does such and such; but a human moves the hand, the foot or the eye merely by willing.

When the Truth deprives a person of his capacity, God forbid, He afflicts him with paralysis. He wills, but the hand or anything else does not respond to him, and he does not know what has been disabled until he goes to the doctors to examine the nervous system and find out why his nerves did not carry out the commands. It is a long process. So when a person wants to move, he directs a power created by Allah alone; he has no real act. Therefore, if Allah rewards me and recompenses me for an obedience, that is because I directed the instrument suitable for action toward doing good. When you hear that no one has in his hand the ability to do anything, this is correct, because no one knows how to do anything at all; he merely wills. If he directs the power toward action, then this is your own deed. The meaning of choice, then, is that you are suitable for doing and for the opposite of doing, namely ceasing and abstaining.

When Allah, glorified and exalted is He, makes clear to you and sends down the method which tells you: direct your power to this and do not direct it to that, this means that your power is suitable for both. Thus you are created with the capacity to do and not to do. What the method has left without saying "do" or "do not do", if you do it in any manner that does not corrupt the universe or disrupt the movement of your life, then this is what is permissible for you.

When Allah, glorified is He, legislated repentance, He made clear that if a person who wills to do something is affected and directs his power toward doing something contrary, perhaps his appetite or his evil nature has overcome him, and in a moment of weakness he turns to an evil deed. That is why repentance was legislated. Why? Because if we were to expel this person from the enclosure of the obedient merely for committing a first evil deed, all his emotions thereafter would become evils, and this is what we call "lost". So the Truth legislates: if you commit a sin, do not despair, for We shall forgive you and accept your repentance.

So when Allah legislated repentance, He had mercy on society from the savagery of the first disobedient person; had this repentance not come, sins would multiply after the first sin. Over against the Truth's words ﴿And Allah desires to accept your repentance﴾ and His alerting you that He will purify you by repentance from the sins you committed before, over against that stand those who follow their desires and want you to bring new sins. Therefore Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿but those who follow their desires desire that you deviate﴾, and deviation is the absolute commission of sins. By it you turn away from the truth, for deviation is departure from a path laid out by a wise One, and the path is the straight way.

Who made this path? It is the Wise One. So if a person deviates once, our Lord sets him straight on the path a second time and says to him: "I have accepted your repentance." He, glorified is He, does this in order to protect the world from its evil. But those who follow their desires do not want you merely to deviate once; rather they want for you a deviation described as a great deviation. Why? Because man by nature, as we said earlier, if he is a liar, respects the truthful, and if he is a traitor, respects the trustworthy; the proof is that if he is a traitor and has something he fears for, he chooses a trustworthy person to place that thing with him.

Thus trustworthiness, truthfulness, fidelity and all these values are matters recognized by innate nature. When a person is found who has not been able to compel himself onto the path of values, and this person finds another who has been able to compel himself onto the path of values, he is struck by severe distress. What then heals him and relieves him? He cannot correct his conduct or rise from the crookedness of his soul; so he tries to make the person of upright conduct deviant like himself. If two people are bound by friendship and one of them deviates, the deviant one is humbled before himself by his deviation, and tries to pull his friend toward deviation so that he will not be humbled in front of him. He does not want him merely to be deviant like himself, but wants him to be more deviant, so that he himself may be distinguished above him. Thus values are recognized even among deviants. And remember well that in Surah Yusuf we read this wise saying:

﴿And there entered the prison with him two young men. One of them said, "Indeed, I see myself pressing wine," and the other said, "Indeed, I see myself carrying bread on my head, of which the birds eat. Inform us of its interpretation. Indeed, we see you as one of the doers of good."﴾ (Surah Yusuf, 36)

They were in prison with Yusuf, but each had a reason for their imprisonment: the cause of these who asked Yusuf is that they committed crimes, while the cause of Yusuf's presence in prison is that he was innocent. The innocent person has all his thought on Allah. As for those who deviated and entered prison with him, when they look at him they find him in a good state, as proven by the fact that a matter attracted them and occupied their minds when they saw a dream, so they went to one whom they knew to be a good man despite his being with them in prison; for they were impressed by him, as shown by their saying to him: ﴿Indeed, we see you as one of the doers of good.﴾ Whoever says ﴿Indeed, we see you as one of the doers of good﴾ must have the capacity to distinguish values; then they measured Yusuf's conduct against them and found it good, for otherwise how would they know? So values are known to them. Then, when a matter occupying their minds came, they went to Yusuf.

An example of this: there is a thief who never tires of stealing and does not stop, and then a matter comes to him requiring him to travel to an unsafe place, so the thief in this situation seeks a trustworthy person to spend the night with, and does not go to a thief like himself. Thus values are the same, and when the companions of Yusuf in prison said: "Indeed, we see you as one of the doers of good," Master Yusuf took advantage of this matter and found them trusting him, so he did not, at the start of their story, interpret the dream for them, but took advantage of their need for him and invited them to faith, saying:

﴿O my two companions of the prison, are separate lords better or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ (Surah Yusuf, 39)

He moved them from their story to his story. Since they wanted to exploit his goodness, why should he not exploit their need of him, advise them, and give them the good news of the religion of Allah? It is as though he were saying to them: "You came to me because you say I am one of the doers of good. But you have not seen all that I have; Allah has given me much of His overflowing bounty and grace." The Truth says, on the tongue of Yusuf:

﴿No food will come to you as provision but I will inform you of its interpretation before it reaches you.﴾ (part of verse 37, Surah Yusuf)

That is, Yusuf the Truthful has much knowledge, and acknowledges to them Allah's grace upon him: this knowledge is not from me:

﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me.﴾ (part of verse 37, Surah Yusuf)

Then he calls them to worship the One God, so that they may seek His help instead of the many gods they take as objects of worship, which neither harm nor benefit.

﴿Are separate lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ (part of verse 39, Surah Yusuf)

Thus values are one, and Allah desires to accept your repentance; but those who follow their desires want you to deviate into a great deviation, so that you will not be distinguished above them in a way that belittles them before themselves. They want you to be more deviant than them, because they want to be distinguished even in goodness too, and they say to themselves: "If we are evil, there are people more evil than us."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 4, verse 28:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿Allah wishes to lighten [the burden] for you, and man was created weak.﴾

Having said, ﴿Allah wishes to make [things] clear for you﴾ so that He may show you the way, and ﴿Allah wishes to turn to you [in forgiveness]﴾ so that He may forgive, He now says, ﴿Allah wishes to lighten [the burden] for you﴾ so that He may make things easy. These are three important matters. Our master Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "In Surat al-Nisa' there are eight verses for the Umma of Muhammad which are better than everything the sun rises upon and sets upon:

The first is the saying of the Truth:

﴿Allah wishes to make [things] clear for you, and to guide you to the ways of those before you, and to turn to you [in forgiveness]. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ (Surat al-Nisa', 26)

The second is the saying of the Truth:

﴿And Allah wishes to turn to you [in forgiveness], while those who follow their desires wish that you deviate into a tremendous deviation.﴾ (Surat al-Nisa', 27)

The third is the saying of the Truth:

﴿Allah wishes to lighten [the burden] for you, and man was created weak.﴾ (Surat al-Nisa', 28)

The fourth is the saying of the Truth:

﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will remit from you your misdeeds and admit you to a noble entrance.﴾ (Surat al-Nisa', 31)

The fifth is the saying of the Truth:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills. And whoever associates others with Allah has fabricated a tremendous sin.﴾ (Surat al-Nisa', 48)

The sixth is His, glory be to Him, saying:

﴿And whoever does wrong or wrongs himself and then seeks forgiveness of Allah will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (Surat al-Nisa', 110)

The seventh is the saying of the Most High:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong [anyone] an atom's weight; and if there is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward.﴾ (Surat al-Nisa', 40)

The eighth is the saying of the Most High:

﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe? And ever is Allah Appreciative and Knowing.﴾ (Surat al-Nisa', 147)

These are the eight verses which no other nation has been given the like of, except the Umma of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him." Among them is the saying of the Truth: ﴿Allah wishes to lighten [the burden] for you, and man was created weak.﴾

And what is the weakness of man? Weakness is that he is swayed by enticements and does not have the ability to keep in mind the reward for obedience or the recompense for disobedience, because the one whose soul opens toward a particular desire generally pushes aside the thought of punishment. For example, if a thief kept in mind that his hand would be cut off if he stole, he would hesitate to steal; but he estimates his own safety and says: "I will scheme and do such-and-such so that I can get away."

So the weakness of man lies in this: that Allah made him a chooser, drawn by immediate desires. But even if he gathers desires or ascends through desires, he will find no desire more deserving of concern than winning the pleasure of Allah and meeting Him in the Hereafter.

In the saying of the Truth, ﴿Allah wishes to lighten [the burden] for you, and man was created weak﴾, we observe that lightening is fitting to weakness. The weakness came from the fact that man became a chooser, especially in matters of obligation. The one in whom weakness was placed was made a chooser who does this or does that, and each matter has its enticements; the enticements of desires are present, while the enticements of obedience lie in the future. So he always prefers the present side over the future side.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 4, verse 29:

﴿O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly except that it be a trade by mutual consent. And do not kill yourselves. Indeed, Allah is ever Merciful to you.﴾

When the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, wishes to draw His creatures to believe in Him, He draws their attention to the cosmos, and to the phenomena that Allah has created, so that they may be certain that these phenomena could only have come into being from One who is All-Powerful, All-Knowing and All-Wise. When they arrive at faith in Him, they then receive the obligation that takes the form of "do such-and-such" and "do not do such-and-such." When He addresses them with obligation, He places before the command of obligation a preface: that you have bound yourself to enter into this obligation. Allah did not compel you to be someone under obligation; rather, you entered into faith in Allah by your own choice and willingness. Since you have entered into faith by your own choice and willingness, make your faith in Allah the ground (ḥaythiyya) of every ruling that Allah issues to you, "do such-and-such" and "do not do such-and-such." Do not say: "Why should I do such-and-such, O Lord, and why should I not do such-and-such, O Lord?" Rather, it is sufficient for you to say: the One in whom I have believed as God, All-Wise and All-Powerful, He, glorified is He, is trustworthy in commanding me and forbidding me. For this reason the Truth always precedes the verses of obligation with His words, glorified is He: ﴿O you who have believed﴾. He did not impose obligation on people in general; rather, He imposed it on those who believed in Him.

So when He imposes obligation on one who believed in Him, He has not been unjust or oppressive toward him, because he believed by his own free choice.

If you draw a person's attention, admonish him, and command him with a command of obligation, such as "pray," or "refrain from evil," and he says to you: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾, here you must say to him: you have not understood the meaning of the Truth's words: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾. The essence of religiosity and faith in Allah is that no one compels you to it; rather, enter into faith in Allah by your own choice. But once you have entered into faith in Allah, then commit yourself to hearing from Allah in "do" and "do not do." When the Truth says: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, He is giving us the grounds of the obligation, that is, the reason for the ruling. The reason for the ruling is that you have believed in Allah as a God who is All-Wise and All-Powerful.

Since you have believed in Allah as a God who is All-Wise and All-Powerful, hand over the reins of commands and prohibitions to Him, glorified is He. If you hesitate over a command to do something or a prohibition against something, then review your faith in Allah.

So His words ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾ mean that you are free to enter into faith in Allah or not to enter. But once you have entered, beware of breaking any ruling of Allah in whom you have believed; if you break one of Allah's rulings, you enter with us into the problem of committing evil deeds or sins.

The rulings that preceded for those who believed were rulings concerning honour and the establishment of the family upon a pure, clean system, so that reproduction may come about pure and clean. The verses spoke of the forbidden women and likewise the permitted ones. Now here He, glorified is He, speaks of wealth, which sustains life. Wealth, as we know, is the fruit of effort and hardship, and everything that is accumulated as property is considered wealth. However, wealth is divided into two kinds: wealth from which you can benefit directly. Some people own food, others own drink, and others own garments; this is a kind of wealth from which one benefits directly. And there is another kind of wealth, which is "cash," from which one does not benefit directly, but benefits by obtaining what one can benefit from directly.

Thus wealth divides into direct provision and indirect provision. The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, wants to protect the movement of life, because by protecting the movement of life He encourages the one who moves to move and increase his movement. And if the Truth did not protect the movement of life and the fruit of the movement of life, what would happen? The movement of life would come to a halt.

We observe that in every society where a person is not secure in the goal and fruit of his work, the movement of work in it diminishes, and each one works according to his strength, saying to himself: why should I work? Because he is not secure. But if he is secure in the fruit of his movement, security over his wealth encourages him to increase the movement of work. When the movement of work increases, society benefits, even if the one who moves did not intend it. It is not necessary that a person intend, in all his movement, to benefit society. No; let him work for the benefit of himself.

We have already given this example: a person, for instance, has thousands of pounds, then he places them in a safe, then he asks himself: why do I place them in a safe? Why not build another house with them and rent out two apartments from it, so that a return comes to me from it? Was society in the mind of such a person? No; his mind is occupied with his own interest. Therefore, let each person's interest be in his mind, and here society will benefit from his movement, whether he intended it or not. Because when he comes to dig the foundation he will pay people their wages; when he brings bricks he buys them at a price, and when it is built he pays the engineer and the workers their wages. So I say: work for yourself in the light of Allah's law, and society will benefit in spite of you.

It is remarkable that you want to benefit yourself, and then our Lord shows you that you will benefit others before you benefit from the return of the house you built. Do not think that anyone will take the provision of our Lord and not let it reach creation. No; society will benefit despite you.

So it is among society's good fortune that we protect the movement of life, and we secure every mover in life over his wealth. But if we are rulers, our eyes must be clear-sighted: does he earn from what is lawful or not? If the earning is lawful, we thank him; but if he earns from what is unlawful, we call him to account. If it operates otherwise, the movement of life comes to a halt, and if the movement of life comes to a halt, this is harmful to those who cannot move. Why? Because Allah apportioned talents among people; not every person possesses the drive for movement, and not every person possesses a mind with which to plan. Thus there may be in society only a few who plan, and the rest are limbs that respond to the planning mind, and the mind works through many limbs. Likewise there is one thinker who sets a plan from which many people benefit.

Therefore we must tend the movement of the mover and foster it, because society benefits from it, even if the mover intends only his own interest. It is true that the one who has nothing in mind but himself nullifies the reward of his work, and it is true that one who keeps people in mind is given the fruit of his work and also receives a reward from Allah.

The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, comes to matters of wealth and explains them thoroughly in order to protect the movement of life and encourage people to move, so that movers multiply and movements multiply, and society benefits. So He said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly﴾. Whenever you find a command addressed to a group concerning a collective matter, distribute it among the individuals.

An example of this: when we say to a group: "Mount your cars," meaning each one of you should mount his car; and the teacher enters the classroom and says to the pupils: "Take out your books," meaning each pupil must take out his book. The address of a plural to a plural requires distribution to individuals. The Truth's words ﴿do not consume﴾ are an address to a plural, and ﴿your wealth﴾ is also plural, so its meaning is: let no one consume his own wealth. And how can it be that each of you does not consume his own wealth? The Truth clarifies: "unjustly." So it is required of each of you that he not consume his own wealth unjustly. A person consumes a thing in order to benefit from it. The Truth advises and commands you: beware of spending a piaster of your wealth and wasting it except in what is right; this applies when we address the singular: let none of you consume his wealth unjustly, but let him direct it to what is beneficial, in which there is no prohibition and which brings no punishment in the Hereafter.

And if the intended meaning is that no one should consume another's wealth, we will clarify it by the following example: suppose a pupil says to his teacher: "Sir, my pen was here and it has gone missing." The teacher says to the pupils: "Do not steal your pens." Does this mean that the teacher says: "Let no one steal his own pen," or "let no one steal his brother's pen"? So the second meaning is intended: ﴿do not consume your wealth﴾, that is, let none of you consume his brother's wealth unjustly.

How does He say "your wealth"? And since it is their wealth, is there no fault in it? No; because its intended meaning is: let none of you consume his brother's wealth. Why did He not say that, and say "your wealth"? Because the custom of the Truth's commands is not addressed to one group created to be consumers and another group created to be consumed; rather, each one is at one time liable to consume the wealth of another, and at another time his own wealth is liable to be consumed. So if I consume the wealth of another, another will consume my wealth. I will have set a precedent for him, and he will consume my wealth as well. Thus when He, glorified is He, says to you: "do not consume your wealth," He is in fact protecting your wealth for you.

The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, wants to make of the community of believers one single society. He says that the wealth each one has belongs to all. If you guard the wealth of others, others will guard your wealth; and if you dare to consume the wealth of another, the collective will dare to consume your wealth. And when you consume the wealth of one person, you embolden thousands of people to consume your wealth. And when you do not consume the wealth of others, it is as if you had not consumed your own wealth.

﴿Do not consume your wealth among yourselves unjustly﴾. The word "consume" ('akl) means taking, because eating is the most important phenomenon of life, since it is the recurring phenomenon: you may live in one house all your life and wear a robe once every six months, but you partake of food every day. When the verse was revealed, the Muslims said: "We do not consume our wealth unjustly," and they felt uneasy about eating at the homes of their brothers. Afterwards the matter was referred to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he clarified that consuming in a spirit of generosity is not unjust, and Allah revealed His words:

﴿There is no fault upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick, nor upon yourselves that you eat from your own houses, or the houses of your fathers, or the houses of your mothers, or the houses of your brothers, or the houses of your sisters, or the houses of your paternal uncles, or the houses of your paternal aunts, or the houses of your maternal uncles, or the houses of your maternal aunts, or what you hold the keys to, or your friend's. There is no blame upon you whether you eat together or separately﴾ (from verse 61, Surah al-Nur).

This removed the sense of fault for them; but when they heard of "consuming unjustly," they said: "I will not take anything from anyone except in exchange."

And what is "unjust" (bāṭil)? Unjust is taking a thing without right to it. An example of this is usury (ribā), because the meaning of "ribā" is that one person has a surplus and another is in need, and the needy person does not have the principal; is it demanded of him that he return the principal plus an increase, and the increase be given to the one who has it?

How does this come about? This is taking by usury, or taking by theft, embezzlement, bribery, or cheating in goods. All of that is consuming wealth unjustly. When you want to consume wealth unjustly, it is as if you want to enjoy the fruit of another's labour, and by doing so you become accustomed to enjoying the fruit of another's labour; your capacity for work withers, and your taking becomes taking from others, taking their wealth by compulsion and without right. Thus the movement of a mover in life is brought to a halt, and that idle thug (the "baltagi") flourishes, and the mover in life, the one upon whom the levy is imposed, fears, and his activity in life diminishes and weakens. What would such a society look like? In that case society will suffer distress and hardship in life.

So His words, glorified is He, ﴿do not consume your wealth among yourselves unjustly﴾, are a command to every Muslim: do not practise usury, do not steal, do not cheat, do not deceive, do not gamble, do not embezzle, do not take bribes, because all these things are consuming wealth unjustly. When we examine the matter of gambling we find something remarkable: those who gamble claim to be friends, they wait for one another and eat together, and each of them sits before the other while being keen to take what is in his pocket; what friendship is this?

Thus when the Truth says ﴿do not consume your wealth among yourselves unjustly﴾, and when the Truth commands you: beware that the obligation should seem hard to you, because it is burdensome to you; but in proportion to what the obligation takes from you by way of restricting the movement of your conduct, and what it gives you by way of restricting the movement of others, the Truth has said to you: do not take another's wealth, so that another does not take your wealth; and thereby you gain and all of society gains. When a command is issued to a person to restrain his hand from theft, it is a command to all people to refrain from stealing from that person; therefore, when you receive any ruling from Allah

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 30:

He, glorified is He, says after that:

﴿And whoever does that in transgression and injustice, We will drive him into a Fire, and that is ever easy for Allah.﴾

"Dhalika" (that): "dha" alone is for pointing, and the "kaf" is for address. When the address is singular, the intended addressee is God's address to His Messenger, with the believers included within that address. Sometimes He says "dhalikum" (that), meaning He is addressing us, as in:

﴿That is purer for you﴾ (part of verse 232, Surat al-Baqarah).

"Dhalika" refers directly to what immediately preceded it in the verse about killing a soul, and likewise what came before it, which is consuming wealth. Some scholars take it as referring to everything mentioned from the beginning of His saying: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already occurred﴾, while others take it as referring to all the commands and prohibitions from the beginning of the surah up to this point. All of these interpretations are valid.

﴿And whoever does that in transgression and injustice.﴾ "Al-'udwan" (transgression) is overstepping, and overstepping may be out of injustice or out of forgetfulness. One who oversteps through injustice is aware and takes the right of another; as for overstepping through forgetfulness, it calls for a person to review his conduct. Why? Because the outcome is bitter.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever does that in transgression and injustice, We will drive him into a Fire﴾. When an action is attributed to its doer, it takes its strength from its doer. So when someone says to you: "If you do this, my young son will slap you with a slap," this is a statement different from the threat that a strong young man will beat you. Why? Because the force of the event is derived from the one who performs it. Who causes the transgressor to burn in the Fire? It is Allah, and glorified is He, who will make him burn in it.

The Truth says: ﴿And that is ever easy for Allah.﴾ This is because the act of Allah is not through processing but is executed immediately. We know that an act requiring processing is every act that requires time: there is work that requires an hour, and each minute of that hour takes a portion of the work; when you divide the work into sixty portions, the work ends in an hour. If the work ends in ten days, you say to him: "Drop the rest times and not practicing the work?" and divide the work over the remaining time. This is what is called "processing" (ʿilaj), because it is the work of a human being. But the work of Allah differs: the Truth says to a thing: ﴿Be, and it is﴾. Thus every act is easy for Allah so long as the matter is: ﴿Be, and it is.﴾ He, glorified is He, said:

﴿Your creation and your resurrection are not but as a single soul﴾ (part of verse 28, Surat Luqman).

He, glorified is He, clarifies: I do not create each one as I created Adam, shaping him, forming him, and then raising him up; no, all creation is as a single soul.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 31:

﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will remove from you your minor sins and admit you to an honorable entrance.﴾

This verse is one of the eight verses about which Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "In this surah, Surat an-Nisa', there are eight verses better for this Ummah than whatever the sun rises upon or sets upon." We have said that these verses begin with His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿Allah wants to make clear to you﴾, ﴿And Allah wants to accept your repentance﴾, ﴿Allah wants to lighten for you﴾, and then came: ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden.﴾ And "ijtinab" (avoidance) does not mean refraining from committing the act or deed, but rather not approaching the places where the act or deed may occur, so that the believer shuts off from himself the imagining of the desire for disobedience, its depiction to him, and its appearing to him.

These noble verses were better for this Ummah than whatever the sun rises upon or sets upon, because they protect from the folly of choice that exists in man when he does not commit to the method of Allah. Had man been directed and compelled to act, he would have been relieved of this choice. Man's hardship came from his being deceived by his distinction over the rest of Allah's creation, and the distinction with which Allah singled out man is the intellect, by which he chooses between alternatives, whereas all the other kinds have accepted from Allah being subjugated and compelled to what He has made them for, without choice. We know that the Truth said: ﴿Indeed, We offered the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they declined to bear it and feared it, and man bore it. Indeed, he was ever wrongdoing and ignorant.﴾ (Surat al-Ahzab).

So man has wronged himself, because he preferred himself when choosing desire or choosing the demands of Allah's method, whereas the compelled or subjugated beings do not have this matter. Each of them performs its task mechanically and is relieved of the folly of choice. So these verses reassure man that if his choice goes astray in something, Allah wants to make him see, Allah wants to accept his repentance, and Allah wants to lighten for him. And Allah wants, if he avoids the major sins, to lift from him his bad deeds and cover them. All of these are reassurances for the human soul, so that it is not seized by despair over the folly of choice. So He clarifies: I am your Creator, and I know that you are weak, because you have two paths: each path tempts you. Allah's obligation, with the good it contains for you and the reward from Allah in the Hereafter you await, tempts, and the soul's hasty desire tempts.

And since the matter has become wavering between choice and choice, weakness arises; therefore He, glorified be He, clarifies: I respect this in you because it is the product of choice, and I am the One who bestowed this choice upon you.

When the Truth bestowed choice upon this kind, which is the master of all kinds, He loves that he come to his Lord desiring and loving, because there is a difference between one who is subjugated and cannot escape what is decreed for him to do, which is what the attribute of power of Allah accomplishes, but the attribute of being beloved was not given to Allah by that; for beloved-ness is that you are free to obey and free to disobey and then obey. This is the attribute of being beloved, and Allah wants man to establish by his obedience the attribute of being beloved to Him, glorified be He. So the man who loves his Master, although he is free to perform obedience or not perform it, inclines by faith to the side of obedience.

﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden﴾: after His commands concerning matters of honor and property, and His commands concerning blood, such as killing a soul and other things, Allah clarified: Beware lest you receive matters in a way that makes you despair of being unable to fulfill some obligations. I will be content with your avoidance of the major sins among the evil deeds: prayer to prayer is expiation for what is between them, Friday to Friday is expiation, and Ramadan to Ramadan is expiation. But on the condition that you do not persist in minor sins. Why? Because if you commit that, consider that you may not be able to remain alive until you seek forgiveness. So do not say: I will commit the sin and then seek forgiveness; this is not guaranteed, and also you would be like one who mocks his Lord.

﴿We will remove from you your bad deeds﴾: regarding bad deeds He says: ﴿We will remove from you your bad deeds﴾. We have said that "kufr" (expiation) means "covering," i.e., He covers them, and to cover them means that We do not punish for them. So takfir (expiation) is the removal of punishment, and ihbat (nullification) is the removal of reward. If a person commits something that deserves punishment, but he has avoided the major sins, Allah expiates it for him, i.e., He sets aside and covers the punishment for him. As for one who does a good deed and Allah does not accept it, He nullifies it. Thus takfir, as we said, is the removal of punishment, and ihbat is the removal of reward, as in His saying:

﴿Those, their deeds have become worthless﴾ (part of verse 217, Surat al-Baqarah).

That is, they have no reward for those deeds, because they did them while the thought of the One who gives reward, Allah, was not in their minds. Rather, the thought of creation was in their minds. Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) said:

"You did it to be said of, and it has been said."

You did it to be said of, and it has been said; they said about you that you are a great benefactor. They said: you built the mosque, and they read the plaque you placed on the mosque amid a great celebration. And the Truth says:

﴿And We will confront what they did of deeds and make it scattered dust.﴾ (Surat al-Furqan, 23).

You did it to be said of, and it has been said. Therefore those who did such deeds and placed marble plaques must heed this matter. If one of them is keen to receive reward from the hand of Allah, let him remove this plaque and conceal it, and the matter ends. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, loves that one who gives charity be like what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said about the seven whom Allah shades in His shade on a day when there is no shade but His:

"And a man who gives charity and conceals it, so that his left hand does not know what his right hand gives."(1)

So when you give charity, why do you expose the one who receives the charity? The Truth says: ﴿If you avoid﴾, and "ijtinab" (avoidance) is giving a thing its side. That is why they say: "So-and-so turned his side away from me," meaning when he met me he gave me his side. The intent in His saying ﴿If you avoid﴾ is distancing, and when the Truth asks you not to commit the act and asks you in another manner to avoid it, this shows that avoidance is more emphatic, because avoidance means that you are not in one place with the forbidden thing. When the Truth says:

﴿So avoid the filth of idols﴾ (part of verse 30, Surat al-Hajj).

And when He says:

﴿And avoid the saying of falsehood﴾ (part of verse 30, Surat al-Hajj).

Avoid it, i.e., keep away from it. Why? Because Allah's sanctuary is His prohibitions.

And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters that many people do not know. Whoever guards against doubtful matters has cleared his honor and his religion, and whoever falls into doubtful matters falls into the unlawful, like a shepherd grazing around the sanctuary who is about to enter it. Verily, every king has a sanctuary, and verily the sanctuary of Allah on His earth is His prohibitions."(2)

And the Truth says:

﴿Indeed, wine, gambling, stone altars, and divining arrows are but filth from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.﴾ (part of verse 90, Surat al-Ma'idah).

Avoidance of it is by not being in one place with it, which entices you, preoccupies you, and presents itself to you. For example, when you are in a place where people drink wine, the Truth says to you: avoid it, i.e., do not go to it, because when wine is before you and you see those who drink, relaxed and happy, you may drink it. But when you avoid wine and its gatherings, you do not fall into its clutches and allure. That is why we said that avoidance is more emphatic than prohibition. There are people who justify wine for themselves and say: no explicit text prohibiting wine has come! We say to each of them: it is enough for you that drinking wine is paired with the filth of idols. The Truth says:

﴿And avoid the Taghut﴾ (part of verse 36, Surat an-Nahl).

So avoiding the Taghut does not mean not worshipping it; rather, beware of even seeing it. Likewise, avoiding wine does not mean not drinking it; rather, beware of being in its presence.

"Al-kaba'ir" (the major sins) is the plural of "kabirah" (a major sin). Since there is a "kabirah," there is its counterpart, which is "saghirah" (a minor sin) and "asghar" (the lesser). The lesser than the "kabirah" is not only the "saghirah," because there is a "saghirah," and there is an "asghar" below the "saghirah," which is "al-lamam" (minor faults).

The Truth says: "If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will expiate your bad deeds," and "bad deeds" are linked to the small matter and the smallest. But this matter has been a point on which the scholars paused. They said: the meaning of that is that we will encourage people to commit bad deeds as long as they have avoided the major sins, since they may commit minor sins. We say: No. Persisting in a minor sin is one of the major sins; therefore do not make minor sins permissible for yourself. The Truth only expiates what slips from you. That is why the Truth says:

﴿Repentance is only upon Allah for those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon after.﴾ (part of verse 17, Surat an-Nisa').

They commit the evil deed without prior arrangement and planning. And He, glorified be He, said after that:

﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now."﴾ (part of verse 18, Surat an-Nisa').

So the meaning of your persisting in a minor sin and repeating it is that by this it becomes a major sin. If we avoid the major sins and fall into them, what then happens? The scholars whom Allah made gifts of gentleness and mercy to creation say: "There is no major sin with seeking forgiveness, and no minor sin with persistence." If you take this, take that too: take both. There is no major sin with seeking forgiveness, and its counterpart is: there is no minor sin with persistence. When the scholars wanted to define the major sin, they said: the major sin is that for which Allah has threatened punishment in the Hereafter, or for which a prescribed penalty (hadd) such as a fixed punishment has been stipulated; this is a major sin. And that for which no prescribed penalty has come has entered the category of forgivable bad deeds through avoiding the major sins, or the minor sin, or the lesser.

Our master 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd was a scholar of Basra and one of its ascetics, and of him one of the caliphs said: "All of them are seekers of game except 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd," meaning that all the scholars go there to take gifts and presents except 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd. So he was testified to. When this scholar wanted to know the meaning of the major sin, and insisted not to know its meaning from the words of scholars, but said: "I want to know it from the text of the Qur'an, which tells me about the major sin, I will bring him a text from the Qur'an." Ibn 'Ubayd al-Basri entered upon our master Abu 'Abd Allah Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq, and we know our master Ja'far al-Sadiq, who is the most worthy of people to be asked, because he is the scholar of the Ahl al-Bayt, and because he has searched the treasures of the Qur'an and brought out its secrets, and lived in the expanse of divine overflow. Ibn 'Ubayd said: "This is the one I should ask." When he greeted and sat, he recited the saying of Allah, glorified be He:

﴿Those who avoid the major sins and the immoralities, except for minor faults﴾ (part of verse 32, Surat an-Najm).

Then he fell silent! Our master Abu 'Abd Allah Ja'far al-Sadiq said to him: "What silenced you, O Ibn 'Ubayd?" He said: "I would like to know the major sins from the Book of Allah."

And look at the confidence in knowing the treasures of the Qur'an, when he said to him: "I would like to know the major sins from the Book of Allah." Abu 'Abd Allah said: "Yes," i.e., you have fallen upon one who knows them; you came to one who knows them. Then he said: "Associating partners with Allah. Allah, the Exalted, said:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ (part of verse 48, Surat an-Nisa').

And He, the Exalted, said:

﴿Indeed, whoever associates partners with Allah, Allah has forbidden him Paradise﴾ (part of verse 72, Surat al-Ma'idah).

He added: and despair of Allah's mercy, for the Truth said:

﴿Indeed, no one despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people﴾ (part of verse 87, Surat Yusuf).

Thus our master Abu 'Abd Allah Ja'far al-Sadiq brought the ruling and brought its evidence, and added: and feeling secure from the plotting of Allah, because He, glorified be He, said:

﴿None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the losing people﴾ (part of verse 99, Surat al-A'raf).

The fourth major sin: disobedience to parents, because Allah described its perpetrator as a tyrant and wretched. Allah, the Exalted, said:

﴿And dutiful to my mother, and He has not made me a tyrant or wretched﴾ (verse 32, Surat Maryam).

And the killing of a soul. Allah, the Exalted, said:

﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein﴾ (part of verse 93, Surat an-Nisa').

And slandering chaste, unaware, believing women. Allah, the Exalted, said:

{Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unaware, believing women are cursed}
