Suppose a man's aim is to travel from Aswan to Cairo; then Cairo is the goal. Then one came and said: we will go on foot. Another said: I will bring good mounts for us to ride. A third said: I will bring a carriage. A fourth said: we will travel by airplane. A fifth said: we will travel by rocket. So every means that brings one nearer to the goal is praiseworthy. And since our goal is to return to the Truth, why do we grieve when one of us dies? So you grieve for yourself and not for the one who died. The one who dies after having guarded Allah's right in this world is happy, because he is in the care of the Truth and with the Bestower; while you are with a temporary blessing. He mocks you for grieving and says: Look at the naive heedless one! He wanted me to remain with the means and leave the Causer!

We find that those who grieve over their loved ones never see them in dreams, because the soul of the dead does not come to visit one who grieves, since he has gone to the Bestower. People must realize the purpose of existence: to be with the means of the Truth in this world and then to be with the Truth. Death is the transition that moves you from the means to the Causer, so what is it that saddens you in this?

We shorten the distance for you. Instead of facing the obstacles of the road, which you may or may not overcome, some say: he died while young and did not see the world. We say to them: Is this good for him or not? For example, you have grown up and may be committing sins; perhaps Allah took the young one so as not to expose him to the trial. Place the matter before you and make it a reality.

It is narrated on the authority of al-Harith ibn Malik al-Ansari that he passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said to him: "How did you wake up, O Harith?" He said: "I woke up a true believer." He said: "Look at what you say, for everything has a reality; so what is the reality of your faith?" He said: "My soul has turned away from the world, so I stay awake at night and thirst during the day; and it is as though I look at the Throne of my Lord laid bare, and as though I look at the people of Paradise visiting one another in it, and as though I look at the people of the Fire wailing in it." He said: "O Harith, you have known, so hold fast," three times. (1)(2)

And for us there is a lesson in our master Hudhayfah (may Allah be pleased with him) when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked him: "How did you wake up?" That is, how is your state of faith? Hudhayfah said: "O Messenger of Allah, my soul has turned away from the world, so its gold and its clay are equal to me," meaning that gold became equal to pebbles. This is the matter of the world. Hudhayfah added: "And it is as though I look at the people of Paradise in Paradise enjoying bliss, and at the people of the Fire in the Fire being punished."

And when the image of the Hereafter does not leave the mind of our master al-Harith, he walks through life upright. So the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "You have known, so hold fast."

(1) Yatada'un: crying out from pain (wailing).
(2) Narrated by al-Tabarani.

Almighty God, when He mentions some of the rulings to us, also mentions to us the account of some people who rebel against the rulings. Then He reminds us of the story of Paradise and Hellfire. That is why He says to us:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Our signs - We will drive them into a Fire. Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment. Indeed, Allah is ever Exalted in Might and Wise.﴾ [4:56]

"Nusallihim" (نصليهم) comes from "al-istila'" (الاصطلاء), meaning to be exposed to heat and burning. Someone may say: since they are being burned in the Fire, and we all know that the fire of this world, when it burns something, reduces it to nothing, and when it reduces it to nothing, then there is no pain! We say: pay attention to the fact that Almighty God says in this matter: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment.﴾ So the punishment is not like the fire of this world, because the fire of this world burns and the matter ends. As for the Fire of the Hereafter, it is everlasting, perpetual punishment, repeated: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment.﴾ So when the skins are burned, other skins will come. Are they the same as the first or different? To clarify this: when you have a ring, for example, and you say: I have made from the ring another ring, the material is also one. So is the punishment inflicted on the skins or on the organs? Punishment is always inflicted on the conscious self (al-nafs al-wa'iya). The evidence is that a person may develop a swelling in which there is some pus, a boil (dummal), which tires him, and he cannot bear its pain. Then he becomes heedless and falls asleep, and as soon as he sleeps there is no pain. But when he wakes up, he feels the pain anew.

So pain belongs not to the organ but to the conscious self. The evidence is that when we advanced in medicine, we said that the conscious self can be made insensible, so that the pain occurs and the person does not feel it, and a boil can be opened with a scalpel without its owner feeling any pain. Thus you find that the skins and organs have no role in the punishment; they are only conveyors to the one being punished, and the one being punished is the conscious self. The evidence is that they will testify against us on the Day of Resurrection: the skins and the limbs will testify, and they will be an instrument for conveying the punishment, and they will be delighted, because they convey the punishment to them.

It is a divine system, so do not be astonished by the Qur'an. Whenever science advances, it guides us to some of the signs of God in the universe. You now numb the conscious self and cut the body with scalpels as you wish, and it causes no pain to it. You have come to know that pain is not in the organ but in the conscious self. So all the limbs are instruments that convey pain to the conscious self, and they are delighted, because the conscious self is being tormented. People liken this to a man who has an "itch" (hikka) in his skin, so he scratches, and the scratching makes his blood flow, and so he takes pleasure in it.

So His words ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment﴾ mean that the skins are replaced and other skins grow from the same material, which convey the punishment to the conscious self, and so on.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Our signs - We will drive them into a Fire. Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment.﴾ We know that Almighty God sent down a Book, the Qur'an, and made it a miracle and a method (manhaj), and this is the feature that distinguishes Islam. The method of Islam is itself the miracle, whereas every messenger among the messengers had a method that was one thing and a miracle that was another.

Our master Musa (Moses), his method was the Torah and his miracle was the staff. Our master Isa (Jesus), his method was the Gospel and his miracle was healing the blind and the leper by God's permission. But the miracle of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was the Qur'an, because his religion would be the final extension until the end of the world. That is why God made his method itself his miracle, so that the miracle would be a proof of the truth of the method at any time. No follower of any prophet before the Messenger of God can say that the miracle of the messenger he follows is his method, because the miracles of the messengers before the Messenger of God were cosmic events that came to an end, like a match that has burned: whoever saw it saw it and it ended. But the Muslim can stand and declare with full mouth: Muhammad is the Messenger of God and truthful, and that is his miracle. So the miracle of Muhammad (ﷺ) remains in perpetual permanence and is always connected to him. As for the miracle of every messenger who preceded the Messenger of God, it fulfilled its task for those who saw it and ended, and the miracle of every prior messenger was separated from his method.

The Qur'anic method contains rulings, and the rulings mean: do this, and do not do that. They are perfectly clear from the time God sent down the Qur'an to His Messenger until the Hour arrives. Whoever does what the rulings require is rewarded, and whoever does not do it is punished. All people are equal in what the rulings require until the Hour arrives.

As for God's cosmic signs, which are not affected... what benefit is there for a person whether he knows them or does not know them? God has concealed and veiled them in the Qur'an with an allusion to them, because the mind contemporary with the revelation of the Book was not able to comprehend them in the time of the message. Had the Qur'an come with a clear sign saying: the earth is spherical and rotates, by God, what would the contemporaries of the Messenger of God have said? Some people even now deny that, so what of the people contemporary with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who, if the Messenger of God had said that to them, would have turned away from following what he brought.

They used to benefit from the sphericity of the earth, just as the farmer or the Bedouin benefits from it, and just as people now who have not studied electricity benefit from watching television and the light of the electric lamp and other uses, without scientific knowledge of the details of that. The sun shines upon the world, and water evaporates from the rivers, oceans and seas to become clouds, and then rain falls from the clouds. All these cosmic signs God has not given their secrets except to the extent that minds can contain them, and He has left in His Book what indicates what ambitious minds may arrive at through scientific research.

When we Muslims come to know a new scientific discovery in the universe, we say: the Qur'an has alluded to it. But before that it is not right for us to say so, lest people deny this miraculous Book. So He, glorified is He, said:

﴿Rather, they denied what they did not encompass in knowledge, and its interpretation had not yet come to them.﴾ [10:39]

If the Qur'an had said: everything in existence multiplies, and in it there is a positive and a negative, male and female, would they have believed that? No; because they knew male and female only in man and woman, and they knew it in animals, and also in some plants such as the date palm. But there are many plants whose reproduction they did not know, such as the wheat we plant and eat, and likewise maize. They did not know that the male element exists in the upper "shawashi" (silk tufts) of the maize cob, and that the wind strikes those tufts so that pollen grains fall from them, and then the grain comes forth. That is why the skillful farmer is the one who opens the maize cob slightly from the top so as to allow the pollen to reach its place. A farmer may open one of the maize cobs and find a dead kernel among the tightly packed grains, and discover that it has no thread, that is, it was not connected to the pollen, and this is what they call in the countryside "an old year's sunna" (sunna 'ajuz).

So every reproduction has a male and a female, and that is why our Lord says:

﴿Glorified is He who created all the pairs, from what the earth grows and from themselves and from what they do not know.﴾ [36:36] (Surah Ya-Sin)

We used to know pairs in ourselves, then we came to know them in plants, and the Truth brought in "what they do not know" so that it would encompass everything, and to reveal the positive and negative in electricity. We have come to know that every living being has male and female, and whenever science advances, it explains the cosmic signs.

Out of the mercy of Almighty God toward the minds of the community charged with the message of Muhammad, He did not wish to make His laws in the universe clear and explicit, lest minds stop at them and become unable to understand them, especially since the Book addressed an unlettered nation without culture. Suppose it addressed the contemporary world: there are matters in the universe that the contemporary world does not know, and if the Qur'an had addressed them openly, they would have been one of the reasons that turn people away from the Book. The Qur'an came as a book of method, and the miracle is something that came to support the method, so He did not wish to make the miracle something that obstructs from the method. But He left in the universe ambitions for the mind created by God and for cosmic matter created by God, and every day the human mind discovers things, and this discovery does not come from nothing, but from things that exist.

So if you traced the finest questions of science that the contemporary mind arrives at, and attributed them to the universe, they would return to the self-evident. No person of intellect has invented or brought something entirely new. Rather, he has used his mind on something existing, and from the existing premises he has derived a matter that did not exist; then the matter that did not exist became a known premise from which whoever comes after him derives. That is why scientists are commonly a people whose courtesy leads them to say: we discovered such-and-such a matter, as if it were already there.

Almighty God gives us an idea that brings understanding closer to us. When we were learning geometry, for example, we came to know that geometry is made up of theorems, beginning with the theorem "one" and ending at infinity. When a teacher came to prove to us a theorem "one hundred," he used in the proof the theorem "ninety-nine," and when he was proving the theorem "ninety-nine" he used what came before it.

So every proof of a theorem rests on what precedes it, and the conscious, thinking, deriving mind is the one that arranges the premises and draws the conclusions from them. Everything in the universe is shared by all people. But the mind that arranges and derives imagines to itself and to people that it has brought something new, and it has not brought anything new. Rather, it has produced something new from what exists. An example of this is the child born of his parents: did they bring him from nothing? No; the child came from a union, and if we trace the matter back, we reach Adam. Then who brought Adam? It is God?

So the self-evident truths in the universe are the leaven of every progress, and they are the creation of God who perfected everything He made. Every theory, however complex, in the universe has its origin in a self-evident matter. An example of this is steam: when they discovered it, and before they used it to run machines, what happened? There was someone sitting, and he turned and found the vessel containing water boiling, then he found the vessel's lid rising and falling. When he learned the secret, he discovered that every steam can give propulsive force, and with that the age of steam began. So he was clever, and he took his discovery from a self-evident truth existing in the universe. So beware of being deceived and saying that the mind invented it. Rather, the mind worked with effort on the hidden treasures of God in existence, and arranged and arranged, and then brought out the discovery.

Therefore, when the human mind invents something new, we say to it: you have not invented, you have only discovered, and Almighty God leaves this process in existence. He says:

﴿We will show them Our signs on the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth.﴾ [41:53]

When humanity discovers something new, we tell them: the Qur'an touched on it and brought it. They say: how strange! Did the Qur'an do that fourteen centuries ago, although it was sent down to address an unlettered nation and came through the tongue of an unlettered prophet? We say: Yes.

The verse we are concerned with contains this:

﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins﴾ [4:56]

We have explained skins and sensations before. The theory of "sensation" (al-hiss), as we know, has occupied materialist scientists, and they wanted to know how we feel. Some of them said: we feel through the brain. We say to them: but there are matters that do not reach the brain and that we feel, as evidence that when someone comes in front of my eye and points his finger to open it and pierce it, before his finger reaches it I close my eye, meaning something did not reach the brain for me to feel it. Some scientists said: sensation takes place through the spinal cord and the reflex action (al-harka al-'aksiyya), and then they concluded that sensation arises through sensory hairs lying flat along the skin, as evidence that when you are given an injection...

Since He had brought the punishment, or the fitting recompense, for those who rejected faith, He did not neglect the counterpart, so that the explanation might cover both ends: the end of the committed and the end of the deviant. Therefore, after that, the Truth says:

﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds – We will admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. For them therein are purified spouses, and We will admit them to a dense shade.﴾ [4:57]

In this verse the Truth describes the reward of the group opposed to the previous group, namely those who believed. We know that the last procession of the messages is the message of Muhammad (ﷺ). Therefore the nation of our master Muhammad is the nearest of the nations to meeting Allah. The nations from the days of Adam took a long time, but we Muslims are near, and therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) said: {I was sent, and the Hour is like these two} (1).

For this reason the Truth did not say in this verse: "sawfa nudkhiluhum" (We will admit them). Rather He said: "sa-nudkhiluhum" (We will admit them). With the others He used "sawfa" because it refers to something distant, or this is an allusion and sign from Allah, granting the disbelievers respite so that they may repent. When Allah brings the distance near to us, He arouses us to obedience: the matter is not distant but near. Therefore He expresses it as: ﴿We will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow.﴾

The word "Jannah" (garden) is derived from "janna" (to conceal, to cover), and "jannah" is the orchard that has trees in which a person who walks is concealed. It differs from flowery gardens that produce flowers close to the ground, representing mere luxury for the eyes. The Jannah has tall, dense trees, so that if someone walks in it, he is concealed; in it there is sustenance and everything. It screens you from turning to anything else, because in it there is what suffices you. The one who has a need that is not met looks toward what will meet it, but the one whose need is met is screened off from the rest of existence. The Truth, glorified and exalted, gives us a picture of something that is now unseen to us and will become, by Allah's permission and will, a visible scene. We know that Paradise contains everything the soul desires, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said:

﴿I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.﴾ (2) The confirmation of this is in the Book of Allah: {No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes as a reward for what they used to do}.

We know that existing things are known by a human according to what suits his perception. Thus He said: ﴿what no eye has seen and no ear has heard.﴾ The eye, when it sees, is limited, but hearing has a wider scope than sight, for one hears from one who has seen; he hears beyond what he has seen. So the sphere of perceptions comes first: that a person sees, then that he hears, and he hears more than he sees. For example, I may see Aswan, but I hear about America: the sphere of hearing is wider.

Then comes His saying (ﷺ): "nor has it occurred to the heart of a human." That is, what is in Paradise exceeds imaginings. So how many attributes are there here for Paradise? The first is His saying: "what no eye has seen," and the eye, however much it sees, has a limited scope. The second: "nor has any ear heard," and the ear, if it hears, has a somewhat wider scope. The third: "nor has it occurred to the heart of a human," and this is wider than imaginings. So, O Truth, glory be to You: if You are going to give us in Paradise what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived, by which words, O my Lord, will these things be conveyed to us? Words of language were only established for known meanings, and since You are going to bring something no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and that has not occurred to a human heart, which words will convey these meanings?

The Messenger (ﷺ) made clear that there are no words for it, because the meaning is known first and then a word is assigned to it. Every word established in a language is known to have a meaning, but since this Paradise has not been seen by an eye, nor heard by an ear, nor occurred to a human heart, there are no words that express it. Therefore the Messenger (ﷺ) did not say, "Paradise is such-and-such," but said: "like the Paradise" (mathal al-jannah). As for Paradise itself, there are no words in our language that convey these meanings. Since these meanings have not been seen by an eye, heard by an ear, or conceived by a human heart, the language of humans does not give us a picture of Paradise. The Truth, glorified, made clear: "I will choose something that is the best of what you have and give you a likeness by it," and He said:

﴿The likeness of the Garden promised to the righteous: in it are rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine delicious to drinkers, and rivers of honey clarified; and for them therein is every fruit, and forgiveness from their Lord.﴾ (Qur'an 47:15)

We see rivers, and the Truth reassures us here that the rivers of Paradise will differ: He will strip from them the quality that might spoil their flowing. Water in a river may stand still and become stagnant and altered, so He says: ﴿rivers of water unaltered.﴾ Thus He gives me an existing name, which is "river," and we all know it, but He clarifies that He will remove from it the turbidities you see in the river of worldly life. Also, the rivers of this world flow in a channel between two banks, but the rivers of Paradise have water seen in them without banks that hold the water back, since it is held by power. And you will also find rivers of milk whose taste does not change.

The Arab used to take milk from camels and store it in waterskins; then the camels would travel far to pastures and wherever they journeyed. When the Bedouin needed milk, he had nothing but the milk stored in the waterskins, and he would find its taste changed, yet he had no other. Therefore the Truth clarifies: I will give you rivers of milk in Paradise whose taste does not change. Then He says: ﴿and rivers of wine﴾, and they know wine; to make us understand that it is not like the wine of this world, He says "like" (mathal)... and He did not state the reality, saying "rivers of wine" but rather "it is wine" ﴿delicious to drinkers.﴾ The wine of this world is not drunk by people with delight, as evidence: when you see someone drinking a cup of wine... he pours it into his mouth at once! Not like you drinking a cup of mango and savoring it; he takes it in one gulp to minimize the speed of its passing over his taste buds, because it is harsh and sour, and it seizes and corrupts the minds. But the wine of the Hereafter has no seizing of minds.

So when the Truth gives me a likeness of Paradise, He negates impurities from the likeness. For this reason we find the parables varied in this field. The Arab, when walking at midday and finding a "nabq" tree, called "sidr," would regard it as an oasis where he rests, and would find on it beautiful nabq fruit. He would stretch out his hand to eat from it, but might find thorns and avoid them; sometimes a thorn would prick him. When he found in such a tree no thorns, he would say: here is "sidr makhdud," that is, a nabq tree with no thorns. The Truth brings all the blights of this world and negates them from the Garden of the Hereafter.

﴿And rivers of clarified honey.﴾ The Arabs used to take honey from the mountains, since bees build their hives in mountain crevices, and when they extracted honey from the mountains they would find sand and gravel in it. So the Truth clarified: what spoils the honey for you here in this world, I will purify it for you there. Although it is a likeness, He still purifies it. And why a likeness? Because, since the bliss of Paradise is "what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived," all human language would fail to convey what is in it. Yet He, glorified, gives us a near image, and Allah strikes the likeness with a near image of things that transcend understanding, to bring them near to the intellect. An example: when He, glorified, wished to give us an image of Allah's illumination of the cosmos, not of His own essential light, but of His illumination of the cosmos, He says:

﴿The likeness of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp, the lamp within a glass.﴾ (Qur'an 24:35)

He gives us a near likeness because your language does not have words that convey the reality, and therefore He says:

﴿And We have prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow.﴾ (Qur'an 9:100)

And since they are gardens, there are dense and tall trees in them, and we know that trees must be in a place with water. Therefore He said: ﴿beneath which rivers flow.﴾ And at another time He says: ﴿rivers flow beneath them,﴾ because what flows beneath them may be coming from another place, its source may be far away, and rivers flow under your garden; one might think the owner of the spring could block it from your garden, so the Truth explains: no, it comes directly from beneath it.

The Truth says of the people of Paradise: ﴿abiding therein﴾, and He, glorified and exalted, addresses a people who witnessed some bliss in their worldly lives from the effects of His favor upon them, but they also witnessed that blessing departs from people, or they witnessed people departing from blessing. So He, glorified, said of the Garden of the Hereafter: ﴿abiding therein forever,﴾ so it neither departs from them nor do they move away from it.

He also gives us an image of the bliss that exists for us in this world but which also departs, or we depart from it: ﴿And for them therein are purified spouses.﴾ "Azwaj" is the plural of "zawj," and when the Truth, glorified and exalted, describes a plural, He brings the attribute in the plural too, as in His saying:

﴿And cooking pots fixed firmly﴾ (Qur'an 34:13).

Because "qudur" is the plural of "qidr." He did not say here "wa-azwaj mutahharat" (purified spouses, feminine plural) but brought it in the singular form, because in this world a man may marry more than one woman, and among the multiple wives shades of discord arise, as if they were mutually repellent. So He said: all of them will be spouses in one form of purity, and in none of them is there anything that would spoil the spouse's serenity as happens in this world. Let no one say: "How would a woman accept having a co-wife in the Hereafter?" Because the Truth, glorified, has removed from the breasts everything that used to trouble the souls in this world, as He said:

﴿And We will remove whatever ill feeling is in their breasts.﴾ (Qur'an 7:43)

So it is as though they, though many in one context of purity, nothing disturbs the husband's serenity; he will like her appearance, she will please him, and her character will have no defect or deficiency such as existed in this world. She is purified from all of that. Thus He gives me the essence of what can be imagined of bliss in spouses.

The Truth continues: ﴿and We will admit them to a dense shade.﴾ When the Arabic language wants to emphasize a meaning, it brings emphasis from the word itself; an Arab says, for example, "hadha layl alyal" (this is a pitch-black night), i.e., a dark night, and when he exaggerates "shade" (zill), he says "zaleel" (dense). What is "shade"? "Shade" is the withdrawal of the sun from a place where it was, or a place the sun has never entered at all, such as a person being inside a cave or cavern.

The phrase "shade dense" is known to those who live in the desert: when a person there sees a tree, he sits beneath it and enjoys its shade. The shade itself may be dense, as in the "air-conditioned tents" they make now, which consist of two layers: the first layer is exposed to the sun and bears the heat, while the second layer blocks the heat, and they call this roof a "double roof." It exists especially in high places, since an apartment on a higher floor, for example, is protected, but apartments on the top floor, especially in hot countries, have intense and difficult heat; therefore they make a roof above the roof, and thus the shade itself is in shade.

Why does a person enjoy shade under a tree more than shade by a wall? Because a wall's shade consists of one layer; it is true that it keeps the sun from us, but it also blocks the air. But sitting in a tree's shade is distinguished by the fact that every leaf of the tree has another above it, and its leaves lie one above another, and each leaf is in the shade of the leaf above. Because each leaf is light, the breeze caresses it, so it screens the one sitting beneath the tree from the sun's heat and gives him air too. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿a dense shade.﴾

Therefore, when the poet wanted to describe the garden, he said:

They shielded us from the scorching blaze, and with abundant rain they watered it; We lodged beneath a branching tree that bent over us, Tenderly, as nursing mothers bend over the weaned child. And we drank, in our thirst, pure water sweeter than wine to the boon companion, It blocks the sun whenever it faces us, and admits the breeze.

Here the poet describes the situation when a person walks in a desert...

(1) Narrated by Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi from Anas.
(2) Narrated by Muslim in the chapter on the description of Paradise.

Thus Allah, glory be to Him, after speaking of the Fire and of the Garden and fixing this matter at the focal point of their consciousness, sends down the rulings afterward. That is why you always find that after Allah mentions the Garden and the Fire, He follows them with the foundational rulings (ummahat al-ahkam), which, if they carry them out, they attain the Garden and keep far from the Fire. So after the focal point of consciousness has been charged with the Garden and the Fire, with the singular goal and the goal that inspires desire, here comes the ruling, and Allah the Exalted says:

﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice. Indeed, excellent is that which Allah instructs you. Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing.﴾ [4:58]

As for His words, glory be to Him, ﴿to render trusts to their owners﴾, Allah has summarized in it all the obligations of heaven for the people of the earth, because the trusts (al-amanat) are: the supreme trust, which is faith in Allah; the trust that relates to the human species; and the trust that is upon the self for all species.

The meaning of trust (amanah) is: what another person has of rights with you, and you are trustworthy regarding them. If you wish, you do it, and if you wish, you do not do it. You say: "I deposited a trust with so-and-so." If this trust were by way of delivery, it would not be a trust, because there would be evidence; and if what you deposited with that person had witnesses upon it, it would not be a trust. So the trust is that you deposit something with him, and his conscience is the judge: if he wishes, he acknowledges what he has of yours when you ask for it, and if he wishes, he does not acknowledge it. The Truth says:

﴿Indeed, We offered the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they refused to bear it and feared it, and man bore it. Indeed, he was ever unjust and ignorant.﴾ [33:72] (Surat al-Ahzab)

So what is the trust that was offered to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, and they refused to bear it, and then man bore it, and the reason for his bearing it is that he was "unjust and ignorant"? The universe, as we know, has kinds: the lowest of them is the inanimate, the middle is the plant, above the middle is the animal, then man. Man is the master of these kinds, because all of them serve him. But the inanimate, the plant and the animal have no choice in whether they act or do not act; rather each kind has been created for something to perform, and it has no choice to refrain from performing it.

The earth, the heavens and the mountains did not accept to be choosing agents, or to bear a trust in which the matter reverts to their choice: if they wished, they would do, and if they wished, they would not do. The earth, the heavens and the mountains feared bearing the trust because of the lack of confidence in the state of the self at the time of performing the trust. It is possible that the being resolves, when bearing the trust, to perform it, but at the time of performing it he does not master himself, for his self may betray him and cause him not to acknowledge it. The heavens, the earth and the mountains took precautions and said: "We do not want this trust, nor do we want to be choosing between doing or leaving, obeying or disobeying; rather, O Lord, we want to be subjected to what You love without choice of our own." So the earth, the heavens and the mountains were spared, but man, with the thought he has, weighs choice among alternatives, and said: "I accept it, and my thought will plan its performance." Man, at the moment he bore the trust, did not look at the state of his performing it.

An example of this: it is possible that a person offers you a sum of money as a trust with you. You take it, certain that you will return it when he asks you for it; but at the time of return you may not master yourself. Circumstances may come upon you so that you spend some of the money, or, may Allah protect us, you may have corrupted your liability.

Thus man does not master himself at the time of performance, even though he masters himself at the time of receiving. Those who take precautions say: "Keep far from us the bearing of the trust; we do not want to bear anything for you." But man, before bearing the trust, because he "was unjust and ignorant," wronged himself and was ignorant of his state at the time of performance. So the trust that was offered to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, and they refused to bear it, and man bore it, is the trust of choice, upon which obligation from Allah is based.

Obligation is confined to "do" and "do not do": if you wish, you do in "do", and if you wish, you do not do in "do not do". And if you wish the reverse. This means that the trust in this sense is restricted to what Allah demanded of man at the time of the offering. But it does not address the trusts that exist among us. The trust is also that which relates to your liability with the right of another. Therefore, when a person gives something to a person, the recipient becomes a trustee: if he wishes he renders it, and if he wishes he does not render it.

But there are other trusts that one person did not give to another person, rather the Lord of the human being gave them to every human being. Knowledge that Allah gave to people is a trust. Is the one who taught you knowledge and gave it to you, and afterward said to you, "Return it to me," like one who is trusted with money?

We say to the scholar: knowledge is not from you, so that you give it to another and afterward he returns it to you; rather Allah rewards you for it with reward. Likewise in forbearance and courage. These matters are not made clear between servant and servant except in money. But in the rest of things, we say to you: you are trustworthy regarding them before your Creator. Your Lord has entrusted you with these things so that you render them to those who do not know. He entrusted you with power and commanded you: give it to the one who lacks power; and He entrusted you with knowledge and made clear to you: give it to the one who has no knowledge.

So who gave you this trust? Allah. It is not necessary that the trust be from its owner who gave it to you so that you return it to him. The trust is: that which makes you trustworthy regarding it, from one who created or from a created being. So render it. The scope of the trust in this sense is wide: Allah's right to tawhid is a trust with you; your competence for obligation from Allah, when He obligated you, is a trust with you; your competence in the various gifts is a trust with you. Every person has a gift of which he is trustworthy and must render it and convey its effects to those who do not have this gift. Our Lord gave one person knowledge... All these things are trusts that Allah deposited in His creation so that creation may be complete: when every person renders his trust to every person, every person comes to have the gifts of all others.

When the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾, we immediately recall the summit of trust: that you worship Him and do not associate anyone with Him; and the trust in the obligations with which Allah has charged you, because it is a trust of yours with another and a trust of another with you. So when Allah charges you not to steal, He has charged all people not to steal from you.

Every trust with another is matched by a trust with you. If you render what the trust requires of you, the society surrounding you renders the trust it has. Thus the trust is: the rendering of a right in your liability to another.

And after the trust there is something called justice (al-'adl) that corresponds to it. If each one rendered to another what he has of right with him, we would not need justice, for justice arises only from dispute and litigation, and litigation means that one person denied the right of another. If each of us rendered what is upon his liability of right to another, there would be no litigation, and no dispute would arise, and there would be no need for justice then.

But the Truth, who created creatures and knows the contingencies within them, decreed that some people are heedless of this matter, and from this arises that a person may not give the right that is upon his liability to another. So He, glory be to Him, decreed another thing called "justice." Had the first matter been completed, we would not have needed justice.

So justice is the remedy for the heedlessness that afflicts humans from the contingencies that arise in their souls. Allah willed to say: ﴿And when you judge between people, to judge with justice﴾. In the first, He did not say, "When you are entrusted, then render"; no. Rather He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render﴾. If heedlessness of this arises from you, what protects this matter? Here comes justice, which is that you judge with a right in the liability of another to another, that is, in your own liability, because you judge in order to weigh a matter and place the affair in its proper place.

Thus we know that the requirements of rendering a trust concern a thing in your possession that you render to another, but the requirements of justice concern things in the liability of another to a third party. Therefore the Truth said: ﴿And when you judge between people, to judge with justice﴾, and just as the verse on rendering trusts is general, the verse on justice had to be general too.

His words, ﴿And when you judge between people, to judge with justice﴾, are not specific to the judge alone; rather every person is obligated to justice. If you are an arbitrator on behalf of a people who have accepted you to judge, then judge with justice, even if the judgment concerns matters in which honor, nobility and gift are involved. It is not necessary that justice be applied only to a matter of material value. For example: our master the Imam 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him and honor his face, saw two boys litigating before his son al-Hasan, so that he would judge between them as to which of the two handwritings was more beautiful. People may regard this as a trivial matter, but since it occupied the two boys and each wanted his handwriting to be more beautiful, justice must be the judgment. So Imam 'Ali said to his son al-Hasan: "O my son, look how you judge, for this is a judgment, and by Allah He will call you to account for it on the Day of Resurrection."

This gives us a picture of the precision of justice even when the matter is small. In football matches, you find the referee who says: "This goal is counted" or "not counted." This referee needs skill, because upon it depends the victory or defeat of a team; the proof is that even while you are watching the ball, when you find the referee did not count a goal, you rise up against him.

Here I ask: why did you apply the law of seriousness to play, and then leave seriousness without a law? This is what happens. We transfer the laws of seriousness to play, and we leave seriousness at times without a law. If we took care of this as we took care of that, matters would be equal. So justice is a right in the liability of one to another, even if it is a match in play; and as long as the matter has occupied two parties and created between them dispute, disagreement and rivalry, you must end this disagreement with justice.

The Truth continues: ﴿Indeed, excellent is that which Allah instructs you﴾. "Ni'ma" means how excellent is what Allah instructs you, that is, there is no better admonition than this one, which is: rendering trusts and judging with justice. By this the movement of life is set right. If people render trusts, there is no dispute or disagreement; and if they render justice in judgment, then if any disagreement exists, it ends. The scholars said: when society knows that a justice guards the rights of people among people, no one will act unjustly after that. The wrongdoer says: "So-and-so wronged and was not brought to trial," and that tempts the wrongdoer to increase his wrong. But at the moment people see someone taking the right of another, and then the judge comes and restrains him and returns the right to its owner, no one will wrong another.

And He, glory be to Him, in this command has no need of whether you do or do not do; these are things that have no effect on Him. They are for your own interests, one with another. The best form of command is that which returns no benefit to the commander, because when a command returns benefit to the commander, it may cast doubt upon the command. But that you command a thing from which you gain nothing is the summit of justice. A person may command what has no benefit for him, yet he may not be broad in knowledge nor broad in wisdom; here the matter differs, because Allah, glory be to Him, has no interest in the command. This is one point; and also He, glory be to Him, is vast in knowledge and wisdom; therefore it was...

﴿O you who believe, obey God, and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. And if you dispute over anything, refer it to God and the Messenger, if you truly believe in God and the Last Day. That is better and more favorable in outcome.﴾ (4:59)

This verse has been discussed at length by us, and on every occasion the discussion has turned to it. Yet we must also restate, briefly, what we have said before about it. God, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿Obey God and obey the Messenger.﴾ Why should I obey God and obey the Messenger? Because there are grounds (ḥaythiyyāt, the justifications) presented for it. When you see a ruling from a judge, you find that there are grounds for the ruling, that is, the legal justification for the punishment or for the acquittal. The judge says: since such and such occurred, its law is such and such according to article such and such; these are the grounds. The word "ḥaythiyyāt" (grounds) derives from: "since such and such happened, we ruled accordingly," or "since such and such did not happen, we ruled accordingly." Thus the grounds of a ruling mean the justifications that indicate the basis of the ruling for the one who issued it.

Here God, glorified be He, says: ﴿Obey God and obey the Messenger.﴾ Did God, glorified and exalted, say: "O people, obey God and obey the Messenger"? No. He did not say that. He said: ﴿O you who believe.﴾ So, since you have believed in God as a god who is wise, a creator, knowing, and who imposes obligations, then listen to what He wants to tell you. God did not impose obligations on all people to obey Him; rather He called all people to believe in Him. And whoever believes is told: "Obey Me, since you have believed in Me."

Thus the ground for obeying God and the Messenger (ﷺ) arises from belief in God and in the Messenger. This is complete justice, because He, glorified be He, does not impose on anyone an act unless that person has believed in Him as the one who commands, who imposes obligations. As for the one who does not believe in Him, He does not say to him: "Do such and such, and do not do such and such." Rather, He requires him first to believe in Him, and once he believes, He says to him: "Listen to Me." This is why you find every obligation introduced with His saying: ﴿O you who believe.﴾

The ground for obeying God and obeying the Messenger is belief in Him; this is the first, faith-based ground. As for whether your mind wanders in order to grasp the secret of obedience, that is another matter. Therefore, I clarify: beware of approaching God's rulings by first examining them, so that if you are convinced you accept them, and if you are not convinced you reject them. No. Such conduct means that you have doubted the ruling. Rather, you must proceed to implement His rulings, because He has spoken them and you believe that He is a wise God. But does that prevent your mind from wandering to understand the wisdom?

We say to you: you may understand some of the wisdom, but not all of it, because the perfections of God's wisdom are without limit. You may know one part of the wisdom and someone else may know another part. This is why they said: the difference between the command of a human to a human and the command of God to those who believe in Him is a very small thing. It is this: God's command to a human is preceded by a cause, which is that you have believed in Him. As for a human's command to a human, you say to the one who commands you: "Convince me why I should do this," because your mind is no more advanced than mine. You do nothing unless you are convinced of it. And the experiences have proven to you the soundness of the opinion of the one you listen to, and that he will not deceive you.

Thus we see that our obedience to God differs from our obedience to a created being. We obey God because we have believed in Him, and when He, glorified be He, asks us to obey Him, we consider whether this obedience is for our benefit or for His benefit. When we are certain that He, possessing all the attributes of perfection, created us, then He does not want any new attribute for Himself, since He created us only through the perfections that are in Him. He, glorified be He, created you without your having any right of creation with Him; He created you by His power, and sustained your life by His self-subsistence. So when the God who possesses those perfections asks you for something, He asks it for your benefit. Just as you see any human being, and to God is the highest likeness, caring for his craft and wanting his craft to be distinguished, so too God, glorified and exalted, wants to take pride in this creation. He takes pride in this creation not by compelling them to do what He commands by subjugation, no. Rather, by the lovability of obeying God, and that we declare by our conduct: "We love You, our Lord." Otherwise, O human, you may choose to be disobedient. And since you are free to be disobedient and then you obey, this establishes for God the attribute of being loved, because, as we know, there is a difference between one who compels by his power and one who gives you the choice, so that you come to Him while you love Him, even though He is able to compel you.

So when the Almighty says: ﴿Obey God,﴾ its meaning is that He has not asked us for something excessive. And how do we obey God? By obeying Him in every command. And did God create His creatures to be separate individuals? No; rather, He commanded them both as individuals and as a community, and He gave them innate faith, which establishes that behind the universe there is another power that created it. No one knows this power's name, its requirements, or what it will give to those who serve it. Therefore there must be a conveyor of the message. For this reason, I see that some philosophers have erred when they said: "Reason is sufficient for grasping religion." I say to them: No. Reason is sufficient for recognizing the one to whom we owe worship, but reason does not bring us the manner of religion and its method.

Therefore there must be a message from Him saying: "Do this, and this, and this." We say to these philosophers: reason is sufficient for deducing the existence of a power behind this universe, but as for the form of this power, its name, and what it wants, no one knows that except through a messenger who conveys this message from that power. And it must be that the power in which you believe by your innate nature has sent one who says: "Its name is such, and what it requires is such." Thus His saying: ﴿Obey God﴾ necessarily entails obeying the Messenger.

After that He said: ﴿and those in authority,﴾ and the verb is not repeated for "those in authority." He did not say "and obey those in authority," so that we understand that those in authority have no obedience except from within the two obediences: obedience to God and obedience to the Messenger. We know that obedience comes in the Qur'an in three forms: ﴿Obey God and the Messenger,﴾ ﴿Obey God and obey the Messenger,﴾ and "Obey the Messenger" alone. So there are three forms of obedience:

The first form: "Obey God and the Messenger," where the act of obedience is one and the one obeyed is God and the Messenger.

The second form: "Obey God and obey the Messenger."

The third form: "Obey the Messenger." Yes. The obligations are commanded by the Almighty and are confirmed by a saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or by his act, or his tacit approval. Here the obedience is in the command of God and of the Messenger, or that God has commanded in general terms and the Messenger has specified in detail. Thus we have obeyed God in the general and obeyed the Messenger in the detail, so obedience is to God, and obedience is to the Messenger; or there is a matter that God did not speak about while the Messenger alone spoke about it. This is established by the saying of the Almighty:

﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God.﴾ (from verse 80, Surah an-Nisa')

And His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it.﴾ (from verse 7, Surah al-Hashr)

So these establish that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) has three aspects in legislation: an aspect in which he legislates what God has legislated, as confirmation of it, or that God has legislated in general terms and the Messenger has specified in detail. Examples of this: God has obligated us to five prayers and obligated us to zakat; these are obligations stated by our Lord, and the Messenger clarifies them: the nisab is such, the share is such. So we obey our Lord in the general command, and we obey the Messenger in the detailed command. Or the matter is one on which God has not spoken as a ruling, but it came from the Messenger by delegation from God. Therefore, if any person says to you about any ruling: "Bring your evidence from the Qur'an," and you do not find evidence from the Qur'an, then say to him: the evidence for any matter the Messenger has spoken is the saying of the Almighty: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it.﴾ (from verse 7, Surah al-Hashr)

This is the evidence for every obligatory command that issued from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Someone may say: there is a difference between a matter established by the sunnah (recommended practice) and an obligation (fard). We say: do not confuse the sunnah, which is a matter that if you do it you are rewarded and if you do not do it you are not punished, with the fard, which is what the responsible person must do, so that if he abandons it he sins and is punished for abandoning it. This obligation was brought by the Almighty and established by evidence, like the five daily prayers and the number of rak'ahs in each prayer. The evidence for the obligation here was established by the sunnah, and this is what is called the sunnah-nature of the evidence (sunniyyat al-dalil). And there is a difference between the sunnah-nature of a ruling, such as a Muslim praying two rak'ahs before the noon prayer and two before the dawn prayer, and the obligatory nature of a ruling, such as the dawn and noon prayers. So there is a difference between a thing that if you do it you are rewarded for it and if you do not do it you are not punished for it, and a thing that is imposed on you to perform, so that if you abandon it you sin and are punished. As for the sunnah-nature of the evidence, it is the practical explanation of what the obligations came with, so that Muslims may follow it.

As for the command to obey those in authority, it came by conjunction to the one obeyed, without a separate command to obey, which indicates that obedience to the ruler is binding only if it is from within the obedience to God and the obedience to His Messenger. In this there is protection for the community of believers from tyrannical rulers who try to humiliate people by the saying of God: ﴿and those in authority,﴾ and claim that their obedience is obligatory. One of them says: "Am I not a ruler (wali al-amr)?" The scholars reply: "Yes, you are a ruler, but you are conjoined to the one obeyed, and the command to obey has not been repeated for you. This shows that your obedience is obligatory only if it is from within the two obediences. If it is not from within the two obediences, then there is no obedience to you, because the rule is: 'There is no obedience to a creature in disobedience to the Creator.'" Thus said Abu Hazim to Maslamah ibn Abd al-Malik when he said to him: "Are we not the rulers, and God has said: ﴿and those in authority﴾?" He said: "We must also be alert to the fact that it was revealed in His saying, glorified be He: ﴿And if you dispute over anything, refer it to God and the Messenger.﴾" So the Muslim ruler is first required to discharge the trust, required to be just, and required also that his obedience be from within the obedience to God and the obedience to His Messenger. If these conditions are not in him, then he is a tyrannical ruler. ﴿And if you dispute over anything, refer it to God and the Messenger.﴾ So the dispute must be over a matter that falls within the scope of things commanded for obedience, and there must be a reference that ends this dispute: ﴿refer it to God and the Messenger, if you truly believe in God and the Last Day.﴾

Those who know these rulings are the scholars. If the ruled dispute with the ruler, we go to the scholars so that they may explain to us God's ruling on this question. Thus, if by ﴿those in authority﴾ is meant the ruler, we say to him: ﴿refer it to God and the Messenger,﴾ meaning the ruler must follow what has been established from God and the Messenger, and the proof in this matter is the scholars who occupy themselves with this affair, and who observe the implementation of God's ruling by what they know of the religion. When the Almighty, exalted be He, asks this of us, He wants to end the matter of dispute, because dispute makes the movements of life conflicting: this one says such, and that one says such. So we must refer it to a higher reference. And the Almighty says:

﴿And if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those who deduce it from them would have known it.﴾ (from verse 83, Surah an-Nisa')

So the intended meaning of "those in authority" may be "the scholars."

We say: the first verse is general, and it is the one that brought the obedience to the ruler within the obedience to God and the Messenger; the second, which concerns deduction, the intended meaning of "those in authority" is the scholars.

As for "those in authority" in the first matter, in which if we dispute with them over something we refer it to God and the Messenger, they are those who supervise the implementation of God's rulings, and this is executive authority; whereas the authority of the scholars is legislative and faith-based.

﴿Refer it to God and the Messenger, if you truly believe in God and the Last Day.﴾ So whoever does not do this risks entering the category of those who do not believe in God and the Last Day. We say to each of them: review your belief in God and the Last Day at the outset of receiving the ruling, and your belief in the Last Day in order to receive the reward for disobeying the ruling, since God did not make this world the abode of recompense.

And the Almighty alerts us at the conclusion of the ver

Do you know that "ألم تر" means "did you not know," whether the thing known was already discussed, or whether the thing known is an apparent, recent event that you can see? We know that the Truth (al-Haqq) used "ألم تر" in many matters that the addressee, our master the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), did not witness, to show us that what Allah says, even if it is news of the past, must be believed with the same faith you have in what you see now, because Allah is more trustworthy in truthfulness than your eyes. Your eye may deceive you, but far be it that Allah should deceive us.

﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you?﴾ The intended meaning is the hypocrites and some of the People of the Book who claimed belief in the message of Muhammad (ﷺ). "Al-zaʿm" (claim) is the mount of falsehood. So "they claim that they believe in what has been sent down to you," which is the Qur'an; "and what was sent down before you," which is the Torah and the Gospel. "They desire" after claiming belief "to refer their disputes to the Taghut" (al-ṭāghūt, the transgressor, the false object of submission).

To refer to something (al-taḥākum) means to seek its help or to turn to it in order to end a dispute. So when we say "we referred to so-and-so," the meaning of our saying is that we have grown weary of the effects of disagreement, of rancor and hatred, and we want to agree on a judge. Two opponents do not agree to refer to something unless both parties have been exhausted by the quarrel, they differ on an issue, and weariness has struck each of them.

﴿They desire to refer their disputes to the Taghut.﴾ As we have known, "al-Ṭāghūt" is the person whom obedience makes more tyrannical; there is a transgressor (ṭāghin), that is, an oppressor, and when people fear him he becomes accustomed to oppression and finds it agreeable, in confirmation of the Truth's saying: ﴿So he made light of his people, and they obeyed him﴾ (Qur'an 43:54).

This is called "ṭāghūt" as an intensive form of transgression. "Al-ṭāghūt" applies to the aggressor who is extremely transgressive, whether he is people worshipped besides Allah who have legislation and command and forbid, or Satan who misleads people, or a tyrant ruler whose evil people fear; any of these manifestations is considered a ṭāghūt. They said: the word "ṭāghūt" applies equally to the singular, the dual, and the plural, so we say: a man is ṭāghūt, two men are ṭāghūt, men are ṭāghūt. It comes for the plural, as in the Truth's saying: ﴿Allah is the Guardian of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light. And those who disbelieve, their guardians are the ṭāghūt﴾ (Qur'an 2:257).

And it comes for the singular, as in the Truth's saying: ﴿And they had been commanded to reject it﴾ (Qur'an 4:60).

So at times it comes for the plural and at times for the singular. In every Qur'anic ruling we may find a specific cause for which the ruling was revealed, so it is not correct to say that a ruling revealed for a particular matter does not extend beyond it; it extends to other matters when they share its causes and circumstances. The lesson lies in the generality of the subject, not in the specificity of the cause.

This verse was revealed concerning a hypocrite named Bishr. A dispute arose between him and a Jew, and the Jew wanted to refer the matter to the Messenger of Allah, while the hypocrite wanted to refer it to Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf. The Jew was confident that the truth was on his side, and he did not seek arbitration from the Prophet out of love for him, but out of love for his justice; therefore he preferred one who is just, so he requested the judgment of the Messenger of Allah. As for the hypocrite, who declares his Islam while concealing and hiding his disbelief, he is the one who said: "Let us go to Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, the ṭāghūt." This gives us a justification for the truthfulness of the Messenger of Allah in conveying from Allah His saying: ﴿And when you judge between people, judge with justice﴾.

That the Jew wanted to refer to the Messenger of Allah indicates his confidence that the Messenger of Allah would not let the truth be lost with him; and he did not seek arbitration from a senior among the Jewish leaders such as Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, because he knew that he accepted bribes.

The Truth concludes the verse: ﴿And Satan wants to lead them far astray﴾. For when the two of them refer to the ṭāghūt, who is Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, and afterward he judges in favor of one who has no right, such a judgment will incite everyone who has a desire to oppress to oppress and go to him to be judged! So "far astray" comes here because oppression will chain itself on, and the unjust judge will bear the burden of every case he rules in falsely. This is the meaning of "far astray," and would that the straying were confined to them, but the straying will be extended.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 61:

When we hear the Truth's saying, "ta'alaw" (come), this means a call with the meaning: come forward. However, the word "aqbilu" (approach) means approaching someone equal to you, whereas the word "ta'alaw" means approaching someone higher. Thus, human affairs have a descending legislation, because it is a product of the human mind. And the product of the human mind in laws for safeguarding societies, on the assumption that we have established the goodness of their intentions and their sincerity, is at the level of their capacity for deduction and for surveying events.

But legislation when it comes from God is elevated, because nothing escapes Him, not even the smallest detail. Human legislation, however, is laid down for a present situation, and then events come after it that necessitate amending it. Amending a law means that events have shown the law to be deficient and that it does not encompass what is new. This arises from the fact that events have occurred which were not in the mind of those who legislated for the safeguarding of society, and the mind of the framer of positive law fell short of them. Likewise, no law is amended except after the legislator sees the harmful effects in society, those effects that arose from his first law, and the events of life have pressed heavily upon them so that they amend the rulings and laws.

As for God's legislation, it protects society from these events occurring in the first place. This is the difference between a human positive legislation that came to rescue us from events, and a divine, heavenly legislation that guards us from those events. Human legislation is like curative medicine, whereas heavenly legislation is like preventive medicine, and prevention is better than cure.

Therefore the Truth, glory be to Him, brought legislations that protect us and shield us from the evil of events; that is, He prevents harm to man before it exists. Thereby His mercy, glory be to Him, is realized for a group of mankind so that events do not afflict them, whereas we find that positive law has victims. The hearts of legislators are moved after seeing these victims, so that they set amendments to rulings they had previously laid down. In positive law we find people upon whom the burden of injustice falls, because it is a law that does not encompass the comprehensive protection of the human being. After a period of time the legislators intervene to amend their laws, and until legislation is completed, people fall into the circle of injury and failure to obtain justice. As for the Creator, glory be to Him, He originated and created His creation and He knows it best; therefore He has not wronged anyone at the expense of another. So He laid down His heavenly legislations, and for this reason the Truth says:

﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy to the believers﴾ (part of verse 82, Surah al-Isra').

"Healing" when a disease arises from heedlessness that befalls us, and "mercy," so that the disease does not come at all. The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, says: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what God has sent down and to the Messenger," you see the hypocrites turning away from you with aversion.﴾ Indeed, He, glory be to Him, places among events what exposes them, so they act in a way that reveals their hypocrisy; after that the Messenger warns them and society comes to know that they are hypocrites.

And they ﴿turn away from you with aversion﴾, meaning they turn away from you, O Messenger of God, because they are hypocrites. Every hypocrite has two matters: a matter of the tongue and a matter of the heart. With the tongue he declares his faith in God and in the Messenger of God, while in the heart his faculties are in conflict, unlike the believer or the disbeliever. The believer's faculties are mutually supportive, because his heart is firmly set on faith, and the harmony of his faculties leads to guidance. The disbeliever's faculties are also mutually supportive, because he has said that he has not believed, and the harmony of his faculties leads him to misguidance. But the hypocrite scatters his faculties!! One faculty here and another there. Therefore they will be in the lowest depth of the Fire. The disbeliever is consistent with himself: he did not declare faith because his heart was not convinced, and it was possible for him to say the word of faith, but his tongue does not consent to utter the opposite of what is in the heart, and his enmity to Islam is clear. As for the hypocrite, he says: "O my tongue, declare the word of faith outwardly, so that I may pass through this declaration to my aims, and that the rulings of Islam be applied to me, so that I benefit from the rulings of Islam; and from the very core of my self, if I find an opportunity against Islam, I will seize it." Therefore the Truth says: ﴿Then how will it be when a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have put forward? Then they come to you swearing by God, "We desired nothing but good and reconciliation." ﴾ (62).

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 4, verse 62:

The hypocrites are faced with a question: "Why did you go to the taghut (false judge) to judge between you, and leave the Messenger of Allah?" They say: "We only intended good, and to be gentle with you, so that you would not wear yourself out with our problems. We wanted to arrange matters in agreement, far from you, so that the issues would not reach you and burden you. We did not intend opposition to you, nor displeasure with your judgment." And they say this after they have been exposed before the people.

﴿So how will it be when a disaster befalls them﴾. The "disaster" (musibah) is a matter that befalls a person and harms him according to his own understanding. Because they are hypocrites, they want this hypocrisy to remain concealed. So when an incident comes that exposes them, it becomes a disaster for them, even though the incident in its reality is not a disaster. When we recognize the hypocrites and reveal them to themselves and to the people, we spare ourselves their evil. They want, through hypocrisy, certain things for themselves.

Thus the exposure of their hypocrisy is a disaster for them. They see hypocrisy as beneficial to them, for through it they benefit from the rulings of Islam, their implementation, and their application to them. When their hypocrisy is exposed, they feel the disaster. Their situation is like that of a man who went to steal, and then, as he was entering the place to steal, was surprised to find the police present to arrest him. In reality this is a blessing, since it checks the hand of the criminal who spreads corruption, but for him it is a disaster.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 63:

When a misfortune befalls these hypocrites, they swear by God falsely, because they want their hypocrisy to continue. They try to excuse what has happened, swearing by God that by going to the tyrant (al-taghut) they only intended good and reconciliation between themselves and their adversaries. But God knows what they conceal and what they disclose.

So He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿Those are the ones whose hearts God knows. So turn away from them, admonish them, and speak to them in their own souls a far-reaching word.﴾ (4:63)

And how sufficient is God's knowledge! For this reason our Lord says:

﴿And had We willed, We would have shown them to you, and you would have known them by their marks. And you will surely know them by the tone of their speech.﴾ (Part of 47:30)

That is: if We had willed to tell you who they are, We would have told you and pointed them out to you, so that you would know them by their very persons. But God has concealed them, sparing them in the hope that they will repent, and you will know them from the substance and manner of their speech.

﴿Those are the ones whose hearts God knows.﴾ They went to seek judgment from the tyrant (al-taghut), and they went there because they knew they were not in the right, and because if they had gone to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) he would have judged with truth, and truth would harm and distress them. So were they really wanting goodness and reconciliation, or were they not wanting the truth? They wanted a falsified judgment.

Therefore the command comes from the Truth to His Messenger: ﴿So turn away from them﴾; for if you punish them, you have taken your right from them, and God wants your right to remain, so that He Himself, glory be to Him, may exact retribution for you from them. And turn away from them also because We want some of them to show, at every period, something that makes the community of faith alert to the fact that there are people infiltrated among them; therefore caution and vigilance are necessary. Moreover, if you turn away from them, you drop them from the account of your call.

"Admonish them" means: say to them, "Be ashamed of your deeds." ﴿And speak to them in their own souls a far-reaching word﴾ means: say to them a word that reaches the ultimate point in the human soul and reaches the ultimate point of admonition, that is, threaten them with a threat that frightens them so that it reaches their souls to a degree. Or ﴿speak to them in their own souls﴾ means: expose to them what they conceal, so that they know that God has made you aware of what is in their souls, and so they feel shame at their deed and do not do it. Say that to them without exposing them before the people, because not exposing them before the people leaves in them some measure of shame. Also, admonition has a good effect when the admonisher is in privacy with the one admonished, conversing with him and not disgracing him. Exposing the one admonished before people may arouse in him the instinct of obstinacy, but when you admonish him in secret he knows that you are still merciful toward him and still treat him with gentleness and kindness.

﴿Admonish them and speak to them in their own souls﴾: if you did that openly, you would be giving an example to others to do likewise. God has informed you of the disbelief in these people's hearts, but God does not inform anyone else of the unseen. If someone accuses another of a sin or disbelief, he may not hit upon the truth and reality. Our legislation tells us: "Avert the prescribed penalties (hudud) by doubts."

The application of this legislation is found when a thief is apprehended but there is doubt in the accusation. This doubt must be interpreted in favour of the accused, and we avert the prescribed penalty because of the doubt. For it is not in the interest of the Muslims to say every day: "We have cut off the hand of a thief or stoned an adulteress." But when crimes are exposed and there is no doubt in committing them and the matter is clear, then we must strike the hands of criminals. So we avert the penalty by doubt so as not to inflict harm or harm an innocent person, and we apply the penalty so that whoever is tempted by his soul toward a forbidden matter is deterred and does not commit the forbidden act. And when the penalty is enforced in any environment, it is only enforced for a short period, after which crimes recede, and no one sees a thief or an adulterer.

So God's words ﴿Admonish them and speak to them in their own souls a far-reaching word﴾ mean: say to them what threatens them with a threat that reaches to the depths of their souls; or ﴿speak to them in their own souls﴾ by uncovering the hidden defects of their faults; or speak to them in their own souls, between you and them, because this is more likely to make them accept it from you and not to embitter their hearts or arouse in them the instinct of obstinacy.

The purpose of the Truth sending the Messenger is that he teach people the law of God embodied in the method (manhaj), and that he guide them to the religion of truth. The method carries rules: do, and do not do. As for matters of life on which there is no "do" or "do not do," the human being is free to choose what suits him. No messenger brings obligations from himself; rather, obligations come by the permission of God, and he is not obeyed except by permission from God. The Messenger, peace and blessings of God be upon him, came with obedience to God, except where he is delegated by God in other matters. The Truth, glorified is He, has delegated His Messenger, peace and blessings of God be upon him, by His true saying: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ (part of verse 7, Surah al-Hashr).

So the believers in the message of Muhammad, peace and blessings of God be upon him, are obliged to obey the Messenger within the scope of what God has delegated, and God has permitted him to legislate.

The Truth continues: ﴿And if they, when they had wronged themselves, had come to you and asked forgiveness of God, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found God Accepting of repentance, Merciful﴾. Wronging oneself is to fulfil a immediate desire that will bequeath lasting misery. Wronging oneself is the most wretched kind of wrong. It is reasonable for a person to wrong another, but for him to wrong himself is not reasonable. Any sinner who abandons an obligatory duty and turns to a forbidden matter may think, on the surface, that he is achieving pleasure for himself, while in fact he is wronging himself with harsh wrong. So the one who abandons prayer and becomes lax, or drinks wine, or commits any act of disobedience, we say to him: you have wronged yourself, because you supposed that you were achieving pleasure for yourself, whereas you have bequeathed to it a misery more severe, more lasting and more enduring, and you are not trustworthy over yourself.

The self (nafs), as we know, refers to the union of the spirit (ruh) with matter (madda), and this union is what gives the human self the attribute of tranquillity, or the attribute of commanding to evil, or the attribute of self-reproach (al-nafs al-lawwamah). At the moment the spirit comes together with matter, the human self comes into being. The spirit, before it is joined to matter, is good by its nature, and matter, before it is joined to the spirit, is good by its nature; matter is subdued to the will of its subduer and does everything it is asked. So beware of saying: "the material life and the spiritual life, and this is such and such." No.

Matter in its absolute sense is good, obedient, subservient, worshipful, glorifying. The spirit in its absolute sense is likewise. So when does corruption come? At the moment the spirit meets matter and this interaction occurs, we say: O you who are accountable, will you be at peace with the judgment of God and the matter is ended, or will your self remain self-reproaching, or will you grow accustomed to disobedience and your self become commanding to evil?

So who, then, wrongs? It is your desire in opposing (the command) that wrongs the whole self, of its spirit and its matter. You, on the surface, achieve a desire for yourself by opposing, but in reality you exhaust yourself. ﴿And if they, when they had wronged themselves﴾. Let us know that there is a difference between a person committing an abomination to achieve a desire for himself, and his wronging himself. The Truth says: ﴿And those who, when they commit an abomination or wrong themselves, remember God and ask forgiveness for their sins — and who forgives sins except God?﴾ (part of verse 135, Surah Al 'Imran).

So committing an abomination is one thing and wronging oneself is another. The one who commits an abomination has given his self a little enjoyment, but how much he has wronged himself by doing that. He has not given it pleasure, nor has he left it in its state; thus he has wronged himself. He has not given it a worldly desire, and he has not spared it from the punishment of the Hereafter. For example, the false witness who testifies so that one person takes another's right: this is harsh wrong to the self, and for this reason the Messenger said:

(Hasten to good deeds before trials come like pieces of the dark night: a man will be a believer in the morning and a disbeliever by evening, or a believer by evening and a disbeliever in the morning, selling his religion for a worldly commodity.)(1)

﴿And if they, when they had wronged themselves, had come to you and asked forgiveness of God﴾. Wronging oneself also includes a person bringing his case before the tyrant (taghut), for example. But when a person brings his case before the ruler, you do not know whether he will judge for us or not; and perhaps God will guide him at the moment of judgment.
