Of course not, for there were disbelievers seeking any gap through which to attack. Then the Qur'an pierces the veil of the future time, which happens while the Muslims cannot protect themselves, and the Truth says: ﴿The multitude will be routed and will turn their backs﴾ (54:45).

Even 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "What multitude is this?" The Qur'an was revealed with verses that are recited, recorded and memorised. Then the Battle of Badr came, and the multitude was indeed routed. Another verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, the tyrant and slanderer: ﴿We will brand him upon the snout﴾ (68:16).

Some of them asked: can we reach it? Then the Battle of Badr came, and they looked at his nose and found that the sword had gashed it and left a mark and sign upon it. So who pierced the veil of the future time? It is God, not Muhammad. If you reflect on these matters with true reflection, you would know that Muhammad is only a conveyor of the Qur'an, and that the One who spoke the Qur'an is the God who has no past, no present, and no future, for all time belongs to Him. And the Qur'an comes saying: ﴿And they say to themselves, "Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?"﴾ (58:8, part).

They said it to themselves and no one heard them. Then the Qur'an was revealed and informed of what they had said to themselves. So what would they say then? And had they reflected upon the Qur'an they would have known that the Almighty and Exalted is the One who informed the Messenger of Allah of what they said within themselves. Thus this verse ﴿Will they not then reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ came after ﴿when they depart from you, a group of them plans other than what you say﴾; so they were exposed. Had they been reflecting, they would have known that Allah, who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, is the One who informed him of what they plotted. Those who do not understand the language rejoice at a supposed contradiction they imagined exists in the Qur'an, saying: a single event attributed to a single agent is not negated at one time and affirmed at another; if you negate it, you do not affirm it, and if you affirm it, you do not negate it. But the Qur'an contains exactly this.

This was made to appear to them in the saying of the Truth: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but it was Allah who threw﴾ (8:17, part).

And ﴿and you did not throw﴾ is n

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 4, verse 83:

Allah, glorified and exalted, trains the community of faith in a manner that secures and protects the secrecy of its movements, especially since they are a people about to face a fierce struggle and have formidable enemies. So He trains them to handle their affairs with wisdom in order to confront spies. He says: ﴿And when there comes to them a matter﴾. That is, when news of a matter reaches them concerning the believing people or their adversaries. For example, they hear that the Prophet (peace be upon him) is going out on an expedition (sariyya, a small military detachment) to such-and-such area, and that the tribe of so-and-so is waiting for him in order to join him. When the weak hypocrites hear this news, they spread it. Then the enemies take precautions by besieging the tribe that promised the Messenger to fight with him, so that it will not go out. Or they say, for instance: "The Prophet will go out to do such-and-such," and they also spread this news! So Allah clarifies for them: Do not do this with any news that concerns you as a group bound to a method (manhaj) that you want to prevail, because this method has adversaries.

Beware of hearing a matter and spreading it before presenting it to the commander and to those whom the commander regards as the people of counsel in it. His saying ﴿a matter of security﴾ means that the matter is in their favour, ﴿or fear﴾, that is, from their enemy, ﴿they spread it﴾.

The expression "adhA'ahu" (he made it known) differs from "adhA'a bihi" (he spread it, with the preposition bi). "Adha'ahu" means "he said it." But "adha'a bihi" indicates that he tells the news to everyone he meets. The news itself spreads itself: there is a matter you relate and the matter ends, whereas with "adha'a bihi" the spreading accompanies the news and clings to it, publishing it and bringing it out from a limited circle into an unlimited one, or from ears that respect the privacy of the news into ears that pursue it. Then He says: ﴿But if they had referred it to the Messenger﴾. The Messenger, or those whom the Messenger (peace be upon him) designates, are the ones entitled to decide what may be said and what may not: ﴿those of them who draw conclusions would have known it﴾. The word istinbat (drawing out a conclusion or inference) is derived from "al-nabT," which is the appearance of a thing after it was hidden. "Istanbata" means he extracted water while striving for it, and "al-nabT" is the first water that emerges when a well is dug. The word was then transferred from the sensory realm of water to the abstract realm of news, and we came to use it for meanings and for sciences as well. For example, you give a student a geometry exercise and give him its data, and then the student takes the data and says: since such-and-such equals such-and-such, such-and-such results. He derives from what exists something that did not exist.

Here Allah clarifies for them: if you hear a matter related to security or a matter related to fear, beware of spreading it before presenting it to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him), or to those in authority whom the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) decided should have some of the authority over it, because they are the ones who draw conclusions: whether this should be said or should not be said.

Allah says: ﴿And if not for the favour of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan, except a few﴾. It is as if they had spread some events that occurred, but they were saved from them by a favour from Allah, glorified and exalted, and some of His inspirations. Among what they spread was what happened when the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) resolved to go to Mecca as a conqueror. Whenever the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) intended a campaign (ghazwa), he would feign (wara) by mentioning another destination, that is, he would not state the true destination, so as to catch the enemy unawares. When the enemy is caught unawares, they are unprepared, and that causes them to lose the ability to resist.

Consider the mercy shown in the events of the Conquest campaign. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) ordered the Muslims to prepare for the campaign against Mecca, so that when the people of Mecca saw that the Messenger of Allah had come to them with troops they could not withstand, they would submit and surrender and not fight, and this was a mercy to them. Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a had heard of this and wrote a letter to the Quraysh in Mecca. A woman took it, mounted her camel and set off. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) sent for Ali and those with him and said: "There is a woman at Rawdat Khakh with a letter from Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a to the Quraysh informing them of our coming to Mecca." So they went to the camel-riding woman (zaina), and she denied it. Then Sayyiduna Ali threatened her and took the letter out of her braids (‘aqas), that is, from the locks of her hair. It was a letter from Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a to the Quraysh. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) summoned Hatib and said to him: "Is this your letter?" He said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "What prompted you to do this?" He said: "By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, I know that Allah is supporting you, and that my letter will neither advance nor delay anything. I am a man attached to the Quraysh; I was not one of them by origin, and I have no tribal kinship with them, but I have a son and family among them, so I wanted to do them a favour with the Quraysh, by which they would protect my kin. I did not do this out of disbelief, nor apostasy from my religion, nor out of contentment with disbelief after Islam." The Prophet said: "You have spoken the truth."

Thus Allah, glorified and exalted, wants to build the matters of faith, especially what concerns the believers and their enemies, upon truthfulness. It is not right for each person to spread whatever he hears. Rather, they must refer such talk to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) and to those in authority, because they are the ones who derive what suits their circumstances. Perhaps they will permit you to say something, or they will permit something else, if the matter of war and deception requires that. This shows that Allah, glorified and exalted, although He has guaranteed them victory and dominance and made clear: "I am the Guardian, I am the One who gives victory, so do not fear them," still wants the believers to take the means, and to rely on Him while acknowledging that He is the Helper.

﴿And if not for the favour of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan, except a few﴾. This shows that this matter did occur among them, but the favour of Allah was what supported and protected them, so He did not allow this matter to have a consequence or outcome that would harm them. ﴿And if not for the favour of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan, except a few﴾. We know that whenever a verb occurs, an exception following it is also possible. So we look: is this exception from the subject (the doer) or from the verb (the act)? Here we find His saying: ﴿you would have followed Satan, except a few﴾. Was following Satan a few instances, meaning that Satan was followed by a few, while many did not follow him? Do we look at the fewness in the act or in the one who performs the act? If we look at the fewness in the act, the meaning is: "you would have followed Satan only with a small following, in which you would be guided by the matter of innate nature (fitra)." If you want the fewness to be in the agent: ﴿you would have followed Satan, except a few﴾, that is, except a small group among you whose innate nature remained sound, so they would not follow Satan.

It is established that before Allah sent and dispatched the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him), some people sat to reflect on the state of the Jahiliyya with its worship of idols and images, and it did not please them or appeal to them. Some of them turned away from it entirely, and some went to seek this knowledge from its sources in other lands. Such were Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, Waraqa ibn Nawfal, who did not accept everything that was presented to him, Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, and Qiss ibn Sa'ida. All of these, by their innate nature, were guided to the conclusion that the things the Jahiliyya was upon were not valid, and that it was not fitting for the Arabs to remain upon them. These were a few, and they were called the hanifs, and many of them had worshipped idols. Then Allah honoured them with the mission of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him).

So the saying of Allah: ﴿And if not for the favour of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan, except a few﴾ means that because Allah, glorified and exalted, by His favour and mercy, will not leave any room for Satan in some matters, rather He exposes Satan's scheme with the hypocrites. When the scheme of Satan is exposed among the hypocrites, He leads you to the side of truth, away from Satan, and this process is part of the favour and mercy of Allah.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 4, verse 84:

After that, the Truth (al-Haqq), glory be to Him, addresses our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying:

﴿So fight in the way of Allah; you are not held responsible except for yourself. And urge the believers. Perhaps Allah will restrain the violence of those who disbelieve. And Allah is more severe in might and more severe in punishment.﴾ [4:84]

When you see a sentence containing the fa' (the particle "fa"), know that it is a consequence (musabbab) of something before it. When you hear, for example, the saying of the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted is He: ﴿Then He caused him to die and then buried him﴾ [80:21] (Surat Abasa).

The meaning of that is that the burial came after the death. So when you find the "fa", know that what precedes it is the cause of what follows it, and they call it "fa' of causation" (fa' al-sababiyyah).

So what was before this verse, such that the causation would follow from it in the saying of Allah, glory be to Him, to our master, the Messenger of Allah: ﴿So fight in the way of Allah; you are not held responsible except for yourself﴾? We say: since the command came as "fa-qatil" (so fight), we must search for the earlier verses about fighting. Did He not say before this verse: ﴿So let those fight in the way of Allah who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter. And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed or overcomes, We will give him a great reward﴾ [4:74] (Surat an-Nisa').

And the second verse: ﴿And what is [wrong] with you that you fight not in the way of Allah and for the oppressed among men and women﴾ (part of 4:75, Surat an-Nisa').

So the command to fight exists from Allah for whom? For the Messenger of Allah. And the Messenger conveys this command to the believers in Him, and the Messenger hears it from Allah once. Therefore he (ﷺ) is the first to affirm the command of Allah in His saying: ﴿So let those fight in the way of Allah﴾. Then he conveys it to the believers, and whoever believes is one who affirms the Messenger of Allah in this command. So the Messenger is the first to be acted upon by the Qur'an. When the Truth says: ﴿So let those fight in the way of Allah who sell the life of this world﴾ (part of 4:74, Surat an-Nisa'),

or when the Truth says to him: ﴿And what is [wrong] with you that you fight not in the way of Allah﴾ (part of 4:75, Surat an-Nisa').

Since the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is the first to act upon the commands of Allah, when the command comes to him he must first bind himself to it, even if no one listens to him, even if no one believes in it, or no one follows him. This is evidence that he is certain of what was said to him: ﴿And what is [wrong] with you that you fight not in the way of Allah﴾. And since the Messenger (ﷺ) is the first to act, he must first apply it to himself; because by his turning to fighting alone, he shows to whoever hears the Qur'an that the Messenger to whom this Qur'an was revealed is the first to affirm it, and Muhammad will not deceive himself. So before he commands the believers to fight, he himself fights alone. For this reason we find that our master Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed to the Highest Companion and the apostasy (riddah) occurred among some Arabs, and the Caliph of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) insisted on fighting the apostates, and said: "If they withheld from me a cord (iqal) of a camel which they used to pay to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I would fight them over it with the sword." Some of the Companions tried to turn Abu Bakr al-Siddiq from his resolve, and he said: "By Allah, if my right hand refused to fight them, I would fight them with my left."

So the saying of Allah to His Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿So fight in the way of Allah﴾ alerts us that there is a difference between conveying (al-balagh) and the one conveyed to carrying it out. Since the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has heard from Allah, he is obliged to apply the act first, and after that the Messenger conveys it to the believers, and whoever listens to him acts accordingly.

And the saying of the Truth: ﴿you are not held responsible except for yourself﴾ is a responsibility for the action, not for conveying only. The Messenger conveys, but whether the believers do what he conveyed to them from Allah or do not do it is not his concern, nor is he charged with it. Rather, the Messenger must bind and charge himself to fight in the way of Allah. ﴿So fight in the way of Allah; you are not held responsible except for yourself﴾.

Does that mean that the Messenger leaves those who believed in him to their own selves? No. The Truth has made it clear: you must also urge them to fight, so do not leave them to themselves: ﴿And urge the believers. Perhaps Allah will restrain the violence of those who disbelieve﴾. The meaning of "urge" (harrid) is derived from "al-harad", which is that by which obstacles are removed, and that which cleans the hands and clothes of the filth and dirt that stain and cover them. So O Messenger of Allah, you must look into the affair of your companions and followers, and know why they do not want to fight, and you must shake off from them the hindrances and remove the obstacles that prevent them from fighting.

﴿And urge the believers. Perhaps Allah will restrain the violence of those who disbelieve﴾. It is as if the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted is He, wants to say to His Messenger: You are not supported by the multitude of those who believe in you; rather the believers are a veil for the hand of Allah in victory. Victory is from Him, glory be to Him: ﴿And victory is only from Allah﴾ [3:126] (Surat Al 'Imran).

The word "ba's" (violence, might) in the verse under discussion is intended to mean strength and severity in war, and it is intended to mean guile, and it is intended to mean the defeat of the enemies. The word "ba's" contains meanings of human capacity: "How can I fight these alone, when the believing people are with you? If they enter the fighting, they do not support you, but they veil the hand of Allah in victory": ﴿Fight them; Allah will punish them by your hands﴾ [9:14] (Surat at-Tawbah).

Why does Allah not give victory to the believers and the Messenger directly, without fighting against others of the disbelievers and polytheists? Because if victory came through an unseen cause from the Truth, they might say it was a natural phenomenon that had arisen. But the Truth wants to show that the small believing group was the one that prevailed. The believer turns to the causes but does not forget the Causer. When the Muslims looked only to causes at Hunayn, and some of them said: "We will not be defeated for lack of numbers, for we are many," then the Muslims tasted the taste of defeat first, and after Allah had given them the disciplinary lesson first, He gave them victory second. The Truth says: ﴿And [recall] the day of Hunayn, when your large numbers pleased you, but they availed you nothing﴾ [9:25] (Surat at-Tawbah).

This is a reminder to the believers that they should be with the causes but always remember the Causer, because causes come only to establish that Allah is with the believers. If the believers had won by some other unseen cause, the enemies would have said: "What happened is the product of a natural phenomenon." The difference between a natural phenomenon and a material phenomenon in the adversaries is what happened to our master Abraham, peace be upon him. The Truth did not merely intend to rescue Abraham from the fire, for if the matter were so, He would not have allowed Abraham's enemies to seize him. And if Allah had done that, Abraham's enemies would have said: "Oh, if only we had caught him," and that would have been an opportunity for their disbelief.

But the Truth caused them to seize Abraham, peace be upon him, and left the fire blazing, and He, glory be to Him, cut off the causes: ﴿We said: O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham﴾ [21:69] (Surat al-Anbiya').

This is the decisive refutation. If Abraham's rescue had come by any other way, through unseen, non-material matters that are not perceived by the senses, Abraham's opponents would have found excuses to justify their defeat.

Therefore the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted is He, makes clear to His Messenger: O Muhammad, I am the One who sent you, and I did not leave you to the support of those who believe in you. I am capable of supporting you alone without anything. But I wanted your nation, which believed in you, to receive the blessing of faith in you, so that some of it would be martyred, and the nation would be rewarded, and would prevail, and its stature would rise above the Arabs. For if the matter had been limited to the victory of the Messenger of Allah, Allah would have granted him victory without war or jihad.

The saying of the Truth, glory be to Him: ﴿Perhaps Allah will restrain the violence of those who disbelieve, and Allah is more severe in might and more severe in punishment﴾ means that He, glory be to Him, is capable of halting and preventing the war and the plotting of the disbelievers, nullifying it and defeating them. And this is what happened: after the battle of Uhud, whose outcome was inconclusive, and no one can determine who was victorious in it and who was defeated, because the Messenger of Allah had first prevailed, then the archers disobeyed the Messenger's command, so a breach occurred in the ranks of the Muslim fighters. But the fighters from Quraysh did not remain in the place of the battle, nor did they go beyond it into the city of Madinah; therefore the battle of Uhud did not end in victory for either side. After that they threatened that the appointment would be at Badr al-Sughra in the coming year.

The year passed, the appointed time came, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wanted to go out. When he called for going out, he found reluctance among the people, and only seventy men obeyed him, and they went out to the appointed place. They demonstrated that they were not afraid of the situation, and Allah cast terror into the heart of Abu Sufyan and his people, so they did not come out. So our Lord is able to restrain the violence of those who disbelieve; the Messenger of Allah remained at the place, sat with the fighters, and they had merchandise with them, which they sold, and the Muslims gained much of this merchandise.

﴿Perhaps Allah will restrain the violence of those who disbelieve, and Allah is more severe in might and more severe in punishment﴾. The word "'asa" (perhaps) in the language takes multiple forms. "'Asa" in the language means hope, as when one says: "Perhaps so-and-so will come," that is: "I hope so-and-so will come." Or one says to his companion: "Perhaps so-and-so will bring you some good." This is a hope that so-and-so will come to so-and-so with some good, and so-and-so may bring good or may not, but the hope has been expressed.

And one may say to his companion: "Perhaps I will bring you some good." Here the hope is stronger, because in the first case the hope is in the hand of someone other than the speaker, whereas the good here is in the hand of the speaker. But can the speaker guarantee that he will have the power and the means to bring good to the one he is addressing?

Truly, he intends it, but he cannot guarantee that he will have the ability.

If someone says: "Perhaps Allah will bring you relief," this is the furthest in hope. But is the one who says it certain that Allah will answer this hope? Allah may answer and may not, according to the will of Allah, not according to the standards of the one who hopes or the one for whom hope is expressed. But when the Truth says of Himself: ﴿Perhaps Allah will restrain the violence of those who disbelieve﴾, this is the utmost statement reaching the ends of all hopes. So "'asa", in its various stages, reaches its peak when the Truth says it.

Thus we see the stages of "'asa". When someone says: "Perhaps so-and-so will do you some good," this is a first stage of hope. When someone says: "Perhaps I will bring you some good," this is a stronger stage of hope, for a person may love to bring good but circumstances may prevent him. When someone says: "Perhaps Allah will do such-and-such," this is a stronger stage still, because the good is attributed to the Supreme Power, though Allah may or may not answer that hope.

And the strongest of all is when Allah says of Himself: ﴿Perhaps Allah will restrain the violence of those who disbelieve﴾.

With respect to Allah, "'asa" is a realized hope, because it is an encouragement from Almighty Allah, and His encouragement necessarily comes to pass, for He, glory be to Him, is the One who urges us and drives us to hope for His grace, because He is Generous. He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Perhaps Allah will restrain the violence of those who disbelieve, and Allah is more severe in might and more severe in punishment﴾, because the people of might among creatures are people of changing states; the strong among them may weaken or be struck with some fear so that their bones loosen. But the Giver of the act and the Giver of strength to His creatures is the One capable of acting, so He is the Most Severe in might, and He, glory be to Him, is most severe in punishment.

Whenever a person hears anything from the root "n-k-l", he must know that it is derived from "al-nakl", which is the shackle. When a ruler, for example, inflicts punishment on one who commits a crime, and the person who sees this punishment fears committing a similar crime, the ruler has shackled them with the punishment he inflicted on the first criminal, so that they would not do what he did. For this reason it is said on the tongues of rulers: "I will make an example (nakalan) of so-and-so." That is, the speaker will punish so-and-so in such a way that he becomes a lesson to whoever sees him, so that he never commits a crime like it, out of fear that the punishment that was inflicted on, and befell, the one who committed the crime will befall him.

So tankil (exemplary punishment), nakal and nakl all return to the shackle that prevents a person from moving toward the crime, or a shackle that prevents a person from returning to the crime he committed first, or that this shackle, which is the punishment with which the criminal was punished, stands before people warning them against falling into it, so that its penalty and exemplary deterrence do not overtake them.

Indeed the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted is He, when He created creatures and distributed among them the bounties of gifts, no single one of them has gathered all...

If one of us is endowed with a gift, let him share his gift with another, until the two become a pair (shaf'an), and thereby the saying of the Truth applies to him:

﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession will have a share in it, and whoever intercedes with an evil intercession will bear a portion of it. And Allah is ever Controller over all things.﴾ [4:85]

What is the good intercession (al-shafa'a al-hasana)? Those from the countryside know the matter of "al-shufʻa" (pre-emption) in custom. It is said: "So-and-so took this land by pre-emption (bi-l-shufʻa)," meaning that after he owned one piece of land, he bought the adjacent piece so that it would join his land. Instead of having one piece of land, he now had two.

When someone comes to buy a piece of land, the neighbour who owns the adjoining land says: "I will enter by pre-emption," meaning that he has the greater right to own the land. Thus the meaning of "yashfaʻ" (he intercedes/pairs) is that he transfers the effect of his gift to another of his fellow believers, and for this he will have a share in it.

The good intercession is mediation by word in securing for a person a worldly or otherworldly benefit, or deliverance from harm, and it is without return. So each person who has a gift must join himself to one who lacks it. Having been a single unit in himself, he becomes a pair. That is why it is said: "So-and-so will intercede for me with so-and-so," meaning that he will add his voice to the voice of the one who seeks his help. The Almighty, in what our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), related, said that Allah said to our master David: "A man does one deed by which I will make him a judge in Paradise."

That is, a man performs a certain deed, and Allah bestows upon him the favour of distributing the places in Paradise among individuals, as if he were an agent in Paradise: he does not take a dwelling for himself only, but also disposes in the granting of dwellings. David asked: "O Lord, and who is that?" He, glorified be He, said: "A believer who strives to fulfil the need of his brother, who wishes that it be fulfilled, whether it is fulfilled or not."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever walks to fulfil the need of his brother and succeeds in it, it is better for him than seclusion (iʻtikaf) for ten years. And whoever keeps seclusion for one day seeking the Face of Allah, Allah will place between him and the Fire three trenches, each farther than the distance between the two horizons."

This is because the servant who strives to fulfil the need of his brother has discharged the right of Allah's blessing in what He has bestowed upon him, and as a result he does not become resentful of or harbour spite against the one who has the gift, though he lacks it. Thus He removes spite from the soul of the one without the gift toward the one who has it. For the one without the gift says: "The gift of so-and-so benefits me too," so he loves its continuance and its growth in his possession.

The Truth says: ﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession will have a share in it.﴾ Then the Truth gives the counterpart. He, glorified be He, does not legislate only for the righteous; He sets out encouragement for the righteous and warning for the wicked, saying: ﴿And whoever intercedes with an evil intercession will bear a portion of it.﴾

Let us observe the difference between the word "naṣīb" (share) and the word "kifl" (portion). The word "naṣīb" often comes with the meaning of good. When someone says, "You have a share (naṣīb) in my wealth," this saying suits any proportion of wealth. But the word "kifl" is a portion proportionate to the evil only. This is a bounty from Allah: whoever brings a good deed has ten times its like, and this is a great share. Whoever brings an evil deed will be recompensed only with its like.

This verse came after the Prophet had urged the believers to fight; that is, you, O Messenger of Allah, are required to gather to yourself people who will fight with you, and that is a good intercession from which they will gain a great share and abundant reward.

As for the Truth's saying ﴿whoever intercedes with an evil intercession will bear a portion of it⦆, meaning he will have a part of it, that is, the ill-omen of the evil deed will befall him. As for the great reward for the good deed, it leads to the diffusion of people's gifts to all people. And as long as people's gifts are shared with everyone, society becomes mutually supportive rather than hostile, and everyone becomes cooperative and pure of heart. When one sees a blessing with his brother, he says: "A day will come when the best of this blessing will come to me."

That is why we have said: whoever wishes that the blessings of others would come to him should love the blessings in their owners' possession. For if you, O believer, love a blessing in its owner's possession, its good will come to you while you sit. And if you are deprived of the effects of a blessing that Allah has bestowed on someone else, then examine your heart regarding your love for the blessing in his possession. You may find yourself afflicted with some jealousy of it, or hating the blessing in his possession, so the blessing becomes, as it were, jealous on behalf of its owner, and says to the one who hates it: "You will never draw near to me, nor will you attain my good."

The Truth concludes the verse: ﴿And Allah is ever Controller over all things (kāna Allāhu ʻalā kulli shay'in muqītā).﴾ This statement comes after the good intercession and the evil intercession, and in it is a warning to all servants: beware lest any of you think that there is something, however small, that escapes the reckoning of Allah. Nothing of a good deed will be lost, and nothing of an evil deed will be wasted. Scholars have written extensive discussions on the word "muqīt" (controller). One scholar said regarding its meaning: "The Truth is a witness." Another said: ﴿Indeed, the Truth is a reckoner (ḥasīb)﴾. A third said: "Muqīt means the giver of sustenance (qūt)." A fourth said: "It means the Guardian (ḥafīẓ)," and a fifth said: "It means the Watcher (raqīb)."

We say to all of them: there is no need for dispute on this matter. There is a difference between explaining a word by one of its necessary implications, and such implications may be many. Each of these meanings may be correct, but the comprehensive meaning is the one that comes from the root of the word itself. "Muqīt" derives from "qāta," meaning he gave him sustenance (qūt). Why does He give them sustenance? To preserve their lives. So He is "muqīt" in the sense that He, glorified be He, gives sustenance so that a human being remains alive. He observes him, so the creature is never absent from its Creator for a moment. And since He gives a human being sustenance according to his need, He is "ḥasīb" (reckoner). And since He watches the conduct of a human being, He recompenses him.

Thus all these meanings are interwoven and implicate one another. Therefore we do not say that the scholars disagreed about this meaning; rather, let us say that each scholar noticed an aspect of the word. The one who noticed the original sense of sustenance is correct, for none gives original sustenance except one who constantly watches over His servants; so He is "Shahīd" (witness), and none gives anyone sustenance unless He is in charge of his affairs, so He is "Ḥasīb" (reckoner). And He does not sustain only human beings; He sustains all His creation. He sustains animals and inspires them to eat a certain kind of food and not to eat another kind.

When we see the scholars looking at "muqīt" from different angles, they are all correct, whether they took it to mean sustenance, or preservation, or power, or observation, or reckoning. Each one looked at a necessary implication of the word "muqīt," and He, glorified be He, sustains everything: He sustains the human being, the animal, the inanimate, and the plant.

Botanists explain this. We plant seeds, and the roots of plants absorb nutrients from the soil. Before a plant has roots, it takes its nourishment from the two cotyledons of the seed, which contain the food, until a root grows for it. After the root of the plant grows, the two cotyledons become two leaves. And He, glorified be He, is Controller over all things. The scientists further say that nutrition is absorbed by the plant through the property of capillary tubes (al-anābīb al-shaʻriyya). That is, the plant draws nourishment from the soil through the fine roots that absorb water in which nutrients are dissolved. The opening of a capillary tube holds only the size of a hair, and when it is placed in a vessel the liquid rises in it, and the water rises above the level of the basin; and when the pressures of air on the surfaces of the water are balanced, the water does not rise.

An example of this: when we bring coloured water and place it in a vessel, and place capillary tubes in the vessel, the coloured liquid rises into the capillary tubes, and no tube takes one substance and leaves another; rather, all the tubes take the same substance. But the hairs of the plant take from the soil what is suitable for them and leave what is unsuitable. Botanists call this "natural selection" (al-intikhāb al-ṭabīʻī). Yet "intikhāb" means choice, and choice requires a mind that thinks and weighs, and a plant has no mind. Therefore they should have said "divine selection," for nature has no mind; rather, it is governed by a Wise One who possesses absolute knowledge, wisdom, and self-subsistence.

He, glorified be He, says about this: ﴿Watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit. Surely in that are signs for a people who reason.﴾ [13:4]

So pepper takes the substance that gives it pungency, cane takes the substance that makes its sweetness, and pomegranate takes the acidic substance. This is divine selection.

﴿And Allah is ever Controller over all things.﴾ When you hear ﴿kāna Allāh﴾, beware of imagining that "kāna" here has a sense of time. When we say of humans "Zayd was rich (kāna Zaydun ghaniyyan)," Zayd is subject to change and his wealth may depart. But when we say ﴿kāna Allāh﴾, we are saying ﴿Allah was and still is﴾, because what was and changes is what is subject to change. He is the One who changes and is not changed; He exists from eternity to eternity. When He, glorified be He, made the intercession clear to us and commanded that each of us extend his gifts to others, so that the capacities of society support one another, this is because it multiplies the benefit for the believing servant and increases it for everyone.

The Almighty then says:

﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet back with one better than it, or return it. Indeed, Allah is ever Accountable over all things.﴾ (4:86)

Here the Truth (al-Haqq) wishes to refine the meaning of life (hayah). What is the meaning of "hayitum" (you are greeted)? The surface-level understanding of it is this: if someone greets you and says, "Peace be upon you," you must return the greeting. The Arabs of old used to say, "Hayaaka Allah" (may Allah give you life). After Islam came, greeting at meeting became "peace": ﴿Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be, "Peace."﴾ (33:44). Or as the Truth said in another place: ﴿So greet one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good.﴾ (24:61).

Let us understand the word "hayaaka." Its root is the letters "ḥāʼ" and "yāʼān," and from it comes the word "ḥayāh" (life), from which our life comes. If we look at life, it may take a superficial meaning among people, which is what gave rise to sensation and movement, the first phenomenon in us, and then in animals. If you deepen your understanding, you will find that the word "life" encompasses all kinds of existence, even inanimate matter. But man only recognizes life in its sensory and kinetic manifestation, while every creature has a life that suits it.

When they taught us the science of magnetism in school, we would observe the experiment of the magnet. We would bring a magnetic rod, then bring iron filings, and pass the rod over them in one direction, so that the particles would be arranged in a way that corresponds to the direction of magnetism in the iron rod. This rod, which we see as a solid substance, contains atoms, beyond human perception, that adapt by a movement specific to them, and the negative and positive ones are rearranged, and no observer has the ability to perceive their movement.

So that the teachers could bring this closer to the minds of the students, they brought a glass tube and placed iron filings in it, and brought the magnetized rod and moved it alongside the filings. The students saw the filings jumping about until they settled. Here the students learn that non-magnetized iron filings, when the magnetized rod passes over them in one direction, have their particles arranged on a clear basis until they become magnetized.

This is evidence from the senses: the negatives have turned to one side and the positives to another. The magnetic rod has movement, but we do not perceive its sensation or its motion because we do not possess the instruments necessary for that.

Another example: suppose we are moving, and an airplane comes from above us and takes a photograph of us. When they take the picture up close, they see the movement. But the further the airplane moves away, the less we see the movement, until it becomes a distant point, as though it were stationary. It is not stationary; rather it is moving in a manner so subtle that it cannot be perceived. Thus everything has a particular life that suits it, and everything has its own particular sensation and movement. When we come to the Qur'an, we see how it addressed this matter, saying: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face.﴾ (28:88).

The verse made an exception: "His Face," meaning His Essence. Everything other than Him is perishing.

The meaning of "perishing" (hālik) is that there is no life in it. Since everything perishes, this is evidence that in everything there is life, until the permission comes from the Truth that life is removed from everything except His Face, glorified is He. Someone may ask: who said that the word "perishing" means there is no life in it? We say: when the Qur'an addresses a matter, it does not divide knowledge into chapters; rather, in each verse it places a particular point that explains to us what was hidden from us in another particular point, so that we understand that the Qur'an is complete. The Truth says: ﴿That whoever perishes may perish upon clear evidence, and whoever lives may live upon clear evidence.﴾ (8:42). Thus perishing is the opposite of life.

If we look at the manufactured goods we make, such as plastic for example, we make from it containers for washing or other uses. When we first buy one for use, we find it bright in color, but after using it for a while, its shine disappears and it becomes pale in color. What happened to it? It has changed. What caused the change? It is said: use, sunlight, and other things. So it has sensation, because it was affected, and movement, because it changed. Likewise precious stones, marble, and granite, and others, whose age is estimated in hundreds of years and sometimes thousands of years, and whenever their age lengthens their color changes due to life and interactions.

When we hold a sheet of paper and place it under the microscope, we see an immense number of small chambers, countless in number. And the believer says: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators.﴾ (23:14).

So everything in existence has a life that suits it. If you survey it and follow it carefully, and you are able to produce the instruments that deduce and help perception, you will see the movement and witness it with the senses.

However, life with respect to the noblest kind, which is man, who benefits from every living creature in the universe, is a life that ends at an unknown time for man but known to Allah. Allah wished to assign him a duty: if he listens to it and carries it out, He, glorified is He, will give him a life that does not end. When we measure the life that does not end against the life that ends, which of them is worthy of being called life? It is the other life, which does not end. Therefore the Truth says: ﴿And indeed, the Last Abode is the true life, if they only knew.﴾ (29:64).

This is the true life. Otherwise, what is the value of this worldly life, in which calamities, pains, disturbances, illnesses, and diseases threaten you, and which then ends? The Truth clarifies: take a life that is neither cut off nor forbidden. This is life in truth. Therefore, when the Truth addressed this matter, He made clear: beware that you think this worldly life is what I want for you. I want for you a life more enduring than this. For this reason He said: ﴿Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life.﴾ (8:24).

He is addressing them, then, as living by the commonly recognized law, and that if they do not respond to what the Truth and the Messenger call them to, they will not attain a higher form of life, which is a life not threatened by calamities, burdens, diseases, or annihilation. It is the true life. That is why the Truth names it "the Spirit" (rūḥ), because it moves the body and gives it life, even though that life ends. He says: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My Spirit.﴾ (38:72). This is the first stage of the life granted to both the believer and the disbeliever. And the greater life, which does not end, the Truth also calls "a spirit": ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit from Our command.﴾ (42:52). This is the one that will give the higher life. The first is called "spirit," giving a perishable life. The second is also "spirit": it is what Allah revealed, because when people act upon it they live an everlasting life free from misery and turbidity. So His saying ﴿when He calls you to that which gives you life﴾ is a call to everlasting life, and the eternal blissful life in the Hereafter is contingent upon a person adhering to Allah's way in his life, even though this life is finite.

In the worldly life, a person sees changes, illnesses, and agitations. When someone comes to him who reassures him and removes from him anxiety and fear, it is as though he has improved his life. The phrase "Hayaaka Allah" or "Peace be upon you" means: "Be secure and at rest." Otherwise, what is the value of life without security and tranquility?

Thus "Hayaaka Allah" or "Peace be upon you" means security and tranquility for you. You do not know whether the one who approaches you brings good or evil, but when he says, "Peace be upon you," this greeting may place security in the heart of the one addressed, and he feels the worth of his life.

So the Truth's saying ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet back with one better than it, or return it﴾ means: when your life has been granted a greeting, which is peace, and which guarantees security and tranquility for you, return the greeting. The word "taḥiyyah" (greeting) gives value to life, and likewise the word "ḥayyū" (greet) means: give the one before you some of a stable, secure, and tranquil life. Life without security and without tranquility is no life at all.

The Arab poet says:
"It is not one who has died and found rest in death;
rather, the dead one is the dead among the living."

So the Truth's saying ﴿When you are greeted﴾ means: when your life has been blessed with security and peace, ﴿greet back with one better than it, or return it﴾ means: you must return it, either with its equivalent or with something better. When the scholars came to speak about this, they restricted the matter to greetings at meeting. So if someone says to you, "Peace be upon you," say to him, "And upon you be peace and the mercy of Allah," meaning that you add to what he said.

On the authority of Salman al-Farisi, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said, "Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah." He said, "And upon you be peace and the mercy of Allah." Then another came and said, "Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah, and the mercy of Allah." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him, "And upon you be peace and the mercy of Allah and His blessings." Then another came and said, "Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings." He said, "And upon you." The man said, "O Messenger of Allah, may my father and mother be your ransom, so-and-so and so-and-so came to you and greeted you, and you returned more to them than you returned to me." He said, "You have left us nothing. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet back with one better than it, or return it﴾ — so We have returned it to you."(1)

When the scholars spoke on the matter of greeting, they classified it and said: the one walking greets the one sitting; the rider greets the one walking; the young greets the elder; the one who can see greets the blind; the few greet the many. Every address directed to the believers encompasses and includes both their males and females, unless the ruling is something specific to women.

Here the Truth says: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet back with one better than it, or return it.﴾ Do women have a greeting? Yes, they have a greeting: a woman greets a woman, a woman greets her husband, a woman greets her mahram relatives, and an elderly woman who has no desire may initiate the greeting and return it. As for a young woman, she does not initiate the greeting to anyone, nor does she return a greeting. She does not begin with peace except when she is with someone like her, because they say: "A woman's eye over a woman is more than a thousand men," meaning that a woman guards another woman more than a thousand men do. So when she is with her counterpart, she protects her. For this reason it is said: if a woman initiates the greeting or returns the greeting, that is forbidden; and if a man initiates the greeting to her or returns the greeting to her, that is disliked. Why? Because her initiating it is arousing, but if he initiates the greeting, it is not necessary that she respond. If someone is with her, or a group that vouches for her, there is no harm in her returning the greeting.

They also said: what if the one who offers the greeting and initiates it with it is not a believer? The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) made clear that they twist their words. So if they say to you, "As-salāmu," say, "And upon you." That means: if they say a good word with a good meaning, then welcome to it, and the same for them; but if it is an evil word, like their saying, "As-sāmu ʿalaykum" (death be upon you), then say, "And upon you," because al-sām means death. So that they will not mock you, say, "And upon you." Some scholars said: what is meant by "greet back with one better than it" is with respect to the believer, and "return it" is with respect to the disbeliever.

But is that greeting alone? If the one who greets you with words has granted you security with words, how can you not be wary of the one who professes faith with words out of hypocrisy, who shows you security and then says, "Peace be upon you," while harboring harm? Just as the Truth taught us to return a greeting with its equivalent, because moving matters from the verbal to the practical is the touchstone and foundation. So if a person greets you with the good he has, then the Muslim must offer a greeting better than it. If he is unable, then at least he should return it with its equivalent. When a person returns with its equivalent, generosity among people becomes such that, if it does not increase, at least it does not decrease, and goodness keeps growing. If a person offers goodness to another, and the other responds with an act better than it, that is growth of goodness. If he is unable, then he should return with an equivalent act, and thus his goodness is not diminished. Thus each person's goodness is restrained for himself, because as long as he will give greeting and...

(1) Narrated by Ibn Jarir.

And after that, He, glorified is He, says:

﴿Allah—there is no god except Him. He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt. And who is more truthful in statement than Allah?﴾ (4:87).

This means that there is no other god who will come to intervene and forbid matters behind the back of the Supreme Creator, glorified is He. ﴿Allah—there is no god except Him﴾: there is no god other than Me. There is no legislation that sets the good of mankind except My legislation, and you will return to Me. There is no one who says "Do" and "Do not," while another says the opposite. He is one God, and His command "Do" is the only command that is good for the human being. His prohibition "Do not" is the only prohibition that the rational person must avoid. Therefore you find Him saying: ﴿Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship, nor do you worship what I worship, nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped, nor are you worshippers of what I worship. For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾ (Surah al-Kafirun, 109:1–6).

He, glorified is He, makes clear that there is no coexistence between two religions, one for disbelievers and one for believers. No. Rather, there is one religion and one method that is good for the human being: the method of monotheism (tawhid), which all the messengers brought, and which was sealed with Islam, after which there is no religion. Therefore immediately after it comes: ﴿When the help of Allah comes and the victory﴾ (Surah al-Nasr, 110:1). And after that comes Surah al-Masad: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he! His wealth will not avail him, nor what he gained. He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame, and his wife, the carrier of firewood, around her neck a rope of fiber﴾ (Surah al-Masad, 111:1–5).

Was it not possible for Abu Lahab to say after that: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah"? He was able to. Had he said it, he would have cast doubt on this verse, and they would have said: "He will not burn in a Fire of blazing flame." This matter was one in which he had a choice, but Allah did not enable him to say it, not even hypocritically. Why? Because the Truth said right after this verse directly: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ (Surah al-Ikhlas, 112:1).

That is, there is no other god whose command overrides His, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Allah—there is no god except Him. He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection.﴾ The word "yajma'" means that He will bring us out together from our graves, all of us, and gather us all before Him. It may also mean "li-yajma'annakum," i.e., He will gather you from your graves to receive the recompense of the Day of Resurrection.

Why did this statement come? It came so that the rational person would reflect on it. He will not let his soul break free from the method of Allah except by considering the recompense for breaking free from the method. If he let his soul break free from the method of Allah without estimating the recompense, he would be foolish and reckless.

Therefore we have said: those who indulge themselves in disobedience do not bring to mind before their eyes the recompense for disobedience. Hence they say: all crimes are committed in the heedlessness of their perpetrator regarding the recompense. The criminal commits his crime while assuming his own safety, and the thief goes to the theft while assuming his safety. But if it were placed in his mind that he could be arrested, he would never have done it.

The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, makes clear: beware, O you who wish to use the choice I have given you to deviate from My method, that you not estimate the recompense for this violation. Rather, you must take it as a clear matter, and ask how much benefit it will give you and how much good Allah will give you for obedience. Place the two in the two pans of a scale. The one that gives you the more lasting good, do it, and keep away from what does not give you good but rather brings you to misery and evil.

﴿Allah—there is no god except Him. He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection﴾, and the Day of Resurrection is the day about which the Truth said: ﴿The Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ (Surah al-Mutaffifin, 83:6).

Why the Day of Resurrection? Because the last manifestation of people's worldly life is that when they die they sleep, and this is what we see. Then we place them in the grave, and we do not know how one comes up standing from his sleep, except by the saying of the Truth: ﴿He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt.﴾

That is, belief in the Day of Resurrection must be without doubt. For if you were to suppose that the world Allah created is one of choice, where if He wills they do good and if He wills they do evil, and He, glorified is He, has provided the servants with the method and given them choice, and that He, glorified is He, is the One able to gather them on the Day of Resurrection—if you supposed this, you would have fulfilled what Allah asked of you.

We give this example not as a comparison, but for approximation, and to Allah belongs the highest likeness. A father gives his son a pound and says to him: "Buy whatever you want, but note that if you buy something useful I will reward you, and if you buy something corrupt, such as playing cards or other things, I will punish you."

When the father gave his son purchasing power and said to him: "Go down and buy whatever you want," the son, when he bought playing cards... Was this purchase done against his father by compulsion? No, because it was the father who gave him the choice, but the son did an act that was not loved by his father.

So what of the servant when the Truth gives him choice? Had Allah willed to guide all people, He would have made them like the angels, and no one would have dared or been able to commit disobedience. The disobedient one, when he commits disobedience, does it only because Allah created for him the faculty of choice. Therefore, when someone says "every act is from Allah," he speaks truly. And why is the perpetrator of disobedience punished, when he directs the faculty of choice toward what it is fit for? We say that he has directed it in opposition to Allah's command. If a knife is for slaughter, and you slaughter a chicken with it, the slaughterer does not deserve punishment for that. But if we slaughter a human being with it, we would have fallen into a prohibited act that the Truth likens to killing all of mankind. Would we say to the one who brought the knife into the house, "You brought the instrument of the crime"? No, because he brought an instrument fit either for slaughtering what is lawful to slaughter or for a crime. So even the one who has choice only exercised his choice from the inner reality that Allah created him as one who chooses.

But did the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, compel him to commit disobedience? No. He, glorified is He, has made clear to you: this I do not love, and this I love. Your choice has its scope, and you may choose what brings benefit and not harm, or choose the opposite.

﴿Allah—there is no god except Him. He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt﴾ is a report from Allah. In our speech, a declarative statement admits of truth and falsehood in itself, but because the report is from Allah, it is true. As for speech in itself, it admits of truth and admits of falsehood. Therefore the Truth concludes the verse with: ﴿And who is more truthful in statement than Allah?﴾ Is there gradation in truthfulness? There is no gradation in truthfulness, for the meaning of truthfulness is the correspondence of speech to reality. A person, before he speaks, while rational, considers the matter on which he wishes to speak so that reason may work on it, and after that he expresses it in speech.

Thus in speech there is a mental relation (nisba dhihniyya), a verbal relation (nisba kalamiyya), and a real relation (nisba waqi'iyya). When someone says, "Zayd is diligent" (mujtahid), before he says it, the idea that he is diligent has come into his mind; this is the "mental relation." When its speaker utters it, it becomes a "verbal relation." But is it true that there is a man named Zayd and that he is diligent? If the real relation matches both the mental relation and the verbal relation, the speech is truthful. If there is no one named Zayd and he is not "diligent," then the external real relation does not match the two relations, "mental and verbal," and the speech is false. Truthfulness requires that the verbal relation correspond with reality, that is, with the external relation that obtains.

Why then does the liar lie? To secure for himself a benefit that he would miss, which truthfulness, in his view, does not secure, or to repel a harm from himself. An example of this: a son breaks something in the house, such as a table. The father says to his son: "Did you break this table?" The son denies: "No, I did not break it." He wants to secure for himself a benefit or repel a harm from himself, which is escape from punishment, because he knows that truthfulness may cause him punishment. Nothing drives him to lie except avoiding a harm that may befall him from truthfulness, so he resorts to lying, and says words that contradict reality.

So he wants to secure for himself a benefit or repel a harm. Whatever benefits a person must be stronger than him, and likewise whatever harms him. But with regard to Allah, there is no one who can bring Him benefit or harm, glorified is He. Therefore, when Allah speaks, His word is true, because the causes that drive to lying are far removed from Him, glorified is He.

And if the Truth gives us speech that clarifies for us the reality of life, and gives us speech that does not enter into the reality of our lives but describes for us the unseen that does not fall within the scope of what we see, then He speaks to us much.

So His word, the Truth: ﴿And who is more truthful in statement than Allah?﴾ is affirmed with respect to us. The comparative form (af'al al-tafdil) here does not come to distinguish between a true statement and a truer statement, but to let us know that Allah's speech to us is abundant. The abundance here comes from the multitude of speech, not from the notion that there is true speech and truer speech.

Gradation may exist in truthfulness too, how? Suppose a man saw an incident in which one person kills another. A witness testifies that he saw blood gushing from the slain man as the killer struck him. But there is another witness who relates all the details, beginning from the quarrel between the killer and the slain until there was a killer and a slain. Thus we find that the second witness is more comprehensive in truthfulness than the first. True, the first witness gave a true testimony, but the testimony of the second witness is more comprehensive regarding the same case.

So His word, the Truth: ﴿And who is more truthful in statement than Allah?﴾ means that the Truth is the most truthful, in the sense that His report to us comes with complete comprehensiveness, and it is a truthfulness in which there is no gradation. Truthfulness is the correspondence of the verbal relation to reality, and since this is so, there is no "truthful" and "more truthful." Yet the comparative form in "more truthful" comes in consideration of the fact that the quantity of truthfulness emanating is without limit, and that He, glorified is He, knows things in accordance with what they are, that is, with complete comprehensiveness. If truthfulness does occur from them regarding one matter, then falsehood may occur from them regarding another. You may state a proposition that you know to be true, but in reality it is not true.

For example, someone may say: "So-and-so visited so-and-so yesterday." He believed that because he saw the reception room in so-and-so's house lit, so he asked who the visitor was, and he was told "so-and-so." He relates the report of this visit according to what he believes, and it is not said that the speaker lied.

We must distinguish between "the report" (al-khabar) and "the reporter" (al-mukhbir). How? If we say, "Zayd is diligent," is there a man named Zayd who is in fact diligent? This is the reality. And do you believe this? Then the person here needs two things: knowledge that the thing exists, and belief in the thing. Thereby the report is true and the reporter is also true.

Suppose you reported that Zayd is diligent on the basis that someone told you so, but he was not so. You are truthful according to your belief, but the report is not true in reality. Thus there is a difference between the truthfulness of the report and the truthfulness of the reporter. If the belief meets reality, the report is true and the reporter is true. If the report agrees with reality but disagrees with belief, the report is true, like the position of the hypocrites about whom the Truth said: ﴿When the hypocrites come to you, they say: "We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah"﴾ (Surah al-Munafiqun, 63:1, part of the verse).

This proposition is true, and they themselves declared it, but the Truth added: ﴿And Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars﴾ (Surah al-Munafiqun, 63:1, part of the verse).

So the proposition is true, but they are liars, because they said it without conviction, and so they were liars. The precision here makes clear the difference between the truthfulness of the report and the falsehood of the belief. Thus the truthfulness of the reporter is that his speech corresponds to his belief. The falsity is evident in their saying "We bear witness," not in the content of what is said, which is "you are indeed the Messenger of Allah," because testimony requires that the tongue agree and conform with the heart.

Therefore, when some people read the Qur'an without understanding the Arabic language, they superficially understand this verse wrongly: ﴿When the hypocrites come to you, they say: "We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah." Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger, and Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars﴾ (Surah al-Munafiqun, 63:1).

They ask: how does Allah bear witness that they are liars, even though He, glorified is He, knows just as the hypocrites testified? We respond: the report here was not a lie, and the Truth did not say anything that contradicts the report, but He made clear the truthfulness of the report and the lying of the hypocrites in their testimony, because they are showing—

And then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿So what is wrong with you that you have become two factions concerning the hypocrites, when Allah has returned them to their state [of disbelief] because of what they earned? Do you wish to guide those whom Allah has sent astray? And he whom Allah sends astray - you will never find for him a way.﴾ (4:88)

Every sentence preceded by "fa" (so/then) necessarily has a cause and an effect, a reason and a result, a premise and a conclusion. All the matters about which the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, has spoken concerning the legitimacy of fighting for the believers are so that they may carry the method (manhaj) to the people, and so that people, after hearing the method, are free in what they choose. Therefore fighting was not legislated to impose a method; rather it was legislated to impose freedom of choice of the method, as evidenced by the words of the Truth: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion. The right course has become distinct from error﴾ (2:256).

Accordingly, Islam does not impose religion, but it came to impose freedom of choice in religion. The forces that obstruct an individual's choice of his religion are confronted by Islam, so that it removes their domination over those upon whom they have imposed their authority, and then leaves people free to adopt whatever they wish. The evidence is that in the lands which Islam conquered by the sword, some of the people remained upon their religions. Had fighting been legislated to impose a religion, we would not have found in any land conquered by the sword a single person who was not of the religion of Islam.

After the Truth had spoken of fighting in several places in Surah al-Nisa, and had said to the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿So fight in the cause of Allah; you are not held responsible except for yourself. And urge the believers. Perhaps Allah will restrain the ferocity of those who disbelieve. And Allah is strongest in might and strongest in punishment﴾ (4:84),

the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, here posed a interrogative matter, which carries the meaning of denunciation and the meaning of reproach, and this is common in all the styles that are similar to it in the Noble Qur'an. When you hear the phrase "fa-ma laka la taf'alu kadha" ("so what is wrong with you that you do not do such-and-such"), it is as though the measure of reason demands that you act, and it is strange that you do not. This style cannot come except when it denounces that you have done something you should not have done, or that you have left undone something you were obliged to do.

For example, a father says to his son: "What is the matter with you that you are not studying, when the exam is near?" As if the logic of reason imposes on the son, if he had neglected the past part of the year, that it was not proper for him to neglect before the exam, and this is an evident matter by rational analogy. So it is as though the legislation and the Qur'an address the believers that they should not proceed with any action except after weighing the choice in it by the proof that stands upon it; it is not proper for the believer to proceed to any deed without thought, nor for the believer to leave any deed without knowing why he did not do it. Thus the style "fa-ma lakum" and "fa-ma laka" is like the statement of the sons of our master Ya'qub: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not trust us with Yusuf?﴾ (12:11).

What is the meaning of their saying this? Its meaning: "What proof do you have, O our father, for depriving us of being entrusted with Yusuf, letting him accompany us on our outing?" As if their analogy was that they are brothers and a band, and it is not proper for their father to fear for Yusuf either from them or from anything else threatening Yusuf, because they are a large and strong group. Likewise the statement of the Truth: ﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ (84:20).

That is, the analogy demands that they believe. And His statement: ﴿So what is wrong with them that they turn away from the reminder, as if they were frightened donkeys fleeing from a lion?﴾ (74:49–51).

The analogy would be that they should not turn away from the reminder. So the style of "fa-ma lahu," "fa-ma laka," "fa-ma lahum," and "fa-ma lakum" all indicate that the believer's action must first be met by weighing what he does or weighing what he does not do. As for performing acts haphazardly without thought regarding the grounds for doing them or for not doing them, this is not the work of reasonable people.

Thus the work of the intelligent person is that before he proceeds to an act, he considers the alternatives from which he chooses the act. The student, if he has before him play and before him study, and knows that after play comes failure, and after failure a non-honourable future, then if he chooses diligence he knows that after diligence comes success, and after success an honourable future. It is therefore the student's duty to exert a measure of effort in order to excel. Every act a person does must be compared with the result it brings and with the preference of the act that has a benefit over the acts that do not achieve the desired goal.

Here the verse says: ﴿So what is wrong with you concerning the hypocrites, [that you have become] two factions?﴾ The analogy would demand that we not be two factions in our view of the hypocrites, but that we be one faction. The word "fi'ah" means a group, and a group means individuals who have joined together with one another despite the difference of desires among these individuals and despite the difference of opinions; yet in faith a single desire unites them, the desire of religion. For this reason the Messenger said: "None of you truly believes until his desire is subordinate to what I have brought."(1)

So the cause of disagreement is that each one has a different desire, and the desire of religion and holding fast to the firm rope of Allah does not unite them. And what is the story of the hypocrites, and how did the believers divide over their matter so as to become two factions?

As we have learned, a "fi'ah" is a group, but not any group: one does not say of a group walking along the road, with no common aim or goal, that they are a "fi'ah." A "fi'ah" or "ta'ifah" is a group of human beings gathered for an aim, because the meaning of "fi'ah" is that some of them return to and take refuge with one another in the one matter that unites them; and similarly the meaning of "ta'ifah" is that they circle around one thing. The Truth says: ﴿So what is wrong with you concerning the hypocrites, [that you have become] two factions?﴾ This is a drawing of attention and an admonition from the Truth, that we should purify our minds from being divided into two opinions on a single matter, especially when we are gathered upon faith in one God and one method. The hypocrites, as we know, are those who show faith and conceal disbelief.

We know that all abstract matters are given names from concrete things, because sensory perception is the first means of the heart's perception, and after that come meanings. When we come to the word "munafiqin" (hypocrites), we find it is taken from a sensory matter that the Arabs witnessed in their environment, where there lives an animal called the "yarbu'" (jerboa), like the mouse and the lizard. The jerboa is well known for cunning and deception, and in order to be safe from the animals that attack it, it builds for itself two burrows, or several burrows, and flees from the attacking animal into one burrow, and the attacking animal tries to wait for it at the mouth of this burrow, so the jerboa leaves it through another opening. As if the jerboa has planned and prepared for itself exits in order to deceive: it makes one opening through which it enters the burrow, and a second and a third, so that it may emerge from any of them. Likewise the hypocrite.

We know that matters of faith or creed are of three forms. There is the believer, who says with his tongue and believes with his heart, and lives with faculties in complete harmony. And there is the disbeliever, who says with his tongue and believes with his heart... [the text here is garbled in the original; the passage ends and the translation follows as given]

There is the disbeliever who does not believe, does not adhere to Islam, and his tongue does not say other than what he believes, and his faculties are also in harmony, even though there awaits him the recompense of his disbelief in the Hereafter; his faculties are in harmony but toward a harmful end, which is the end of disbelief. As for the "hypocrite," he is one who believes in disbelief and his heart is fixed upon it, but his tongue says the opposite; his faculties are not in harmony, for his tongue has said the opposite of what is in his heart. Therefore he lives divided and anxious, wanting to take the good of faith and the good of disbelief. This is the hypocrite.

There is a group in the history of Islam who, when they saw the victory of the Muslims at the Battle of Badr, said to themselves: "The wind is on the side of the Muslims, and we do not believe that after the victory of Badr and the killing of the chiefs of Quraysh and their obtaining all these spoils, they will come to us." This group tried hypocrisy and claimed Islam while they were in Makkah, so that when the Muslims entered Makkah they would have secured themselves. Or they were a group who went to Madinah as emigrants, and did not endure the bitterness of emigration and of living far from homeland, family and wealth, so they thought about these matters, wanted to renounce the religion and return to Makkah, and said to the believers in Madinah: "We have wealth in Makkah, and we will go to recover it and return."

The Muslims heard the news, and the Muslims divided into two parts: a part that said, "We will fight them," and a part that said, "We will not fight them." Those who said "We will fight them" were driven to that by the zeal of faith. Those who said "We will not fight them" said: "This group has shown faith, and we have not split open their hearts, and perhaps they said that out of sympathy toward them because of ties or bonds." So the Qur'an came to settle the matter of the Muslims' division into two parts and to resolve the disagreement. When the Qur'an comes to settle a matter, this means that the Lord of the Qur'an fashioned the mass of believers under His own eye, and whenever He sees any flaw among them, He, glory be to Him, settles the matter, and so He said: ﴿So what is wrong with you concerning the hypocrites, [that you have become] two factions?﴾

The address is directed to the Muslim community. His saying ﴿fa-ma lakum﴾ means that they are united upon one aim, and His saying ﴿fi'atayn﴾ (two factions) indicates that they are in disagreement.

So "two factions" contradicts the address that the Truth began with "fa-ma lakum." The one receiving the Qur'an was required to infer the meaning as follows: "What is wrong with you that you have divided over the hypocrites into two factions?" So this is a style of reproach and threat, and such a matter should not happen. Does this speech fall upon all the addressees? Let us look: is the Qur'an with the one who said, "Kill the hypocrites," or with the one who said otherwise? If it is with the first group, then it does not rebuke that group but honours it. The Qur'an is with the group that calls for fighting the hypocrites and not with the second group; therefore it rebukes that second group and reproaches it. When the style is a reproach to the one who holds one opinion, it is an honouring of the one who holds the opposite opinion, and the honoured holder of opinion is not included in the reproach, because the Truth has given him the ground that raises his head.

The Truth says: ﴿So what is wrong with you concerning the hypocrites﴾ — that is, the Truth says: What proof do you have for splitting into two factions regarding the matter of the hypocrites? The analogy demands that you study the matter by rational study and by faith study, so that you arrive at the conclusion that you must be upon one opinion. The meaning of denunciation is: You have no proof, O believers, for dividing into two factions.

And the Truth says: ﴿And Allah has returned them [to their state] because of what they earned.﴾ When you hear the word ﴿arkasahum﴾ (He has returned them), what do we gain from it even if we do not know the meaning of the word? We gain that the Truth has placed them in an unbecoming position. We feel that the style indicated their overturning and made their front their back, that is, that they were turned upside down, even if we do not understand the root from which the word is taken; and this is among the suggestions of the Qur'anic style, the suggestions of the wording and the harmony of its letters.

﴿Wa-llahu arkasahum bi-ma kasabu﴾ — "arkasa" is derived from "rakasa," and its meaning is "to return something." As if they were upon something and then left it, then Allah returned them to the first thing. They were disbelievers first, then they believed, then He returned them. But did Allah return them as harshness toward them or by compulsion? No; this happened "because of what they earned," so that no one may enter with us into the maze of the question of why Allah punishes and reproaches them, since He is the One who did this to them; therefore the Truth told us that He "returned them because of what they earned." The root of "arkasa" is taken from a thing called "al-rikas" (with a fatha on the ra), which is the returning of a thing upside down; and from it "al-rikis" (with a kasra on the ra), which is the refuse that returns from a person's stomach before the food has been assimilated. It is like our saying: "So-and-so's stomach has turned against him," or "So-and-so brings back what is in his belly."

When we look at this process, we find that the food which a person desires, loves, approaches and eats with pleasure, and his eyes look at it with longing, and his hand cuts the food with pleasure and chews the food with pleasure — this food, once it is chewed together and enters the stomach and digestive secretions are added to it, if it returns in this state it is no longer pleasant in smell. Indeed, if a person digests the food, takes what is beneficial from it and expels the remainder afterward, the smell of the natural waste is no worse than the smell of food that returns without being assimilated. If you were to see a person relieving himself and another...
