(1) Narrated by al-Baghawi in Sharh al-Sunnah, and Ibn Asim in al-Sunnah, al-Muttaqi al-Hindi in Kanz al-Ummal, and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi in Tarikh Baghdad.

**Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 89:**

"﴿They wish[^1] ...﴾": its pronoun refers to the hypocrites (munafiqun) about whom the Muslims divided into two groups. God's judgment favoured the group that wanted to confront them with a stance of strength, force and tyranny. Then, explaining their hypocrisy, He, glorified and exalted is He, said: ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved﴾. Furthermore, their hypocrisy means anxiety that afflicts them about the state of their condition with the future or present of Islam, because they are disbelievers in their hearts. But they fear that Islam will prevail and treat them as those who disbelieve in it, so they try to show that they are Muslims in order to take precautions for the support and spread of Islam. They are thus in distress and fatigue, and this fatigue makes them wish for many ideas in their heads: they say, "We will declare before the Muslims that we are Muslims, and we will declare before the disbelievers that we are disbelievers."

What has compelled them to this state, when they were formerly of one consistency, their tongues with their hearts, before Islam came? Therefore, what restores them to a state of psychological stability and draws them out of anxiety, turmoil and fear for their present and future is that the question of Islam should end, so that there are no longer Muslims, disbelievers and hypocrites, but rather everyone becomes a disbeliever.

﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved﴾. The wish (al-widad) is an act of the heart, and all the limbs submit to the act of the heart when they are able. So as long as they wish that the Muslims would be disbelievers, they will stand in the way of the victory of the Muslims and will place obstacles that achieve what their hearts desire. Therefore, beware of them; I will expose their affair to you so that you may be aware of all their conduct, the treachery of their eyes and the treachery of their tongues.

﴿They wish that you would disbelieve﴾. We know that the word "kufr" (disbelief, literally "concealment") means "concealment": the verb "kafara" means "he concealed." And from the greatness of faith in Islam and the greatness of the truth in itself is that its opponents can never extinguish it. The word that came to define the opposite of God is itself evidence of belief in God. When we say "kafara billah" (he disbelieved in God), it means "he concealed His existence," as if the existence is present before he conceals it; therefore we find that the word "kufr" itself is evidence of faith, for the word "kufr" in itself means an existing faith which its bearer struggles to cover and conceal.

﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved﴾. This statement came after the Truth said: ﴿Why are you divided into two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾ (Quran 4:88).

It indicates that they are described at one time as hypocrites and at another time as disbelievers. God named them in one verse "hypocrites," and the Truth describes them in this verse as having disbelieved: ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved﴾. The disbelief described here indicates what is concealed in the heart. Hypocrisy gave them only the outward appearances of Islam, but they did not take its inward realities. Therefore they will be in the lowest level of the Fire in the Hereafter. Although in this world they are treated as Muslims out of respect for the words "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," God will treat them in the Hereafter as disbelievers, and additionally they will be in the lowest level of the Fire.

Thus, the people of falsehood, if they have power, make their tongues agree with their hearts in openly proclaiming falsehood; and if they are weak, they make their hearts incline to falsehood while their tongues speak truth. This process is not comfortable in either position. What is comfortable for them is that there should be no group of truth at all. Therefore He, glorified is He, says, describing the reality of their feelings: ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be alike﴾. They wish the removal of the group of truth so that no one would be better than anyone else, just as we say: "There is no one better than anyone."

For example: we find a group of employees in a government department, among whom is one who embezzles, or who does not perform his work in the refined manner required. Therefore he does not like others to perform their work with perfect excellence; he wants them to be corrupt, and tries to entice them to corruption so that they become like him, so that they do not show him to himself in the light of deficiency, and so that he does not appear diminished in their eyes.

It is strange that we find the thief respects the trustworthy, and we often hear of a thief who, as soon as he learns that there is an ambush awaiting him to arrest him, looks for a trustworthy man in whose custody he may place the stolen goods as a trust.

The Truth's statement about the wish of the hypocrites who are disbelievers in their hearts is that the believers should be like them: ﴿so that you would be alike﴾. This is a testimony that the holder of falsehood loves that the holder of truth be with him, because when he finds him in the truth, the holder of falsehood despises himself. Wonders have occurred with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): they disbelieved in him and tortured his companions, yet he was the trustworthy one by the acknowledgment of them all. Here is the Messenger (ﷺ) emigrating from Makkah and leaving behind "Ali" (may Allah ennoble his face) to return the deposits and trusts that were with him.

They denied him regarding the message, but he was the trustworthy by the acknowledgment of them all; therefore they deposited their trusts with him. Thus the person of virtue is respected even by the person of vice. To understand this meaning fully, let us suppose that a person got into a problem: he insulted someone, and the one insulted filed a legal case against this insulter. The insulter had a dear friend whom the one insulted cited as a witness. The insulter says: "Will you testify against me?" The friend goes to the court and says: "My friend does not say such abuse." Here the friend has given false testimony for his friend. Now suppose this insulter repented, turned to God, and became one of the pious, and people made him a judge among them, and the friend who gave false testimony for his sake came to testify before him: would he accept his testimony? Of course not.

Thus the person of virtue is respected even by the person of vice. If anyone among the people of vice tries to pull the person of virtue into error, he is seeking to mislead him, and the Truth's statement applies to that: ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be alike﴾. As long as this is their goal and their idea, they will not leave the believers in their faith, in order to take them to the side of disbelief. In this way they are hypocrites, disbelievers in heart, not sincere to the side of faith. They do not stand toward faith in a position of neutrality, but rather in a position of obstinacy and enmity. ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, so that you would be alike﴾. In this is a clear warning to the believers: beware of trusting them in anything that touches your interests and your faith.

The Truth issues the ruling on this matter with complete clarity: ﴿So do not take from among them allies﴾, that is, beware of taking hypocrites as your helpers or as advisers, because God, glorified is He, has exposed to you the secrets of their souls. This matter is not an inescapable decree: if one of them returns and repents and goes back to the fold of faith, God will not reject him, for He, glorified and exalted is He, does not persecute anyone merely because he committed a sin, since He is the Truly Forgiving, the Merciful. So long as a person has returned to what is right and distanced himself from error, the believers must accept whoever returns to them sincerely. Hatred is not established against anyone because he erred, for hatred is directed at the wrong act, not against the human being created by God. If they give up the error, they are accepted by the believers.

Here is the killer of Zayd ibn al-Khattab passing before Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), and some people said to him: "Here is the killer of your brother Zayd." Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "What should I do with him, when Allah has guided him to Islam?"

Thus we see that hatred did not extend to the person of the speaker; rather the detestation is for the deed. If the person gives up the deed, then the person has his standing. Thus the divine judgment is issued: ﴿So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of Allah﴾.

Emigration in the way of Allah (hijra) used to require a person to leave his wealth, his homeland and his family, and go to a life of austerity, fatigue and hardship, and in this there is that which expiates for him. The believers here recognise that he has repented to Allah, so Allah has accepted his repentance, and it is time for him to enter the domain of faith. If he does this, he has returned to faith. Therefore, people must separate persons from their deeds. Why? Because persons in themselves do not deserve to be hated; rather, the deed of the person is what is hated if it is ugly and evil.

When we read the Quran, we find it presents this very matter. Our master Noah (peace be upon him), when he received God's revelation to build the ark, sat building it while people passed by and mocked him. Noah said to them: "We will mock you tomorrow just as you mock us." His son, who was not on his path, came to him, and Noah invited him to the path, but the son said: "No." Noah boarded the ark and said to God: "You promised me that You would save me and my family."

Here the Truth clarifies: "It is true that I will save you and your family; but what made you consider your son among your family? Indeed, persons, in the case of the prophets, have no lineage; rather, the lineage of the prophets is their deeds": ﴿He is not of your family; indeed, his conduct is unrighteous﴾ (Quran 11:46).

It is the deed that is evaluated. Therefore the Truth says: ﴿So do not take from among them allies until they emigrate in the way of Allah﴾. Emigration (al-hijra) comes from "hajara," and "hajara" means that a person has moved from one place to another, or from one affection to another, or from one quality to another. The one who forsakes (yahjur) is usually one who wrongs the one he forsakes. Note that God, glorified and exalted is He, in His Book, when He presents the event, uses "hajara" (he emigrated) and does not use the word "hajara" (he forsook). The Prophet (ﷺ) did not forsake Makkah, but he emigrated from it, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By Allah, you are the dearest of Allah's lands to me, and you are the dearest of Allah's lands to Allah; and if your people had not expelled me from you, I would not have left."[^2]

Emigration came about because the people of Makkah first forsook him, so he was compelled to emigrate. And "hājara" is on the pattern of "fā'ala" (the form of mutual action). Al-Mutanabbi says:

*When you depart from a people who have resolved not to part from you,*
*the departing ones are they.*

Therefore the Truth prescribed emigration in the form of mufā'ala. They disliked his call, and the Messenger responded to the dislike and emigrated.

God, glorified is He, makes clear that what frees these hypocrites from our judgment against them, that the believers not take them as allies, is that they emigrate in the way of Allah, because that is the proof of the sincerity of faith. The emigrant lives a difficult life, and the emigrants lived on the bounty of Allah and the goodness of the Ansar, and did not establish their lives in a fitting manner. Therefore whoever joins that procession is a believer who has purchased faith and is able to expiate what has befallen him. Emigration is not mere migration, but emigration in the way of Allah.

Therefore we see the principle of faith in the prophetic hadith: "Actions are only by intentions, and every person has only what he intended. Whoever's emigration was to Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is to Allah and His Messenger; and whoever's emigration was to worldly gain he will obtain, or to a woman he will marry, his emigration is to what he emigrated for."[^3]

Thus the believers treat the hypocrite if he returns from his disbelief and hypocrisy to faith. But what if the hypocrites turn away? ﴿If they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take from among them any ally or helper﴾. Seizing (al-akhdh), when it comes in the context of conflict, means capture. Killing them on the battlefield is a binding duty, and it is not proper for the believers to take them as allies or helpers, because each hypocrite is a spy among the believers, who seeks to learn the affairs and conditions of the Muslims, informs the enemies of Islam about what the enemy may penetrate through, and strives eagerly to learn what the Muslims are plotting against the disbelievers.

Taking as an ally or helper one whom we know does not love faith and is not on the principle and creed of Islam is a matter that casts doubt on the soundness of the insight of the person who takes as ally and loves non-Muslims who are sincere. When one of us sees a person whom he does not love and who plots schemes, and that one sees you trusting him and doing him good, this hater says: "This person lacks insight; if he knew what is in my heart, he would not have done that." So if the Muslims take hypocrites as allies or helpers while the hypocrites remain as they are in hypocrisy, the hypocrites would say: "The Muslims lack insight and do not know what is in our hearts." Therefore the Truth illuminates the insight of the believers so that we do not take an opinion from the hypocrites that harms us.

And the hypocrites may say: "These Muslims have no Lord to give them insight, so why do they claim that they have a god?"

*[^1]: Here the source begins with a pronoun reference to the hypocrites in the verse ﴿They wish...﴾ (ودوا), translated as the opening of the verse.*

*[^2]: Narrated by Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi.*

*[^3]: Narrated by al-Bukhari.*

The verse begins with an exception, so that it does not open a door to angering those who have a covenant and treaty with Islam. Those who arrive at and take refuge with a people who have an alliance or pact with the Muslims are not subject to what was mentioned in the previous verse, which is seizing and killing.

An example of this is the agreement that took place between the Muslims and Hilal ibn Uwaymir al-Aslami, that they would not aid against him nor help others against him, and that whoever reached Hilal and took refuge with him would have the same protection as Hilal has. The exception also includes those who came to the Muslims. Thus, if a hypocrite goes to those with whom the Muslims have a covenant, he obtains safety, and likewise the Messenger (ﷺ) gives security to hypocrites who came to him and who, for reasons that compel them to seek the protection of the Messenger and Islam, say so. Despite his hypocrisy, Islam grants him security.

﴿Or those who come to you, their hearts constricted at fighting you or fighting their own people.﴾ One of them would say: "I am not able to fight you, nor am I able to fight my people, so forgive me this and accept me among you." The Messenger (ﷺ) accepts such people because they acknowledge the straitened state they are in. They cannot act before the Muslims by declaring faith, nor before the disbelievers by working in the camp of disbelief. They cannot take a decisive, firm position between the Muslims and the disbelievers, so they admit their weakness and confess it.

﴿And had Allah willed, He would have given them power over you.﴾ What then makes them seek refuge with a people who are allied with the Muslims by a pact, so that they take shelter among them? Or they acknowledge that their hearts are constricted and that they are unable to act, declaring: "We are not able to fight you, nor to fight our own people." Truly, the Real makes clear: I did this and cast terror into their souls; had I willed, I would have empowered them and emboldened them against you, and they would have fought you. Thus, glorified is He, Who supports us with terror and prevents them from fighting us. ﴿So if they keep away from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, then Allah has not made for you any way against them.﴾

If they keep away from you, do not fight you, offer peace, and acknowledge that they have no capacity to choose between fighting the Muslims or fighting their own people, then you, O Muslims, have no justification to attack them; attacking them in such a situation is something Allah forbids.

The sight of the Real is not limited to what we know, but extends to the most subtle details; it is a sight that does not see only what we have known, but reveals to us the veils we do not know. So Allah, glorified is He, says:

﴿You will find others who wish to be secure from you and secure from their own people. Every time they are returned to disbelief, they are plunged back into it. So if they do not keep away from you, nor offer you peace, nor restrain their hands, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them. And those – We have given you clear authority over them.﴾ [4:91]

This verse begins with a verb in the future tense: ﴿You will find others who wish to be secure from you and to be secure from their own people﴾. This means that at the moment this verse was revealed, the Muslims had not yet encountered people like those the Truth describes. Had the contemporaries of the Qur'an's revelation not later encountered such people, what would they have said about this report? If they had not found such people, they would have doubted the Qur'an. He, glorified is He, makes clear that He is with you and for you. He informed you of what happened and you disagreed about it, and He informs you of what has not reached your minds and knowledge, so do not dispute it. This is evidence that you are under My care and My protection.

﴿You will find others who wish to be secure from you﴾. These people were from the tribes of Banu Asad and Ghatafan, and they lived on the outskirts of Medina. They would meet the Muslims and say: ﴿We are with you﴾, and they would also meet the disbelievers and say: ﴿We are with you﴾. In reality, they were unable to confront either camp. For this reason the Qur'an describes them: ﴿You will find others who wish to be secure from you and to be secure from their own people. Whenever they are returned to disorder, they are plunged into it﴾. Whenever a test came to them, they ﴿were plunged into it﴾, meaning they failed in choosing. Their faith had not yet grown strong, and they remained in confusion about their affair. When the trial came to melt them down and expose what was in their depths, their confusion increased. Fitnah (trial, test) is an examination and is not in itself something blameworthy. When it is said that so-and-so is in fitnah, the believer should pray that he succeeds in it. A trial is not a calamity that befalls a person; rather, calamity befalls a person when he fails in the trial.

We know that fitnah is derived from a sensory matter: the fitnah of gold and likewise of iron. The fitnah of gold is melting gold in the crucible until it liquefies, so that all the impure elements mixed with the gold float up like foam. Likewise iron is smelted until its tightly bound particles separate from one another, and the dross rises to the surface.

We know that iron comes in types. Cast iron has its impurities plainly visible in it and breaks easily, while we find steel with no dross, so it is hard. The fitnah of gold and iron reveals the foreign metals mixed with them. The word "fitnah" was transferred from sensory things to meanings, and fitnah became the test by which a person either succeeds or fails. It is not harmful in itself, but it is harmful to the one who fails in it.

Thus was the Qur'an's prophecy, which informs the Muslims about a people on their borders whom trial prevents from being able to hold firm in faith. Whenever their own people call them to polytheism and to fighting the Muslims, they turn back on their heels and overturn upon their heads, in the most ugly and shameful way, and they became worse than any enemy against you. The Qur'an then explains how the believers should behave toward these people who revert and turn back in trial: ﴿So if they do not withdraw from you and offer you peace and restrain their hands, then seize them and kill them wherever you overtake them. And those — We have made for you against them a clear authority﴾. We note that the Truth commanded the granting of safety to those who sought refuge, through their weakness, despite their hypocrisy, either with the Muslims or with the allies of the Muslims, when He said in the previous verse: ﴿So Allah has not made for you a way against them﴾ (Qur'an 4:90).

This is justice and a divine warning from the Truth: no one should heed his own anger and prey upon weak people. As for those who try to rebel and submit to the voice of disbelief and inflict harm on the Muslims, and who do not offer peace to the Muslims or restrain their hands from them, the divine command applies to them: seize them and kill them. Allah has made for the Muslims a clear authority over these people. Authority, as we know, is power, and power takes two forms. There is power that compels a person to act: one person commands another to stand and he stands, or a strong man commands a weak one to prostrate and he prostrates. This is the authority of force, which subdues the body but can never subdue the heart. The second authority is the authority of proof: the strength of argument, the force of expression, and the evidence that persuades a person to act.

The difference between the authority of force and the authority of proof is that force may compel a person to prostrate, but the authority of proof makes a person prostrate by conviction. The clear authority that Allah has given the believers over the hypocrites who fight the believers is this: O Muslims, you have a power by which you may do to them what you wish, as long as they attempt to fight and inflict harm on the Muslims. Firmness and justice mean seizing them with force.

To understand the meaning of authority well, let us recall the argument that will take place in the Hereafter between Satan and those who followed him. You will find Satan saying: I did lead you astray, that is true, and you followed me, so you are responsible for that. I had no authority over you of force or of persuasion: ﴿I had no authority over you except that I invited you and you responded to me﴾ (Qur'an 14:22).

After the Truth spoke of fighting and its legitimacy, the fighting of the hypocrites, and the fighting of others, the discourse arrives at the subject of killing. He made clear to them: the matter is that I am the One who fashioned the human structure, and I am the One who gives life. It is not easy for the builder of a structure to incite its destruction. Rather, I incite the destruction of those who fight you, so that the rest of the structure may be preserved for you. Beware of daring against the structures of people, for cursed is the one who destroys the structure of Allah. The soul that Allah created: beware of approaching it except by right, and that is when you transgress the limits of Allah, because He, glorified is He, is the One who created life and the One who takes life. The lives of people are not their own possession, and a person's life itself is not his own possession. Therefore, whoever kills one person unjustly and without right, we exact retribution from him. As for one who killed by mistake, we take diyah (blood money) from him, and the matter ends there. But the one who kills himself, Paradise is forbidden to him.

So before He said to me, "Do not kill others," He said to me, "Beware of killing yourself." Thus He, glorified is He, is not only jealous for people from you, but He is also jealous for you from yourself. Therefore, when He, glorified is He, legislated qisas (retributive justice) for homicide, He legislated it to protect you, not to embolden you to kill. As for His command, glorified is He, that whoever kills shall be killed, He is establishing justice and equity. The purpose of this is the preservation of two lives, because if you know that if you kill him you will be killed, you will not kill. As long as you do not kill, you have protected two lives: the life of the one you would have killed, and your own life from being retributed against. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And in retribution there is life for you, O people of understanding﴾ (Qur'an 2:179).

So the one who philosophizes and says, "This is brutality, and so on," we say to him: Does He who legislated qisas want to kill? No, rather He wants to protect your life, because the killer, when he knows that if he kills he will be killed, does not kill, and as long as he does not kill, we have preserved his life and the life of the other. Therefore His saying, ﴿And in retribution there is life﴾, is a true statement.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 4, verse 92:

When the Truth (al-Haqq) spoke of fighting and killing, He alerted us: "Beware lest, on account of these matters, you become bold against people's blood or their lives." Therefore, Glorified is He, speaks of the killing that is forbidden in faith and in Islam, and says:

﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake. And whoever kills a believer by mistake, then [he must free] a believing slave and pay blood-money to his family, unless they forgo it. But if the victim was from a people hostile to you and he was a believer, then [free] a believing slave. And if he was from a people between whom and you there is a covenant, then blood-money must be paid to his family and [free] a believing slave. But whoever does not find [the means], then [he must fast] two consecutive months as repentance from Allah. And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾

This statement came after He spoke of fighting, to establish the matter of the call (to Islam). Since fighting requires the killing of a disbelieving soul by a believing one, it was fitting for the Truth, Glorified is He, to speak about killing.

Killing, as we know, is the taking away of a living being's soul by destroying its structure. The living being, even if we do not destroy its structure, dies when its term comes. Thus, destroying the structure of a human being by one who intends to end a person's life is an act whose aim is ending life. Let no one suppose that the killer who wished to destroy a person's structure possesses the power to end that person's life; rather, he coincides with the ending of life, and the one who ends life is Allah, Glorified and Exalted. For this reason we have said: the punishment falls upon the killer not because he caused the slain to die, but because the killer hastened a matter that Allah alone has reserved, while the slain died at his appointed term. Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is the One who appointed man as vicegerent (khalifah) on earth, and the meaning of this vicegerency is stated by the Truth in His words:

﴿And He made you inhabit it [and develop it]﴾ (Qur'an 11:61).

So Allah is the One who made man a vicegerent in the universe in order to cultivate it, and the cultivation of the universe arises from thinking about the advancement and the good in the universe. What is good, we leave as good; and if we can increase its goodness, let us do so.

The earth, for example, produces crops, and even if man does not sow it, he finds crops growing from it. The Truth wants man to develop this property in the earth, so man brings seeds, plows the land, and plants it. This increases the good that already exists. And all of this is a branch of the existence of life.

Thus the vicegerency on earth for its cultivation requires life and the preservation of life for the vicegerent. And since the preservation of life is a necessity, O vicegerent, do not go to another vicegerent like yourself to end his life, thereby disabling his revival of the earth and his developing of it. Fighting was legislated for the believers against the disbelievers, because the movement of the disbelievers in life is a corrupting movement, and repelling corruption always takes precedence over bringing about benefit. So whoever corrupts life, the believers fight him so that his life is ended and life is freed from an obstacle within it.

Thus the Truth wants life to belong to those who improve the earth through their lives. The disbelievers spread corruption in the earth, live without a method, and take the wealth of the weak so that they themselves become strong through it. So Allah legislated fighting either so that they believe and submit to the method, or so that life is rid of their evil. Therefore, if a person directs killing at a believer who is himself fit to develop life, he has committed a crime against life. Likewise, if a person kills himself, he has committed a crime against life too. Why? Because he has deprived life of one who could have developed the earth through his activity.

If a person is bold against his own life or the life of another, then he must be disciplined. How? Allah, Glorified is He, says:

﴿And those who earn evil deeds—the recompense of an evil deed is its equivalent﴾ (Qur'an 10:27).

Islamic legislation has prescribed for the killer who acts with premeditation and ambush a punishment of death. Thereby legislation protects life and does not encourage killing; rather, it prevents killing. Thus the hudud (fixed penalties) and the retaliation (qisas) were established in order to give life breadth in its necessities, not to constrict those necessities. When the Truth, Glorified and Exalted, spoke of lawful fighting, He wanted to make clear to us: beware lest you transgress in this matter and use fighting in other than a lawful cause. So if a person is bold against another person to end his life outside a lawful believing war, what then is the position?

Legislation says: he is killed. And it should have been in your mind not to be bold in taking away anyone's life, unless it was a mistake on your part. But if you do commit an error that results in the effect, which is killing, then what is the matter? There is one affected by you, namely the slain, and you are the killer, but you did not intend it. There are thus two matters: the absence of intention in committing the mistaken killing, and the second is the occurrence of the killing.

Legislation says on this matter: the killer without intent has taken away a human life, and this person's life has many connections within his general believing environment, and he has connections within his particular family environment, such as his household, the family to which he belongs or which belongs to him, or the family in its broader sense, namely the lineal ascendants and descendants. How many circles, then? A general believing circle, the circle of kin in its broad sense, the circle of the family, and the particular circle of the family in its ascendants and descendants. When you end a person's life within the general believing environment, that environment will be affected by the loss of one believer who submits to Allah's method and is useful in his movement, because the believing circle has general benefit.

But the circle of kin has a somewhat limited private benefit, and in the family circle his benefit is of a particular kind, while in the ascendants and descendants we find his benefit to be significant and very particular. Thus this killing involves terrifying a general environment, a family environment, and the environment of ascendants and descendants.

For this reason I want you to notice something that passes over all of us, and perhaps many of us do not attend to it, though it occurs very often. For example: when we are sitting in a gathering and someone comes and says, "So-and-so has died," and in this gathering there are people who know him in a general way, others who know him in a particular way and have a connection with him, some of his relatives, and the father or son of the deceased is present. Look at the effect of the announcement or the news on the faces of the people. Each one will be moved to the degree that it reaches him and connects him to the one who died. One says, "May Allah have mercy on him," another asks in alarm, "How did that happen?" A third weeps bitterly, and a fourth weeps flowing tears in order to see the dead man. The news is one, so why does the effect and echo of the emotions multiply, and why is the emotion not one?

We say: emotion arises by compulsion, through a non-conscious process, in proportion to the benefit the deceased was to the one who is moved by his death. The one who met him occasionally and briefly at long intervals says, "May Allah have mercy on him." The one who sat with him every festival thinks of his memories with him. And when we come to his children, we find that the employed graduate with a family differs in emotion from the one recently graduated or still studying, or the little girl who is still receiving education. These children receive the news with varying emotions: the son who has a family and a home receives the news with an emotion different from the son who is still in school, and the emotion of the daughter who is married and has a family differs from that of the daughter who has not yet been married off.

Thus emotion occurs in proportion to usefulness, and that is why we may find it for a friend more than for a brother. They said: Which is dearer to you, your brother or your friend? He said: The one who is more useful. So the reception of news of the end of life is different; grief over him and sorrow at his parting arise in proportion to the spread of his benefit in society.

The one for whom you find the whole society agitated, rebellious, and grieving at his parting was useful to the whole society. And the one whom only his family mourns, we say: he was in proportion to his benefit to his family and children. A person may die and no one feels that the universe has diminished. This is the reason they wanted each person to have a homeland. They said: people's homelands are in proportion to their aspirations. One whose only homeland is himself sees everything for himself and does not see himself for anyone, even if they are his children.

There is one whose homeland is his family, working in proportion to its benefit; one whose homeland is his clan and village; one whose homeland is his nation; and one whose homeland is the whole world. Thus when society is struck by the loss of one person, the shock comes in proportion to his homeland. When people are surprised by one who is killed by mistake, the doer is excused. But does his excuse prevent that his act reached beyond him, and that the other was killed? The effect has occurred, and the shock falls upon those nearest to him in benefit. And since the killing was a mistake, retaliation will not be carried out against the killer; but he must pay blood-money, and this blood-money is distributed among the people who were affected by the loss of his life, because there is a principle that says: "The expansion of benefit and the contraction of harm."

When you see something that will benefit you, the soul expands; when you see something that will harm you, the soul contracts. When news of the death of someone dear to a person comes, his soul contracts; and when good comes to him afterward, namely receiving a portion of the slain's blood-money, the soul expands, and thereby the effect caused by the mistaken killing is treated.

By the ruling of the law, blood-money is paid by the 'aqilah (paternal kin who bear the obligation), on condition that it is not taken from the ascendants and descendants, so that a calamity of losing a person at the hand of one of their ascendants or descendants is not piled upon them, since they would be frightened by it, and so this matter is not combined with their participation in the blood-money. It is as if the legislation wanted to treat the shock produced by a deviation with a remedy that is a protection against reaction, thereby achieving balance in society. So the one who kills by mistake is not retaliated against by society, but there is the blood-money. And for the sake of spreading responsibility, the killer does not pay it himself; rather the 'aqilah pays it, because when the 'aqilah knows that whoever among its members commits a crime will be borne with him by them, they teach their members the art of safeguarding the rights of others, since each of them will have to pay, and thereby balance is achieved in society.

The Truth, Glorified and Exalted, teaches us to rule out that a believer would kill a believer except by mistake. So it is not right that this should happen intentionally; He says:

﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾, meaning that such killing should not occur deliberately, because the bond of faith (al-luhmah al-iman, with the lam vowelled with a damma) prevents this. But if it does happen, what is the remedy?

﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake. And whoever kills a believer by mistake, then [he must free] a believing slave and pay blood-money to his family.﴾

Glorified is He does not mention retaliation (qisas) here, because retaliation was already mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah in His words:

﴿Prescribed for you is retribution for the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾ (Qur'an 2:178).

Retaliation is the right of the guardian (wali); he may pardon or take the blood-money. It is as if he says: "I have pardoned retaliation in exchange for the blood-money." We must distinguish between the hadd (fixed penalty) and qisas. Qisas is the right of the guardian, while the hadd is the right of Allah. The guardian may waive qisas, but no one can waive the hudud, because they are not the right of anyone but are the right of Allah.

So for mistaken killing He said: ﴿then [he must free] a believing slave﴾. Here we may ask: what does the family of the one killed benefit from the freeing of a believing slave? Does that return to the family of the slain as an expansion of benefit? It may not benefit them in anything, but it benefits society, because the one held in bondage, the male slave or female slave, belongs to his master, and the master controls the slave's movement; but when the slave is free, he is free in movement. The slave's movement with his master is limited, and in his freedom there is a movement beneficial to society.

Thus the contraction that resulted from the killing of a believing soul is matched by an expansion in the freedom of one who was restricted in his movement, and we say to him: "Go forth in your movement to serve all your society." The Truth, by this, intends to open a channel for the freedom of slaves among the many channels that Islam established for that purpose.

After this statement, ﴿and blood-money paid to his family﴾, in order to produce expansion in the souls of his family, so that the contraction resulting from the news of the killing is followed by expansion. Therefore we find that a family struck in one of its members by an incident lives in grief for days, then they take the papers and receive the blood-money or compensation with them, which shows that in this there is some consolation, some solace, and some compensation. If the matter were disdained, they would say, "We do not want that," but this does not happen.

Afterward we find that the one who has lost the life of a beloved does not remain in a state of grief in order to lose his own life; in reality the grief of the mourner...

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 4, verse 93:

When the Truth (al-Haqq) legislates, it must necessarily prescribe the recompense and the punishment for the one who kills deliberately. And He says:

﴿Whoever kills a believer deliberately, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever, and Allah will be angry with him and curse him and prepare for him a great punishment.﴾ (4:93)

Killing here is of a believer, by deliberate intent, so the matter is different from unintentional killing (al-qatl al-khata', killing by mistake), which the killer does not realize until after it has happened. The recompense of one who kills a believer deliberately is Hell, and there is no expiation (kaffarah) for him ever. In this way the Truth shows us the ugliness of the crime of deliberate killing. For deliberateness (al-ta'ammud) means that the killer has lived with the idea of killing, and for this reason the law says "killing with premeditation" (qatl ma'a sabq al-israr). That is, the killer has lived the killing in his imagination and then in his act. In the period in which he arranges the killing, his religious restraint (wazi'uhu al-dini) should have checked him, and this means that Allah had been absent from his mind during the time of preparing the crime. Since he has lived in that state, he has been absent from Allah, and had Allah come into his mind, he would have held back. And since a person's mind has been absent from Allah, Allah makes him absent from His mercy.

﴿Whoever kills a believer deliberately, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein﴾. The scholars mentioned the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse: a man named Miqyas ibn Dababa had a brother named Hisham, and he found his brother killed among Banu al-Najjar, a people of the Ansar in Medina. When he found Hisham dead, Miqyas went to our master the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him of the news, so he sent with him a man from Banu Fihr and wrote to them that they should hand over to Miqyas the killer of his brother. Banu al-Najjar said, "By Allah, we do not know of any killer for him, but we will pay the blood money (diyah)." So they gave him one hundred camels, and then the two returned to Medina. Miqyas then attacked the Fihri man and killed him in revenge for his brother, took the camels, and went back to Mecca as an apostate (murtaddan), and he began to recite:

"I killed Fihr in return for him, and I carried his blood-money,
The chiefs of Banu al-Najjar, lords of... 
I dismounted with him, and you see my vengeance was attained,
And I was the first to return to the idols."

When this reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he declared his blood lawful to be shed (ahdar damahu). The meaning of "ahdar damahu" is that he made his blood permissible, that is, whoever kills him bears no punishment. Until the day of the Conquest came, when he found Miqyas clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah seeking refuge in it, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered him killed. ﴿Whoever kills a believer deliberately, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever, and Allah will be angry with him and curse him and prepare for him a great punishment.﴾

Here we find more than one stage of punishment: the recompense of Hell, abiding forever in the Fire, anger from Allah, a curse from Allah, and preparation by Allah of a great punishment. So Hell is not the whole of the punishment; within it there is punishment, and there is abiding in the Fire, and there is anger, and there is a curse, then the preparation of a great punishment. This is what we seek refuge in Allah from. Some of us imagine that punishment is Hell alone, and some may overlook that there are many kinds of punishment. In life we see a person imprisoned and think that imprisonment is everything, but when we learn what happens inside the prison, we realize that there is something worse than imprisonment.

Here there is a pause at which the scholars stopped: Does this killer have repentance (tawbah)? The scholars differed on this. One scholar says: there is no repentance for such a killer. Another says: no, there is repentance. Ibn 'Abbas (raḍiya Allahu 'anhu) came and sat in a gathering, and a man came and asked him: "Does the one who kills deliberately have repentance?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "No." After a while, another man came and asked Ibn 'Abbas: "Does the one who kills deliberately have repentance?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "Yes." His companions said: "How can you say that, when you said no before, and today you say yes?"

Ibn 'Abbas said: "My first questioner wanted to kill deliberately, but my second questioner has already killed. I frightened the first, and I did not despair the second of the mercy of his Lord."

How did Ibn 'Abbas distinguish between the two states? It is the faith-based discernment (al-fitnah al-imaniyyah) and insight that Allah spreads over the mufti. When a companion asked the Prophet (ﷺ) in the presence of his Companions, "Which Islam is best?", he (ṣallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam) said: "Feed the food, and give the greeting of peace to those you know and those you do not know" (1). Another asked him and he answered: "The one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe." Thus he (peace be upon him) would answer each questioner with what he saw as most suitable for his condition or the condition of the listener, and would answer each group with what was most beneficial for them. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (raḍiya Allahu 'anhu) asked him: "Which deeds are best?" He (peace be upon him) said: "Prayer at its proper time." I said: "Then what, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "That people be safe from your tongue" (2).

We know that the verse on deliberate killing requires more reflection on its text: ﴿fa-jaza'uhu jahannamu khalidan fiha﴾. Is khulud (abiding) a long stay, or is it in the sense of perpetuity (ta'bid), meaning that the duration of abiding never ends? If the duration of abiding never ended, the Truth would not have described staying in the Fire once with His saying: ﴿abiding therein﴾ (3:88), and once again with His saying: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾ (4:169).

This statement indicates that the word "abadan" (forever) carries a nuance beyond khulud without perpetuity. If the two statements agreed that khulud in its absolute sense implies perpetuity, and that ﴿abiding therein forever﴾ also implies perpetuity, then the word "abadan" would add nothing. The Qur'an is the speech of Allah, and the speech of Allah is free from futility or repetition. Therefore we must pause to understand that khulud is a long stay, and that khulud abadan is a stay that never ends in length; on this basis we have understanding. Every word of the Qur'an is precise (muhkam) and has meaning. Moreover, when the word "khalidin" appears in the Qur'an, we find the Truth, glory be to Him, saying of the Fire's abiding: ﴿On the day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission; then among them are the wretched and the happy. As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, having therein groaning and wheezing, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills. Indeed your Lord is the Accomplisher of what He intends﴾ (11:105–107).

So the Truth, glory be to Him, made an exception from abiding: ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾. An exception must have a time-period, so we do not take khulud to mean perpetuity, but khulud is a long time. Likewise He says of the abiding of Paradise: ﴿As for those who were made happy, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills — a gift never cut off﴾ (11:108).

His saying: ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ indicates that abiding for them ends, as long as there is an exception; the exception must have a time-period, and the time is excluded from abiding, so abiding is not perpetual.

We must approach the verses in this spirit. On this question we find a pause by a scholar of the doctrinal sciences (a'lam al-'aqa'id) in the Abbasid era, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd. 'Amr was among the scholars known for guarding the dignity of knowledge and the honor of scholars, to the point that the caliph of that time said of him, among some who claimed affiliation to knowledge: "They are all hunters of prey except 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd." His scholarly standing was high, and his soul had a faith-based dignity that rises above the trivialities of life. 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd was precise in opinion, and Qays ibn Anas narrates this story about him: "I was in the gathering of 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd when 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd said: 'I will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and it will be said to me: Why did you say that the killer by intent has no repentance?' He said: I recited the verse: ﴿fa-jaza'uhu jahannamu khalidan fiha﴾."

'Amr ought to have noticed that the inspiration that came to him, or the vision Allah showed him that he would be brought on the Day of Resurrection to be asked why he issued a fatwa that the deliberate killer has no repentance, should have led him to notice that it implies the deliberate killer has repentance, because his being questioned about it on the Day of Resurrection indicates reproach for that.

We say this so that we know that the Truth, glory be to Him, placed above every possessor of knowledge one who is more knowing. But 'Amr mentioned what came in the Truth's saying: ﴿fa-jaza'uhu jahannamu khalidan fiha﴾. Qays ibn Anas said: "I was the youngest of those sitting, so I said to him: 'If I had been with you, I would have said as you said: ﴿fa-jaza'uhu jahannamu khalidan fiha﴾, and I would also have said: ﴿Indeed Allah does not forgive that He be associated with, and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ (4:48).'" Qays said: "By Allah, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd did not reply to what I said." That meaning indicates 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd's agreement. What does this indicate? It indicates that we should not take the words ﴿khalidin fiha﴾ in the sense of an endless perpetuity, because Allah has made an exception from abiding in another verse.

When the Truth, glory be to Him, had explained the rulings on deliberate killing and unintentional killing, scholars investigated and found that there is a killing called "quasi-deliberate" (shibh al-'amd), meaning it is neither deliberate nor mistaken. For example, a person strikes another with an instrument that does not ordinarily kill, and he dies from it. Here deliberateness exists: the striker strikes, holds an instrument and strikes with it, and it happens that the instrument kills, which it does not usually do. The scholars said: the killing is with it, not by it, so there is no retaliation (qisas), but there is blood money (diyah).

2 Narrated by al-Tabarani.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 94:

Allah, glory be to Him, wished to clarify: after what has occurred, and after I have spoken to you about killing in all its forms and shades, whether the killing is permissible, such as killing disbelieving enemies in war between them and you, or deliberate killing, or accidental killing, or killing that is quasi-deliberate. Therefore He alerts us: you must be extremely cautious in this matter, taking care to verify where your swords fall upon the necks of your brothers. So He says:

﴿O you who have believed, when you go forth in the cause of Allah, investigate carefully, and do not say to one who gives you [a greeting of] peace, "You are not a believer," seeking the goods of worldly life; for with Allah are abundant spoils. Thus were you before, and Allah conferred His favor upon you. So investigate carefully. Indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾ (4:94)

O believers, when you strike in the cause of Allah, investigate and make certain, so that your swords, your spears, or your arrows do not act until you have verified: ﴿And do not say to one who gives you [a greeting of] peace, "You are not a believer," seeking the goods of worldly life; for with Allah are abundant spoils. Thus were you before, and Allah conferred His favor upon you. So investigate carefully. Indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾

So this verse combines all the meanings: in it is the ruling, its justification (haythiyyah), and its purpose. Allah begins it with His words: ﴿O you who have believed﴾. The address of faith is the justification for adherence to the ruling. He did not say: ﴿O mankind, when you strike, investigate﴾; rather He said: ﴿O you who have believed, when you go forth in the cause of Allah, investigate carefully﴾. He addresses those who believe in Him with a ruling, because they have believed in Him as God, and so long as they have believed, it is incumbent upon them to follow what Allah requires. The justification for every ruling among the rulings is that the believer has believed in the One who issued the ruling. So beware, O believer, of saying, "What is the cause?" or "What is the wisdom?", lest you enter yourself into a labyrinth. We continue to repeat this matter, because it often surfaces in people's minds, and some of them ask about the wisdom of everything. Therefore we say: when you know the wisdom of a thing, you arrive at the wisdom, not at the One who commanded the ruling.

Now we see those who are wasteful toward themselves, who do not believe in Allah, or who believe in Allah but have committed major sins, from false testimony, to usury, to drinking wine. When doctors examine the liver of a wine drinker, for example, they find it has become cirrhotic, and that any dose of wine will cause death. Here he abstains from drinking wine. Why did he abstain? Because he understood the wisdom. And it may be that the one who said it to him was a Magian. Was his abstention from the ruling in obedience to a divine command? No. Rather, the believer abstains from wine because it has been prohibited by a ruling from Allah, and the believer implements all the rulings, even in matters that are not harmful. So who said that Allah prohibits only what is harmful? He may prohibit something as a discipline for a person. We give this example, and to Allah belongs the highest example: a husband says to his wife, "Beware of giving our son some of the sweets you have brought." He forbids the sweets to his son not because they are harmful, but because he wants to discipline the son and train him.

And Allah says: ﴿For wrongdoing from those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them﴾ (4:160). So the one who goes to implement the command of Allah goes to it because Allah has said it, not because the wisdom of the ruling benefits him. If a person goes to a ruling for its benefit or its harm, his faith is deficient. Allah, in many instances, manages His wisdom in the rulings until a person sees one of the infinite aspects of Allah's wisdom that was hidden from him, and the person says: "I used to stand at such-and-such a wisdom, then events and days showed me that Allah spoke the truth in what He said." This encourages a person to take Allah's rulings while submitting to them. And Allah says: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, and faith is the justification: O you who have believed in Me as a powerful, wise God... listen to what I want from you: ﴿O you who have believed, when you go forth in the cause of Allah﴾. And striking, as we know, is the violent and forceful movement of a limb upon something else. And His words: ﴿And when you travel through the earth﴾ (4:101).

Its meaning is that all of life is movement and activity. Why striking through the earth? Because Allah has deposited in it all the sustenance of creatures; when they wish to bring forth its good, they plough it until it is stirred, sow the seeds, and after that irrigate. Afterward the fruits emerge, and this is the process of stirring the earth. Thus every movement requires exertion and striving. And Allah says: ﴿And others travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty﴾ (73:20).

Since the matter is striking through the earth, it requires resolve from a person and strength. Therefore it is said: the earth loves whoever humbles it with digging and tilling. The more a person's movement in the earth intensifies, the more good it brings forth for him. Striking in the cause of Allah is jihad, or preparing the requisites of jihad. And Allah, glory be to Him, says to us: ﴿And prepare against them whatever you are able of power﴾ (8:60).

Preparation is something that precedes battles. And how is preparation accomplished?

We prepare bodies, and bodies need the requisites of life. We prepare equipment, and equipment needs research into the elements of the earth and research into the various industries, so that we choose the best of them. All processes of preparation require human research and craftsmanship. Therefore it is said in the righteous report: "A single arrow in the cause of Allah, by it Allah forgives four persons."

Why? Because there is a person who cut the wood from which the arrow is made and polished it, and there is a person who put feathers on the arrow so that it would fly forward, and there is the one who fixed the arrowhead, and there is the one who shoots the arrow with the bow. Allah wants us to be strong so that our striking may be strong, and so He says: ﴿When you strike in the cause of Allah, investigate carefully﴾. We know that striking in the cause of Allah is not only at the time of jihad, but in all circumstances of life, because whatever a duty cannot be completed without is itself a duty. "Investigate carefully" means: do not take matters at their face value, and do not carry out a command or do an act until you have verified and made certain, lest you harm a people through injustice.

There is a story concerning this ruling. There was a man named Muhallam ibn Jaththama, and between him and another named Amir ibn al-Adbat al-Ashja'i there was enmity, that is, some hatred. Afterward Muhallam was in a detachment, a small band of soldiers of limited number, and he encountered Amir al-Ashja'i. Amir had embraced Islam, so he gave the greeting of peace to Muhallam. Muhallam said: "Amir has only become Muslim in order to escape from me." Muhallam killed Amir. Then he went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the Messenger asked him: "Why did you not investigate? Did he not give you the greeting of peace? How can you say that he said 'Peace be upon you' only to save himself from being killed?"

Muhallam said: "Ask forgiveness for me, O Messenger of Allah."

When someone says to the Messenger of Allah: "Ask forgiveness for me, O Messenger of Allah," the Messenger of Allah, with his faithful insight, immediately knows the state of the one seeking forgiveness. If the Messenger of Allah says, "May Allah forgive you," he knows that the man was excused; and if the Messenger does not say that, the one seeking forgiveness knows that he is sinful. Because there was rancour and enmity between Muhallam and Amir, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Muhallam: "May Allah not forgive you," because the Messenger ﷺ knew that the rancour and hatred were what made him not scrutinize Amir's situation.

The narrators said: Muhallam died seven days after this incident. They buried him, but the earth expelled him. They came to the Prophet ﷺ and told him of that, and he said: "The earth accepts one who is worse than your companion, but Allah wished to admonish you." Then they cast him between two cliffs of a mountain and threw stones upon him.(1)

When a verse came that contradicted the known laws of the world as people understand them, the Prophet wanted people not to be tempted by these signs. An example of this is when Ibrahim, the son of the Prophet, died, and the sun was eclipsed. The people said: "The sun was eclipsed because of the son of the Messenger of Allah." But since the matter concerned beliefs, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ clarified it, as in the noble hadith:

On the authority of al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, who said: The sun was eclipsed in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the day Ibrahim died. The people said: "The sun was eclipsed for the death of Ibrahim." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The sun and the moon do not eclipse for the death or the life of anyone. So when you see that, pray and call upon Allah."(2)

They said this out of honor for the Messenger of Allah and his son Ibrahim, but the Messenger wanted to correct the people's concepts and beliefs. Likewise, when the earth expelled Muhallam, so that no one would be tempted or say anything: every one whom the earth does not expel is of good deeds, for there are many disbelievers who were buried and were not expelled. Therefore the Messenger of Allah said: "The earth accepted one who is worse than Muhallam, but Allah wished to admonish people so that they would not return to the like of it." If he had not said that, what would have happened? A slight tremor in one part might have occurred, and people would have assumed and said: "Everyone whom the earth does not expel is of good deeds," and Abu Jahl would have been in an acceptable state, and likewise al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. But the Messenger of Allah ﷺ places such matters in their correct position; therefore he said: "The earth accepts one who is worse than Muhallam, but Allah wished to admonish the people so that they would not return."(3)

﴿O you who have believed, when you go forth in the cause of Allah, investigate carefully, and do not say to one who gives you [a greeting of] peace, "You are not a believer"﴾. And in connection with this, a noble brother said to me: I was listening to one of the radio stations, and they erred and said "fa-tathabbatu" (so verify) instead of "fa-tabayyanu" (so investigate) in the words of the Truth: ﴿If there comes to you a defiant one with news, investigate carefully﴾ (49:6). I say: this is one of the recitations, and the meanings always converge; "tabayyana" means "seek clarification so as to be certain." We know that the Qur'an was revealed in seven modes (ahruf), and the writing of the Qur'an was without dots and without vowel marks, and this is a situation different from ours, where we find the letters vocalized with fatha, damma and kasra.

We know that there are letters similar in form. The "ba'" resembles each of: the "ya'", the "nun", the "ta'" and the "tha'". These dots were not present, and these marks were not present before al-Hajjaj al-Thaqafi; they used to read from linguistic faculty (malakat al-'arabiyya), and from instruction and following of revelation. Therefore: ﴿fa-tabayyanu﴾, of what is it composed? It is composed of: the "fa'", about which there is no disagreement, and the "ta'", and the remaining letters are the "ba'", the "ya'", and the "nun".

Each of these letters can be made "tathabbatu" by placing dots, or made "tabayyanu"; the disagreement is about the dots. If we removed the dots, we would read it in more than one form. What we follow in this is what has come down from the revelation sent to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Therefore, when they brought a person who did not memorize the Qur'an and brought him a copy of the mushaf to read what was in it, he said: "The workmanship of Allah, and who is better than Allah in workmanship?"

There was no disagreement about the "sad", but there was disagreement about the "ba'", for it may be a "ba'" or a "nun"; likewise the "ghayn" may be an "'ayn". The reading of this verse in the reading of Hafs is: ﴿The dye of Allah, and who is better than Allah in dye?﴾ (2:138).

When the person who does not skillfully memorize the Qur'an read it, he said: "The workmanship of Allah, and who is better than Allah in workmanship?" The meaning is one.

But the recitation of the Qur'an is by transmission (tawqifiyya), and following the revelation that Jibril, peace be upon him, brought from the Lord to His Messenger ﷺ. It is not permissible for anyone to recite the Qur'an according to what he thinks, even if the form of the word accepts that and admits it and does not prohibit it. Therefore they said: the correct recitation has pillars, which are:

1. That it conforms to one of the aspects of the Arabic language.
2. That it conforms to the orthography of one of the Uthmanic copies (masahif).
3. That its chain of transmission is authentically attributed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ by a certain, mass-transmitted path that admits no doubt.

These conditions were versified by the author of Taybat al-Nashr, who said:
"Whatever agrees with a mode of Arabic grammar, and with the orthography of the rasm, even if only as a possibility,
And whose chain is authentically sound, that is the Qur'an. These three are the pillars."

And the words of the Exalted:

{"He said: My punishment I afflict with whom I will..."

(1) Tafsir al-Qur'an al-'Azim of the Imam Ibn Kathir.
(2) Related by al-Bukhari.
(3) Related by Ahmad and Ibn Jarir.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 95:

Then Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, wished to make clear the distinction between those who stayed back from jihad in the way of Allah and those who strove, so He said, glory be to Him:

﴿Not equal are those believers who sit at home, other than those with a harm, and those who strive in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives. Allah has preferred those who strive with their wealth and their lives over those who sit at home by a degree. And to each Allah has promised the best reward, and Allah has preferred those who strive over those who sit at home with a great reward.﴾

There is a story behind this verse. Drawing lessons from this story requires alertness, for it teaches us how the Truth addresses His creation. Our master Zayd ibn Thabit, who was trusted with writing down the revelation of the Messenger of Allah, and trusted with collecting the Book of Allah from the flat white stones (al-lakhaf)(1), from the shoulder bones, and from the breasts of the Companions, related to us, saying:

"I was beside the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when tranquility (al-sakinah) overcame him, and this always used to precede the descent of revelation upon the Messenger of Allah. His thigh fell upon my thigh until I feared it would crush it."

That is, the thigh of the Messenger of Allah was heavy.

When revelation came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, it perhaps produced a physical effect upon his body, such that if he was on a mount, people knew he was being revealed to, because the mount would groan beneath him. So when the thigh of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was upon the thigh of Zayd ibn Thabit, Zayd must have felt the weight of the thigh of the Messenger of Allah, and the revelation had come. Zayd said: "I feared that his thigh would crush my thigh," meaning it would be struck with a severe blow or broken. When the tranquility lifted from him, he said: "Write: ﴿Not equal are the believers who sit at home and those who strive﴾." Then our master Ibn Umm Maktum, who, as we know, was blind, said: "What about those believers who are unable to strive, O Messenger of Allah?"

This is the faith-based alertness of Ibn Umm Maktum, for he understood his own position with regard to this statement, that he is unable to strive, and he knew that if the verse remained this way, he would not be equal to those who strive. Therefore he spoke this alert word: "What about those who are unable to do that, O Messenger of Allah?"

Then the tranquility came upon the Messenger again, then it lifted from him, and he said to Zayd ibn Thabit: "Write: ﴿Not equal are the believers who sit at home, other than those with a harm, and those who strive in the way of Allah﴾."

It is as though it descended as a reassuring answer for those who cannot fight, such as Ibn Umm Maktum. And one may say: Was the verse waiting for Ibn Umm Maktum to interject so that he would say this?

We say: Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, wished to alert every believer that when he receives a word from Allah, he should reflect and determine his own position with respect to that word. If this was the state of our master Ibn Umm Maktum when the Messenger of Allah heard from his Lord, then it teaches us how to recall our role from any matter we hear. When Ibn Umm Maktum heard the verse, he saw his position with respect to it, and this is what the Truth desires from His creation.

Zayd ibn Thabit said: "So I wrote it down."

This is the precision of Zayd ibn Thabit in conveying, which indicates the truthfulness of the narration. When he first wrote ﴿Not equal are the believers who sit at home and those who strive﴾, did the word ﴿those who strive﴾ not stick to the word ﴿the believers﴾? Then when Allah added ﴿other than those with a harm﴾, where would he write it?

Zayd ibn Thabit had to reduce the size of the writing so as to write ﴿other than those with a harm﴾ between the words ﴿the believers﴾ and ﴿those who strive﴾. Our master Zayd ibn Thabit said: "It was revealed alone, and as if I am looking at its attachment at the crack of the shoulder," for they used to write on shoulder bones. The shoulder bone on which Zayd ibn Thabit wrote was cracked, and this was a sign in it.

Allah wishes by this to alert the believers that when they receive the Book of Allah, they must receive it with faith-based alertness, such that their ears hear nothing except what first passes over their minds, so that every believer understands his position with respect to it, and the verse passes over their hearts a second time so that a conviction settles within their selves.

Thus was the story of Zayd ibn Thabit and Ibn Umm Maktum and the revelation in this verse: ﴿Not equal are the believers who sit at home, other than those with a harm, and those who strive﴾.

There are situations in which a verb occurs and cannot have only one agent, but must have two. An example of this is when we say: "Zayd and Amr took part together." And when we describe football players, we find one catching the ball after another, so we say: "The players caught the ball one after another."

When Allah says ﴿لا يستوي (not equal)﴾, this indicates that there are two things that are not equal. Which of them is unequal to the other? Each of them is unequal to the other, and therefore both are "fa'il" (agent) in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis), for the strivers are not equal to those who sit, and those who sit are not equal to the strivers, because each of them is both agent and object.

When we say ﴿لا يستوي القاعدون من المؤمنين (not equal are the believers who sit)﴾, what is the counterpart of "those who sit" (al-qa'idin) in the noble verse? It is "those who strive" (al-mujahidin). But the counterpart of those who sit in ordinary life is those who stand (al-qa'imun), and the counterpart of those who strive is "those who do not strive." So it would have been possible to say: "not equal are those who sit and those who stand," or to say: "not equal are those who strive and those who do not strive." What then is the wisdom in the use of "those who sit" and "those who strive"?

Allah wishes to show that at the beginning of Islam, every believer, upon entering Islam, considered himself a soldier in a state of readiness, and they were always at a supreme level of preparedness to answer the call immediately. The Muslim was not in a state of relaxation, but in readiness, as though standing at all times to answer the call, and the one who sat was the one who was not among the ranks of the believers. The saying of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, illustrates this: "The best of people's livelihood is a man holding the bridle of his horse in the way of Allah, flying upon its back; whenever he hears a cry (haY'ah) or a call to arms (fazi'ah), he flies to it, seeking death or being killed where it is expected; or a man in a sheep-pen on the top of one of these mountain peaks, or in one of these valleys, establishing prayer, paying zakat, and worshipping his Lord until certainty comes to him; he is among people only in goodness." (2)

So if the believer is not ready, then he is sitting, and sitting, as we know, is the opposite of standing. And Allah says: ﴿So remember Allah standing and sitting﴾ (part of verse 103, surah an-Nisa').

From this saying we know that the counterpart of standing is sitting.

We must know that every word has a specific meaning. Some of us imagine that qu'ud (sitting, staying back) is the same as julus (sitting down), but precision requires us to know that qu'ud occurs from standing, and julus occurs from lying down. One says: "He was lying down, then sat (jalasa)," and "He was standing, then sat down (qa'ada)."

When Allah says here ﴿لا يستوي القاعدون من المؤمنين غير أولي الضرر (not equal are the believers who sit, other than those with a harm)﴾, qu'ud is the counterpart of standing. So the state of the striver is always standing; he does not wait until he stands, but is alert and ready. The noble hadith expands the scope of the striver's responsibilities, drawing a picture of the fighter who is fully prepared, on the back of the horse, holding the reins, so that no surprise may overtake him.

Was there any suspicion that the one who sits and the striver would be equal? No, but Allah wishes to clarify a hidden matter of faith, and He shows it clearly to every understanding.

We say to the student: "The one who studies succeeds, and the one who does not study fails." This is a self-evident matter, but we say it so that it becomes clear in the focus of the student's awareness, and he turns to his responsibilities.

When Allah says ﴿لا يستوي القاعدون من المؤمنين غير أولي الضرر والمجاهدون في سبيل الله﴾, does that mean that in the time of the Messenger of Allah one mind imagined equality between the one who sits and the striver? No, but the Truth wishes it to be a matter of faith at a level of faith from Allah. Then He draws attention to the quality of those who sit and are not equal to the strivers, saying: ﴿غير أولي الضرر (other than those with a harm)﴾. Harm (darar) is what corrupts a thing, such as sickness, and this is what the Truth's saying clarifies:

﴿There is no blame upon the weak, nor upon the sick, nor upon those who find nothing to spend, if they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger. There is no cause for blame against the good-doers, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. Nor is there blame upon those who came to you to be provided with mounts, and you said: "I cannot find anything to mount you upon," and they turned away while their eyes overflowed with tears of grief that they could not find what to spend.﴾ (Surah at-Tawbah).

So weakness is a harm that removes a person from the elements of health and well-being, and sickness is a harm, and those who find no wealth to spend from, and those who come to the Messenger and there is no mount with the Messenger to carry them, so they depart with their eyes overflowing with tears of grief because they cannot find what to spend. Among these believers was one who grieved because the Messenger of Allah had not found a horse or mount to carry him to the place of battle: ﴿Nor upon those who came to you to be provided with mounts, and you said: "I cannot find anything to mount you upon," and they turned away while their eyes overflowed with tears of grief that they could not find what to spend.﴾ (Surah at-Tawbah).

They turned away while their eyes overflowed with tears. The word "turned away" (tawallaw) here carries great meaning. The Truth did not say that their eyes overflow with tears apart from turning away; they do not weep in front of the Prophet, but they weep in the state of their turning away, and this is a psychological reaction from the excess of being affected, because they do not take part in fighting. The word "overflow" (tafid) indicates that the tears have overcome the whole eye. They do not feign this, but the emotion overwhelms them; for one who feigns it squeezes his eyes and makes an effort at showing off, whereas the emotion of the believers who do not fight overcomes them, so their eyes overflow with tears.

There is another verse in which the Truth specified the situations in which the believer is not required to fight: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor blame upon the lame, nor blame upon the sick. And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ (part of verse 17, surah al-Fath).

These, then, are the people of harm.

﴿Not equal are the believers who sit, other than those with a harm, and those who strive in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives﴾. And since they are not equal, which of them is the better?

This is what the rest of the verse clarifies, which carries the clear statement of faith: ﴿Allah has preferred those who strive with their wealth and their lives over those who sit by a degree. And to each Allah has promised the best reward﴾. Allah promised both the faith-based best reward, because each of them is a believer, but the striver has a degree over the one who sits. If someone asks: "Why did Allah promise the one who sits among those with a harm the best reward?" I say: We must be attentive, and must understand and reflect well when we read the Qur'an; for the one who has been struck by an affliction and suffered harm from it, and then patiently accepted Allah's decree in himself, will he not take a reward for this?

He has taken the reward, and so the Truth must give the one who did not take a reward like it an opportunity to take another reward, so that all are equal in the faith-based path. Therefore He says: ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best reward﴾.

The "best" (al-husna) for the one with a harm is that he takes the reward of patience in the affliction that befell him, and the one who was not harmed will take the reward of striving; thus all have attained the best from Allah.

﴿And to each Allah has promised the best reward, and Allah has preferred those who strive over those who sit with a great reward﴾.

He, glory be to Him, places a new reward for the one who stands striving over the one who sits: at the beginning of the verse He mentioned a higher "degree" for the one who stands striving, and here, "a great reward." What is the explanation of this great reward? The explanation comes in His saying: ﴿Degrees from Him, and forgiveness and mercy. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (verse 96).

(1) al-Lakhaf: white, thin stones; its singular is lakhfah.
(2) Narrated by Muslim in al-Imarah and Ibn Majah in al-Fitan, and narrated by Ahmad. Al-Haya'ah is the sound upon the enemy's arrival. Al-Fazi'ah is the rising up to the enemy. Al-Sha'fah is the top of the mountain.

Thus He (Glorified is He) has granted those with a valid excuse (ulu al-darar) a rank, and has preferred the mujahid in the way of Allah over the one who stays behind, other than those with a valid excuse, by several ranks. Whenever we hear the word "daraja" (rank), it means a station, and a station alone does not fully convey the meaning; rather, it is an ascending station. But if the movement is to other stations that are lower and more base, we say "darakat" (degrees of descent), and we do not say "darajat."
