But are the ranks for all the mujahidin? No, because we must note the difference between leaving one's homeland and abandoning one's family for jihad, and the act of jihad itself. The act of jihad itself requires a resolve of faith (himma imaniyya). Therefore the Truth has stated in explicit text in Surat al-Tawba:

﴿It was not fitting for the people of Medina and the Bedouins around them to remain behind from the Messenger of Allah, nor to prefer themselves over his own self. That is because they are not afflicted by thirst, nor fatigue, nor hunger in the way of Allah, nor do they tread a path that enrages the disbelievers, nor do they inflict any harm on an enemy except that a righteous deed is recorded for them thereby. Indeed, Allah does not waste the reward of the doers of good. And they do not spend any expenditure, small or large, nor do they cross any valley, except that it is recorded for them, so that Allah may reward them with the best of what they used to do.﴾ (Surat al-Tawba)

Here the Truth makes clear that it is not proper for the people of Medina and the Bedouins around them to remain behind from jihad with the Messenger of Allah, nor to be content for themselves with ease, comfort and rest while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is in hardship and difficulty. Just as he went out to fight, they must go out; for the reward is great. So no fatigue befalls them except that they have for it the reward of a righteous deed; no hunger afflicts them except that they have for it the reward of a righteous deed; and they do not walk in a place that enrages the disbelievers except that they have for it the reward of a righteous deed. And they do not inflict any harm on an enemy except that Allah records for them a righteous deed. So He (Glorified is He) rewards with the best of what they used to do.

The scholars have counted these divine gifts as seven degrees. One person attains all the degrees together; another is afflicted only by thirst and so attains the degree of thirst; another is afflicted by fatigue (nasab), that is, exhaustion, and takes the degree of fatigue; a third is afflicted by hunger (makhmasa); a fourth gathers three degrees; and a fifth gathers all the degrees.

When we calculate these degrees, we find them to be: being afflicted by thirst; fatigue (nasab), that is, exhaustion; hunger; "they do not tread a path that enrages the disbelievers," that is, they do not descend into a place where the Muslims could gain control over the disbelievers and extend their authority over them, the intended meaning being the disbeliever's impregnable fortress; infliction of harm (nayl) on the enemy, meaning punishing the enemy; a small or large expenditure; and crossing any valley in the way of Allah. These are the seven degrees for which Allah rewards with better than what their doers have done, as the scholars have explained. Whoever attains the seven degrees has attained a great station, and every mujahid is according to the effort he has exerted. Among the mujahidin are those who attain one degree, or two, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven degrees.

When we read the two verses together:

﴿Those believers who sit at home, other than those with a valid excuse, are not equal to those who strive in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives. Allah has preferred those who strive with their wealth and their lives over those who sit at home by a degree. And to each Allah has promised the best reward; but Allah has preferred the strivers over those who sit at home with a great reward, ranks from Him, and forgiveness and mercy. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (Surat al-Nisa')

We find that Allah desires the believers to be mujahidin, and to exert effort so that the word of Allah may be supreme. When a person believes, it is not for him to remain behind from the ranks of faith; for since he has benefited himself with faith, why would he not join the caravan of those who benefit others with faith? Allah wants every heart touched by faith to be mobilized, and even if one is present in a place controlled by the disbelievers, He calls him to free himself from the encirclement of the disbelievers and to come out joining his fellow believers, so that faith may spread to others and he may practically express his love for people by what he loves for himself. But there are those who say: "We are weak and unable to emigrate or to fight in the way of Allah." So the Qur'an cuts off the excuse of any person who stays behind from the caravan of jihad in the way of Allah and in support of the religion of Allah, and the Truth says:

﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves, they will say, "In what state were you?" They will say, "We were oppressed in the land." They will say, "Was not the earth of Allah spacious that you could have emigrated therein?" For those, their refuge is Hell, and evil is the destination.﴾

Those are the ones who wrong themselves by not taking part in jihad, and this is what happens to them when the angels take their souls.

The word "tawaffi" (tawaffi, literally "taking"/"seizing") means "qabd" (qabd, seizing). It is said: "tawaffaytu dayni" (tawaffaytu dayni), meaning I seized it in full, having received it fully. It is also said: "tawaffa Allah al-insan" (tawaffa Allah al-insan), meaning Allah seized the person to Himself in full. The seizing has a supreme commander, and He is the Truth. After that there is a general appointed agent, who is "Azra'il" ('Azra'il), the Angel of Death, and there are helpers to 'Azra'il, who are the angels. When death is ascribed, it is ascribed at times to Allah, so Allah takes (yatawaffa) because He is the supreme commander, and death is ascribed to the angels in His saying: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him (tawaffathu rusulunaa)﴾ (part of verse 61, Surat al-An'am).

And death is ascribed to 'Azra'il: ﴿Say: The Angel of Death who has been charged with you takes you (yatawaffakum)﴾ (part of verse 11, Surat al-Sajda).

When the Truth employs these three styles in describing the process of death, is this a contradiction, a conflict, or an inconsistency in the styles of the Qur'an? No. Rather, it is a clarification of the stages of the authority (wilaya) that Allah has established. He, the supreme commander, issues the command to 'Azra'il, and 'Azra'il issues the command to his soldiers. In our life there is an example that explains this, and to Allah belongs the highest example: a pupil goes to school after the final examinations of the year and returns home saying: "I found myself failing, and the reason for that is the teachers who intended not to pass me."

His father replies to him: "The teachers did not do that, but the regulations that the Ministry set for correcting examinations are what made you fail." The pupil responds: "The headmaster made me fail." This is a correct statement, because the headmaster applies the rules by which the student is judged to be passing or failing. The pupil may also say: "The Minister of Education is the one who made me fail." This is also correct, because the Minister, together with his assistants, draws up the basic lines according to which each pupil's marks are calculated. If the pupil says: "The state made me fail," that is a correct statement too, because he has understood the sequence of legislation through its various levels, and any link in these links may serve as the agent. From here we understand that when the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death (yatawaffa al-anfusa hina mawtiha)﴾ (part of verse 42, Surat al-Zumar),

this is a correct statement, like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Say: The Angel of Death who has been charged with you takes you﴾ (part of verse 11, Surat al-Sajda),

and like His saying: ﴿Our messengers take him (tawaffathu rusulunaa)﴾ (part of verse 61, Surat al-An'am).

All these statements are correct, because they relate to the levels of the command.

﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾. Wrongdoing (zulm) is to place something in other than its rightful place and to give to one what is due from another. Wrongdoing requires a wrongdoer, a wronged party, and a matter in which the wrong occurred. How, then, can a person be wronging himself, and the angels take him in that state? Certainly they did something that merits that. When a person comes to the moral-faith personality (al-shakhsiya al-ma'nawiya al-imaniya) after he has believed in Allah and believed in the methodology (al-manhaj), and then his own self (nafs) speaks to him of opposition, he here faces a conflict between two matters: the responsibility of the faith-based personality that accepted the methodology from Allah, and the restraint of the self (wazi' al-nafs) that insistently pushes him toward deviation. A dialogue takes place that is close to a conversation between the faith-based responsibility and the self's insistent drive toward deviation. When the faithful self prevails, a person knows that his self has become tranquil and happy, and he says to himself: if you obey the drive to deviate, you will have achieved a hasty desire for which you will be burned in the end, and by rejecting the desire you will have dealt justly with your self. If you obeyed your hasty desire, you would have wronged your self. The same thing happens in our ordinary life: when a mother spoils her son while his father asks him to study and tries to restrain him so that he fulfils his academic responsibility, this mother is wronging her son. Likewise, the Truth gives us an idea of the conflict between the faith-based personality and the deviant self that wants only desire, saying: ﴿And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam in truth, when they both offered an offering, and it was accepted from one of them and not accepted from the other. He said: I will surely kill you. He said: Allah only accepts from the righteous (al-muttaqin)﴾ (Surat al-Ma'ida, 27).

Here Habil says to Qabil:

Why would you kill me? I am not the one whose offering was accepted; it is Allah who accepted it, so what is my fault?

Then the dialogue follows: ﴿If you stretch your hand toward me to kill me, I shall not stretch my hand toward you to kill you; indeed I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ (Surat al-Ma'ida, 28).

Let us consider this wise statement: ﴿So his self made the killing of his brother seem good to him﴾ (part of verse 30, Surat al-Ma'ida).

It is as if there were a conflict in the soul of Qabil between two matters: "kill" and "do not kill." The faithful self says: "Do not kill," and the appetitive self says: "Rather, you must kill."

The appetitive self prevailed when it made the killing of his brother seem good to him and smoothed the way for it. After he killed his brother, and the fury of anger had passed, he became one of the regretful, and then the particulars began to appear and become clear. Allah sent a raven that searched and dug in the earth to conceal the corpse of another raven. Here Qabil said: ﴿Have I been unable to be like this raven and conceal the shame of my brother?﴾ (part of verse 31, Surat al-Ma'ida).

Thus we see that wronging the self is to oppose what Allah has legislated for the self in order to benefit it with an everlasting, complete benefit. But the self may rush after its love of desires and its longing for immediate benefit that has no permanence, and when a person achieves this immediate benefit for himself, he is wronging himself.

﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves; they say: In what were you?﴾ So the angels ask those who wronged themselves: ﴿In what were you?﴾, that is, in what matter of your religion were you? The interrogation here is for rebuke and reproach: why did you wrong yourselves? Why did you not do as your brothers did, emigrating and joining the procession of faith and the procession of jihad? Why did you remain in your places, confined and besieged, unable to move and unable to escape? The answer of those who wronged themselves is: ﴿They say: We were oppressed in the land﴾. By Allah, when Allah recounts for us this scene that will happen on the Day of Resurrection, will we have time to benefit from it? Certainly not, because we will have no capacity to make amends and correct the error.

When the Truth recounts this scene to us, that is from His kindness to us, and a warning to each of us: beware lest a situation arise in which what I have explained to you happens, and no one is able to make up for life so as to do good deeds. Each of you must now examine the state of his own self.

﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves; they say: In what were you? They say: We were oppressed in the land﴾. The phrase ﴿We were oppressed in the land﴾ indicates that a people oppressed them, that is, they were not able to leave and emigrate, and did not know the way to it, and they feared for their wealth and homes, and those who oppressed them said to them: if you leave, do not take anything of your wealth. These are some of the manifestations of oppression (istid'af). Here the angels say something that indicates this speech is neither fitting nor beneficial. The angels say: ﴿Was not the earth of Allah spacious, so that you could emigrate in it?﴾

This was another warning, and a declaration that such a statement and such an argument have no value, because whoever holds on to his place and his wealth instead of Allah has placed and tied his certainty to the causes. But whoever places the methodology of Allah above his place, his child, and everything else, is the one who trusted in Allah, because He is the Causer and the Giver of causes.

﴿Was not the earth of Allah spacious, so that you could emigrate in it?﴾ This statement on the tongue of the angels comes from the supreme law. Allah created all creatures and settled them in the earth, and this earth belongs to no one exclusively. Whoever is confined by a place should go to another place.

If, through man's injustice, arrogance and tyranny, he has set limits on place, then no one moves from one place to another except after a long chain of complications that prevent movement from place to place, and that contradicts the matter of vicegerency (khilafa) on earth, because vicegerency was not distributed so that each group is assigned a particular land. Rather, man, every man, is a vicegerent on the whole earth, in confirmation of the Truth's saying: ﴿And the earth He laid out for the creatures (al-anam)﴾ (Surat al-Rahman, 10).

Allah made the earth lowly, subjected and made submissive for man; the earth is any earth, and the creatures (al-anam) are all creatures. If the world does not take notice of this matter and make it a cosmic, social issue, the world will remain in corruption and misery. What makes life on earth corrupt is the emergence of opinions saying that population density prevents finding food for the people of a country. They say this while another land needs working hands, and so humanity faces an inverted situation: land in countries that needs people, and people in countries that need land.

It is necessary for the matter to flow so that land without men takes from the countries without land what it needs of men. The clamour that rises in the cosmos is due to the fact that in Allah's cosmos there is land without men and men without land. If a place becomes too tight for a person, he may go to another place, and if the matter were so, humanity would be happy. Whoever refutes this matter must know that he is taking vicegerency on earth without its conditions. What corrupts affairs on earth is that the human vicegerent has forgotten he is a vicegerent and considered himself an originator in the cosmos. Since he considers himself an originator in the cosmos, this is corruption:

﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves; they say: In what were you? They say: We were oppressed in the land. They say: Was not the earth of Allah spacious, so that you could emigrate in it? Those—their refuge is Hell, and evil is the destination (masir)﴾ (Surat al-Nisa', 97).

So, if a person remains under oppression and does not employ his thought and reason, and does not raise before himself the question of the cosmos to see the earth that is wide enough for him to emigrate in it, then he must know that he is threatened with an evil end, because Allah has made the whole cosmos for him to be a vicegerent in it. As for those who will be saved from this punishment and from the angels' rebuke at the time of death, they are those whom the Truth describes in the next verse: ﴿Except the weak men, women, and children, who have no power to devise and do not find a way﴾ (Surat al-Nisa', 98).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 4, verse 98:

It is incumbent upon us to know that there is a difference between "the nominal weak (mustada'af da'wa)" and "the truly weak (mustada'af haqiqi)." There is one who has accepted another's subjugation of him and made himself weak. This is the "nominal weak."

As for "the truly weak," they are those whom the Truth has specified: ﴿except the weak among men, women, and children, who have no means and do not find a way﴾. These are the ones who are truly weak, according to the nature of their helplessness, among men, women, and children.

Is a child among the children weak? Yes, because weakness is either incidental or inherent. Some men are owned by others and cannot act or go freely, and likewise women: a woman cannot walk alone and protect herself, but must have with her someone who protects her, such as a husband or a mahram relative. Likewise children, because by their nature they are not legally responsible, and by that they fall outside the scope of accountability from the angels, since they have no means and do not find a way.

This is a precision in the Qur'anic expression. A person is obligated to escape the oppression of others against him, even by means of cunning (ihtiyal). Cunning (ihtiyal) is the application of thought in a way that gives a person an opportunity greater than what is actually available to him. Strength may be small, but through cunning a person may widen his opportunities for strength. An example of this: when a person wants to lift a rock, and he cannot do so with his hands, he brings an iron bar, makes from it a lever, and places a wheel beneath the lever in order to roll the rock. This is one of the kinds of cunning. Likewise the scaffolds upon which we build: they are a cunning.

And the one who built the pyramid, how did he place the final stone at the top? He did that through cunning. And the one who sat to carve an obelisk of granite whose length exceeds ten meters, then moved it and erected it: he did that through cunning. Cunning is thought that gives a person a capacity beyond his own capacity in what is within his reach. Likewise, knowing the way to emigration (hijra). Knowing the routes of emigration from Makkah to Madinah in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) required experience so that one would avoid the deserts and the trackless wastes. When the Messenger (ﷺ) made the hijra, he brought a guide for the road, and his guide was a disbeliever, for such a land cannot be crossed without a guide.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 99:

Let us consider the words of the Truth, glorified is He:

﴿Then those – it may be that Allah will pardon them, and Allah is ever Pardoning and Forgiving.﴾

"Then those" refers to those mentioned in the verse preceding this one: ﴿Except the oppressed among men, women, and children who are unable to devise a plan and do not find a way.﴾ Nevertheless, when Allah referred to these truly oppressed people, He said: ﴿Then those – it may be that Allah will pardon them﴾ (part of verse 99 of Surat al-Nisa'). The expected form of speech would have been for the Truth to say: ﴿Then those – Allah has pardoned them﴾, but the Truth used "ʿasā" (it may be, perhaps) in order to urge them to hope that Allah will pardon them, and hope may or may not come to pass. We know that "ʿasā" (perhaps; an expression of hope) is used to express hope, and that it is used when what follows it is a desirable matter that we love to occur.

You may hope for something from another and say: "Perhaps you will do such-and-such." A person may also say: "Perhaps I will do such-and-such," where the speaker is the one who controls the action; this is somewhat stronger. But a person's strength may fail him; therefore he should say: "Perhaps Allah will do such-and-such," and in this there is reliance upon absolute power. And when it is Allah who says ﴿it may be that Allah will pardon them﴾, this is an encouragement of hope from One who is Generous and Able.

Following the story of those who die while wronging themselves, whom the angels take in death, having remained in a land and dwelt in it when it was possible for them to migrate to another land of faith and Islam, the one who sets in his soul something he wishes to accomplish for a matter of faith is helped in it, because Allah, glorified and exalted, says:

﴿And whoever emigrates in the way of Allah will find on the earth many a refuge and abundance. And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger and then death overtakes him, his reward has already fallen upon Allah. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (100)

So whoever emigrates in the way of Allah will find abundance, if he has set in his soul the practice of faith. In the beginning, the Muslims used to emigrate to Abyssinia, because they were not safe in Makkah with regard to their religion.

For this reason it was said that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was given insight by Allah, and he examined the question of justice in the world, so the Prophet did not accept anything except that the emigrants should go to Abyssinia. And it is certain that the Truth had informed him that Abyssinia in that time was a land free of tribulation.

Someone may say: why did the Prophet not choose for the first emigrants to go to an Arab tribe in the south or the north?

Quraysh held sovereignty over the entire Arabian Peninsula with its tribes, for all the tribes would make pilgrimage to Quraysh, and there was no Arab environment able to stand against the desire of Quraysh. Therefore the Master of Messengers, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), surveyed all the lands until he commanded them to emigrate to Abyssinia. The reason for going to Abyssinia was that there was a king under whom no one was wronged. Justice in itself was the distinguishing mark of that king, and the believers called it "the abode of security", though it was not "the abode of faith". As for emigration to Madinah, it was to an abode of faith. And we who live in this age must know that there is no emigration after the Conquest, except an emigration whose doer intends by it assistance in obeying Allah. This is what his saying (ﷺ) clarifies: "The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe, and the emigrant is the one who abandons what Allah has forbidden." (1) There remains for us a continuing emigration, which is the Hajj, or emigration in pursuit of knowledge, or emigration because there is a greater scope for obedience. Let us suppose there is a place where the rulers restrict people from going to the mosque, so the people of faith leave that place for a place where a person has the freedom to perform the religious obligations. All of these are emigrations to Allah. And the intention in these emigrations cannot be confined only to seeking abundance of livelihood. Therefore it is not proper that the preoccupation of people in this age should be solely the abundance of livelihood.

Here is Imam ʿAli, may Allah honour his face, saying: "I am amazed at the people who strive for what is guaranteed to them (بالبناء للمفعول: passive form), and leave what is demanded of them." Most of people's striving is only for provision and livelihood, which is a matter guaranteed to them by their Creator, may He be exalted:

﴿And whoever emigrates in the way of Allah will find on the earth many a refuge and abundance. And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger and then death overtakes him, his reward has already fallen upon Allah. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (Surah an-Nisa')

The emigrant will find nothing but abundance from Allah. The poet says:

"By your life, lands did not become narrow for their people, but the characters of men became narrow."

A person may say: "I seek abundance of provision through emigration." We say: you are seeking a job whose form is work but whose inner reality is idleness, for in your field of life you find many jobs.

And we find some who seek abundance of provision who want one of them to sit at a desk and collect a salary, while society searches with difficulty for a skilled worker, as if those who seek abundance of provision want this abundance together with idleness, not with the exertion of effort.

﴿And whoever emigrates in the way of Allah will find on the earth many a refuge﴾ When you read the word "muraghim" (refuge/place of humbling of an opponent), you know that it opens the field before the oppressed whom the tyrants subdue. The root of "muraghim" is "r-gh-m", and its basic meaning is "al-rughām", that is, "dust". It is said: "I will do such-and-such, and the nose of so-and-so is in the dust", meaning: so-and-so's nose goes into the dust, and I will do what I am determined upon. As long as there is a person who will do something in spite of another person's nose, it means that the second was wanting to subdue him and wanted to force him to something, but he refused and did what he wanted.

When a person sees a tyrant who lifts his nose high and is arrogant, he tries to oppose him and does something other than what he wants, and makes the standing of that nose in the dust. The popular saying goes: "I want to break so-and-so's nose."

When one who was oppressed and suffering humiliation in his land emigrates, he will find a land where he finds what puts his enemy's nose in the dust. The enemy says: "Despite my having restricted him, he went to something better than I expected." Through his emigration a person humbles the noses of tyrants.

The word "muraghim" is a noun of place (ism maf'ul, in the sense of the place where the opponent is humbled), meaning a place which, when you reach it, humbles the nose of your adversary who was oppressing you. Is there anything better than this?

﴿And whoever emigrates in the way of Allah will find on the earth many a refuge﴾ That is, He, glorified, gives the emigrant things that make the one who was oppressing and humiliating him feel disgrace to the degree that his nose is in the dust.

The one oppressed in a land finds someone who restricts his movement, but when he emigrates in the way of Allah he will find abundance and provision.

The Truth continues the verse: ﴿And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger and then death overtakes him, his reward has already fallen upon Allah. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ No one knows the time of death. If a person emigrates in the way of Allah, he may not reach the refuge, because death may come to him, and here his reward has fallen upon Allah. If He, glorified, has promised the emigrant in His way the place that humbles the nose of his adversary, and that is a means, then whoever dies before reaching that means has gone to the Lord of the means, and it is certain that going to the Lord of the means is more bountiful. Thus we find that the emigrant gains whether alive or dead.

"And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger and then death overtakes him, his reward has already fallen upon Allah, and Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful." The word "waqaʿa ajruhu ʿala Allah" means that his reward has fallen upon Allah. As if the Truth, glorified and exalted, says to the servant: when you emigrate to the wide earth of Allah, if death overtakes you before you reach the abundance and the refuge, you are going to My presence. The refuge is one of My means, and I am the Causer.

And to understand the meaning of "waqaʿa ajruhu ʿala Allah" we must read His saying, the Truth: ﴿And when the word has fallen upon them﴾ (part of verse 82, Surah an-Naml).

The "waqaʿa" (falling) here is a falling, but not like the falling we know; rather it is going to Allah. And why does the Truth use "waqaʿa" with the meaning of "saqaṭa" (fell)?

He, glorified, draws our attention to an important point: that the reward is more eager for the servant than the servant's eagerness for it, so when death overtakes the servant, the reward seeks him while he is with Allah, and the reward knows whoever goes to it with complete knowledge.

Thus we must understand His saying, the Truth:

﴿And whoever emigrates in the way of Allah will find on the earth many a refuge and abundance. And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah and His Messenger and then death overtakes him, his reward has already fallen upon Allah. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (100) (Surah an-Nisa')

And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful even toward one who was slack for a while, so that he may join the ranks of faith and make up what he missed, for Allah forgives what has passed if the servant tries to make it up. Emigration requires travel in the earth and requires striving (jihad).

(1) Narrated by al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i from Ibn ʿAmr.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 4, verse 101:

Having made pillars (arkan) for Islam, God then came to the believer and laid upon him what he could carry of these pillars. The pillars of Islam are: the testimony of faith (shahada), prayer (salat), fasting (sawm), almsgiving (zakat), and pilgrimage (hajj) for whoever is able to make his way to it. The Muslim pronounces the testimony and performs the prayer, but he may not possess wealth, so the Truth excuses him from zakat. He may have a lasting illness, so he cannot fast, and God excuses him from fasting. He may not have the capacity for pilgrimage, so the Truth excuses him from hajj. As for the testimony, "There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," a Muslim may say it only once in his life. Only the pillar of prayer remains, and it never falls away from a person as long as he retains the capacity to perform it. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

("The head of the matter is Islam, and its pillar is prayer.")(1)

And because prayer is the pillar that never falls, God has gathered all the pillars within it. When a person establishes prayer, he bears witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. During prayer a person abstains from food and drink, and in addition he abstains from speech as well. Thus we find that prayer involves a wider abstention than the abstention of fasting. A person, while praying, restrains himself from many things he might otherwise do while fasting. Fasting, for example, does not prevent a person from moving to any place, but prayer prevents a person from everything except standing before God.

So prayer involves a form of abstention broader than the abstention of the believer in fasting. And zakat is the giving of a portion of wealth, and wealth comes from a person's movement and work. Movement and work take time, and when a Muslim prays, he is in essence paying zakat: he pays out the time, which is the vessel of movement. So within prayer there is a broad zakat.

The pilgrimage to the Sacred House of God is also present in prayer, because the Muslim seeks out the direction of the Sacred House as the qibla in every prayer, and so on.

Prayer thus differs from the other pillars: it was not legislated through revelation alone, but was ordained by direct communication between the Lord and Muhammad (ﷺ). Because prayer holds this station, we find that the Truth warns us lest journeying in the land distract us from it. Rather, He (glorified is He) legislated a special prayer called "the prayer of war and the prayer of fear," so that no one would say that war prevents us from prayer; for in war it is more fitting for the Muslim to cling to the method of his Lord.

Likewise, during travel God has legislated the shortening of the prayers.

﴿And when you travel in the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer, if you fear that those who disbelieve may harm you. Indeed, the disbelievers are to you a clear enemy.(101)﴾

Journeying in the land is meant to describe the believer walking upon the earth with firmness, resolve, and strength. Shortening (qasr) in prayer is the reduction of the numerical count of its units (rak'at). In the language there are "ikhtisar" and "iqtisar." "Iqtisar" means taking a part and leaving a part, while "ikhtisar" means taking the whole in a concise manner. An example of this: when we abridge (ikhtasara) a book, we condense all the meanings in it into a smaller number of words.

A person may intend to write a letter and then say to himself: I will send a telegram on the same subject. Here he must abridge the words so that they carry many meanings in concise expressions.

Verbosity, as we know, does not take as much time as brevity does, for when a person wants to be brief he must exert his mind for a longer time to reach meanings in fewer words.

It is related of Sa'd Zaghlul, leader of the Egyptian Revolution of 1919, that he wrote a letter to a friend, made it long, and concluded his letter with the words: "I apologize to you for the length, for I do not have sufficient time to be brief."

History also relates of the Muslim caliph who wished to threaten the commander of the Byzantines, and wrote to him: "As for what follows: I will bring you an army whose first part is with you and whose last part is with me." Thus the caliph condensed the magnitude of the imminent danger that the King of the Romans would face from a vast army that would fill the earth, and so on.

History also transmits of one of the Arab commanders, in his difficult battle position at Dumat al-Jandal, that he wrote to Khalid ibn al-Walid two words and no more: "Iyyaka urid" ("It is you I want"), and did not say more than that, so that the magnitude of the hardship he was suffering would become clear through this brevity. We have cited this account while speaking about shortening and brevity.

The shortening of prayer means that the believer performs each of the noon (zuhr), afternoon (asr), and night (isha) prayers as two units (rak'at) instead of four. As for the dawn (fajr) and sunset (maghrib) prayers, both remain as they are: the dawn prayer is two units and the sunset prayer is three units. The wisdom behind this legislation is that prayer in a time of war requires that the fighters not be distracted from the enemy, and not be distracted either from the words of the Truth:
﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at fixed times﴾ (Qur'an 4:103).

So if God has legislated a prayer for fear and a prayer for war, this means there is no way at all for the servant who believes to forget establishing prayer. And if prayer is obligatory in war, there will be no concerns in life greater than the concerns of war and the sword. The prayer of war, that is, the prayer of fear, was brought by the Qur'an, while the travel prayer was also brought by the Sunnah, and in it the believer likewise shortens his prayers:

﴿And when you travel in the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer, if you fear that those who disbelieve may harm you. Indeed, the disbelievers are to you a clear enemy.(101)﴾ (Surah An-Nisa)

If the disbelievers were to see the believers lined up together in prayer, they might attack them in a single onslaught; for this reason the Truth legislated the shortening of prayer.

1 Narrated by al-Tirmidhi and Ahmad.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 102:

The address now turns to the Messenger ﷺ:

﴿And when you are among them and establish the prayer for them, let a group of them stand with you and let them take their weapons. Then when they have prostrated, let them be behind you, and let another group who have not prayed come and pray with you, taking their precaution and their weapons. Those who disbelieve wish that you would neglect your weapons and your belongings, so that they could attack you in one single assault. And there is no blame upon you if you put down your weapons because of rain or if you are ill, but take your precaution. Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾

If the disbelievers were to see the believers lined up together in prayer, they might launch a single assault upon them; for this reason the Truth (al-Haqq) legislated the shortening of the prayer (qasr al-salah).

When the Truth says, "let a group of them stand with you," we understand that the believers are divided into two groups: a group that prays with the Messenger of Allah, and another that watches over the enemy and protects the believers.

But how can one group pray behind the Messenger of Allah while another does not, when all of them are believers seeking the honour of praying with the Messenger of Allah? The Truth commands that the Prophet ﷺ divide the prayer so that he leads each group once, so that every fighter may be honoured by praying behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

The shortening of the prayer, as we have known, applies to the four-rak'ah prayers: Dhuhr, 'Asr and 'Isha'. As for the Fajr prayer and the Maghrib prayer, there is no shortening in them, for it is not conceivable that someone should pray one and a half rak'ahs; and in arithmetic we round fractions up to the larger whole number.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf) in several forms, and there is no harm in briefly touching upon them, because teaching this prayer is ordinarily an obligation upon the imams and scholars who lead armies in a state of war. The prayer of fear has methods and modes: the Messenger ﷺ would divide the army into two parts, one part praying with him and another part watching the enemy, and he would pray with each division two rak'ahs.

There is another method, which is that he prays with one division one rak'ah, then they depart, and the group that had been protecting the first group comes during the prayer so that this second group may pray one rak'ah with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Here the Messenger of Allah gives the salam, because he has completed the prayer.

After that, the first group prays the second rak'ah that remains for them in the shortened prayer and gives the salam; then the second group prays the second rak'ah that remains for them in the shortened prayer and gives the salam.

There is a third mode, which is that the first group comes and prays one rak'ah with the Prophet ﷺ, and the Prophet ﷺ does not pray the second rak'ah with them but remains standing until they finish their prayer with the salam. Then he calls the group that stands facing the enemy to pray behind the Prophet ﷺ the second rak'ah, which for him is the second rak'ah while for them it is the first rak'ah. The Prophet ﷺ remains seated until the second group comes with its second rak'ah, and the Prophet ﷺ gives the salam with them. Thus the first group attains the honour of beginning the prayer with the Messenger ﷺ, and the second group attains the honour of the salam with him ﷺ.

Here we ask: is this manner of prayer restricted to the time of the Prophet ﷺ, and merely a following of him, because praying with him is the honour? How then do fighters perform the prayer of fear after his death ﷺ? The scholars said: if you regard those who hold the command as the successors (khulafa') of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in authority, then the prayer of fear is established in the form in which it came in the Qur'an; but if each group has its own imam, then each group should pray the complete shortened prayer behind its imam.

﴿And when you are among them and establish the prayer for them, let a group of them stand with you and let them take their weapons﴾. These weapons are real weapons, such as the sword, the spear, the arrow or the rifle, which the fighter takes with him; as for one who carries heavy weapons, he will not take them into the prayer by the nature of things.

﴿Then when they have prostrated, let them be behind you, and let another group who have not prayed come and pray with you, taking their precaution and their weapons﴾. The Qur'anic statement here is not merely words spoken, but words with meanings from the Lord of the worlds. Those who went forward to the prayer first left behind them those who would protect them.

But the second group, which will leave their positions for the second rak'ah behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, their minds are occupied with themselves and with protecting those who pray; perhaps when they go to pray with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the matter will distract them. Therefore Allah said: ﴿and let them take their precaution and their weapons﴾. Thus we find that the first group is obliged to take up weapons, and the second group is obliged to take up precaution and weapons.

Someone may say: it is true that weapons are taken, but how is precaution taken, since it is an immaterial matter?

We say: He, glory be to Him, depicts immaterial things and gives them bodies as if they were material, so that a person does not neglect them; it is as though precaution were an instrument of warfare, and you, O fighter, must beware of neglecting it.

This is a common feature of the style of the Noble Qur'an. The Truth says:

﴿And those who had settled the abode and the faith before them﴾ (part of verse 9, surah al-Hashr)

The "abode" (dar) is a place a person can settle in and dwell; so what is meant by a person settling in faith, which is an immaterial matter? In this statement He describes the Ansar, who honoured the hospitality of the Muhajirun, and the abode, as we know, is the place to which a person returns, while faith is the place of return for every matter.

So the Truth, glory be to Him, has made faith as though it were something one settles in, that is, something a person descends into and dwells in; and faith is indeed so. In this verse the "abode" is intended to mean here the city of Madinah, where the Ansar received the Muhajirun.

﴿And those who had settled the abode and the faith before them love those who emigrate to them, and find not in their breasts any need for what they have been given, and prefer them over themselves, even though they themselves are in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul—it is those who are the successful﴾ (verse 9, surah al-Hashr).

Thus the Truth depicts immaterial things so that we understand the matter as though it were sensory, just as the Truth said: ﴿So let them pray with you and let them take their precaution and their weapons. Those who disbelieve wish that you would neglect your weapons and your belongings, so that they could attack you in one single assault.﴾

This clarifies for us why Allah commanded the Muslims to take precaution and weapons: the fighter must be concerned for his weapons and his belongings, for if the fighter loses them he loses the instrument of fighting, and his instruments of fighting become a strength for his enemy. When the fighter takes a weapon from his enemy, the weapon turns into a strength against the enemy.

Therefore the warning against losing weapons and belongings was given, so that the strength of the weapons and goods is not added to the strength of the enemy, for that weakens the believer and strengthens his adversary. The enemy of Islam wishes that the Muslims would be heedless of weapons and goods. The believer at the time of prayer is absorbed in his vigilance with Allah; but a person must not lose his vigilance if he is praying during war. It is not right for a person to forget his weapon during combat, even while praying, for fighting is a standing for Allah, and so one must not separate fighting in the way of Allah from prayer to Allah.

﴿Those who disbelieve wish that you would neglect your weapons and your belongings﴾. Heedlessness (ghaflah) is a passing forgetfulness of what should not be forgotten, and in this there is a clear warning, for heedlessness during fighting is the dream of the disbelievers, so that they may achieve their goal stated in Allah's words: ﴿so that they could attack you in one single assault﴾. The camp of disbelief wishes to fall upon the believers in a single moment; this is what is meant by His words: ﴿in one single assault﴾.

But let us now consider the Truth's words: ﴿And there is no blame upon you if you put down your weapons because of rain or if you are ill, but take your precaution. Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.﴾

Here we find the word "precaution" (al-hadhar) repeated, and He, with the majesty of His dominion, has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment; in this is a good tiding from Him that the disbelievers will gain nothing from the believers. Why then does the command to take precaution come here? Taking precaution does not mean that Allah has abandoned the believers, but rather it is an admonition to the believers to take the means and not to neglect the One who causes the means to act, for He has prepared and readied the humiliating punishment for the disbelievers: ﴿Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾.

This is what we must understand, so that no one imagines that when Allah repeatedly warns us of the necessity of taking precaution, He then abandons us. No. He, glory be to Him, makes clear to us that we should take the means and not neglect them, and He is the One who said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment﴾.

And after that, the Truth (Allah) said:

﴿So when you have completed the prayer, remember Allah standing, sitting, and on your sides. And when you are secure, establish the prayer. Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at specified times.﴾

It seems that the believer is required not to procrastinate or delay the prayer beyond its time, and to remember Allah standing, sitting, and lying on his side, so that prayer may always be the focus of a person's consciousness. Rather, the believer is required to remember Allah even while he is fighting his enemy and engaging him in combat: he carries the sword while his tongue is moist with the remembrance of Allah, saying: "Subhan Allah, wal-hamdu lillah, wa la ilaha illa Allah, wallahu akbar, wa la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah al-'Aliyy al-'Azim" ("Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, Allah is greatest, and there is no power and no strength except with Allah, the Most High, the Mighty").

When a person glorifies Allah even while he is engaged with the enemy, Allah does not forget him. The believer may delay the prayer while engaged in combat and in close contact with the enemy, but he must urge his heart and soul toward the remembrance of Allah. At the time of prayer he is with his Lord, so let him remember Him standing, sitting, and in every state. After the Muslim feels secure in his fighting position, let him then perform the prayer. He never abandons his Lord; indeed, during war this is even more fitting, because in a state of need for Him, and in fighting, the believer is driven to seek help from his Lord. If the Muslim knows that Allah has manifestations (tajalliyat) at His times, then let no one deprive himself of these manifestations at any time. The remembrance of Allah brings the servant close to his Master: He is with His servant when the servant remembers Him. So if a person is filled with tranquility at a time of fear and fighting, let him remember Allah to strengthen his position with the Supreme Power.

As for His saying, "But when you are secure, establish the prayer": that is, when the fighting ends, the believer must move from remembrance of Allah during the engagement to the prayer whose time has come during the battle. The remembrance of Allah during the engagement was so that the prayer time would not be lost, without honoring that time and without honoring the meeting of the servant with the Lord. And why all of this? The decisive statement comes: ﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at specified times.﴾

Allah has clarified for us the rule of the prayer of fear, and He legislated for us His remembrance when the time of prayer arrives in the midst of fighting, and when its timing coincides with the prayer time. The Sunnah of the Prophet (ﷺ) explained to us how to shorten the prayer during travel. And why all of this? Because prayer is an obligation that is absolutely indispensable: "Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at specified times," that is, prayer has a set time.

It is not correct for anyone to understand this meaning as some do, that the time of the noon prayer, for example, extends from midday until the afternoon. It is true that if a person lives until shortly before the afternoon prayer begins, the obligation of the noon prayer falls from him. But what happens if the servant dies after a period has passed that could have contained it? Then the servant has sinned. And who guarantees his life until he performs the prayer after its appointed time?

Someone may say: "Sometimes I hear the call to prayer while I am in a task I cannot leave; perhaps I am performing surgery or riding an airplane." We say: I ask you by Allah, if you are in this task that you imagine you cannot leave, and you wish to relieve yourself, what do you do? You go to relieve your need. So why did you set aside part of your time to relieve your need? And you may find people, disbelievers, who make it easy for you to ask about the restroom so you can relieve yourself.

When these people see you praying, you see on their faces the mark of joy, because within them is the innate servitude to Allah. And you find some of them who make it easy for you and bring you a sheet to pray upon, and they stand trembling, caused by the innate servitude to Allah. So never say: "The time is not enough for prayer," because Allah never burdens His servant with anything beyond his capacity, and the Truth has obligated the servant to pray and has provided the time that suffices for it.

To Allah belongs the highest likeness. We see the foreman at a site distributing work among his workers according to the time each of them has. So what of the Lord, the Creator? That is why the Truth says:

﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out, and will provide for him from where he does not expect.﴾ (Surah At-Talaq, 65:2–3)

Prayer is a servant's provision that frees you from every fear, and its virtue has no limit, because the One who prescribed it is the Creator and Sustainer. So how can you be stingy with yourself in not being connected to your Lord?

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 104:

And the Truth says, after that:

﴿And do not weaken in pursuit of the people. If you are suffering, then indeed they suffer as you suffer, and you hope from Allah what they do not hope. And Allah is ever Knowing, Wise.﴾

﴿And do not weaken in pursuit of the people. If you are suffering, then indeed they suffer as you suffer, and you hope from Allah what they do not hope. And Allah is ever Knowing, Wise.﴾

This verse is a reminder to us of how to respond to those who claim liberation and try to present Islam as suitable for the age we live in, when we interpret it and bend it to the desires of the age, forgetting the aims of Islam. They say: "The Truth has legislated war in Islam only to repel aggression." We say to them: It is true that war in Islam is to repel aggression, and war in Islam is also to widen the scope for the freedom of belief for the human being.

What frightens these people is that fighting in Islam should be an obligation, so that Muslims resist tyranny wherever it may be. This is an attempt by the enemies of Islam to divert Muslims so that they do not resist the subjugation of people and tyranny over them, because the enemies of Islam know well the latent strength of Islam, which it bestows upon whoever believes in it as a religion. Some Muslims are deceived by the claims of the enemies of Islam who say: "Islam legislated war only to repel aggression."

So we say to these and those: No. Islam came with fighting to liberate the human being's right in belief, and the Muslim is required to proclaim the word of Allah and to stand against whoever resists its proclamation. But Islam does not impose belief by the sword; rather, it protects freedom of belief by the sword. The Truth says: "And do not weaken in pursuit of the people" — i.e., do not be weak in seeking out the people who fight Islam. Ibtigha' (pursuit, seeking out) is for a person to make something his object of desire, i.e., a goal and an aim, and to mobilize for it all the plans of thought and the resources of energy. It is as if the human being does not only repel the disbelieving people at the moment they attack the abode of Islam, but the Muslim must also pursue them, in compliance with the saying of Allah: "And do not weaken in seeking Allah." So the Muslims must raise the word of Allah and call all people to faith in Allah. In this call they do not impose the word of Allah, but they raise the sword against the tyranny that prevents a person from freedom of belief. It is upon the Muslims to lift tyranny from mankind, even if that entails hardship for them, because the Truth said:

﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, while it is hateful to you.﴾ (Part of verse 216, Surah al-Baqarah).

Allah has created in the believer the capacity to pursue the enemy of Islam so as to lift tyranny from other people. It is true that war is a matter disliked by people and is not an easy journey, but it is sometimes obligatory. Those who lived through the Second World War knew that Churchill came as prime minister of Britain after Chamberlain, who was known as a man of peace. Chamberlain tried to procrastinate and hold out the prospect of peace with Germany until England was prepared for war. When England had prepared, Chamberlain announced that his policy was not beneficial, and Churchill came and steered the course of the war and said to the English:

"Expect dark days and expect hunger."

Churchill said this to the English so that, when reality came with less than what he had said, they would rejoice and be glad.

And Allah, glorified is He, says: "And do not weaken in pursuit of the people. If you are suffering, then indeed they suffer as you suffer." War exhausts them too just as it exhausts you, but you, O believers, are distinguished from the disbelievers in the following: "and you hope from Allah what they do not hope, and Allah is ever Knowing, Wise." So you and they are equal in suffering, but the difference is that the believers hope for what the disbelievers do not hope for. The believers know, at the moment they enter war, that Allah is with them and that it is He who gives them victory, and whoever of them dies goes to a Garden whose width is the heavens and the earth, and this is what the disbelievers do not hope for.

The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, addresses the believing group whose matter of creed has ended in faith in one God, who created them and brought them into being, and to Him they return. This matter governs the movements of their lives. He, glorified is He, requires them to fulfill the requirements of this matter and to defend this creed, which proves to all people that there is no one worshipped, i.e., no one obeyed in any matter, except the Truth, glorified and exalted is He.

When this matter governs people, it unifies their directions and their movements are not in conflict; they become all cooperative, mutually supportive and reinforcing. Therefore Allah made the believing community "the best nation brought forth for mankind," because its Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the best messenger sent to mankind. The Truth required of the people of faith that they strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, so that the realm of faith may be purified of what troubles the clarity of life's movement.

The Truth deals with His creation as humans. He created them and knows their natures and instincts, and does not address them as if they were angels, but addresses them as humans, and they are changeable. Among the characteristics of changeability is that the matter of creed is clear to them at one time, and their desires cloud the clarity of creed at another time. Therefore He affirms to them that the path of creed is not strewn with sweet basil and roses, but is strewn with thorns, so that none bears the message of the Truth on earth except one who is patient with these trials and these tribulations. For if the matter were on the edge of thumam(1), i.e., easy to obtain, with no hardship in acquiring it and without hardships, every person would claim it and it would become unsafe to entrust with bearing the creed.

For this reason Allah did not give victory to Islam first; rather, He made Islam at the beginning of its affair weak and oppressed, its people unable to protect themselves, so that only one who has tasted the sweetness of faith would endure this harm, which makes him not feel the bitterness of oppression, the weight of torture and its hardship. Thus the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, said: "And do not weaken in pursuit of the people" — i.e., do not be weak in seeking them out.

The phrase "do not weaken in pursuit of the people," i.e., in seeking them out, indicates that the Islamic community is not only required to repel aggression from itself, but must also discipline those who stand in the way of the call, so that they leave people free to choose the creed.

So the command from Him, glorified is He, is: do not weaken and do not be feeble in pursuing the people who stand in the way of the call. Then He, glorified is He, said: "If you are suffering, then indeed they suffer as you suffer, and you hope from Allah what they do not hope." That is, if the pain of war and its preparation afflicts you, then you too are fighting a people whom the pain of battles, wars and their preparation afflicts; you and they are equal in perceiving pain, hardship and fatigue. But you must not neglect the assessment of strength, so do not overlook it, for it is the decisive strength; you have an advantage over them in that you hope from Allah what they do not hope.

Things must be carried to their ends, and reward follows deeds. Therefore the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, explains this equation so that minds may be clear about it, in preparation and in entering war and bearing its pains: ﴿Say: Do you await for us except one of the two best outcomes?﴾ (Part of verse 52, Surah al-Tawbah).

"O disbelievers, know that what awaits us is one of the two best outcomes: either we will be victorious and subdue you, or we will be martyred and attain the other life." And what of the believers' waiting upon the disbelievers?

﴿And we await for you that Allah will afflict you with punishment from Him, or at our hands.﴾ (Part of verse 52, Surah al-Tawbah)

Which side, then, is the heavier in the equation? It is the side of the believers. Therefore the Truth said: "And do not weaken in pursuit of the people. If you are suffering, then indeed they suffer as you suffer, and you hope from Allah what they do not hope." So do not be weak, O believers, in pursuing the people, for they suffer as you suffer, but you have a higher weight, which is that you hope from Allah what they do not hope.

The Truth concludes the matter of urging the believers to pursue the disbelievers, and how the believers surpass the disbelievers in that they hope from Allah what the disbelievers do not hope for, saying: "And Allah is ever Knowing, Wise." He is Knowing, Wise: He knows every pain that afflicts the believer, so do not think, O believer, that any reward of yours will be lost. The thorn that pricks you in fighting is counted for you. He, glorified and exalted is He, leaves you to suffer in the presence of the disbeliever as he suffers, and that is for a wisdom: that you may march to fighting while confident in the power of your faith to bear the consequences of this religion.

On the authority of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, she said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "No affliction, not even a thorn or more than that, befalls a believer except that Allah raises him a degree thereby or erases a sin from him." (2)

1. Thumam: a grass that does not have a long flower, easy to take and pluck.
2. Narrated by Muslim in al-Birr.

Having spoken of fighting in defence of His religion, the Truth (al-Haqq) does not deprive the believers of guidance that likewise purifies the movement of life. Why? Because He knows that there are people who believe in Him and gather under the banner of the Messenger (ﷺ). So He makes clear: your joining, O believers, under the banner of Islam carries consequences. You are the first to whom the judgment of God applies. Beware lest you think that by your faith, by declaring your Islam to God, and by following the Messenger of God, you have acquired something that distinguishes you from the rest of God's creation. Just as we told you, "Repel the disbelievers and repel the hypocrites," we also tell you: repel your own selves. For one may join Islam and then think that Islam will give him an opportunity to be distinguished over others. To such a person we say: No. Therefore He addresses His Messenger (ﷺ) and says to him:

﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, that you may judge between people by what Allah has shown you. And do not be an advocate for the treacherous.(105)﴾

The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted is He, when He speaks of Himself, speaks regarding actions with the attribute of magnification and plurality. An example of this is His saying "Indeed We sent down," and this is the "plural of the collective" (nun al-jama'ah), since the sending down of the Qur'an requires multiple powers that are available only to one who holds dominion over the whole of existence. Let us strike an example for this, and to God belongs the highest likeness: we find that the head of a state or the king of any country issues a decree and says, "We, so-and-so, have issued the decree." The king or the president knows that he is not alone in issuing the decree, but rather all who cooperate with him and all who work under his leadership issue it with him. How much more so, then, the Highest Truth, glory be to Him and exalted is He? Therefore, when He, glory be to Him, speaks regarding His essence, the speech comes through the pronoun of the singular, so He says:

﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.(14)﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha).

Here the plural pronoun never appears, nor does the "nun of majesty" (nun al-ta'zim). But in this verse we find the Truth saying, "Indeed We sent down to you the Book in truth," and we see the "nun of majesty" clearly. The Qur'an is the speech of God, and the sending down of the Qur'an requires mutually supporting attributes. So, glory be to Him, at one time He says:

﴿We have sent down to you the Book﴾ (part of 29:47)

And at another time He says:

﴿We have sent down to you the Book, to be recited to them﴾ (part of 29:51)

And a third time He says:

﴿We have certainly sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder. Will you not then reason?(10)﴾ (Surah al-Anbiya').

What is the purpose of sending down? The purpose of sending down is that there exist on earth a methodology that governs the movement of life. The Qur'an was sent down to the Messenger and to those who believe in the message. When the Truth says, "We have sent down to you," this means the descent of obligation (al-taklif). Whenever we hear the word "We sent down," we must know that everything that comes from the Truth descends to us from Him, glory be to Him. The word "anzala" (sent down) makes the hearer or reader feel that the party which sent down is a higher party, not equal to the one to whom it is sent down, nor lower than him either.

The word "anzalna" indicates that there is a party that sent down and a party to which it was sent down, and a thing sent down by the party to the one it is sent down to. The Book that was sent down and the One who sent it down is God, and the one to whom it was sent down is the Messenger of God and his community. Did the Truth, glory be to Him, send down only the Book, or did He before that send down everything related to the foundations of life?

When we read this noble saying: ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to cover your private parts and as adornment; but the clothing of righteousness is best(26)﴾ (part of 7:26).

It is a garment that came from above, therefore the Truth used the word "We sent down," and it is not merely a garment, but also adorns you, taken from the feathers of a bird, because it is its clothing and its adornment. It does not only cover the nakedness but is also beautiful, and most beautiful of all is that it is the garment of righteousness.

The Truth brought what sustains life as covering and comfort, and afterwards the Truth sent down the garment of righteousness, which is good. The first garment covers a material nakedness, while the garment of righteousness covers moral and spiritual nakedness, and all of that is a sending down from above. In another verse the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear evidences and sent down with them the Book and the balance so that people may maintain justice; and We sent down iron, wherein is great military might(25)﴾ (part of 57:25).

Thus the word "sending down" indicates that everything that comes from the Supreme Truth to us descends to us with something that treats our material existence and our stability, and with something that treats our spiritual and moral values.

In the verse we are now discussing, the Truth says: "Indeed We sent down to you the Book." When the Book is mentioned without qualification, the meaning goes to the comprehensive, preserving Book that is dominant over all other books, which is the Qur'an, although "the Book" is also used for the written revelation that descended upon any messenger of God, glory be to Him and exalted is He.

"Indeed We sent down to you the Book in truth." The truth is that which is firm and which no other reality comes to overturn. For example: in your ordinary life, when you tell a true matter that narrates a reality, however many times you repeat this account over a period of twenty years, it does not change, because it corresponds to reality, and when you tell it you recall the reality that occurred before you. But if a person narrates a false matter, it has no reality. What then is his position? He will relate the matter one way, and if a week passes he forgets some of what he said the first time, so he narrates other events, because what he recounts has no reality behind it. Therefore he says something different from what he said the first time, and here the listener knows that this matter is false.

Thus the Truth is that which is firm, which no reality ever overturns. God sent down the Book in truth, meaning He sent it down with firm matters, to which falsehood cannot come from before or behind it; it is firm, and no reality overturns it.

In our lives it is said to a successful student by his teachers: "We have given you first place over your classmates in truth," meaning that this student has taken his right, because he deserves this position. His, glory be to Him, saying "Indeed We sent down to you the Book in truth" means that the sending down of the Book upon our master, the Messenger of God, that he might convey it, came bound to and connected with the truth, and that it does not separate from it; and that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was fit to have the Book sent down upon him. The presence of one meaning alongside another meaning in the Qur'an is among the secrets of the radiance of Qur'anic words; they do not contradict one another, but are placed by the wisdom of the Creator to clarify the meanings for us.

﴿Indeed We sent down to you the Book that you may judge between people﴾. This shows us that the government of the Islamic religion, headed by its first ruler, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), came not only to judge between those who believe in it, but to judge between people. And among the conditions of judging between people is upholding justice in what they dispute. So no one should say, "This one is a Muslim and that one is a disbeliever": if the truth is with the disbeliever, you must give it to him; and if the truth is with the Muslim, you must give it to him, because you do not judge only between believers, but between people.

If you judge between people with a judgment that accords with the logic of reality and truth, you make the one for whom you judged bear witness that your religion is true. When the truth is with the disbeliever and you rule against the believer with a just judgment free of bias, even if it is a punishment, the disbeliever will reproach himself for not being of this religion which acknowledges the truth and judges by it, even if it be against a Muslim. And the Muslim too, at the moment he is judged in favour of a non-Muslim, knows that the matter is not a formal attribution to Islam, but an objective attribution. So let no one think that Islam came to favour a Muslim over any other human being; rather, Islam came to hold everyone to the logic of truth, to apply to everyone the methodology of truth, and so that the Muslim may always be on the side of truth.

Glory be to Him and exalted is He gives this case in an incident that occurred during the lifetime of the Messenger of God. The incidents that occurred in the lifetime of the Messenger of God were like the sky pouring down rulings: the matter happens and the ruling descends concerning it. Even if the rulings had come arranged by chapters and had descended all at once, when an incident occurs the believers have the ruling and try to seek it in the Book; but when the ruling comes at the moment the incident occurs, it bears down upon it, and the matter is more conducive to submission to it, because it is established, confirmed and documented by a practical event.

The ruling that descended is: "Indeed We sent down to you the Book in truth, that you may judge between people by what Allah has shown you, and do not be an advocate for the treacherous." When He, glory be to Him, says "shown you" or "taught you," know that the teaching of God is more certain than your human seeing; it is as if you were envisaging the thing that God teaches you, as though it were embodied before you, though not with the eye.

The incident that occurred was this: in the clan of Banu Zafar there was a man named Ta'mah ibn Ubayriq, and Ta'mah stole a coat of mail, and this coat belonged to Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man. Ta'mah feared to keep the coat in his house, lest people learn that he had stolen it, for Ta'mah was apparently known as a thief. So he went to a Jew and deposited the coat with him. The coat was in a sack of flour, and as he went out carrying it, the flour began to spill through a tear in the sack, leaving a trail of flour on the ground leading to the house of the Jew, whose name was Zayd ibn al-Samin. When they followed the trail of flour, they found it led to Ta'mah's house, but he swore that he had not taken it and that he had no knowledge of it, so they left him and followed the trail of flour until it ended at the house of the Jew, and they took the coat and said, "Ibn al-Samin has stolen." Then Ibn al-Samin said, "I did not steal the coat, but Ta'mah ibn Ubayriq deposited it with me." They went to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the Banu Zafar came, and they were Muslims, and Ta'mah ibn Ubayriq was among them, and they said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "If you rule against the Muslim in favour of the Jew, the matter will be against the Muslims, and shame will fall upon the Muslims."

We know that the Truth, glory be to Him, sent His Messenger to correct the method of human instincts, and human instinct, according to its impulsiveness and short-sightedness, may imagine that ruling against a Muslim and acquitting a Jew weakens the Muslims. But the Truth, glory be to Him, wants to establish the matter with justice, and so He sent down to His Messenger: ﴿Indeed We sent down to you the Book in truth, that you may judge between people by what Allah has shown you, and do not be an advocate for the treacherous.(105)﴾ (Surah an-Nisa').

That is, beware lest you say: "This one is a Muslim, and it is not right that we attach to him the crime he committed, lest it be a disgrace upon him." And beware lest you fear the raising of the Jew's head because a thief has appeared among the Muslims. It is an honour to Islam that any person who commits a wrong be punished, for as long as he has attached himself to Islam, he must safeguard this attachment; and the punishment of a Muslim for a wrong is a testimony for Islam that it did not come to flatter a Muslim, and every Muslim must know that he entered Islam by the right of Islam.

Some superficial people looked at His saying: "and do not be an advocate for the treacherous," saying: "If there is a thief, a traitor, or one who exploits his power, leave him alone and do not look at him or pay attention, so that he does not cause you trouble." To these we say: No. For He, glory be to Him, says: "and do not be an advocate for the treacherous," and the "lam" that is at the beginning of "lil-kha'inin" (for the treacherous) denotes possession or benefit, meaning that the Truth commands the Prophet (ﷺ) not to take a position in favour of the treacherous, but rather to contend on behalf of the interest of truth.

Some scholars tried to narrow the gap, saying: perhaps no one notices the matter of the "lam" and that it here denotes benefit, so the prohibition would be that a Muslim take a position that benefits a traitor; rather, it must be against the traitor and not with him. So the "lam" here would have the sense of "'an" (on behalf of / against), as if the Truth said: "and do not be against the treacherous as an advocate," meaning, O Muhammad, do not be a defender of the treacherous.

Why did the Truth not say "'an" instead of "lam"? We say: the purpose of defending an adversary is that you tip his case in his favour, so that he is the one who benefits, not the one against whom it is held. Therefore the Truth used "lam" here, so that the purpose of "'an" would be clear; the "lam" conveys that a Muslim should not benefit a traitor, so the matter does not become his. The Truth used it for clarity and brevity, so that we may know that His Messenger will not stand on the side of the traitor nor bring anything that benefits him. This is why the scholars said: the "lam" here has the sense of "'an." The Qur'an contains much of this kind.

And some people say: why does He not use a clear wording that makes us know the meaning directly? We say: the matter of the observed... [text ends mid-argument]

Then the Truth (exalted is He) says: ﴿And seek forgiveness from Allah. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [4:106]

The command to seek forgiveness came merely upon the occurrence of a passing thought of hesitation between supporting the Muslim or supporting the Jew, for the Messenger had not yet ruled in favour of one against the other. Yet this mere passing thought requires seeking forgiveness, and it is Allah, glorified is He, who issues this command to His Messenger. There is no objection or embarrassment in our Lord amending a matter for us.

Or, every address of this kind is directed at those who made the matter a subject of bargaining in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), like the statement of "Banu Zafar" when they wished that the Messenger would not judge the thief among them, and they made excuses regarding Islam. Therefore, the Truth commands those who spoke to the Messenger of Allah about this matter to seek forgiveness, or commands the Messenger to seek forgiveness from Allah on their behalf, because they only said that out of desire that the affair of the Muslims not be exposed.

Then, after that, the Truth says:

﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves. Indeed, Allah does not love one who is a habitual betrayer, sinful.﴾ (4:107)

He, glorified is He, wishes to thoroughly examine this matter, for it would have sufficed for Him to say what came before. But He wants to settle such matters decisively, so there is no arguing on behalf of those who betray themselves. And al-jadal (argument, dispute), as we know it, is al-qatl (twisting). When a person twists something, such as taking some hair, wool or fiber and braiding it to make a rope, he twists this yarn to strengthen it, so that it is not brittle and can bear pulling and tugging. For this reason it is said of such a process: "We braid the rope so as to give it strength." So it is with the two disputants: each one wishes to strengthen his argument, and strives hard to reinforce it by whatever methods he can, twisting the speech, adorning it, or using eloquence in expression. Hence the command comes to the Messenger: do not strengthen the position of anyone who betrays himself.

When the Qur'an turns away from saying "yakhunūna" (those who betray) to "yakhtānūna anfusahum" (those who betray themselves), there must be a great meaning in this, because khiyana (betrayal) is taking what is not right. It is possible for a person to betray another, but is it reasonable for a person to betray himself? Such a process requires considerable fabrication. A person may betray another for the sake of his own benefit, or to give himself a desire and a sin that carries a punishment; this is a betrayal of the self, because in such a case a person overlooks the deferred punishment for the sake of the fleeting, immediate desire.

Thus we see that one who betrays people is in fact, implicitly, betraying his own interest. And when a person betrays himself, this is not easy and requires fabrication. Therefore the Truth says: "And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves. Indeed, Allah does not love one who is a habitual betrayer, sinful."

The verse that spoke earlier about this stance did not use the word "khawwanīn" but rather "al-khā'inīn" (the betrayers). Here the Truth uses the word khawwān (habitual betrayer), and there is a difference between khā'in and khawwān. The khā'in is one from whom betrayal proceeds once, whereas the khawwān is one from whom betrayal proceeds repeatedly. Or the meaning is: the khā'in commits betrayal in a small, minor matter, whereas the khawwān commits betrayal in a major matter. So in one sense the intensification is in repeating the act, and in another in magnifying the act.
