We are astonished, because the donkey, for example, does not do this, since its flesh is not lawful; but the beast knows its usefulness to humans, so it stretches out its neck seeking slaughter. As we know, during its life it serves man, either by carrying loads, or by giving milk, wool, fleece or hair. And at the moment when harm befalls it or overtakes it, it stretches out its neck as if asking for slaughter so that man may benefit from its flesh; it is subjected to man and knows this by inspiration and subjugation.

Since God has made all this available to us, why should we accept the prohibition of what is not forbidden, or the permitting of what is not lawful? But the custodians used to perform wonders to control people. When a she-camel gave birth to four litters and the fifth birth was a male, the custodians would say: "It is enough that she bore four litters, and the fifth was a male stallion," and they would slit the ear of the she-camel and leave her. When someone saw her and found her ear slit, custom decreed that she should not be used for anything: not for suckling, not for carrying, her milk was not to be milked, and she was not to be prevented from water or pasture. She was called "bahira," and the custodians would take her at any time, because they did not want to store meat; they wanted it alive, to slaughter at whatever time occurred to them. For this reason the Truth said:

﴿God has not appointed any bahira, sa'iba, wasila or ham.﴾ (5:103, part).

The bahira, then, is the she-camel whose ear is slit, meaning that she bore four litters in succession, and then bore a male in the fifth litter; and her owner dedicates her to the idols. The sa'iba is also distinct, along with another sa'iba: though she did not bear four litters, nor a male in the fifth litter, her owner offers her as a vow or gift to one of the idols. She is called "sa'iba" because no one takes charge of her affairs; she grazes on any land and drinks from any water, and no one takes from her milk or rides her, and the custodians take her when they need fresh, tender meat. If a ewe gave birth to a female, they kept her for themselves; if she gave birth to a male, they dedicated him to their gods; and if she gave birth to a male and a female, they did not slaughter the male for their gods, and they said of the ewe: "She has joined her brother"; this is the "wasila." For people used to keep the females of livestock, since they are the vessels of offspring; therefore the giving of the stallion to the custodians was something within reach. The poet says:

"Indeed, the mothers of people are but vessels,
newly made; and for lineages there are fathers."

In farming we find that females of livestock need one stallion, and in a whole town there may be one or two stallions for the females of the same kind. Children in the countryside rejoice when livestock gives birth to a male, because it will be fed a little and then slaughtered, and they will eat from it; and children become angry when livestock gives birth to a female, because she will be raised and they will not eat from her.

That is, when livestock gave birth to a female and a male in one litter, they did not slaughter the male; they would say: "The female has joined her brother," and the male would have his life guaranteed and be used as a stallion to impregnate the rest of the females, and he would be called "wasila."

Thus we find the bahira is the she-camel that bore five litters, the last of which was a male; the sa'iba is the vow from the outset; and the wasila is the one that bore...

1 Narrated by al-Wahidi in Asbab al-Nuzul, and in Abu al-Nu'aym's al-Tibb al-Nabawi; Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi attributed it in his Bustan to Abu Umama al-Bahili, as a marfu' report.

Al-Sha'rawi said, commenting on the words of Allah, the Exalted:

﴿He promises them and arouses their desires; but Satan promises them nothing but delusion.﴾ (4:120)

This means that Satan presents false promises to his followers and tells them something that pleases them. A promise (wa'd) is when one person tells another of something that will please him, that it will come to exist.

We see an example of this in ordinary life. A person loves his wealth, which came with effort, and charity (sadaqah) apparently diminishes wealth. Allah says:

﴿Satan threatens you with poverty﴾ (2:268).

Why?

Because Satan whispers into the breast of the owner of wealth, saying: "If you give some of your wealth in charity, your wealth will decrease." Woe to whoever yields to the whisperings of Satan, for he leads him to the places of ruin. Satan also presents false hopes (amani) in his whisperings: "and arouses their desires" (wa yumanihim). An example of this is what was said by the one who boasted over his brother with a kind of mockery, and Allah's refuge is sought:

﴿And I do not think the Hour will ever come. And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a return.﴾ (18:36)

The boaster says: since Allah has given me in this world, and since Allah's task is constant giving, then my Lord must give me in the Hereafter many times what is in this world, for the fortunate one in this world is fortunate in the Hereafter. So what was his reward?

He saw the collapse of his crops and learned the evil outcome of delusion, because he responded to the promises of Satan, and the promises of Satan are nothing but delusion: "but Satan promises them nothing but delusion."

What is al-ghurur (delusion)? There is "ghurur" with a damma on the ghayn and "ghurur" with a fatha on the ghayn. Ghurur with a damma is the thing that is made to appear to you as a reality while in fact it is an illusion. Ghurur with a fatha is the one who performs this action, and so the ghurur with a fatha is Satan, because he adorns for man an illusory matter, and he acts just as a mirage does. When a person sees the refraction of light, it appears to him that he sees water. Allah says about this:

﴿Like a mirage in a desert plain, which the thirsty one takes to be water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing﴾ (24:39).

Likewise, delusion is when Satan adorns something for a person and makes him imagine that he will enjoy it; when the person goes to it, he will find no reality in it, but the opposite. Therefore Allah details for us the deeds of the disbelievers, saying of them:

﴿And those who disbelieved, their deeds are like a mirage in a desert plain, which the thirsty one takes to be water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing; but he finds Allah with him, and He pays him in full his account. And Allah is swift in account.﴾ (24:39)

The disbeliever is surprised by the presence of Allah, Whom he used to deny, and he finds himself before two calamities: the first is that he was heading toward water and finds none, so his hope is dashed; the second is that he finds Allah, who calls him to account for his denial and disbelief.

Allah says: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust.﴾ (25:23)

Someone may come and claim humanity for himself, thinking he speaks with logic, and say: "Will these people who gave humanity all these inventions that benefited people, such as transportation and others, end up in punishment?" We say: these will receive the reward of disbelief, because each of them did his deeds while Allah was not in his mind; rather he performed those deeds with the genius of invention and humanity in his mind. He takes honor from humanity, and he must seek his wage from the one for whom he worked, not from one for whom he did not work. The saying of the Messenger applies to him:

On the authority of Abu Hurairah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The first of people to be judged on the Day of Resurrection will be a man who was martyred. He will be brought forward and his blessings will be made known to him, and he will recognize them. He will be asked: 'What did you do with them?' He will say: 'I fought for You until I was martyred.' He will be told: 'You lie. You fought so that it might be said, "He is brave," and it has been said.' Then he will be ordered, and he will be dragged on his face until he is thrown into the Fire. And a man who learned knowledge and taught it and recited the Qur'an, will be brought forward, and his blessings will be made known to him, and he will recognize them. He will be asked: 'What did you do with them?' He will say: 'I learned knowledge and taught it, and I recited the Qur'an for You.' He will be told: 'You lie. You learned knowledge so that it might be said, "He is a scholar," and you recited the Qur'an so that it might be said, "He is a reciter," and it has been said.' Then he will be ordered, and he will be dragged on his face until he is thrown into the Fire. And a man whom Allah made wealthy and gave all kinds of wealth, will be brought forward, and his blessings will be made known to him, and he will recognize them. He will be asked: 'What did you do with them?' He will say: 'I left no path in which You would love money to be spent except that I spent in it for Your sake.' He will be told: 'You lie. You did it so that it might be said, "He is generous," and it has been said.' Then he will be ordered, and he will be dragged on his face, and then thrown into the Fire." (1)

Allah did not deprive them of the reward of their deeds in this world, for they took from this world all honor.

Allah, glory be to Him, distributed the excellence of these gifts among people, but those who have Allah in mind are the ones to whom it belongs. Therefore you see the untrained Muslim boarding an airplane to perform Hajj to the House of Allah, and recording the discourses of faith on cassettes so that those who were not present may hear them, and witness this rite. Thus these disbelievers are made subservient to the believers, for they have enabled them to benefit from their knowledge and discoveries. The believers are also obligated to take the means of Allah so that they may attain the generosity of Allah in the bounty of knowledge; indeed, this is a duty upon them, and they sin if they do not do it, so that they do not become dependent upon others and thus be humiliated.

(1) Related by Imam Muslim in his Sahih, in Kitab al-Imarah (the Book of Leadership/Jihad), and also related by al-Nasa'i, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah.

"And Satan promises them nothing but delusion." And what will be the portion of these people in the Hereafter? He, glorified is He, says:

﴿Those, their refuge is Hell, and they will not find from it any escape.﴾ (4:121)

The word "maʾwā" (refuge, dwelling place) means the place to which a person is compelled to resort. Now, is this compulsion a pushing or a pulling? He, glorified is He, says about the Fire that it will speak, saying:

﴿Is there any more?﴾ (50:30)

It is as if the Fire will draw its people toward it, while they will not find from it any "maḥīṣ," that is, no escape, no flight, and no way of refuge. A single one of them could have fled from a creature like himself in the world of contingent things, but when the matter belongs to God alone, there is no escape.

﴿Whose is the dominion today? It is God's, the One, the Subduer.﴾ (40:16)

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 122:

The opposite of that is brought by the Truth (al-Haqq):

﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds – We will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. The promise of Allah is true, and who is more truthful than Allah in statement?﴾ (4:122).

When He, glory be to Him, brings up a matter concerning the disbelievers and their punishment, souls are prepared and ready to hear about the opposite. If the reward of the disbelievers repels a person from being among them, the listening soul is drawn toward the opposite, which is speech about the reward of the believers who do righteous deeds. He, glory be to Him, had said earlier:

﴿Then We will give him a great reward﴾ (part of 4:114).

Here He says: "We will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow." The one who is certain of Allah and trusts in Him knows that there is no distance that puts him beyond the giving of Allah. An example of this is when the Prophet asked one of the Companions, whose name was al-Harith ibn Malik al-Ansari: ("How have you woken up, O Harith?").

He said: "I have woken up as a true believer (mu'min haqqan)." The Companion answered with a word of great meaning, which is faith "in truth" (haqqan). Therefore the Messenger said: "Consider what you say, for every matter has a reality (haqiqah). So what is the reality of your faith?"

The Companion answered: "My soul has turned away from this world, so I stay awake at night for it and I endure thirst during the day. It is as if I look at the Throne of my Lord set out openly, and as if I look at the people of Paradise visiting one another, and as if I look at the people of the Fire wailing therein (i.e., crying out therein)."

He said: "O Harith, you have known, so hold fast to it, three times" (1).

Sometimes the Truth says "sa" (we will) and sometimes He says "sawfa" (surely we will). Each of the particles that enter upon the verb has its own nuance and purpose, and every gift from Allah is beautiful: "And those who believed and did righteous deeds – We will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow."

As we said before, the word "Paradise" (al-jannah), when used absolutely, refers to the Paradise of the Hereafter, which is truly Paradise. As for the garden of this world, its plants and trees may wither, dry up and scatter, or it may be struck by drought. But the Paradise of the Hereafter has food that never ends. Even when the word "Paradise" is not unrestricted but qualified, its intended meaning is something else, as in the saying of the Truth:

﴿Indeed, We have tested them as We tested the people of the garden, when they swore that they would surely harvest its fruit in the morning﴾ (68:17).

And His saying, glory be to Him:

﴿Like a garden on a height, struck by heavy rain﴾ (part of 2:265).

The garden on a height (bi-rabwah) is an orchard on an elevated place, and it has qualities higher than what modern science has reached, because if the land is high, groundwater cannot rot the roots of the plants grown in it, so the plant remains green. The Truth says of such a garden:

﴿It brought forth its produce twofold﴾ (part of 2:265).

Beyond that, it is on a height, and it is watered by rain from above and by dew: the rain supplies water to the roots and the dew washes the leaves. All of this is called a garden.

Here the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, says: "gardens beneath which rivers flow," and He reassures them that they will keep their freshness and greenness. The first thing that prevents greenness is that water diminishes, and then the greenery wilts.

We find the Qur'an sometimes says: "gardens in which rivers flow beneath them," and this means the source of the water is distant; and at other times it says: "gardens beneath which rivers flow from under them," meaning that the source of the water cannot be blocked by anyone, because the rivers flow and spring forth from beneath them. The Truth promises the believers who do righteous deeds the eternal abiding in Paradise, and "abiding" is staying for a long time. So when the Truth says: "abiding therein forever," the meaning is that the stay in Paradise moves from staying to lasting staying.

And whose promise is this? "The promise of Allah is true, and who is more truthful than Allah in statement?" When One who is not diverted from fulfilling His promise by anything makes a promise to you, that is the promise of the Truth, glory be to Him. As for a promise from one who is equal to you in humanity, it may not be fulfilled: perhaps at the time of fulfilment he changes his mind, or he does not find the means, ease and wealth to fulfil what he promised, or his heart may change toward you. But Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, is not subject to change, nothing overcomes Him, and there is no other god with Him who could say to Him "no." His promise, glory be to Him, cannot be reversed, and there is no escape from its fulfilment.

Allah's saying here, "The promise of Allah is true, and who is more truthful than Allah in statement?", is a statement from Him to make clear to each one of us: I do not want to ask you a question, yet it comes in the form of a question so that the answer from the creatures will be an acknowledgment by them of the truth of what He says. Is there anyone more truthful than Allah?

The answer is: No, it is impossible; far be it from Allah, because lying comes only from a liar who seeks to achieve for himself something that truthfulness would not achieve, or out of fear of someone before whom he lies. Allah is exempt from all that, so when He says a word, it is true.

(1) Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Kabir and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah; al-Daraqutni and Ibn Hibban declared it weak.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 4, verse 123:

And after that, the Truth (al-Haqq) says:

﴿It is not by your wishful thinking, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book. Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it, and he will not find for himself, besides Allah, any protector or helper.﴾

Wishful thinking (umniyyah), as we have known, is that a person aspires to something pleasant and joyful without any capital of action. When Almighty and Exalted Allah appointed man as vicegerent (khalifah) on earth, He required him to receive every good thing in existence as one who guards it, so that he does not corrupt the good that already exists. And if a person aspires to what brings happiness, he must increase the good in it.

An example of this: there is a well from which people drink. This well has a rim, sides and edges, and the well is corrupted if someone comes to its rim and pushes into it the dirt so as to bury the well.

Whoever wishes the well's goodness to continue leaves it as it is, and thus leaves the good in its goodness. And if a person wishes to aspire to a joyful and pleasant work for himself and for others, he works to increase the good, such as coming to the sides of the well and building around it a wall of brick so that dust does not seep into the water, or at least making a cover for the well. If a person aspires further, he thinks of the comfort of the people and tries to spare them the trip to the well to fill their jars and water-skins, so he considers raising the water by a suction and pressure pump into a high tank, and then the pipes come out of this tank to reach the houses, so that each one takes the water while at ease. In this way he has increased the good in goodness.

As for a person who wishes to aspire to pleasure without work, these are false wishes. Even if a person keeps dreaming of wishes and does not carry them out with a plan of work, these are the wishes that bear no fruit but disappointment and backwardness.

So wishful thinking is that a person aspires to a pleasant, joyful matter without any capital of action. We know that Almighty and Exalted Allah has given us a means (sabab) for everything, and let us note that the Truth has said: ﴿So he followed a means﴾ (surah al-Kahf).

That is, man is required to make things that elevate the ways of life on earth. Allah has guaranteed the vicegerent the essentials of life, and when man wants luxury and comfort, he must toil. An example of this: the Truth gave man rain, so water descends from the sky, and rainwater flows in specific channels that the rain has dug for itself, and in each channel there may be dirt of stones or silt, so man purifies the water and lifts it into tanks so that it reaches his home. Instead of drinking it directly from the river with his hand, he makes a beautiful cup. Man first made the cup of pottery, then of various materials such as copper, then of crystal, and thus we find that every luxury needs a work that leads to it. The matter is not one of wishes.

Likewise with affiliation to religion: the matter is not that a person merely conforms and affiliates to religion in outward form. The Messenger (ﷺ) came to judge between all people, and no one can affiliate outwardly with Islam in order to take its privileges and distinguish himself from the rest of Allah's creation of other religions. No. A person is judged by what he professes, and the Muslim is the first to be judged by what he professed.

Likewise the Truth said: "not by your wishful thinking." To whom is the address here? If the address is to the believers, then the Truth clarifies to them: O believers, the matter is not one of wishes but one of action, because your affiliation to Islam does not exempt you from work. How many people pass through this world and their lives end in it without doing a single good deed; when they are asked, "Why do you live life without work?" they say, "We think well of Allah." We hear al-Hasan al-Basri say to these: "Faith is not by wishing, but what settles in the heart and is confirmed by deeds." Some people were distracted by wishes for forgiveness until they left this world with no good deed, and they said, "We think well of Allah," and they lied; had they truly thought well of Allah, they would have done good work for Him.

And Allah, glorified is He, says to these: "not by your wishful thinking." But if the address is directed to non-believers, then the Truth does not withhold the provision of this world from one who takes the means, even if he does not believe. As for the reward of the Hereafter, it is a promise from Him, glorified is He, to the believers who did righteous deeds, and it is the true promise. This true promise is not by wishes; rather, reaching this promise is by action.

Thus it may be correct that the address in "not by your wishful thinking" also includes the disbelievers, the hypocrites and the People of the Book. The disbelievers had some wishes, like the words of one who denies the Resurrection:

﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established; and if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a destination﴾ (surah al-Kahf).

These are the wishes of the disbelievers, and this promise of Paradise will not be realized for them. As for the People of the Book, the Truth has said about their wishes:

﴿None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian﴾ (part of verse 111, surah al-Baqarah). And they said: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾ (part of verse 80, surah al-Baqarah).

All these wishes are deceptive, because the method of Allah is one for all people. Whoever affiliates with Islam, which came as the seal, let him act, because the clear principle by which Allah judges His creation is His saying, glorified is He: "Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it, and he will not find for himself, besides Allah, any protector or helper."

Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: When this verse was revealed, it weighed heavily upon the Muslims, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "Be steadfast and seek nearness (to what is right), for in everything a Muslim is afflicted with there is an expiation, even the thorn that pricks him and the misfortune that befalls him."

Some scholars said: the intended "evil" in this verse is shirk (associating partners with Allah), because Allah promised to forgive some sins, and they relied on His saying: ﴿Thus We recompense every ungrateful disbeliever﴾ (part of verse 36, surah Fatir). As if the painful recompense is for the disbelievers, while for those who believe, faith raises them to the honour of standing, so that Allah accepts their repentance and forgives them. Glorified is the Truth, who made prayer an expiation for what lies between one prayer and the next, made Friday prayer an expiation for what lies between one Friday and the next, and made Hajj an expiation for what came before it. All of these are privileges of faith. But the recompense of the disbelievers is: "Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it, and he will not find for himself, besides Allah, any protector or helper."

One does not say "so-and-so does not find" unless this person searched for something and did not find it; man in himself is not self-sufficient, but whoever does evil should seek for himself a protector or helper, and he will not find one.

The walī is the one who is close to a person (yalī), i.e., draws near to him, and likewise the naṣīr is the helper and aide. Only one who loves a person draws near to him and is close to him, and as long as he loves him, he is strong against the weak and able to defend him and aid him.

Why did the Truth mention here "walī" and "naṣīr"? As we have known, walī is the close one who is near the person. As for the word "naṣīr," it suggests that there are battles and enmity between the believer and others, and there is a great power which may appear to a person as not concerned with him, because he is at peace and prosperity. When this power learns that the believer has adversaries, it comes to his support, whereas the disbeliever finds no walī or naṣīr, and no one will come near him, and no one will help him if the events bite him. The "biting" of events is what makes people sympathize with the afflicted, so that even one far from a person comes to his aid, but no one can aid against Allah.

1 Narrated by Muslim, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i, from the narration of Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 4, verse 124:

And after that, the Truth says:

﴿And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer—those will enter Paradise, and they will not be wronged the least bit (naqir).﴾

The two words "male" (dhakar) and "female" (untha) have come here so that no one understands that the masculine form of the verb in His words "does" (ya'mal) means that women are excluded from it. In many rulings we find that the ruling concerning women is hidden within the matter of men, and this carries a suggestion that their affair is built upon concealment.

But matters that need an explicit text, He explicitly states them: "whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female." He, glory be to Him, has also come here with the particle "min" (from), which indicates partiality, that is, a part of a whole. He says: "whoever does of the righteous deeds (min al-salihat)," and did not say: "whoever does the righteous deeds (al-salihat)," because He knows His creation: there is no person who does all the righteous deeds. There are those who try to do some of the righteous deeds according to their ability, and what is required of the believer is that he do some of the righteous deeds according to his capacity and talents. The righteous deeds begin with a person leaving things that are good in their goodness; for preserving the good in its goodness means that the believer will not commit corruption. This is the first rank. After that, a person advances in righteous deeds that accord with his vicegerency (khilafa) on earth. Every action by which the vicegerency of man on earth is made right is a righteous deed. So the one who paves a road so that people may rest from fatigue does a righteous deed; preparing transportation for people so that they reach their destination is a righteous deed; and whoever works so that people's minds are not occupied with things that are necessities of life, this is a righteous deed.

Everything that aids the movement of life is a righteous deed. A person may perform righteous deeds without God being in his mind, like the scientists of advanced states that do not believe in one God. Likewise, atheist scientists may perform deeds that are good for mankind, such as paving roads and manufacturing some machines from which people benefit, and they do these things out of a restless ambition for discovery. One of that group wants to prove that he invented, discovered and served humanity, and we consider him to have done a righteous deed; but he is not a believer, so these scientists will receive their recompense from the humanity for which they worked, and they have no reward with God.

As for the one who does righteous deeds while being a believer, he has a clear recompense, namely:

﴿And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer—those will enter Paradise, and they will not be wronged the least bit.﴾ (Surat al-Nisa').

Some may say: "The non-wronging includes the one who does a good deed or an evil deed." And some say: "The one who does evil is the one who must receive punishment, and receiving punishment is not an injustice." And the Truth says:

﴿The recompense of an evil deed is one like it﴾ (part of verse 27, Surat Yunus).

Whoever does a good deed receives ten times its like, and the recompense may be seven hundred-fold, and that comes to him as a bounty from God. Bounty from God is not restricted; it is a bounty without limits. How then does His saying (wa la yuzlamuna naqira, "and they will not be wronged the least bit") come in this position, when they have been given multiplied manifold of good recompense? We say: bounty from creatures is not binding upon them, like one who hires a worker and gives him a hundred pounds as a monthly wage, and at the end of the month gives him fifty pounds or a hundred above the wage, and in another month gives him nothing beyond his wage. This extra giving and bestowing is a bounty from the employer. As for bounty in relation to God, its matter is different: it is unlimited and cannot be retracted. This is the meaning of "and they will not be wronged the least bit." He, glory be to Him, does not suffice with recompensing the doer of a good deed with one good deed, but gives the recompense of a good deed as ten times its like, up to seven hundred-fold, and does not retreat from the bounty. Retreating from bounty in relation to God would be an injustice to the servant. Bounty from God cannot be compared with bounty from humans: humans may retract their bounty, but with God there is no retraction of bounty.

And He says:

﴿Say: "In the bounty of God and His mercy—in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they accumulate."﴾ (Surat Yunus, 58).

Those who do righteous deeds together with faith enter Paradise, in confirmation of His saying: "those will enter Paradise, and they will not be wronged the least bit." The naqir is the small mark on the back of a date pit (nawa), which is an extremely tiny thing. There is another thing called the fatil, which is the material resembling a thread in the hollow of a date pit, and a third thing resembling a skin that covers the pit, called the qitmir.

God struck these examples with these small things so that we might know the extent of His bounty, glory be to Him and exalted, in His giving to the believers.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 4, verse 125:

Then He says:

﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah while being a doer of good and follows the religion of Abraham, inclining (to truth), and Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend.﴾ (4:125)

When we hear an interrogative such as His saying, the Truth: "And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah," then good inference (istinbat) requires that we understand that the one who submits his face to Allah is the better in religion. In our everyday speech we say: "Who is more generous than Zayd?" The meaning is that the speaker does not wish to state explicitly that Zayd is the most generous of people, but leaves that good inference to the listener. Such a question in interrogative form is not used except when the one spoken of is specific and defined, and the speaker is confident that whoever hears his question will find no answer except the specific, defined matter he asks about. It is as if people, when they turn their heads searching for an answer to the question, will find nothing but what the questioner has specified.

"And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah?" The answer to such a question is: no one is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah. Thus we see that God presents a firm statement in the form of a question, although if He had spoken it as a statement it would have been wholly true: ﴿And who is more truthful in statement than Allah?﴾ (4:122).

He, glory be to Him, puts the question to us so as to leave us free to answer in speech, as if He, glory be to Him, were saying: "I put the question to you, O human, and leave the answer to you within the framework of your conscience and judgment. So tell Me: who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah?" You search for the answer and find nothing better than one who submits his face to Allah, and so you say: "No one is better than one who submits his face to Allah." Thus the answer from the addressee becomes an affirmation (iqrar), and affirmation, as we know, is the master of proofs (sayyid al-adilla).

"And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah?" We know that when a word is used in several places, it does not carry one single meaning; rather each place requires a meaning imposed by the context of the speech. So when God, exalted is He, says:

﴿On the day when faces will be whitened and faces will be blackened﴾ (3:106),

that is because the face (wajh) is the facing organ in which are the distinguishing features that reveal and clarify the features of persons, for we would not recognize someone by his shoulder or his leg; people are recognized by the marks of their faces.

When we hear the Truth's saying: ﴿Everything perishes except His face﴾ (28:88),

we ask: what is meant by "face" here?

If we take it to mean a face like our faces, that is falling into what is forbidden, because everything related to Allah, glory be to Him, we take in the light of "There is nothing like unto Him." We say this so that no speaker says: since the face of Allah is what will not perish on the Day of Resurrection, will His hand or anything else perish?

No. When the Truth said, "Everything perishes except His face," what is intended is His Essence. He, glory be to Him, is exalted above resemblance, and He, glory be to Him, said:

﴿Wherever you turn, there is the face of Allah﴾ (2:115).

Thus the face of Allah here is the direction He approves, and a person turns his face toward the Ka'bah during prayer. Beware lest you think that when you turn your face toward the Ka'bah, it is the face of Allah, for Allah exists in all existence; any direction a person faces contains Allah. The proof is that we pray around the Ka'bah, and there is one east, another west, a third north, and a fourth south; all directions are present during the circumambulation (tawaf) around the Ka'bah and during prayer, and the Ka'bah is there thus so that we circle it, and so that our direction to Allah is in all directions.

﴿Wherever you turn, there is the face of Allah﴾ (2:115), that is, the direction He, glory be to Him, has approved.

And here in this verse we see the saying of Allah: "And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah."

"Submits his face" means submits his direction, because when a person is going toward an aim, a purpose, or an objective, his face is the one turned toward it, since a person does not walk with his back. So the face here means the direction.

Why did the Truth mention only the face, although the believer submits with the face all the limbs? Because the face is the most noble of the organs, and therefore Allah, glory be to Him, made prostration the most noble position of the servant, for the lofty stature and the face that a person takes care to keep clean prostrate to Allah.

So "submits his face to Allah" means submits his orientation and direction to Allah. "Submits" (aslama) comes from Islam: "aslama" means he handed over the reins of his affairs to one. When a person hands over his reins to an equal, that is a testimony to that equal that he knows better than him in this matter; a person does not hand over to an equal unless, before he gives him the reins, he has witnessed for him that he possesses wisdom, knowledge and insight. If a person does not perceive that, he will not submit to him. And how worthy is a person to submit himself to the One who created him; is this not the best of matters?

A person may hand over his reins to another person because he thinks him wise, but can he guarantee that this person will remain wise? He, as a human, is a son of changes; his heart may change, or the matter he has entrusted may become beyond him. But when I submit my reins to the One who created me, this is the utmost wisdom. Therefore we have said: Islam is that you hand over your reins to the One in whom you believe as a mighty, capable, wise and all-knowing God, who holds the qayyumiyyah (self-subsistence and sustaining of all) at every time and place. When a person submits his face to Allah, he will do no deed except that his direction is toward Allah.

﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah while being a doer of good﴾ (4:125).

Why did the word "muhsin" (doer of good) come here? The Prophet (ﷺ) spoke of ihsan, and we know that we believe in Allah unseen; but when we enter faith into the station of ihsan, we worship Allah as if we see Him, and if we do not see Him, He sees us. The dialogue that took place between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and one of his companions named al-Harith: he said to him, "How have you risen, O Harith?" He said: "I have risen a true believer." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Look at what you say, for every truth has a reality; what is the reality of your faith?" He said: "My soul has turned away from this world, so I have kept my nights awake for it and my days thirsty, and it is as if I see the Throne of my Lord manifest, and as if I see the people of Paradise visiting one another in it, and as if I see the people of the Fire crying out in it (crying out to one another)." He said: "O Harith, you have known; then hold fast to it," three times. (1)

A person from among the righteous knows that he is in constant meeting with Allah; therefore he sets for himself a program whose summary is that he knows he is never out of Allah's sight (and He is with you wherever you are). He keeps in mind that he is never absent from Allah for the blink of an eye, so he is ashamed to disobey Him.

What clarifies this is the hadith narrated by our master Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, when he asked Gabriel, peace be upon him, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and said to him: "Tell me about ihsan." He said: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him; and if you do not see Him, then He sees you." (2)

When you are certain that Allah is looking at you, how could you disobey Him? You would not dare to do that with a servant equal to you... so how would you do it with Allah?

The greatness of the Truth appears in: "And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah while being a doer of good and follows the religion of Abraham, inclining (to truth)." Why then "the religion of Abraham"? Because the Qur'an says of Abraham: ﴿Indeed Abraham was a nation, devoutly obedient to Allah, inclining (to truth)﴾ (16:120).

To be "a nation" means that he gathered all the qualities of goodness that scarcely gather in one individual, unless we distribute the qualities among an entire nation: this one is brave, that one forbearing, a third a scholar, a fourth strong. These good qualities do not all gather in one person unless we gather them from a whole nation. The Truth, glory be to Him, wanted Abraham to be a gatherer of much good, so He described him with His saying: ﴿Indeed Abraham was a nation﴾ (16:120).

Here He says of the religion of Abraham: "and follows the religion of Abraham, inclining (to truth)." "Millah" is the religion, and "hanifan" means "turning away from falsehood toward truth." The linguistic meaning of "hanif" is "the one who inclines." Abraham was hanif, turning away from falsehood. When messengers are sent to peoples, we know that messengers come when corruption has overspread and become general. When societies are still able to correct the corruption within them, the Truth gives people respite and time; but when corruption reaches its height, the Truth sends a messenger, and when the messenger comes to a people in which corruption has spread, he inclines away from corruption. Thus inclining away from crookedness becomes uprightness.

"And follows the religion of Abraham, inclining (to truth)."

Then the Truth brings the clear goal: "And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend (khalil)." What then are the grounds of the friendship? He followed the best religion, submitted his face to Allah, was a doer of good, followed the religion, and was hanif. These are the grounds of the friendship, and all of them were attributes of our master Abraham, peace be upon him.

We have been told that Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to Abraham when his people threw him into the fire, and Gabriel said: "O Abraham, do you have a need?" Abraham said: "As for you, no." Gabriel said: "Then ask your Lord." He said: "My knowledge of my state suffices me as a request." Allah said: "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham." (3) That is, he did not ask Gabriel for anything by himself, and that is the summit of submission to Allah. As we also know how dear people are to their children, and we know that Ishmael was born to him in the last part of his life, and the Truth made clear to him that He would test him. But the trial is extremely severe: the son does not die, nor does anyone kill him, but the father slaughters him. How many degrees of trial did Abraham, peace be upon him, pass through?

Abraham set out to carry out the command of his Lord. Therefore we read on the tongue of Abraham, peace be upon him:

﴿O my son, indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you, so see what you think﴾ (37:102).

The Truth made that through a dream, not by direct revelation. Let us look at what Ishmael, peace be upon him, said. He did not say, "Do what seems right to you, O father," but said: ﴿O father, do as you are commanded; you will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast﴾ (37:102). That is, Ishmael and Abraham both submitted together to the command of Allah. So what did Allah do?

﴿And We called to him, "O Abraham, you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, thus We reward the doers of good. Indeed, this was the clear trial. And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice. And We left for him among later generations: Peace upon Abraham. Thus We reward the doers of good. Indeed, he was among Our believing servants. And We gave him good tidings of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾ (37:104–112).

The Truth does not stop at giving Abraham Ishmael as a son, with a ransom, but Allah granted Abraham another son, Isaac. "And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend."

The scholars sat to examine the meaning of the word "khalilan," and to examine the attributes it carries and all the usages in which it occurs. The word is derived from kha', lam, lam. "Al-khal" with a fatha on the kha' is the path in the sand, which in our custom we call "madaq," and usually it is a passage; when two walk in it, they lean on each other if there is strong affection between them, and if there is no affection between them, one walks behind the other. Therefore they called the two who walk leaning on each other "khalil," for each of them penetrates the other, that is, enters into him. The khalil is also one who fills the gap of his companion, and the khalil is one who unites and agrees with his friend in qualities, traits and characters; or he is one to whom a person is intimate in his private places, and who in turn penetrates into the private places of a person. A person may receive one of his companions in any place, whether in the salon, the office, or the bedroom, but there are some he receives only in the salon or the office.

"And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend," that is, the Truth chose him with a special choosing. Love may be shared, for He, glory be to Him, loves one, another, a third, a fourth, and all believers. He is the One who says:

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant﴾ (2:222).

And He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the righteous﴾ (3:76).

And He teaches us: ﴿And Allah loves the patient﴾ (3:146).

And He tells us: ﴿And Allah loves the doers of good﴾ (3:148).

And He also says: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the just﴾ (60:8).

But He chose Abraham as a khalil, that is, no one shares in his station; love is general, but khullah (intimate friendship) admits no sharing. Therefore we see

1 Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya; al-Daraqutni and Ibn Hibban declared it weak.
2 From a long hadith narrated by Imam Muslim.
3 From al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an by al-Qurtubi; a similar report is mentioned in the tafsir of Ibn Kathir and in al-Kashshaf of al-Zamakhshari.

Then the Truth says afterward:

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and Allah is ever, of all things, Encompassing.﴾ (4:126)

Glorified is He. In an earlier verse He made clear that there is no protector and no helper for the disbelievers or for the hypocrites, and here He reinforces that meaning for us: beware lest you think there is any escape (mahrab), any refuge (mahīs), any place of seclusion (ma'zal), or any means of flight (mafarr). To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. The heavens do not shelter one who flees from Him, and those in the heavens do not assist one who flees from Him. He, glorified is He, is the One who encompasses everything in knowledge and is capable of everything.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 127:

Then the Truth (al-Haqq) says:

﴿They ask your ruling concerning women. Say: "Allah gives you His ruling concerning them, and what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women whom you do not give what is prescribed for them, and whom you desire to marry, and concerning the oppressed among the children, and that you should maintain justice for the orphans. And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is ever Knowing of it."﴾ (4:127)

"They ask your ruling" means they seek a fatwa (fatwa: a legal opinion). We know that the religion passed through stages, one of which is the Truth's saying: "They ask you" (yas'alunaka). This expresses the questioning of the believers in many places. The second stage is: "They ask your ruling" (yastaftunaka). What is the difference between the two?

They asked about wine, the crescent moons, menstruation, and spending, and the questioning was directed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), although he said: "Leave me as I leave you, for those before you were destroyed by their excessive questioning and their disagreement with their prophets. So when I command you to do something, do of it what you are able, and when I forbid you from something, avoid it" (1).

That is, he asked them not to probe or to search into matters through which they might bring upon themselves new obligations. Nevertheless, they asked him out of a desire to know which ruling determines a person's movement in life.

And if they did not want to define their lives, why would they ask him? The question was evidence that the questioner had come to love the method of Allah, and so wished to make the method of Allah govern all his actions. Whatever Allah has summarized and made concise, one loves to ask about it.

Also, Islam came to address the customs of the Jahiliyyah and of the Arabs, and their rulings by which they walked, which they had devised for themselves. Islam did not change anything of them. They did not wish to continue in them merely because they were the practice of their fathers, but they wished that every conduct be from the essence of the command of Islam. Therefore they asked him about many things.

As for seeking a fatwa, it concerns a matter in which a ruling may be ambiguous. That is why a person says about a matter: "Let us seek the ruling of a scholar in this matter," because the meaning of seeking a fatwa is the inability of one person or a group of people to derive a ruling or to know it, and so they refer the matter to its people.

And the Truth says:

﴿If they had referred it to the Messenger and to those of authority among them, those who derive it from them would have known it﴾ (4:83).

Seeking a fatwa, then, is for a ruling that exists, but the one seeking it does not have the ability to derive it. That is why we find Muslim societies designating a house of fatwa (dar al-ifta'), because the believer may not know all the details of the religion, and may live his life without these particulars arising for him, such as the chapters on endowments (waqf), partnership (mudaraba), or inheritance. If a matter befalls him, he seeks a fatwa from the people of knowledge (ahl al-dhikr). So the question is about routine practice, whereas the fatwa concerns a matter in which knowledge is not required to be general, and therefore the one seeking turns to the people of knowledge asking for a fatwa. And the Truth says: "They ask your ruling concerning women," as if they had said to the Messenger: "We want Allah's ruling regarding women, in permissibility, prohibition, and conduct."

So how is the answer? "Say: Allah gives you His ruling concerning them." Allah did not postpone the fatwa until their asking, but had already said it before; despite that, He gives them the ruling again.

Perhaps the ruling revealed first was not on their minds, or they were not mindful of it.

So the Truth said:

﴿They ask your ruling concerning women. Say: Allah gives you His ruling concerning them, and what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women﴾ (4:127).

That is, the Truth gives you His ruling about their matter, and it had previously been revealed in the Book, in a verse of Surat al-Nisa' where the Truth said: ﴿And if you fear that you will not deal justly with orphans, then marry those women who please you, two or three or four﴾ (4:3).

And verses followed after that concerning the matter of women.

So His saying, the Truth: "Allah gives you His ruling concerning them, and what is recited to you in the Book," only teaches us that a person should not hasten to seek a fatwa about something unless he first reviews what knowledge he has, perhaps finding in it the answer that makes him independent of asking.

Although the asking about women is general, young and old, orphans and non-orphans, why did the answer come concerning orphan women? Because mature women have the capacity to manage their own affairs and are not weak, whereas the orphan girl is the weakest of the weak. We have understood the meaning of orphan: an orphan is one who has not reached the stage at which a person becomes independent. So one who has reached maturity, whether man or woman, is not called an orphan. Therefore the answer came specifically concerning orphan women, because orphan women are always under guardians (awliya'), those guardians whom in our age we call "trustees" (al-awsiya'). And guardians had two conditions: if the girl was beautiful and had wealth, the guardian wished to marry her in order to enjoy her beauty and seize her wealth; and if she was plain, the guardian did not desire to marry her, so he would withhold her (ya'dilu-ha), that is, prevent her from marrying, because if she married, the husband would have the better claim to the wealth.

This matter therefore required clear legislation. Here we find our master 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), with his perceptiveness known as the Faruqi insights, when a man came to him asking about an orphan girl under his guardianship. Our master 'Umar said:

"If she is beautiful, leave her to take someone better than you; and if she is plain, take her as a wife, and let her wealth be an intercessor for her plainness."

And the Truth says: ﴿And what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women whom you do not give what is prescribed for them﴾ (4:127).

What is prescribed for them is either dower (mahr) or inheritance (tarika). The wise saying came to lift from the woman the oppression of the guardian, and the command came in this lofty style which none but a Generous Lord could utter. We find that the root "raghiba" means "to love." When the situation is "to love that it be," one says "raghiba fihi" (he desired it); and when "he loved that it not be," one says "raghiba 'anhu" (he turned away from it). Therefore the Truth said:

﴿And who turns away from the religion of Abraham﴾ (2:130).

Since "'an" came as in the verse, what follows it is the thing abandoned. But if the phrase were "raghiba fi," it would be for something beloved. The word "targhabuna" in this verse is found with its transitive particle omitted, whether in love or in aversion, because it intends both meanings: if the desire is for the woman, it becomes "targhabuna fi"; and if the woman is plain and one renounces her, the phrase becomes "targhabuna 'an." No one other than Allah can produce a style that combines two contradictory situations, and the Truth came to legislate for both matters together.

Then the Truth continues with: "and the oppressed among the children," alongside the orphan girls, being the other weak category, that is, the orphan who has not reached the stage of men. When He, glory be to Him, speaks of guardianship and trusteeship over such people, He speaks in two modes. If a person lacks the faculty to receive eloquent style, he may say: "This is contradictory speech." But if a person possesses the faculty to receive eloquent style, he may say: the greatness of this style could only come from a Generous Lord. The Truth said:

﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾ (4:5).

Allah said this although the property is originally the possession of the foolish. The wealth is not his until his right judgment returns to him. Islam made faith-brotherhood a basis for mutual support and social solidarity, and when Muslims see one of the foolish, they restrain his conduct to protect his wealth from his foolishness. Wealth is preserved and safeguarded, and it is required of the trustee and guardian to protect it. This is what the Truth said concerning the foolish.

The Truth speaks of orphans, saying: ﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age; then if you perceive in them sound judgment, deliver to them their property﴾ (4:6).

Because the foolish or the squanderer has no authority to dispose of property; rather the authority to dispose belongs to the guardian, and in this case the property is attributed to the guardian, since he is the one in charge of it and its keeper. But as soon as the minor attains sound judgment, the guardian must return the property to him.

Here we have a verse laying down the rules for orphan women and oppressed children:

﴿...what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan women whom you do not give what is prescribed for them, and whom you desire to marry, and concerning the oppressed among the children, and that you should maintain justice for the orphans. And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is ever Knowing of it.﴾ (4:127)

What is the meaning of "standing for the orphans with justice"? "Qist" with a kasra on the qaf means justice, and it differs from "qast" with a fatha on the qaf, which means injustice. "Qasata yaqsitu" means he was just; "qasata yaqsitu" also can mean he was unjust. The noun for justice is "qist" with a kasra on the qaf, and the noun for injustice is "qast" with a fatha on the qaf.

Some who want to take exception to the word of Allah, foolishly and without knowledge, say: the Qur'an uses "qist" in the sense of justice in several verses, then it comes in another place saying:

﴿And as for the unjust (al-qasitun), they will be fuel for Hell﴾ (72:15).

"Al-qasitun" is the active participle from "qasata." Who told you that "qasata" is used only in the sense of "adala" (to be just)? It is used both for "adala" and for "jara" (to be unjust). And He, glory be to Him, says of the just:

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly (al-muqsitin)﴾ (5:42).

The unjust (al-qasit) goes to the Fire, derived from "qasata yaqsitu," while the just (al-muqsit) goes to Paradise, derived from "aqsata."

When we see "aqsata," we find it begins with the hamza of removal, meaning there was injustice and we removed it; whereas "qist" with a kasra is justice from the beginning, and "muqsit" is one who found injustice and removed it. What distinguishes the two is the present-tense verb: in justice it is "yaqsitu" with a kasra on the sin in the present tense, whereas "yaqsatu" with a fatha on the sin in the present tense means "he is unjust and oppresses." Among the beauties of the language is that a single word is used for more than one meaning, so that a person learns courtesy in reception and understands words in light of context.

In earlier times language was a faculty, not a craft as it is now in our age. Language was a faculty to the degree that if they vocalized the writing to the recipient, he would be angered and return it to its sender, saying to him: "Do you doubt my ability to read your letter without vocalization?" Vocalizing a letter is an insult to the one addressed; and in our age we find someone delivering a speech who asks that the speech be vocalized so that it may be pronounced correctly.

The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, says: "and that you should maintain justice for the orphans." The ruling came in His saying, the Truth: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ (4:2). He speaks of dowers and wealth, and raises the matter to the level of considering good conduct in the affairs of orphans as a matter of faith-responsibility. An orphan girl may have no wealth and be unattractive, so that no one is tempted by her or her wealth; in this case the guardian must still care for her and care for the right of Allah concerning her.

His saying, the Truth: "and that you should maintain justice for the orphans" is a command that the believer stand over the affairs of orphans with justice, because an orphan girl may be with the guardian and his family, and if she has some comeliness, the guardian may hasten to her with excessive affection and tenderness beyond his own children. The Truth warns that caring for an orphan girl must be marked by justice and must not exceed it. And He, glory be to Him, says:

"And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is ever Knowing of it," to teach us that the act itself and the performance of it is not the basis of reward, but the intention in the act is the basis of reward. So beware, O believer, of saying "I did," but say "I did with such-and-such intention."

Whoever wipes the head of an orphan has a great share of reward, and whoever sponsors an orphan is with the Prophet (ﷺ) in Paradise. The one who assesses this is Allah, glory be to Him, the All-Knowing of hidden things according to the intention of the person doing the deed. A man may show closeness to an orphan and feign affection and tenderness while intending to draw near to the orphan's mother. Therefore the basis of reward is the intention that moves and prompts the deed, and it is not enough for a person to say "my intention is good" and not act. The noble hadith says:

("Actions are only by intentions, and every person shall have only what he intended. Whoever's emigration was to Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is to Allah and His Messenger; and whoever's emigration was for a worldly thing he would obtain or a woman he would marry, his emigration is to what he emigrated for.") (2)

That is, there must be a connection and conjunction of intention with action, because Allah wants us to do good, and by this a person extends good from himself to others.

(1) Narrated by Muslim and others.
(2) Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim and others from the authors of the Sunan.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 128:

Then, after that, the Truth (al-Haqq) speaks about matters concerning women, saying:

﴿And if a woman fears ill-treatment (nushuz) or aversion (i'rad) from her husband, there is no blame upon them if they make peace between themselves in settlement, and settlement is best. And souls are present with stinginess. And if you do good and fear God, then indeed God is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾ (4:128)

When we see "in" (inna) followed by a nominative noun, as in His saying: ﴿And if one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection﴾ (9:6),

let us know that this "in" (in) governs a verb, meaning that its basic order is: "And if one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection." Here in this verse the construction is: "And if a woman fears from her husband ill-treatment (nushuz)." And what is fear? It is the anticipation of a matter that is distressing or harmful, which has not yet happened but which a person awaits. When a person fears, he anticipates the bad matter occurring. Thus we find that fear is the anticipation of something that may be troubling. The Truth says: "And if a woman fears from her husband ill-treatment or aversion," meaning that the ill-treatment has not yet occurred, but the woman fears that it may occur. The Truth has based the ruling on the mere fear of ill-treatment, not on its actual occurrence. This is a lesson for each of us: not to leave matters until they happen, but to address their causes before they occur, because once they occur it may be difficult to remedy them. If a woman sees some signs of her husband's ill-treatment, she must deal with the matter.

We note that the Truth here speaks of the ill-treatment of the man, having earlier spoken of the ill-treatment of the woman:

﴿And those whose ill-treatment you fear﴾ (4:34).

What is nushuz? When we hear about music, we find someone saying: "This is a discordant note (nagham nushaz)," meaning that it is a note that has departed from the sequence and rhythm of the notes. Its origin is derived from nashz, which is what is raised and appears above the ground. The ground is supposed to be level; if we find in it a protrusion, this is called nushuz.

The basis of the relationship between a man and his wife is that the man has taken the woman as a source of tranquility (sakan), affection and mercy, and they have become intimate with one another (afda). The jurists stipulated in marriage the principle of equality (takafu'), that the spouses be close to one another in standing. For this reason the Truth said:

﴿Wicked women are for wicked men and wicked men are for wicked women, and good women are for good men and good men are for good women﴾ (24:26).

Even equality lies in goodness or wickedness. Thus no one should give a wicked woman in marriage to a good man so that she does not weary him, nor give a wicked man in marriage to a good woman so that he does not weary her, because when a good man marries a good woman, she comforts him and honours him.

Likewise, when a wicked man marries a wicked woman, they agree in temperament and conduct, and in this there is balance. If the wicked man is not ashamed of scandal, the wicked woman is not ashamed of it either. As for the good man and the good woman, each of them fears for the feelings of the other and preserves the other's dignity. So if a woman fears from her husband nushuz, meaning a rising above the expected standard of treatment in cohabitation, affection and mercy that ought to exist between the spouses, and she has become intimate with him and he with her, then if she fears that he will domineer over her with his person or with maintenance, or hold her in contempt, or if his affection or mercy towards her is lost, all of this is nushuz. Before this occurs, the intelligent wife must be attentive to herself and watch for the signs of that nushuz in her husband before it happens. If the causes lie on her side, she must treat these causes, return to herself and correct the matter; and if they lie on his side, she must try to win back his affection.

"And if a woman fears from her husband nushuz or i'rad." I'rad means that he has not yet risen above her, but he does not keep the wife company, does not speak to her, and does not show her tenderness, although he gives her all her rights. The woman must address this matter too. The matter lies between two people, as we have said, and God said of them:

﴿And some of you have gone in unto others﴾ (4:21).

And He said also concerning this:

﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾ (2:187).

That is, the man covers the woman and the woman covers the man; she is a shelter and protection for him. We know that when her father or brother enters upon her, she covers any visible part of her body, but when her husband enters upon her, she does not conceal or hide anything.

Every married man and every married woman knows that between them there is mutual intimacy (ifda'). God has permitted the man from his wife what He has not permitted to anyone else, and likewise the woman. So the man should not utter any cutting description or insulting epithet about the woman, and the woman must also guard her husband. She should remember that she has seen his nakedness by the right of God, and he has seen hers by the right of God.

The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, wishes to end this disagreement before it occurs. Therefore He obliged the woman to seek the cause of the nushuz and the cause of the i'rad, for perhaps she has grown old in years, or illness has befallen her, while there remains in the man some vigour of youth; and it may be that another woman has attracted him, or he desires to marry another for some reason. Here the woman must treat the matter with the treatment of the wise: she should relinquish her turn (qism) to him. Perhaps she is not beautiful and he wishes to marry, so let her permit him that, or relinquish to him some part of the dowry. The important thing is that reconciliation take place between the man and his wife, and this is the task of the man just as it is the task of the woman.

"There is no blame upon them if they make peace between themselves in settlement." Settlement here is the task of both together, because every problem that does not exceed the man and the woman has a solution that is easy. What makes problems difficult are those who interfere in the relationship between the man and the woman, when there is nothing between them that concerns others. A man may disagree with a woman, go out of the house, calm down and return, and the wife says a word that ends the dispute; but if a relative intervenes, the problem may become complicated, since one who has no means of causing or averting a solution has intervened.

Therefore we must pay attention to the Truth's words here: "There is no blame upon them if they make peace between themselves."

The first degree of settlement between a man and a woman is that each of them performs his or her responsibility, and let both remember the Truth's words:

﴿Perhaps you dislike a thing while it is good for you﴾ (2:216).

And likewise His saying, glory be to Him:

﴿If they are disliked by you, perhaps you dislike a thing and God places in it much good﴾ (4:19).

Let no man think that there is a woman who gathers all beauty and goodness, for the qualities of goodness that life requires may not be found in the beautiful woman, but may rather be found in the woman who is not blessed with beauty, since the beautiful one may rely on the capital of her beauty, whereas the one who has no share of beauty tries to be trustworthy, obedient, a good manager and well-behaved with her husband's family, because she wants to preserve for herself a capital of preservation.

Therefore we find that those who have no share of beauty are the great majority in bearing the burdens of building a family. It is not right for a man to take the single corner of sensual beauty; rather he must take beauty in all its aspects and corners, for sensual beauty may captivate men's minds, but its life is short, whereas there are aspects of beauty that have no end except the end of life.

They have related to us of one of the righteous who had a wife of great harshness and domineering over him, and he was a good man. He said to her: "Oh, if you could see me while I am in lessons of knowledge and people are eager to hear me!" He thought that when she saw him in a session of knowledge she would be restrained and become tender towards him.

She went to attend a lesson of knowledge, and saw him, and he thought that this would plant awe of him in her heart. He returned to her at the end of the day and said to her: "You have seen me today." She said: "I saw you, and alas for what I did not see! I saw everyone sitting with composure except you, for you were shouting."

They have also related of this man that God used to honour him with aid in recompense for his patience with his wife, and his disciples would see the illuminations of God in his conduct. Then his wife died, and the disciples went away and did not find with him the illuminations that he had had before. They asked him why, and he said: "The one for whose sake God used to honour me has died."

Just as it is required of the woman to be patient with the man, so the man is required to be patient with the woman, and whoever is patient with her, God gives him her good. Therefore they said: "Imran ibn Hittan was a Kharijite, and he had a beautiful wife while he was ugly of features. His wife once looked at him and said: 'Praise be to God!' He said to her: 'For what do you praise God?' She said: 'That you and I are in Paradise.' He said: 'Why?' She said: 'Because you were granted me and you were thankful, and I was granted you and I was patient, and the thankful and the patient are both in Paradise.'"

No one should think that he will find a woman who is the gathering of beauty and excellence in everything. If she is lacking in one aspect, she is distinguished in another, so do not lose the excellence that is in her because of her deficiency in some aspect. The corners of life are many. We have said previously that no one is a son of God; rather all of us are servants of God. Since we are all servants of God and none of us is His son, and He has given us the causes of excellence in equal measure, one individual has taken excellence in one respect while another has attained excellence in another; this one's deficiency in one corner and that one's excellence in another corner, God willed that the sum of the qualities and virtues of any person should equal the sum of another person, so that the world may be in balance.

If a man finds something in a woman that does not please him, and a woman finds something in a man that does not please her, then the man must gather all the corners so that he sees the complete picture of the woman, and the woman must gather all the corners so that she sees the complete picture of the man.

The man who looks at all the corners lives at ease of mind, for he sees of the good corners many times over those that are not so. The one who is pleased is the one who looks at the good qualities, and the one who is angered is the one who looks at the ugly ones; the one who is just in anger and pleasure is the one who looks at the sum of this and the sum of that. Indeed, the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, wishes that the family be built on soundness, so He makes clear to us:

Do not wait, O man, nor wait, O woman, until the dispute occurs. As soon as the signs appear, then both of you should resolve the problems, for there is no one more capable of resolving problems than you two, because there is no one who has such ties and bonds between himself and another as there are between a man and his wife. Therefore He, glory be to Him, said: "There is no blame upon them if they make peace between themselves in settlement."

Sometimes we find that settlement takes only the form of settlement, while its substance, which is ending estrangement and inner resentments, may not exist. What obstructs settlement is that we perform the formality and do not address the real causes buried in souls, which seep into other matters. Therefore settlement must be made and carried out in its reality, as God the Exalted says: "that they make peace between themselves in settlement, and settlement is best." When souls are reconciled, good spreads over the two spouses and over society.

Then the Truth continues: "And souls are present with stinginess, and if you do good and fear God, then indeed God is ever, of what you do, Acquainted." God, glory be to Him, makes clear to us: I am your Creator and I know your natures and dispositions, and I know that when I ask the woman to relinquish part of her maintenance, such as her dowry or the first betrothal gift (al-shabaka), or to relinquish to him her night so that he may sleep with the other wife, this may be hard on the soul; likewise it is hard for the man to relinquish his measures. Beware lest stinginess take hold of your conduct towards one another. The Truth has come in a verse saying:

﴿And how would you take it back when you have gone in unto one another, and they have taken from you a solemn covenant?﴾ (4:21).

Here He says: "And souls are present with stinginess, and if you do good and fear God, then indeed God is ever, of what you do, Acquainted." There is a difference between the rights that one of the spouses may insist upon and the kindness that one volunteers. We know what a virtuous judge did when he said to two litigants: "Shall I judge between you with justice, or with what is better than justice?"

One asked: "Is there anything better than justice?" The judge said: "Yes, it is grace (fadl). Justice is only the giving of right, while grace is that a person relinquishes his right by mutual consent to his brother."

The Truth concludes the verse: "And if you do good and fear God, then indeed God is ever, of what you do, Acquainted." Glory be to Him and exalted, He wishes to resolve a psychological problem to which families may be exposed in which there is no leaven of con

The Exalted Lord is the One who created creation and commanded justice within what is within one's capacity. It is incumbent upon the man to be just with regard to time, to be just with regard to maintenance, to be just with regard to smiling and cordiality, and to be just with regard to companionship and consolation. The man is able to do all of that, but he is not able to be just in the inclination of the heart, which is a hidden matter. Therefore the Truth said:

﴿And you will never be able to be just between wives, even if you should strive. So do not incline completely [away from one], leaving her as if suspended. And if you amend and fear Allah, indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (4:129)

That is, the justice of love is impossible. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, this is my division in what I possess, so do not blame me for what You possess and I do not possess," meaning the heart.(1)

Thus there is a difference between the inclination of the heart, which consists of inner emotional sensations and psychological tendency, and the emotional process, over which no one has power. There is no regulation that says to a man, "Love so-and-so," except when the intended love is intellectual love. As for emotional love, there is no regulation for it at all. What the Shari'ah commands is that a person love with the intellect, while the love of emotion is never subject to regulation.

A person may love bitter medicine with his intellect, not with his emotion, and a person may be pleased with a friend who brings this medicine from outside, because the medicine will cure him by Allah's permission.

So, "And you will never be able to be just between wives, even if you should strive. So do not incline completely": what is "complete inclination"? Allah explains it with His words: "leaving her as if suspended." This refers to a woman who is neither an *ayyim* (that is, one without a husband who seeks marriage) nor married, so that she enjoys the presence of a husband; the man holds her back without fulfilling his responsibility toward her. So the Truth clarifies: I am not asking you to incline your heart here or there, because this matter is not yours to own. Rather, I want justice in other matters, such as equality in lodging and maintenance, the needs of your children, and justice among your wives in companionship. As for the other meaning, which is the inclination of the heart, I do not burden you with it.

When Allah legislates for His creatures, He knows best whom He has created. He has given every one of us emotions from which inclination arises, and He has given us instincts and choices in emotional responses. Had Allah wished to restrict inclination, He would not have created it. But He, glorified and exalted, releases inclinations so that the interests of the universe are accomplished together through them. When He grants the heart the capacity to love, He knows that the building of the universe arises through love. If the scholar did not love to discover the secrets of Allah in His creation, he would not bear the hardships of research, exploration, experimentation, and all that follows from them of difficulties.

If a person did not love to perfect his work, you would not see any work done well. If a person did not love his children, he would not bear the hardship of their upbringing. Thus love has a purpose, and Allah does not want us to prevent love; rather He wants us to elevate the aims of love, so that we give love its lawful domains, rather than letting love run loose in the universe to wreak havoc on people's honor.

When you direct love toward good, no evil comes to you or to people from it. For example, when we look at the drive and instinct of curiosity, we find that Allah created it in human beings so that they might advance their innovations that bring happiness to life. Had the instinct of curiosity not existed, the discoverer would not have toiled to invent or discover something to give relief to us humans, and man would not have thought of using steam to carry off from people the hardships of travel and the hardships of carrying heavy loads. That discovery relieved us by the invention of the steamship or the train.

But Allah, glorified and exalted, wants to elevate the instinct of curiosity, so we should place it in its lawful domain and not let it become espionage upon people's private affairs, for example. Likewise, Allah placed the instinct of love of wealth in human beings, because love of wealth drives a person to work, and people benefit from his work whether he intends it or not. Likewise, Allah placed the sexual instinct in human beings, and it has its fervor, so that through it the human species is preserved. He, glorified, does not want it to rush out in a way that transgresses upon people's honor. Thus Allah created the instincts for a purpose, and the laws came to preserve the instincts within the domain of their purpose and to prevent them from their raging excesses in domains other than those the method has defined for them.

So inclination is an innate matter in the human soul.
