If anyone tries to cast doubt on this matter, we say to him: every matter at which the intellect may stop, the Truth (glorified and exalted is He) treats it in a broad manner, for He (glorified is He) is a Creator, Merciful, who does not present a text before which the intellect would halt. If the intellect accepts the text, it is well, and if it does not accept it, it finds an alternative, because it is a matter that does not touch the core of belief.

Suppose a person said that Jesus was not raised but died. What has been added to the articles of faith, and what has been diminished? That is a matter that neither harms nor benefits. Similar to this is the Night Journey (al-Isra'), concerning which the Truth gave the Qur'anic statement:

﴿Glory be to the One who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed, to show him of Our signs. Indeed, He is the Hearing, the Seeing.﴾ (1) (Surah al-Isra')

The Truth did not make any statement about the matter of the Ascension (al-mi'raj), because the Night Journey is an earthly sign, in which the Messenger (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him) moved from Makkah to Bayt al-Maqdis. We know that the Messenger of Allah had not gone to Bayt al-Maqdis before the Night Journey, as evidenced by the fact that the disbelievers of Makkah wanted to embarrass the Messenger. They said to him: "Describe Bayt al-Maqdis to us." They were confident that he had never gone there before. There were caravans of theirs on the road that he (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him) had seen. He (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him) described Bayt al-Maqdis and told them about the news of their caravans, and the caravans came, confirming the truthfulness of Muhammad (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him).

Thus the Night Journey of the Messenger of Allah (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him) was an earthly sign that could be established by evidence, and that is why the Truth brought it explicitly, saying: "Glory be to the One who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa."

But the Ascension (al-mi'raj) the Truth did not mention explicitly. No one of the Quraysh nor of the people of the earth saw the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (sidrat al-muntaha), and no one of the people of the earth had the ability to describe the way of the Ascension.

So the verses in which the intellect may halt are treated by the Qur'an in a broad manner, out of mercy toward minds. If a person believes in them, this is permissible, and not believing in them does not affect the core of belief or the foundations of the obligations. Their basis is affirmation. Since the Truth (glorified and exalted is He) has delegated to His Messenger the authority to give us rulings, which if we act upon them we are rewarded by Allah, and if we do not act upon them we incur punishment: "And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it" (Surah al-Hashr, 59:7). How, then, would He not delegate to him the authority to tell us some reports?

The Messenger of Allah (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him), as narrated from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) and mentioned by al-Bukhari in his Sahih, said:

"By the One in whose hand my soul is, the son of Mary will surely descend among you as a just judge. He will break the cross, kill the pig, abolish the jizyah, and wealth will overflow until no one accepts it, and one prostration will be better than the world and everything in it." Then Abu Hurayrah said: "Recite, if you wish: 'And there is none of the People of the Book but that he will surely believe in him before his death, and on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them.'" (Surah an-Nisa', 4:159)

Then Abu Hurayrah said, "...and on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them." (The passage breaks off here.)

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 4, verse 158:

﴿Nay, Allah raised him up to Himself. And Allah is ever Almighty, All-Wise.﴾

He raised him up, the Almighty, whom no one can overpower in any way. He is the Strong, the Mighty, whom no one can harm. So although they intended to kill His messenger, Jesus, son of Mary, Allah prevails over His affair, and He is Almighty in His wisdom.

The Lord, exalted is He, then says:

﴿And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in him before his death. And on the Day of Resurrection, he will be a witness against them.﴾ (4:159)

The "in" (إن) here is the negating "in" (in al-nafiyah, the negative particle), and it is different from the conditional "in" (in al-shartiyah). Here is an example of the negating "in" from another place in the Qur'an, when the Lord said:

﴿Those who divorce [by zihar] from among you their wives - they are not their mothers. Their mothers are not but those who bore them.﴾ (58:2)

Here the Lord corrects the error of those who make zihar (zihar, the pre-Islamic practice of declaring one's wife unlawful by likening her to one's mother) from their wives, by the statement of one of them to his wife: "You are to me as the back of my mother." So He, glorified is He, says:

﴿Their mothers are not but those who bore them. And indeed, they say an objectionable statement and falsehood.﴾ (58:2)

So He clarifies: "Their mothers are not but those who bore them." And the "in" in this verse that we are now pondering is the negating "in."

It is as if the Lord is saying: "There is not any one of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in him before his death." This is an explanation of the meaning of the negating "in."

Someone may say: what about the referents of the pronouns in this verse? The verse contains more than one pronoun, such as the Lord's statement: "And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in him before his death." To whom does "him" (به) refer? And to whom does the "his" (هـ) at the end of "his death" (موته) refer? Is it the death of Jesus or the death of any one of the People of the Scripture? Jesus is mentioned, and the People of the Scripture are also mentioned. So it is valid for the statement to be as follows:

No one of the People of the Scripture will die except after he believes in Jesus. And it is also valid: Jesus will not die except after every one of the People of the Scripture believes in him. Since a pronoun is only known through its referent, and the referent clarifies the pronoun, if there are preceding words, each of them may be valid as the referent, or the pronoun may refer to part of its referent, as in the Lord's statement:

﴿And none is granted long life or has his life shortened but that it is in a register.﴾ (35:11)

The one granted long life (المعمر, al-mu'ammar) is the person who has advanced in years. And the life of this one granted long life is not shortened except as God wills. The "his" (هـ) in "his life" (عمره) refers to a part of the one granted long life, because the word "mu'ammar" is composed of two elements, which are "the person of the man." So when the pronoun referred back, it referred to the essence (الذات) and not to the lengthening of life. So the meaning is: "And none is granted long life, nor has the life of a self be shortened, to which lengthening has not been ascribed." And what is the situation when there are two referents? As in the Lord's statement:

﴿He raised the heavens without pillars that you can see.﴾ (13:2)

Here we find two referents: "the heavens" (السماء) and "the pillars" (العمد). So to which of them does the "it" (ها) in the word "you see it" (ترونها) refer? Does the "it" refer to the first referent, which is the heavens, or to the second referent, which is "the pillars"? It is valid for the "it" to refer to the heavens, meaning: the creation of the heavens raised, standing by His power, not supported by anything, while you look at them and witness them without supports. And it is also valid for it to refer to the pillars, meaning: without pillars that we know, but the Lord raised them by the laws of gravity, or: He raised the heavens "without pillars that you can see," meaning the pillars are hidden from human sight. Thus it is valid for the pronoun to be attributed and to refer to one of the two referents.

In the verse we are discussing, two things have preceded: the Messiah and the People of the Scripture, and in them are two pronouns. Do the two pronouns refer to Jesus, or do they refer to the People of the Scripture? Or does one of them refer to Jesus and the other to the People of the Scripture? And which of them refers to Jesus and which refers to the People of the Scripture? Or there is a third referent that is not mentioned but is known from the context, which is Muhammad, may God's blessings and peace be upon him. We find that the two pronouns may refer to the third referent, that is, to Muhammad, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, whose coming was announced by Jesus, son of Mary, and the frequently transmitted reports that Jesus is about to descend, break the cross, kill the swine, and that Jesus, son of Mary, will indeed pray behind one of the community of the Messenger of God, Muhammad, may God's blessings and peace be upon him.

Why did the Christians agree with the Jews on the matter of killing and crucifixion? They are excused in that, because the Lord had not given a clarification about it at that time, and His statement: "And they did not kill him, nor crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them" indicates that they are excused if they said that. But it was obligatory for them to reject the matter of crucifixion if it involved divinity or a part of divinity, and it was obligatory that they should conceal the matter of crucifixion, and that Islam should come to absolve Jesus, peace be upon him, from this matter and help the followers of Jesus to absolve him of it.

But the followers of Jesus did not heed the saying of Islam on this issue: "But it was made to appear so to them." The followers of the Messiah should have heeded it. When the Lord narrates all of that, He then judges with a divine judgment after that: "Rather, God raised him to Himself." The Christians speak of the raising, but after the crucifixion. We Muslims say: the raising, and no crucifixion: God raised him to Himself, and he will descend. The wisdom in this is that no messenger among the earlier messengers was tested by his people in such a way that they made him part of a god or a god, so the heaven did not remain silent about that. So He, glorified is He, raised him, and He will send him down to refute this matter. After that, God's decree will apply to him in His creation, which is death.

Those who stop at this matter should not stop, because the matter of our master Jesus, peace be upon him, was initiated by God with a wonder that broke the customary laws, since he was born of a mother without a father. If you have accepted the wonder at the birth, then why do you not accept the wonder in the matter of the raising?

And if one of us says: Jesus, peace be upon him, has died, we say: What do you say about your Prophet Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him? Was he raised to heaven, ascended to it bodily? Was the Messenger of God not alive by the law of life? Yes, he was alive by the law of life. The Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, remained in the heaven for a brief period and then descended to us. So the matter is that a creature of God's creation goes to heaven by the will and power of the Truth, while alive, and then descends to the earth while alive, and this is not a wonder.

The difference between the raising of Jesus and the ascension of Muhammad, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, by the Mi'raj (al-mi'raj, the Night Ascent) is a difference in duration, and this does not nullify the principle. The important thing is that he ascended with his life, descended with his life, and remained for a period of time with his life. So the matter of ascending to heaven and remaining there for a period is something admissible in our Islamic law. And to confirm this matter, the Lord says:

﴿And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in him before his death.﴾ (4:159)

The superficial hearer of this verse may say: they are people of a scripture, so they must have believed in him. I say: No. They believed in him with a belief that was for themselves, not the belief that is for God. They believed in him as God and a part of God, which is what is called among them the Trinity: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But God wants them to believe in him as a messenger, a human being, and a servant.

When the Lord says: "And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in him before his death, and on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them," the meaning of this is: none of the People of the Scripture will fail to believe in Jesus, peace be upon him, as a messenger, servant, and human being before he dies.

The pronoun in His statement "he will surely believe in him" refers to Jesus, and the other pronoun in "before his death" may refer to Jesus, meaning: before the death of Jesus. He, peace be upon him, will not die the actual death that ends his term in life except after they believe in him as a servant, messenger, and human being. This will not be realized unless he comes with his flesh, bone, and blood, to say to them: "You are wrong in denying my good news of Muhammad the Seal, and you are wrong in accusing my mother. The proof of your error is that I came bringing good news of a messenger for all people, who is Muhammad son of Abdullah, and here I am praying behind one of the community of that messenger. So Jesus, peace be upon him, will not bring a new legislation, but rather will pray behind one of the believers in Muhammad son of Abdullah, may God's blessings and peace be upon him."

When Jesus son of Mary does that, what will those who were tested in him say? Undoubtedly they will declare belief in the message of Muhammad, may God's blessings and peace be upon him. Or every People of the Scripture who lived in the interval from his raising until his descent again will declare belief in Jesus as a human being, messenger, and servant before he dies, even in the final unconsciousness when the soul reaches the throat and rattles in the throat at death. So it may be valid for the verse to be general: "And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in him before his death," and the pronoun in it refers to every People of the Scripture before he dies.

The human soul has a desire that may veil the truths from it, close the door of certainty before it, and push it toward that through the delusion of life. When the agony of death comes with the truth, every matter that distances a person from the path of the certain truth ends, and only matters remain in their truth, their veracity, and their certainty. The human soul awakens at a moment when it thinks it will meet God, the delusion of life falls away, and a person among them reviews himself at this moment and says: "I followed my soul's desire." But will such a kind of faith benefit its possessor? No, because his case in that is like the faith of Pharaoh, for he said when drowning overtook him:

﴿Until, when drowning overtook him, he said: I believe that there is no deity except the one in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the Muslims.﴾ (10:90)

Then the voice of the Truth is heard at that moment: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before and been of the corrupters.﴾ (10:91), so Pharaoh did not benefit at the moment of drowning from faith.

And He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And repentance is not [accepted] from those who do evil deeds until, when death comes to one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now," nor from those who die while they are disbelievers. For those, We have prepared a painful punishment.﴾ (4:18)

The Lord concludes the verse: "And on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them." This affirms that Jesus, peace be upon him, will bear witness against those who were contemporaries of his descent in the world, and he will bear witness on the Day of Resurrection against those who ascribed divinity to him: ﴿And [mention] when God will say, "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as deities besides God?'" He will say, "Exalted are You! It was not for me to say that to which I have no right. If I had said it, You would have known it. You know what is within myself, and I do not know what is within Yourself. Indeed, it is You who is Knower of the unseen."﴾ (5:116)

Continuing with His discussion of the atrocities of the Jews, the Truthful (al-Haqq) the Glorified says:

﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things which had been lawful for them, and for their hindering many from the way of Allah,﴾

He, glory be to Him, makes clear that the prohibition of some good things upon the Children of Israel came as a result of attitudes that Allah enumerates. They committed the great sins they committed, wronged themselves and wronged others, and barred others from the religion of Allah, meaning that they did not enter into Islam.

The Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 161:

The reasons (hathaith) for the prohibition of some good things continue, adding to these two positions:

﴿And their taking of usury, although they had been forbidden from it, and their consuming of people's wealth by falsehood. And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment.﴾ (4:161)

What injustice is the Truth speaking of in His saying: "For the injustice of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them"? Injustice (zulm) means that one judges for someone who has no right to a right. The peak of injustice is that one judges that God has a partner, and for this reason He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Indeed, association [with Allah] is a great injustice.﴾ (part of 31:13, Surah Luqman).

The reasons for God's judgment in forbidding things that had been lawful to the Children of Israel are many. When God forbids something, it is certain that it is limited in relation to what is permitted: what is forbidden is little, and the rest of what God has not mentioned falls within the scope of the lawful.

An example of this is His saying:

{Say, "Come, I will recite what your Lord has prohibited to you: that you associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents, and do not kill your children out of poverty; We provide for you and for them; and do not approach immoralities, what is apparent of them and what is concealed; and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right. This He has commanded you that you may use reason. And do not approach the property of an orphan, except in the way that is best, until he reaches maturity. And give full measure and weight in justice. We do not burden a soul except [with that within] its capacity. And when you speak, be just, even if it should be [against] a near relative. And the covenant of Allah fulfill. This He has commanded you that you may remember."} (Surah al-An'am, 6:151-152)

Here the Truth mentions the prohibitions, which are specific and limited, whereas all blessings are lawful. From this matter we understand the breadth of the mercy of the Truth toward creation: He has granted us much and very much of blessings that cannot be counted, and has forbidden only a little. The restriction to a little came so that each blessing would remain within its own domain.

If a person says: "God forbade this thing because it is harmful," we say: what you say is permissible, but harm is not the cause of the ruling for all prohibitions. God, glory be to Him, may forbid a matter to discipline a people. And to God belongs the highest likeness: we see that the one responsible for raising a family may forbid a child in it a kind of food or part of his pocket money, and the purpose of that is punishment.

Why did the Children of Israel deserve the punishment of prohibition? They went against the method of God and made lawful for themselves what God had forbidden. Since they had deviated and made lawful what God had forbidden, the Truth responds to them: "You have dared against what I forbade, and so you made it lawful. It is my right to forbid to you what I had made lawful for you before that, so that a person does not understand that by making lawful for himself what God forbade, he has taken something beyond God. No one can overpower God, and therefore He, glory be to Him, forbids him some of His lawful things."

Prohibition is either a prohibition of legislation (tahrim tashri') or a prohibition of nature, disposition (fitrah), or necessity. We find the man who has been excessive toward himself in consuming forbidden things, such as wine for example, God forbids him things that were lawful to him, and the doctor tells him: "Your liver has deteriorated, and it has become forbidden for you to eat many kinds of food and drink." Thus we see man's injustice to himself and how it resulted in the prohibition of things that had been lawful to him.

As for one who has been excessive toward himself in consuming a certain kind of food, such as sugar for example, eating it beyond what need calls for, we find God's cosmic law (sunnat Allah al-kawniyyah) saying to him: "You have taken more than your right, and you have disabled in your body the ability to use sugar well, so you have become ill. Beware of eating sweets again." The sick person craves sugar and sweets and has the ability to buy them, but they are forbidden to him. It is as if the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, is saying to him: "By your injustice to yourself, you have forbidden what I had made lawful to you."

And another who owns wealth, servants and vast farms, has others grind the grain for him, and orders them to make bread for him from the purest kinds of flour free of any "bran" (nukhalah). They make him white bread, and he eats it, while his followers make bread for themselves from less pure flour. God's law says to him: "You will eat bread made with bran, by a doctor's order, as a treatment for your intestines, because you were excessive toward yourself in eating bread made from the purest kinds of flour. And let your subjects and workers eat bread made from the finest kinds of flour." So, by your injustice, We have forbidden what was made lawful for you.

When we see a person deprived of a blessing of God which is lawful for him, we know that he has made lawful for himself something God forbade him, or was excessive in using a right God had permitted him. None of us escapes God's observation. So prohibition may be by legislation, when the punishment is prohibition from the Legislator, and it may be prohibition by nature and disposition when the matter involves excess on the part of the self.

Let us always read this verse: "For the injustice of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them, and for their hindering many from the way of Allah." And likewise those who take wealth through usury: they took usury so that their wealth would increase. Why do you want wealth? Do you want wealth for its own sake, or for another purpose? It is true that wealth is provision, but it is indirect provision, because with it one buys the things a person benefits from, which are direct provision. We have said in the past: suppose a person is in a desert with a mountain of gold, but his food has run out. A mountain of gold in such a situation does not benefit him; rather, a loaf of bread and a cup of water become, in that state, more precious than gold. And one who increases his wealth through usury, does he want that increase for pleasures? God erases that wealth and destroys it in calamities.

Whoever wishes to keep what God has made lawful for him until his term comes, must not permit himself anything God has forbidden, and by this he remains enjoying God's blessings upon him. The Truth is the One who says: ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants.﴾ (41:46)

Man, then, is the one who wrongs himself, in confirmation of the saying of the Truth: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people at all, but the people wrong themselves.﴾ (Surah Yunus, 10:44)

Thus the Jews wronged themselves, so God forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them. And who transformed a good matter into something not good? It is man. But did he change the thing itself or the ruling on the thing? He changed the ruling on the thing, making what was forbidden into something lawful. "For the injustice of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them, and for their hindering many from the way of Allah."

How could they be able to hinder from the way of Allah? They wronged themselves and took usury, and these are matters that place them on the side of misguidance and in the sphere of falsehood. And would that the matter stopped there; rather, they also wanted to misguide others, and this is the essence of hindering from the way of Allah. This matter made them bearers of another burden upon their burdens, so they were not content with their own misguidance but bore the burdens of others.

﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Unquestionably, evil is that which they bear.﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 16:25)

A skeptic who hears this saying may ask: how does the Qur'an contradict itself, saying: ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another.﴾ (part of 6:164)

We say: every burden has its path and its reckoning. A person bears the burden of his own misguidance alone, if he has not misguided anyone else; but if he tries to misguide others, he bears the burden of that misguidance.

The Truth says, completing their wronging of themselves: "And their taking of usury, although they had been forbidden from it, and their consuming of people's wealth by falsehood. And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful punishment." We have already dealt with usury, and they took bribes, which is consuming people's wealth by falsehood; likewise theft and cheating in goods. All of that is taking people's wealth without right, and what is taken without right is falsehood, and God, glory be to Him, has prepared for them in advance a painful punishment. Every person has two seats: a seat in Paradise if his faith is decreed, and a seat in Hellfire if his disbelief is decreed. There is no room to suppose that Paradise or Hellfire could become crowded. God created the seats of Paradise on the basis that all people are believers, and made the seats of Hellfire on the basis that all people are disbelievers.

For this reason the Truth says: ﴿Those who will inherit Paradise, they will abide therein forever.﴾ (23:11, Surah al-Mu'minun)

When the believer takes his seat in Paradise, God gives him the other seat that He had prepared for the disbeliever. For the disbeliever, before he disbelieved, had a seat in Paradise had he chosen faith. And the Truth has prepared for them a painful punishment, that is, one whose pain is severe, and it is also humiliating, for He has the power to subdue any person who steels himself against hardship; no one can endure the punishment of God.

Is this all that was among the People of the Book? Was there not among the People of the Book one who pondered the matter of faith in the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in his mind, and investigated the qualities and signs that came announcing him ﷺ in the Torah and the Gospel? Among them there were those who did so. And the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, relates the true history, excepting from the People of the Book those firm in knowledge, saying: ﴿But those firmly grounded in knowledge among them and the believers believe in what has been revealed to you, and what was revealed before you, and the establishers of prayer and the givers of zakah and the believers in Allah and the Last Day. Those - We will give them a great reward.﴾ (4:162)

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 4, verse 162:

﴿But those firm in knowledge among them, and the believers, believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and those who establish prayer and give zakah and believe in Allah and the Last Day — those We will give a great reward.﴾

So Allah did not generalize the ruling against the People of the Book, which had preceded regarding their disbelief, their wronging of themselves, their taking of riba and other things. Rather, He placed an exception, and an example of this is "Abdullah ibn Salam," who had the question of faith in the Messenger of Allah on his mind, and who knew that the Jews were a people of deceit.

So he said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I believe in you as a messenger. By Allah, I recognized you when I saw you, as I recognize my son, and my recognition of Muhammad is stronger."

And the Truth (Allah) says about this same position: "Those to whom We gave the Book recognize him as they recognize their own sons." No one loses track of the recognition of his own son. Likewise, those firm in knowledge recognize Muhammad as a messenger from Allah and one who conveys from Him. The one firm in knowledge is the one who is steadfast in his faith, who does not waver from it, and whom desires and whims do not seize; rather, he is one who has reached a pure elevation in certainty, which is not tainted by any blemish or doubt.

"But those firm in knowledge among them, and the believers, believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you." His saying, "what has been revealed to you," is the Qur'an, and it is the origin to which every book revealed before it is referred back. So when they believe in what was revealed to our master the Messenger of Allah, they must necessarily believe in what came in earlier books.

Whoever observes the stylistic pattern will find that there is a variation in what follows His saying: "and those who establish prayer." The verse began: "But those firm in knowledge among them, and the believers, believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and those who establish prayer."

We know that the sound masculine plural is marked by a waw in the nominative and by a ya' in the accusative and genitive, and here we find "al-muqimin" (those who establish) comes with a ya', even though it is coordinated with a nominative word. Grammarians call this phenomenon "kasr al-i'rab" (breaking of the case-ending), because i'rab requires a ruling, and here we turn our attention to the breaking of the ruling. The Arab ear upon which the Qur'an was revealed is disposed to eloquence and becomes alert at the moment the case-ending is broken.

Therefore, when an Arab hears a grammatical error, he is startled. Everyone knows the story of the Bedouin who heard one of the caliphs giving a sermon. The caliph committed a grammatical error, so the Bedouin cupped his ears, that is, placed his fingers behind his ears, turning and raising them, to listen carefully to what the caliph was saying. Then the caliph committed another error, and the Bedouin jumped to his feet. Then the caliph committed a third error, and the Bedouin said: "I testify that you were appointed to this matter by decree and destiny," as though he wanted to say: "You do not deserve to be in this position."

When a verse appears in the Book that challenges with eloquence and contains a breaking of the case-ending, the people of eloquence should have said: how can Muhammad claim that he challenges with eloquence when his grammar is not sound? But no one said it, which indicates that they perceived the secret in the breaking of the case-ending, by which the Truth draws every soul to the awareness of this matter upon which the mind must pause: "and those who establish prayer."

Why? Because prayer encompasses and includes the essential pillar among the pillars of Islam. Each pillar has a time, a duration, and a basis of obligation. The testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah suffices to be uttered by the Muslim once in his lifetime. Fasting is a month in the year, and a person may not fast and may take the concessions of breaking the fast if there are reasons in his life for taking them. Zakah is paid by a person each year, or with each harvest if he has property subject to zakah. Hajj may be performed by a person or he may not be able to perform it. But prayer remains the essential pillar of the religion. For this reason we find this noble statement:

﴿"What led you into Saqar?" They said, "We were not of those who prayed."﴾ (Surat al-Muddaththir)

The pillars of Islam, as we know, are five, and they are clear. It is permissible that a Muslim may not be able to establish all of them, but may establish only two, such as the testimony and the establishment of prayer. When the Truth says: "and those who establish prayer," He draws every believer to the continuity of love for Allah. They may love Allah for one month a year through fasting, or show love by paying zakah whenever they receive produce from land or wealth, or they may love Allah only if they are able to go to Hajj. But through prayer the believer loves his Lord five times every day. It is thus a constant declaration of loyalty. We have said that prayer combines all the pillars of the religion: in it we say, "I testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and messenger." We know that we purify through wealth, and wealth is a branch of labor, and labor requires time, and a person who prays purifies through time. A person who prays abstains from everything lawful to him, so there is fasting in prayer, and the Muslim faces the Sacred House in every prayer, as though he were on Hajj.

Thus, when the Truth breaks the case-ending at His saying "and those who establish prayer," He has only come to draw our attention to the importance of this worship. That is why they say: this is a breaking of the case-ending for the purpose of praise. It is in the accusative by way of specification (al-ikhtisas), and the Truth specifies those who establish prayer, because the establishment of prayer contains a continuous declaration of loyalty to Allah, and this loyalty is never severed in any state of the Muslim nor at any time of the Muslim, as long as he has reason.

Then the Truth says afterward: "and those who give zakah and the believers in Allah and the Last Day." It is as though all the acts of worship are for the sake of perpetuating the servant's declaration of loyalty to faith in Allah. Faith, as we know, has two parentheses: the first parenthesis is that a person believes in the summit of faith, which is belief in Allah; the second parenthesis is that a person believes in the end to which we return, which is the Last Day. And He, glorified is He, says as a recompense to these: "those We will give a great reward." It is a great reward, because each one of them has separated from the rest of the People of the Book and stood in a stance of refusal, rebelling against the deception of others, and because he did this in order to demonstrate the truthfulness of the Qur'an in that the announcement of the Messenger had already been foretold in the Torah.

Then the Truth says:

﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him. We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron and Solomon, and to David We gave the Psalms.﴾ (4:163)

We know that when the Truth speaks, He uses the first-person pronoun, and the first-person pronoun has three forms. Sometimes He says "innā" (إنا, "indeed We"), sometimes a second time "innanī" (إنني, "indeed I"), and a third time He addresses His creation with "naḥnu" (نحن, "We"). Here He says "innā awḥaynā ilayka kamā awḥaynā" (إنا أوحينا إليك كما أوحينا, "Indeed We have revealed to you as We revealed"). In another place in the Noble Qur'an we see His saying:

﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me﴾ (20:14)

And in a third place He says:

﴿Indeed, It is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ (15:9).

This is because the Reminder requires many and varied attributes gathered together to send it down and preserve it. When Allah addresses His creation, He addresses them in a way that makes manifest the places of the attributes in the universe in which we live. The universe in which we live is full of beings that serve man, and these beings needed much to prepare the universe for man before man existed, so that when he came into the universe he would find the blessings of Allah for him. Man is the one who came newly upon the creation of Allah.

This universe, which has reached a great level of creativity, needed many attributes to prepare it. It needed knowledge of things, wisdom to place everything in its proper place, power to bring it forth, and a Rich One with His treasuries, so that He might pour out on each position a good that differs from the good of another position. When the work requires the fields of many attributes of the Truth, He, glorified be He, says "innā" (إنا) or "naḥnu" (نحن). When the discourse turns to the Essence of the Truth, glorified and exalted be He, He says "innī anā Allāh" (إني أنا الله, "indeed I am Allah"). In this case "innā" does not come, and "naḥnu" does not come.

The Truth here says "innā awḥaynā ilayka" (إنا أوحينا إليك), meaning that He has revealed a method by which man becomes a master in the universe, preserving himself and the universe together. Preserving the creature and the universe requires knowledge, wisdom, power and mercy. Therefore revelation requires many attributes working together, which created the universe. And out of Allah's mercy toward His creatures, He gave them a share of participation. He says, for example:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth thereby fruits of varying colors?﴾ (35:27)

He is the One who sends down water from the sky; none of His creatures has any part in this, because water evaporates without man knowing it, and man did not know this except in the last few centuries. We have come to know how clouds form from vapor, and then rain falls afterward. Thus man has no part in this matter. Therefore the Truth says: "Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky" (أ لم تر أن الله أنزل من السماء ماء). Then comes the Truth's giving justice to the creation, and He says: "fa-akhrajnā bihi thamarātin mukhtalifan alwānuhā" (فأخرجنا به ثمرات مختلفا ألوانها, "then We bring forth thereby fruits of varying colors"). He did not say "fa-akhrajtu" (فأخرجت, "then I brought forth"). Rather, the Truth gave justice to His creation, who are the ones moving in His blessings through the intellects He created for them. So He, glorified be He, measures the work of the creatures, such as plowing, sowing and irrigating, so that the fruit may come forth.

Thus the Qur'anic style, when it uses "innī" (إني), points to the unity of the Essence, and when it uses "innā" (إنا), points to the gathering of the attributes of perfection, because every act of Allah requires a mustering of attributes: knowledge, will, power, wisdom, grasping and extending, honoring and humbling, dominance and mercy. Therefore the pronoun of majesty is necessary, which the grammarians speak of, saying that "naḥnu" (نحن) and "nā" (نا) are for the one who is magnified, and the Truth has magnified Himself, because the matter here is a mustering of attributes required for the bringing into being of the universe and for its governance. For this reason we find some of the knowers of God, who have glimpsed the majesty of Allah in His Essence and the beauty of Him in His attributes, saying:

Glory be to a Lord above every conjecture, exalted in majesty beyond being encompassed in His Essence.
If He says "innī," that is the unity of His holiness,
And if He says "innā," that is the mustering of His attributes.

When we look at this matter, we find that the Truth, glorified and exalted be He, has given justice to His creatures so that they might know Him. He made for them the bringing about of things. And when He, glorified be He, addresses a matter in which He has an action, and in which one of His creatures whom He has empowered also has an action, He uses the pronoun of magnification, because He, glorified be He, is the One who gave them this power.

When the Truth brought His creation into being from nothing, He made it possible for some of His creatures to bring about things too. But there is a difference between bringing matter into being and bringing into being what is composed of matter. He, glorified be He, created everything from nothing, but He gave His creatures the ability to create things, though not from nothing. He did not withhold from them the mention of the word "creation" (الخلق), so He said: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ (23:14).

It is as if He, glorified and exalted be He, made some of His creatures creators. But the creators among His creatures do not create from pure nothingness; rather they form a composite from what already exists in its materials. They take from materials that Allah created, then they assemble and bring into being. The human who makes a water cup does not produce the cup from pure nothingness, even though the universal (الكلية) of the cup did not exist, the particulars of making the cup do exist. Sand exists in many environments, and also exists what melts sand, and the intellect that takes those elements, and the thought that makes glass paste from sand, and the designer of the machines that make this cup exist. So man has brought forth a cup from existing particulars. The difference, then, between the creation of Allah and the creation of the creatures of Allah is that Allah creates from pure nothingness. Therefore He described His Essence by saying: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾.

You, O humans, only create from the creatures of Allah, and you do not create from something other than what Allah has created. So He, glorified and exalted be He, is the best of creators. Just as the Truth gave justice to His creation by attributing to them a creating, He must describe Himself as the best of creators. Also, if the creatures create, as we have said, and I will keep repeating it so that it may settle firmly in minds, the thing becomes fixed in the form in which they brought it into being. They make the cup so that it remains a cup in its size, shape and color. But they have not created a male cup and a female cup so that they might come together and produce small cups that grow and get bigger. Rather, Allah breathes the secret of life into everything and brings it into being. For this reason He is the best of creators.

And if you look at everything in existence, you will find in it the secret of the active Essence. If you look at your own self, you will find for yourself means of perception: you will find for yourself hearing, and you will find for yourself eyes, and you will find for yourself a nose, and touch and taste. But some of these instruments are under your control in choosing. When you open your eyes you see, and if you do not want to see, you close your eyes. But if you want not to hear, can you put in your ear a device that says "I do not hear"? And you open your mouth to eat and to taste, but you do not open your nose to smell. You stretch out your hand to touch. And tell me, by God, what emotion do you have when you want to laugh? What is the instrument in your body that you move to laugh? You know nothing except a stimulating cause that makes you laugh, but you do not know which instruments in your body work to make you laugh. Likewise, when you weep, what are the instruments that work within your self to make you weep? You do not know. For this reason Allah made laughing and weeping, along with bringing into being by life and non-existence by death, belong to Him, glorified and exalted be He.

﴿And that it is He who causes laughter and weeping, and that it is He who causes death and gives life﴾ (53:43–44).

The Truth placed within your human self things that act, but you do not know by what you act or by what you are acted upon. The ear has nothing that blocks it from hearing, therefore the Truth does not command you not to hear anything. But the righteous saying commands: "Do not eavesdrop on gossip" (لا تتسمع إلى القيلة).

It did not say "do not hear anything but gossip," because man cannot plug his ears against what goes on around him. But he can avoid eavesdropping by not turning his ears toward what is being said. Thus the Truth has placed the obligation within the scope of the believer's choices. For this reason He said: ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in a conversation other than that﴾ (6:68).

He used the word "ra'ayta" (رأيت, "you see") here, because the Muslim does not possess anything with which he can block his ears so as not to hear the talk of those who engage in vain talk about the verses of Allah. But Allah commanded those who hear that to go away, turning aside from those who indulge in vain talk. And He, glorified be He, clarifies for us what is hidden from us. Everything in the universe, although its outward appearance is that it "acts," is in reality subdued in what it undergoes, to the desires of Allah, by the command of Allah. For this reason the knowers of Allah say: "Among the beauty of His kindness to you is that He acted and attributed the action to you."

So He, glorified and exalted be He, is the One who does everything, and man has nothing but to direct the acting instrument. From the greatness of the Truth, glorified and exalted be He, is that when a man is strong he cannot give his strength to a weak person. None of us says to a weak person, "Take some of my strength so it helps you endure," whereas Allah makes clear to the weak person in practice: "Come to Me, and I will give you from My absolute power a measure of strength so that you may act."

Thus strength in a created being is never given to its like; rather its effect is given. An example of this is when a person cannot carry a heavy thing and another strong person comes to carry it for him. The strong person, by his action, transmits the effect of his strength to the weak one, but he cannot transfer his strength into the weak person's own self so that he can carry the heavy thing.

But Allah does not merely transmit the effect of His strength; He bestows and gives strength to every weak person who turns to Him and to every strong person too. He, glorified be He, bestows wealth and abundance on every rich and poor person, and by His mercy on every merciful one, and by His power on every capable one, and by His wisdom on every wise one. Therefore all of these are supplies from the Truth, glorified and exalted be He. This is our discussion of "innā" (إنا).

And when the Truth speaks saying "awḥaynā" (أوحينا, "We revealed"), He, glorified be He, uses the plural form. And what is revelation? The scholars said: revelation is informing by way of concealment, because the means of informing are various. The means of informing are what conveys a speech said by a communicator so the hearer knows it, or a gesture by which he points so that the observer understands its meaning. These informings are not concealed but clear. When He says "awḥaynā," He means that He has informed, but by a hidden way. When the word "waḥy" (وحي) is used, it has various meanings: every informing by concealment is revelation. But who revealed in concealment? And to whom was it revealed in concealment? And what was revealed in concealment? We find that the Truth, glorified and exalted be He, has come in the kinds of existence, and He spoke of the earth, which is inanimate matter:

﴿When the earth is shaken with its [final] earthquake, and the earth brings out its burdens, and man says, "What is wrong with it?" That Day it will report its news, because your Lord has revealed to it﴾ (99:1–5).

That is, the Truth has set the earth on a timed span until the establishment of the Resurrection, at which point it will speak. And to Allah belongs the highest likeness: we estimate the expected lifespan of what we make so that it ends at a specified time. Thus Allah revealed to the inanimate, which is the earth.

And in creating the creatures, He leaves us something that brings us close to the craftsmanship of the Creator. When a man wants to wake at three in the morning, a time at which he is not accustomed to waking, he sets the alarm so that its bell sounds at the appointed time. It is as if the man, by this action, has revealed to the alarm clock. Likewise the Truth created the earth and revealed to it: at the appointed time you will burst open by My natural decree for you. And the Truth reveals to the animal kind:

﴿And your Lord revealed to the bee: "Take for yourself dwellings in the mountains and in the trees and in what they construct"﴾ (16:68).

This is an informing by concealment from Allah to the bee, for Allah placed in its instinctive constitution what leads to that. There is a difference between instinctive constitution (التكوين الغرزي) and chosen constitution (التكوين الاختياري). Instinctive constitution proceeds by an automatic system from which it does not deviate, whereas chosen constitution may deviate from it.

Another example of automatism is the computer called the electronic brain. A person stores information in it, and this computer cannot tell the one who put the information in it, "Do not say this fact," nor can it refrain from giving what is in it to whoever asks for this information, if he knows how to retrieve it. The computer has no choice.

The situation is different with the human intellect, which is distinguished by the capacity to select information and knows how to present this information according to different situations. It consciously controls what must be concealed and what must not be concealed. Indeed, the human intellect may lie and distort information, and it is able to change facts and manipulate them, whereas the computer called an electronic brain cannot do that, because it presents information according to what has been "barmaja" (برمجة, "programmed") into it, stored in it and placed in it. And thus man rises in thought.

And the Truth, s

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 4, verse 164:

Then the Truth (al-Haqq) says:

﴿And messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you. And Allah spoke to Moses with direct speech.﴾

The messengers mentioned by Allah in the preceding verse are not all the messengers in whom belief must be held in detail. As our teachers at al-Azhar al-Sharif taught us, we must believe in twenty-five messengers, and some poets have arranged them in verse:

"Those are our proof: eight of them,
after ten, and seven remain, and they are:
Idris, Hud, Shu'ayb, Salih, and likewise
Dhu al-Kifl, Adam, and with the Chosen One they are sealed."

In Surat al-An'am we find His saying, the Truth:

﴿And that was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people. We raise by degrees whom We will. Indeed, your Lord is Wise and Knowing. And We gave him Isaac and Jacob, each We guided. And Noah We guided before; and among his descendants David and Solomon and Job and Joseph and Moses and Aaron. Thus do We reward the doers of good. And Zechariah and John and Jesus and Elias, all of the righteous. And Ishmael and Elisha and Jonah and Lot, and each We preferred over the worlds.﴾

In these verses there are eighteen messengers. Adding the seven—Idris, Hud, Shu'ayb, Salih, Dhu al-Kifl, Adam, and Muhammad (ﷺ)—there are twenty-five messengers whom Allah mentioned. However, the verse preceding the one we are discussing did not mention all the names of the messengers; He mentioned the names of some messengers in Surat al-An'am, some of them in Surat Hud, and some of them in Surat al-Shu'ara'. The Truth says:

{And messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you. And Allah spoke to Moses with direct speech.} (4:164)

That is, the twenty-five messengers are not all the messengers whom the Truth sent to creation, for He said:

﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them.﴾ (35:24)

That is, He has related to us the notable messengers whose nations had density or wide scope, or whose messengers had a dense mission. But there are some messengers whom He sent to a hundred thousand or more, such as Jonah (peace be upon him): ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more.﴾ (37:147)

The world in ancient times was isolated, and did not possess the means of contact that would make nations merge. Every environment had its own ailments, and every environment had its distinct character in conduct. Therefore Allah sent a messenger to every environment to treat these ailments, and He did not mention the other ailments, lest they transfer from one society to another by imitation. When the Truth, with His eternal knowledge, knew that His creation, by what He had empowered them with in thought, production, and research into the secrets of the universe, would invent means of contact so that the world becomes one unit, and that a thing happens in the East and the West learns it in the same moment, and that ailments would become one ailment throughout the world, then it was necessary that there should exist a messenger who treats the gathered ailments. So he (ﷺ) was the Seal, the comprehensive messenger and the restraining messenger.

﴿And messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you. And Allah spoke to Moses with direct speech.﴾ (4:164)

The Truth, glorified be He, speaks of the history of the prophethoods with their peoples using the word "related" (qasasna), and there is wisdom in that. Qasas means that the messenger has no role in the events; rather the events come in their context as they occurred, and He, glorified be He, knows from eternity that His creation would invent an art called "the art of narrative."

It is strange that they call it the art of narrative, and authors weave imaginary tales or tales with no reality. When they come to real history, the author adds part of the events or adds things from his imagination, and they say these are requirements of mastering the art of storytelling, and they deprive themselves of the trust of transmission. Therefore the Truth comes to clarify for us that the narrative concerning the messengers and others in the Qur'an is real, true narrative that actually happened.

The word "qasas" is derived from qass al-athar, meaning that we follow the footprint as it goes, so we do not go here nor go there. The stories of the prophets in the Qur'an are realistic and are from the narration of the Truth, not the narration of creation. There is a difference between what the Truth narrates to His creation so that they may walk by the method, and what creatures narrate to one another for entertainment or other purposes. We find the narrations of creatures sometimes crowded with human imagination, such as the novels of Jurji Zaydan about Islam and the prophets; and when they asked him why he added from his own to reality, he gave the conventional answer: "I did that for the sake of the plot of the story."

We must distinguish and differentiate between the narrations of creatures and the stories of the Truth, and place this in the focus of awareness, so that no one enters by his imagination into the Qur'anic stories what is not in them, and so that no one comes one day and says: all stories are one. In the Qur'an we are not before an author; we are before the Supreme Creator who narrates to us what teaches us, and He, glorified be He, knew from eternity what would occur in His universe. Therefore He said:

﴿We relate to you the best of stories by what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an, although you were before it among the unaware.﴾ (12:3)

He, glorified be He, related to His Messenger (ﷺ) in the Qur'an the best of stories, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would address the kinds of humanity that were distributed among all the messengers, his brothers. Since the work of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would be with all human kinds who had been scattered earlier among the messengers, his brothers, it is necessary that He, glorified be He, clarify to the Messenger (ﷺ) and to his community after him: that such-and-such happened to the messenger so-and-so, and he was sent to a people whose stance toward him was such-and-such, and the ailments of that society were such-and-such. Muhammad (ﷺ), as we know, is charged with treating all kinds of humanity, and likewise his community after him, and they must know the news of all the societies and messengers. (We relate to you the best of stories by what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an, although you were before it among the unaware.)

Thus the word "qasas" indicates that they are narratives of the movement of the creed that was with all the messengers. History, as we know, is linking events to their times: sometimes we make the event the focus of the historical account, then we bring many persons who revolve around the event; and sometimes we make the person the origin, and the events revolve around him. So when we say "sira" (biography), we mean that we have made the person the axis of speech, and events revolve around him; and if we record an event chronologically, we make the event the origin and the persons revolve around it.

For example: when we come to speak of the event of the Hijra, we make this event the axis and narrate how the Messenger of Allah emigrated with Abu Bakr, and how Umar ibn al-Khattab and other Companions emigrated, and thus the Hijra is the axis and how persons revolved around this great event.

Another example: when we narrate a biography such as the biography of the Prophet (ﷺ), we make the Prophet (ﷺ) the axis of the speech and history, and we narrate how events unfolded in his life.

Thus the reports of the stories of the messengers are the axis, and we pick up the events that passed over them, because when the messages come with the method of heaven they divide into two parts: a theoretical part that the Truth wishes to teach His creation through the Messenger, which is the scientific part, for these are matters they must know; and a practical part, because the Truth wants of His creation that they know, and wants of them also, after they know, that they adapt the movement of their lives in light of what they know. The matter is not a luxury of knowledge, but a responsibility of applying what they know within the axis of "do" and "do not do." Had the matter been only that the creation know, it would have been possible to say: how easy a journey it is.

We found the Quraysh disbelievers, when the Messenger asked them to testify that there is no god but Allah, resisting that; and had they thought it was merely a word to be said, they would have said it. But they understood the demand of the word, and understood that there would be no sovereignty, no servitude, and no commands for anyone other than Allah, and that this meant absolute equality among the servants.

Thus every obligation from heaven has been sent down, and the purpose of knowing it is to act upon it, that is, to employ knowledge in practice; there is no value in knowledge without action. When the Messenger conveys to the people: this is the ruling, and each one of you is required to adapt the movement of his life in light of this ruling, the rulings always come within human capacity.

There are people who knew and acted, and these are their stories: this is the story of so-and-so and the story of so-and-so. The stories give us the practical side required of the method. Therefore the Truth related to us the stories of the messengers in the Qur'an, and the Truth informs us of the faithful lineage and teaches us the lineage acknowledged by the prophets. He narrates the story of Noah (peace be upon him), when it was revealed to him that he must build the ark, and his people mocked him; and after he built it, the divine command came to him that he should carry in it two of each kind. The Truth says:

﴿And he was constructing the ship, and whenever a company of his people passed by him, they mocked him. He said: If you mock us, then we will mock you as you mock. So you will know to whom will come a punishment that will disgrace him and descend upon him a lasting punishment. [And so it was] until when Our command came and the oven overflowed, We said: Load into it of each pair two, and your family, except those against whom the word has preceded, and those who believed; and none believed with him except a few.﴾ (11:38–40)

The Truth's words "except those against whom the word has preceded" should not have passed unnoticed by the insight of Noah, for it implies that there were people of his family who would not believe. So he says to his son:

﴿And Noah called to his son, and he was apart. O my son, board with us and be not with the disbelievers.﴾ (11:42)

And the reply was:

﴿He said: I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water.﴾ (11:43)

So Noah said:

﴿He said: No protector today from the command of Allah, except for whom He has mercy.﴾ (11:43)

And after Noah's son drowned and the earth swallowed its water, Noah called to his Lord and said:

﴿My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and indeed Your promise is true, and You are the most just of judges.﴾ (11:45)

So we are before a narrative scene in the story of Noah, by which the Truth draws our attention to the matter of the sonship of the messages: sonship here is methodological, and whoever follows the prophet is the one who belongs to his lineage, and whoever does not follow the prophet is not of his lineage. Therefore the Truth said: ("O Noah, indeed he is not of your family"). The people of prophethood are those who followed the prophet's method, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explains this to us when he said of Salman al-Farisi:

("Salman is one of us, the People of the House.") (1)

He did not say: Salman is Arab, or that he is one of the Muslims; but he said: he is of the People of the House. And the Truth clarified this in the story of Noah's son: ("Indeed he is not of your family; indeed he is of unrighteous conduct.")

Some who delved into the meaning of "he is not of your family" engaged in idle talk and said: Noah's son's mother committed evil. To these we say: seek forgiveness from your Lord and consider the basis of the ruling.

﴿Indeed he is not of your family; indeed, he is of unrighteous work. So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge.﴾ (11:46)

Thus the lineage of children to fathers among the prophets is a lineage of deed, not a lineage of blood, nor of marriage or procreation. As for those who spoke evil of a woman, they must seek Allah's forgiveness. The Truth, glorified be He, is exalted above deceiving His Messenger. Suppose the mother of the son did that—God forbid—what is the son's fault when his mother comes to this? The son has no share in that; but the saying of Allah, "indeed he is of unrighteous work," shows that the establishment of faithful sonship is by deed alone.

Let us consider the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to his family and kin. On the authority of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), he said: When the verse was revealed (And warn your closest kindred), the Prophet (ﷺ) began calling out to the clans of Quraysh, clan by clan: "O Banu so-and-so, save yourselves from the Fire! ... " until he reached Fatimah and said: "O Fatimah, daughter of Muhammad, save yourself from the Fire; I possess nothing for you against Allah, except that you have kinship which I will keep in its moisture (i.e., keep ties with it)."(2)

Allah gives the example of wives, saying:

﴿Allah presents an example for those who disbelieved: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot. They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them, so they availed them nothing against Allah, and it was said: Enter the Fire with those who enter.﴾ (66:10)

The betrayal meant here is not sexual betrayal; rather, to derive the proof that the messenger, even if he is a messenger, has no power to compel his wife or spouse to a creed. She possesses freedom of belief, so there is no guardianship for the man over the woman in creed, even if he claims divinity, as Pharaoh, for example, said—

1. Narrated by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, from Amr ibn Awf.
2. Narrated by Imam Ahmad; and narrated by Muslim in Iman, al-Bukhari in al-Adab, al-Tirmidhi in Tafsir, and al-Nasa'i in Wasaya.

Then the Truth says: "Messengers as bearers of good news and warners, so that people will have no argument against God after the messengers. And God is Mighty and Wise" (165).

We know that good news (bushra) is information of something pleasing that comes afterward, and warning (nadhara) is information of something displeasing that comes afterward. The Mighty (al-'Aziz), glory be to Him, is never overcome, and the Wise (al-Hakim), glory be to Him, places everything in its proper place. Why? Because the messengers bring good news and warning that there is a Paradise, a Fire, and a reckoning. So beware lest you think that one who disbelieves is able to do anything for himself, for God is Mighty and Independent of all His creation.

We know that the Truth does not make any conduct a crime except by a text, and before He punishes, He lays down the rules from which it is not right to depart. When the Truth says, "And God is Mighty and Wise," it is His might and His wisdom that have made it possible for us to know His method.

God says: "But God bears witness to what He has sent down to you—He has sent it down with His knowledge—and the angels bear witness. And God suffices as a witness" (4:166).

When we hear "but" (lakin), it means that there is a corrective addition (istidrak). His saying, the Truth: "But God bears witness," we take from it a message of truth: Your opponents, O Muhammad, do not bear witness that you are fit for this message, so God corrects them and makes clear to them that He, glory be to Him, is the One who created man, and He is most knowing of the law of his upkeep. The method of God for mankind through the messengers is the law of upkeep for that human being.

And if the People of the Book do not bear witness to what God sent down to His Messenger, peace and blessings of God be upon him, and deny what is in their scriptures of the good tidings of Muhammad, peace and blessings of God be upon him, as the final messenger, then God bears witness, and God suffices as a witness.

The Qur'an was sent down with His knowledge, and He is the One from whom nothing is hidden. He created all creation, and He knows what laws are suitable for mankind. In our human customs we find that whoever makes a manufactured item sets down the law for its maintenance so that it performs its task as it should. Likewise God, who created man, has laid down for him the law of his upkeep through "do" and "do not." Therefore the Truth says:

"Does not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware" (67:14).

We find that one of us takes his watch to a watch repairer, who examines it and determines what defect is in it. How much more so the Creator of man! The corruption found in the world is caused by people receiving the creation of God for them, while no one claims that he created himself or created others, and yet they try to legislate laws for the upkeep of man that are outside the method of God.

We say: Let the Creator of man set down for you the law of man through "do" and "do not." And if you wish to legislate, then legislate in the light of God's method. If any malfunction occurs in man, let us return it to the maintenance law of the First Maker, which is the Qur'an, because hardships only spring from man forgetting at times that he is the work of God, and trying to make for himself a maintenance law far from the method of God. What removes the troubles of humanity is that it return to its law of maintenance, which the Creator, blessed and exalted, has laid down.

"But God bears witness to what He has sent down to you—He has sent it down with His knowledge—and the angels bear witness." The angels bear witness because they attained the honour of being among the ones who convey to the Messenger of God, namely Jibril, peace be upon him. They are also those who record the reckonings of a person's good or bad deeds and write them in his record, and they are those who carried what is in the Preserved Tablet and conveyed what they were commanded to convey, and they know much. "And God suffices as a witness." Why did God not say here, "God and the angels suffice as witnesses"? Because the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, does not take the testimony of the angels as a reinforcement of His testimony.

We do not take the testimony of the angels as a reinforcement of God's testimony, for otherwise the angels would be more trusted by us than God. He, glory be to Him, records the testimony of people and the testimony of the angels, but you, O Messenger of God, the testimony of God suffices you.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 4, verse 167:

After that, the Truth (al-Haqq) says:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah have certainly strayed far astray.﴾

The disbelief of the disbeliever returns only to himself, and he has the choice between disbelief and faith. But if the disbeliever bars others from faith, this is a straying that extends to others. He has gone astray in himself, and he is trying to lead others astray. Therefore he bears not only his own burden, but also the burdens of those he misleads.

And how does barring from the way of Allah occur? By the people of misguidance trying to prevent the signs of guidance from reaching people's ears. They say, as the Truth has related of them:

﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it that you may overcome.﴾ (Part of verse 26, Surah Fussilat)

Had they understood the meaning of this verse, they would not have said what it contains. Their saying, "Do not listen to this Qur'an and make noise during it," means: create an uproar that disrupts the hearing of the Qur'an. And they knew that this Qur'an, when it reaches the ears, conveys guidance. Had the Qur'an not been effective, they would not have said that. Thus they acknowledge that they will be overcome when the voice of the Qur'an reaches the ears of humans who are called to guidance.

"Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah have certainly strayed far astray." The Truth could have said only, "They have strayed," but He brought the emphatic infinitive, "have strayed a far straying." That is, it is straying in its very essence, and beyond that it is a far-reaching straying.

When we consider the word "far" (ba'eed), we know that a far thing is one between it and its source there is a long span of time. The one who merely strays, at most his straying ends with the end of his life. But the one who works to lead others astray makes the straying extend; that is, in this case the straying will take a longer time than the life of the misleader, and the straying passes on from the misled to generations, and thus the straying becomes extended.

The straying known in worldly material matters, for example, is that a person walks on a road and then strays onto another road, and at most he goes into a desert (mafaza), that is, a wasteland, finds no water or food, and dies. But the astray misleader makes his straying take the time of this world and the Hereafter, and thus his straying is extended.

Then the Truth (al-Haqq) says:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and do wrong—Allah would never forgive them, nor would He guide them to a path, except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever. And that is ever easy for Allah.﴾

The discussion here begins with disbelief and wrongdoing: "Indeed, those who disbelieve and do wrong." Kufr (disbelief, literally "covering") is the concealing of the Supreme Existence, and zulm (wrongdoing) means that they lived by a human method that does not provide them with enjoyment or happiness in their worldly life; in this way they have wronged themselves. Then this method leads them to the punishment of the Hereafter. Whoever disbelieves has concealed the existence of Allah and deprived himself, by concealing the Supreme Existence, of the method that Allah brings. By doing so he has certainly gone far astray. And the One who said:

﴿Then when there comes to you guidance from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor suffer.﴾ (Part of verse 123, Surah Ta-Ha).

There is another verse in which the Truth says: ﴿Then whoever follows My guidance—there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾ (Part of verse 38, Surah al-Baqarah).

As for one who follows his own desire and human methods, he has a ma'ishah dankan (a constricted, narrow, severe life). Let no one suppose that one who takes and handles matters according to his desire has taken off into boundless freedom and endless rest. No, for the one who does this may find rest once, but he meets fatigue and lives in it, and does not part from it afterward. Thus he wrongs himself.

Someone may say: "They have wronged themselves, so this means there must be a wrongdoer and a wronged party. Who is the wrongdoer and who is the wronged?" Each one of them is both the wrongdoer and the wronged, because the human being is composed of multiple faculties: a faculty of desires that wants to rush toward appetites, and a faculty of values that wants the person to preserve himself and walk upon the straight path of values.

In the case of one who disbelieves and does not follow Allah's method, he leaves the opportunity to the faculty of desires to wrong the faculty of values. Islam came to balance between the faculties so that they support one another within the human soul, so that the current of one faculty does not overpower the current of another.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and do wrong—Allah would never forgive them, nor would He guide them to a path, except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever. And that is ever easy for Allah.﴾ (Surah an-Nisa').

This is the judgment of the Truth concerning those who disbelieve and wrong themselves: they will not attain Allah's forgiveness, and before them there is nothing but the path of Hell, abiding therein forever.

And the discussion here begins with disbelief and wrongdoing: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and wronged [themselves]...﴾. Disbelief (kufr) is concealing the Supreme Existence, and wrongdoing (zulm) means that they lived by a human method that does not bring them enjoyment or happiness in their worldly life, and by this they have wronged themselves. After that, this method leads them to the punishment of the Hereafter. Whoever disbelieves conceals the existence of God and deprives himself, by concealing the Supreme Existence, of the method that God brings; by this he has indeed gone far astray. And He, glorified is He, says: ﴿So if guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor be distressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 123].

There is another verse in which the Truth says: ﴿Then whoever follows My guidance, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38].

As for one who follows his own desire and the method of men, he has a life of dhank (dank), that is, narrow and severe constriction. Let no one suppose that one who takes and handles matters according to his desire has obtained unrestricted freedom and a rest without end. No! For the one who does this may find rest once, but he meets fatigue and lives in it, and does not part from it afterward; thus he wrongs himself.

Someone may say: "They wronged themselves, which means there must be a wrongdoer and a wronged party. So who is the wrongdoer and who is the wronged?" Each one of them is both the wrongdoer and the wronged, because the human being is composed of multiple faculties: the faculty of appetites, which wants to rush toward desires, and the faculty of values, which wants the person to preserve himself and walk upon the straight path of values.

In the case of one who disbelieves and does not follow God's method, he leaves the opportunity for the faculty of appetites to wrong the faculty of values. Islam came only to balance the faculties so that they support one another within the human soul, so that the flow of one faculty does not overpower the flow of another. ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and wronged [themselves], God would never forgive them, nor would He guide them to a path, * except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever. And that is ever easy for God﴾ [an-Nisa: 168-169].

This is the judgment of the Truth regarding those who disbelieve and wrong themselves: they will not attain God's forgiveness, and before them there is nothing but the path of Hell, abiding therein forever. Then the Truth says after that: ﴿O mankind...﴾.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 4, verse 170:

Then the Truth (al-Haqq) says:

﴿O mankind, the Messenger has certainly come to you with the truth from your Lord, so believe; it is better for you. But if you disbelieve, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. And ever is Allah Knowing and Wise.﴾ (170)

﴿O mankind, the Messenger has certainly come to you with the truth from your Lord, so believe; it is better for you. But if you disbelieve, then indeed, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. And ever is Allah Knowing and Wise.﴾

After He has described to us, in a firm and concise manner, the chain of battles that arose between the Messenger and the Jews on one occasion, and on another between him and the polytheists, here He, glorified is He, addresses all of mankind in order to purify the position of the method of Allah on earth. He says, warning every person: the message of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, has come as a purification of all the messages that preceded it, and all people must distinguish, so that they may choose the new life of faith, because the Messenger has come with the light and the proof. The proof is that which outweighs what he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is upon over what they are upon, and the light is that which guides them to the right path (sawa' al-sabil).

The people, before the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, were upon various creeds (milal), religions and sects (nihal). Then the proof came that Islam has come as an abrogating (nasikh) and final (khatim) religion. The proof is the teachings of this religion and its evidences.
